I moved the mail to a pg-boss job that is queued inside the transaction, so it only exists if the transaction commits. The job reads the stored data and does not depend on the webhook any more.

I wrote tests for three cases: a crash after the insert, a duplicate delivery at the same moment, and an error in the logic. For the crash I killed the handler with a thrown error after the insert and checked that the next delivery was processed. All three pass. The older duplicate test from the outage still passes as well.

I also ran the replay script against the test account with fifty events sent twice. Each event produced exactly one receipt job. The lock waits were short, below ten milliseconds in the log.

The change goes out with the next deploy. The reconciliation job will show whether any mismatch is left after that. If it stays quiet for two weeks, I will think about the repair step again.

summary: The usage meter double counted events when nebula resent a batch after a timeout; the meter now stores a batch id and ignores one it has seen.
body:
Ines found a customer with usage about 4 percent above what nebula showed. I compared the meter rows with the source counts per hour and found one hour counted twice.

nebula's export had timed out and then retried the same batch. Our meter received both and added both. The batches did carry an id, but we did not store it.

I added a unique constraint on customer, hour and batch id, and the insert now does nothing on conflict. I fixed the affected hour by recomputing it from the source.

The invoice for that customer had not been finalized yet, so no credit note is needed. I checked the other customers for hours with two batch ids: none found. A test sends the same batch twice and checks the count.

summary: Reviewed how the webhook handler treats unknown Stripe event types and changed it to acknowledge and log them, since a 400 made Stripe retry them for days.
body:
The Stripe dashboard showed a growing list of failing deliveries. They were all events of types we do not handle, for example a new type for the customer portal. The handler returned 400 for unknown types, so Stripe kept retrying.

Unknown events are not errors for us. The handler now verifies the signature, stores the event in the events table, logs the type at info level, and returns 200.

I kept the 400 for failed signature checks. I also added a counter per type so we can see which unknown events arrive often and decide if one is worth handling.

After deploying to staging, I resent a few of the failed events from the dashboard and they were all accepted. A test posts an unknown type with a valid signature and expects 200 and one stored row.

summary: Started the slow query investigation on the invoices list endpoint: the filter by customer and status scans the whole table, and the plan shows no use of the existing index.
body:
The invoices list endpoint for the admin screen takes 1.8 seconds for customers with many invoices. I ran explain analyze on the query with a customer that has 400 invoices.

The plan is a sequential scan over the invoices table. The existing index is on customer_id alone, but the query orders by created_at descending and filters on status, and the planner picked the scan because the status filter matches about half the rows.

I tried a composite index on customer_id, created_at desc. In a copy of the production data on my machine, the query dropped to 6 ms. An index with status as the third column made no difference, so I left it out.

Creating the index on the live table takes a lock if done normally. I wrote the migration to use create index concurrently, which cannot run inside a transaction, so the migration runner needs a flag for it. Mara showed me that the runner already supports it with a comment at the top of the file.

I did not run it on production yet. The table has about 600k rows, so the build should take under a minute, but I want to do it outside of month end. Scheduled for the weekend.

I also noticed that the endpoint loads all lines for every invoice in the list, which the screen does not show. That is a second fix for later, and I noted it.

summary: Ran the concurrent index build on the invoices table during a quiet hour; the admin list endpoint went from 1.8 seconds to 9 ms for the heaviest customer.
body:
I ran the migration with the concurrent flag. The build took 38 seconds and no writes were blocked. I watched the active queries during the build and saw no waiting.

After it finished, I checked that the index is valid in pg_index, since a failed concurrent build leaves an invalid one. It was valid.

The heaviest customer, with 400 invoices, now loads in 9 ms. Customers with few invoices were already fast and did not change.

The old index on customer_id alone is now redundant. I will drop it next week after a few days of looking at index usage statistics.

summary: Dropped the unneeded lines join from the invoices list endpoint, so the admin screen loads only line counts, which cut the response from 600 KB to 40 KB.
body:
The list endpoint returned every line of every invoice, but the screen shows only totals and a line count. I changed the query to select a count of lines per invoice and removed the lines from the response.

The detail endpoint still returns all lines. I checked the admin frontend code for any use of lines in the list and found none.

The response for a customer with 400 invoices went from about 600 KB to 40 KB. I updated the endpoint tests and the schema in the Fastify route so the response is validated against the smaller shape.

summary: Spam complaints for receipts reached a clear pattern: nearly all come from two big mail hosts, so the provider move is worth doing; wrote the numbers for Mara.
body:
Mara asked for numbers before deciding. I went through the support tickets of the last six weeks and tagged each one that mentions receipts or reminders in spam.

There were 31 tickets. 22 are from addresses at two big mail hosts, 6 from company domains with their own filters, and 3 unknown. The reminder mails are affected less than the receipts, which carry a PDF attachment.

I also counted from the status table how many receipts were sent in the same six weeks, about 2,900. So tickets are about one percent, but customers who do not write are not counted, and some customers told support they check spam only when they look for an invoice.

One more thing I checked: the receipt mail has a PDF of about 90 KB and a very short body. A short body with an attachment is a known spam signal. I rewrote the template text to include the invoice number, the amount, the period, and a link to the billing page. That is a free change and can go ahead whichever provider we use.

I sent test mails to accounts at the two hosts. With the new text, one went to the inbox and one still to spam, so the text helps but does not solve it.

The summary for Mara says: spam is a real problem concentrated in two hosts, the text change helps a little, and the sending reputation is likely the main cause. She will decide this week.

summary: Walked through the first quarter-end close with Ines and listed what billing-api must give the accountants: a locked period, a ledger export and credit notes included in the totals.
body:
Ines asked for a meeting before the accountants start their quarter-end work, and I joined to write down what they need from billing-api. This entry holds the list, since it will drive the next weeks.

First, the period must be lockable. Once finance closes a quarter, no invoice or credit note in it may change. Today an admin could still edit a line on an old invoice, and nobody would notice. I propose a closed_periods table, and every write path checks it. A correction after the close must go through a credit note dated in the open period.

Second, the ledger export. Ines now builds the ledger from the CSV report and fixes it by hand. The accountants want one row per invoice and credit note with net, tax, gross, tax rate, country and the reverse charge flag. The rows must add up to the totals shown in the PDFs. I checked the current CSV against ten invoices and found that it lists tax per line while the PDF shows it per rate, so the grouping differs.

Third, a view of unpaid invoices at the closing date. The accountants need the open amount per customer at the end of the quarter, not today. That means we must keep the payment time for each payment and not only the final status. We do keep it in payment_attempts, but not for payments marked paid by hand. Those need a paid_at field.

Fourth, the VAT summary per country. The EU return needs the net amount and tax per country and rate. The data exists in the invoice lines, but nobody has built the query. I ran a first version for last quarter, and it matched Ines's spreadsheet except for a few cents on five invoices. I will look at those cent differences separately, because they may come from the way each line is rounded.

We agreed on an order: the period lock first, then paid_at, then the ledger export, then the VAT summary. Ines will check each against the quarter that just ended. I started with the closed_periods migration and a guard function in the invoice repository. Nothing is deployed yet.

summary: Ines found invoices whose totals differ by one cent from her spreadsheet; traced it to rounding each line differently from the way she sums, and listed the affected invoices.
body:
Ines sent a list of 14 invoices from last month where our total and her spreadsheet differ by 0.01. She recomputes the totals from the lines for the accountants, and the accountants want the numbers to agree exactly.

I recomputed the same invoices in a script. The cause is in how the builder rounds. It computes the tax on each line, rounds each line, and sums the rounded lines. Ines computes line amounts, sums them, then applies the tax rate to the sum. For most invoices both ways give the same cent, but with many small lines they drift apart.

I checked a few by hand. An invoice with eleven lines of 0.35 at 19 percent tax shows the difference clearly. Each line's tax is 0.0665, which rounds to 0.07, and eleven of those give 0.77, while the tax on the sum of 3.85 is 0.7315, which is 0.73.

So neither number is wrong. It is a question of which rule is the right one for the invoice. I asked Ines to check with the accountants which rule they need. For now nothing is changed in the code.

I also found that the rounding in the usage preview endpoint uses the same code, so the preview and the invoice agree with each other, which is good.

The second finding: our rounding of a half cent uses the default of the language library, which always rounds up at exactly half. If the accountants want a different rule at exactly half, that is a separate change. I wrote the 14 invoices into a table with both totals and the line detail, so Ines can show it to them.

The next step depends on their answer. I expect a change in the rounding function and a rerun of the dry run over past invoices to see how many would change.

summary: Moved the billing page endpoint tests to the fixture builder and added a test for a customer with an invalid billing email, which had no coverage.
body:
The billing page tests still used the old setup. I moved them to the fixture builder, which removed about 120 lines.

While doing it I saw that no test covers a customer whose billing email was marked invalid after a hard bounce. The page should show a notice asking for a new address. I wrote the test, and it passed, so the behavior was right but unprotected.

I also added a case for a customer without a Stripe customer id yet, as with a new trial. The endpoint returns a clear 409 in that case. The suite runs in 9 seconds.

summary: Upgraded the PDF worker's headless browser package to the latest minor; render time for a 40-line invoice went from 2.6 to 2.1 seconds.
body:
The browser package had a minor release with a note about faster page printing. I upgraded it in the worker and ran the render benchmark script on ten sample invoices of different sizes.

For a 3-line invoice the time is about the same, 0.7 seconds. For a 40-line invoice it dropped from 2.6 to 2.1 seconds. For a 120-line invoice it is still 9 seconds, so the slowness with many lines is not fixed by this.

The visual output was compared with the old PDFs for the ten samples by rendering both to images and diffing. No pixel differences except one font hinting change in the footer of a single sample, which I consider harmless.

The 120-line case is the real problem and it grows faster than linearly, so the layout of the table is the likely cost. I did not look further today.

summary: Profiled the PDF render of a 120-line invoice and found that the table layout uses nested flex boxes that the browser recomputes per row; noted as the main cost.
body:
I recorded a performance trace of the browser while rendering the 120-line sample. Most of the time is layout, not script and not network. The lines table is built from nested flex containers for each row, with the description column set to wrap.

The trace shows layout running many times as rows are added, since each row's height depends on wrapped text and the page break logic reads the height again.

As a quick test I changed the template to a plain HTML table with fixed column widths in a copy. The render time for 120 lines dropped from 9 seconds to 3.4 seconds, and the layout looked the same in the diff apart from small spacing.

I did not apply it to the real template yet, because the page breaks in long invoices need a check, and the repeating table header on each page must still work. That is the next step, with a few long invoices from real customers.

summary: Applied the plain table layout to the invoice template and checked page breaks on long invoices; 120 lines now render in 3.5 seconds with the header repeated per page.
body:
I moved the fixed width table change from the experiment into the real template. The thead is marked to repeat on each page, and rows are set to avoid breaking inside a row.

I picked five of the longest real invoices from last quarter, 60 to 210 lines, and rendered them with old and new template. The page count is the same for four of them. One long invoice has one page more in the new layout, because rows no longer split across pages, which leaves a little white space. That is acceptable.

Times: 60 lines went from 4.1 to 1.9 seconds, 120 lines from 9 to 3.5, and 210 lines from 22 to 6.8 seconds.

I found one problem: the reverse charge note was placed after the table in a flex container and now overlaps the last row on a page boundary. I fixed it by putting the tax block in its own section with page-break-inside set to avoid.

I also checked the totals block stays on the same page as the last lines, so a total is never alone on a new page. For the 210-line invoice it was alone at first. I added a rule to keep at least three rows together with the totals, using a wrapper on the last rows.

The PDF worker tests render a fixture invoice and check the text content for the number, the totals and the note. They pass.

Finance should look at the new layout before it goes out. I attached the five old and new PDFs to the ticket for Ines.

summary: Built the quarterly VAT summary query and export, and checked it against Ines's spreadsheet for last quarter; it matches except five invoices that differ by one cent.
body:
After the planning meeting with Ines, I built the VAT summary that the accountants need for the EU return. It is a SQL query that groups invoice lines by country, tax rate and the reverse charge flag, with net and tax sums. A small script runs it for a chosen quarter and writes a CSV.

The rate comes from the invoice date lookup that we added for rate changes, so old invoices keep their old rate. Reverse charge invoices go into their own group with no rate, as Ines confirmed earlier. Credit notes are included as negative amounts, which keeps the sums in line with the ledger.

I ran the query for last quarter and compared the groups with Ines's spreadsheet. Twenty-two of the groups matched exactly. Two groups differed, by one cent in one and two cents in the other. I looked at the invoices behind them and found five where the tax sum per invoice differs from the sum of the rounded line taxes.

The reason is that the invoice builder rounds tax per line, while the query sums the unrounded tax and rounds once per group. I changed the query to sum the stored per-line tax amounts, which is what the PDF shows. The two groups then matched Ines's totals for the tax column.

The net column still shows one cent on three invoices, in the same five. Ines sums the gross amount and takes the tax out of it, and this gives a different split. Both ways are fair, but the accountants should get one rule. I wrote the five invoice numbers, with both calculations, in a note for Ines to take to them.

I also added tests with six invoices that have mixed rates and one with a credit note. The export takes about 300 ms for a quarter of the current size. With the large invoices table, I used the existing index on invoice date, and the plan shows it is used. Next step is the paid_at field, and then the ledger export.

summary: Shipped the new invoice template to production and checked the first hundred rendered PDFs for overlaps and missing footers; found none, and the queue time at month end dropped.
body:
The template with the larger tax block font and the footer number went to production this morning. I did not use a flag for this one, since the old template was only a layout, and the rollback is a revert of one file.

After the first hundred invoices were rendered, I wrote a script that reads each PDF text and checks that the invoice number appears on every page, that the total appears once, and that the page count is not larger than the line count allows. All hundred passed.

I also looked at the render times in the job table. The median is 1.3 seconds now, from 2.4 before the change. The 95th percentile dropped from 14 to 5 seconds, which is where the long invoices were.

The backed up queue at month end was the reason for the concurrency limit of last year. With the faster render the queue should be empty faster, and I can look at raising the limit later, though the pool of database connections in the worker is a limit as well.

One customer with a very long invoice had a page with a large blank area at the bottom, because of the rule that keeps rows with the totals. It looks odd but is correct. I mentioned it to Ines in case a customer asks.

Next is the rounding rule for exact half cents, which I plan to start tomorrow.

summary: Checked the first night of PDF renders with the new invoice template and found two invoices with a clipped footer, both with very long plan names.
body:
After the template went to production this afternoon, I looked at the renders of the first night run. Of 412 PDFs, two had a footer clipped at the bottom of the last page. Both belonged to a customer whose custom plan name is 74 characters long.

The cause was the plan name wrapping to three lines in the summary box, which pushed the footer block past the page margin. I set a max height on the summary box and let the name truncate with an ellipsis, and the full name stays in the line table.

I re-rendered the two invoices by hand and compared them with the old versions. The footer is intact and the totals are the same as before, to the cent. I added a fixture with a 90 character plan name to the template tests so this layout case is covered.

I also checked the queue depth during the run. The longest wait was 40 seconds, against several minutes at the last month end. The job runner logged no retries for the render queue.

Nothing else is open for the template. Next I want to clean up the invoice number handling in the filenames, which still carries the old format in a few places.

summary: Fixed the clipped footers from the first night of the new template: very long plan names pushed the footer block off the page, so names are now wrapped and capped at two lines.
body:
Yesterday's check found two invoices with a clipped footer, so I picked them up first. Both belonged to customers on a custom enterprise plan whose plan name is 74 and 91 characters long. The name sits in the header table, and the plain table layout gave that cell no width limit, so the line grew, the row got taller and the footer block lost its space on the last page.

I reproduced it locally by rendering a test invoice with a 90 character plan name. The footer was cut at the bottom edge in exactly the same way as in production. Short names rendered fine, so only the name length mattered, not the number of lines.

The fix has two parts. The plan name cell now has a fixed width and wraps its text. The template also limits the name to two lines and cuts the rest with an ellipsis. The full name stays in the invoice data and in the plan description line, so nothing is lost for the customer. I also reserved a minimum height for the footer so a tall header can never push it out of the page again.

I added a snapshot test with three names: short, 90 characters and one long word without spaces. The long word case broke the first version of my fix, because it did not wrap, so I added a word break rule for it. After that all three cases passed.

I re-rendered the two affected invoices and compared them by eye with the old PDFs, and the footer is complete now. The render time for the 120 line invoice stayed at 3.5 seconds. The two customers did not get new PDFs sent; the stored files were simply replaced. Next I will check the second night of renders for other layout problems, and I will ask Mara whether plan names can be limited at creation time.

summary: Checked the second night of PDF renders after the footer fix: no clipping across all invoices, and one customer name with an ampersand showed up escaped twice, which is now fixed.
body:
After the footer fix I went through the second night of renders. The queue created 212 PDFs, and I ran a script that checks each file for a footer text at the bottom of its last page. All 212 had it, so the clipping is gone.

While looking at a sample by eye I found one different problem. A customer whose company name contains an ampersand showed the text as the raw escaped form in the address block. The name was escaped once when the invoice data was built and a second time by the template engine. Earlier invoices of that customer, made with the old template, were fine, so the problem came with the template change of last week.

I removed the early escaping in the data builder, because the template engine already escapes every value by default. Then I searched the other fields that went through the same builder: customer name, address lines, plan name and the purchase order reference. I rendered test invoices with an ampersand, angle brackets and a quote in each of them. All came out as plain text in the PDF, and the angle brackets did not turn into markup.

I added these cases to the template tests so the double escaping cannot return silently. The email receipts use the same builder, so I also checked one receipt body, and it was correct there because that template uses its own path.

The invoice of the affected customer was rendered again and replaced. No other customer in the last two nights had special characters in the visible fields. The render time stayed near 2 seconds for a 40 line invoice and the queue time at the end of the night was normal. I consider the new template stable now. What is left is a short note for Mara about the new tests, and I will watch the third night only through the existing failure alert.

summary: Explained to Mara why one customer's invoice list shows two invoices with the same period: the second is a proration from a mid-cycle plan upgrade.
body:
Mara asked why a customer had two invoices for the same month. I looked at the invoice and its lines.

The first invoice was the regular subscription charge at the start of the period. The second was created eleven days later, when the customer moved from the Team plan to the Business plan. Stripe created the proration, and our sync stored it as its own invoice with a credit line for the unused part of the old plan and a charge line for the rest of the new plan.

The amounts add up. The credit was 18.40 and the new charge was 61.20, so the customer paid 42.80 for the change. Both invoices have the right status and number.

I told Mara it is correct behavior and that support can point customers to the lines. I also proposed a short text on the invoice page saying that mid-cycle changes appear as a separate invoice. She will decide whether to add it.

summary: Found why the nightly Stripe comparison reported 14 mismatches: all were invoices voided in Stripe, a status our mapping did not know.
body:
The nightly comparison between Stripe's invoices and ours reported 14 mismatches this morning, more than the usual one or two. I looked at them before touching anything.

All 14 had the Stripe status void, while ours showed open. Our status mapping knew draft, open, paid and uncollectible, but not void, so the sync ignored the event instead of failing, and the invoices stayed open.

To find out why so many came at once, I checked the events. Support had cleaned up a batch of old test customers in the Stripe dashboard the day before and voided their open invoices. That explains the number, and it is also why nobody noticed the gap earlier: voiding was rare.

The fix has three parts:
- The mapping now has void, which sets our status to void and clears the invoice from the dunning schedule.
- The sync logs an error for any status it does not know, instead of skipping it.
- A one-time script set the 14 invoices to void after I checked each one against Stripe.

I also checked that dunning did not send emails for those invoices. The reminder job had sent nothing, because the customers were test accounts with a blocked email domain.

I wrote tests for the void transition, including a void after a partial payment, which Stripe does not allow, so the test expects the error log. The comparison ran again with zero mismatches.

One question stays for Ines: how should a voided invoice appear in the ledger export? For now it is listed with the amount zero and the status void. I wrote this in the notes for the next close.

summary: Added the locked period for quarter close: invoices and credit notes inside a closed quarter can no longer be edited, only corrected by a new credit note.
body:
This was the first item from the list that Ines and I made at the quarter-end close. The accountants want the numbers of a closed period to stay fixed, so I built the lock.

There is a new table, closed_periods, with a start, an end, who closed it and when. A service function, assertPeriodOpen(date), is called by every code path that changes an invoice, a line or a credit note. If the date of the document is in a closed period, it throws a PeriodClosedError and the API answers with 409 and a clear message.

I went through the write paths one by one. There were seven: invoice finalize, line edit, status change by hand, credit note create, refund record, manual payment record and the import script. The webhook sync is the tricky one. A paid event from Stripe for an invoice in a closed period must still be recorded, because the money did arrive. So the sync stores the payment, but books it as a correction entry dated in the open period, and flags it for Ines.

The close itself is an admin endpoint that needs the finance role. It refuses to close a period when invoices in it are still in draft or open without a dunning schedule, and it lists them in the response.

Tests cover the 409 case for each of the seven paths, the webhook correction entry, and the refusal to close with drafts. I also tested that the end of the period is inclusive, since the first version of the check missed invoices dated on the last day.

Not done yet: the ledger export has to mark correction entries, and reopening a period needs a decision from Ines about who may do it. I wrote both as open items. I ran the whole thing on staging with last quarter's data and closed the period without errors.

summary: Ledger export now marks correction entries from the period lock, so Ines can see which payments arrived after a quarter was closed.
body:
I added a column entry_type to the ledger export with the values normal and correction. A correction is any entry booked in an open period for a document of a closed one. A second column holds the original document number.

I tested the export on staging by forcing a late payment for an invoice of the closed test quarter. The row appeared once, as a correction, dated today, and referred to the right invoice.

The CSV header changed, so I told Ines and kept the old column order, with the new columns at the end. Her spreadsheet import should not break.

summary: Decided with Ines that reopening a closed period needs the finance role and a written reason, stored in an audit table.
body:
Ines and I talked about reopening a closed period. She wants it to be possible, because mistakes in a closed quarter do happen, but rare and visible.

I added a reopen endpoint that needs the finance role and a reason text of at least 20 characters. It writes a row to period_audit with the user, the reason and the time, and it clears the closed flag. Closing again is a normal close.

Tests check that a missing reason or a missing role gives 403 or 422. Ines will tell the accountants about the audit table.

summary: Built credit notes into the invoice totals and the VAT summary, so a credited invoice shows its net amount and the quarterly report no longer overstates VAT.
body:
The close list had a third item: credit notes included in the totals. Until now a credit note was a separate record, and the invoice total ignored it, so the VAT summary for a quarter counted the full VAT of an invoice that was later credited.

I added a function netTotals(invoice) that takes the invoice lines and subtracts the credit note lines that refer to it, per VAT rate. The invoice page and the API response now show gross, credited and net. The PDF is not changed, because an issued invoice must stay as it was; the credit note has its own PDF.

The VAT summary query changed more. It now groups credit note lines by their own VAT rate and period, and subtracts them in the period of the credit note, not of the original invoice. Ines confirmed that this is how the accountants want it: the correction falls in the period where it happened.

I checked the numbers against last quarter. There were 9 credit notes, together 412.30 net and 82.46 VAT. Before the change the report was too high by that VAT, and now the VAT total matches Ines's sheet, except for the known one cent differences on five invoices that come from the rounding of lines.

Edge cases I tested:
- a credit note for part of one line
- a credit note larger than the line, which is rejected
- two credit notes for the same line, together within the line amount
- a reverse charge invoice with a credit note, where VAT stays zero

The partial refund from the refund endpoint creates a credit note too, so it flows into the same totals. I checked this with a test refund on the Stripe test account.

Open: the invoice list endpoint still shows the gross total only. I will add the net column in the next step.

summary: Added the net total column to the invoice list endpoint and the admin screen, using the new credit note function.
body:
The list endpoint now returns gross and net per invoice. To avoid an extra query per row, I load credit note sums for the page of invoices in one grouped query and join them in memory.

On the heaviest customer, 200 invoices per page, the response time stayed at 11 ms, so the grouped query is cheap with the index from earlier.

The admin screen shows net in a new column, and a small mark when it differs from gross. I wrote a test for a page with a mix of credited and normal invoices. Mara checked the screen on staging and had no comments.

summary: Investigated a customer whose VAT was charged although they entered a valid EU tax ID; VIES had been unavailable at signup and the check was never repeated.
body:
Mara passed on a complaint from a German business customer who was charged 19 percent VAT even though they gave a tax ID at signup. I started with their record.

The tax ID was stored with the validation status unknown. The log from the signup showed that VIES had answered with a service unavailable error for that member state. Our code treated that as unknown, charged VAT to be safe, and never tried again. That choice was correct for the first invoice, but the missing retry was a gap.

I checked how many customers are in this state. There were 23 with the status unknown, 6 of them with an EU tax ID that could have reverse charge. Four had paid at least one invoice with VAT.

The fix is a retry job. It runs every night, picks customers with the status unknown, and asks VIES again, at most five times, with a pause between calls so we do not hit the rate limit. When the answer is valid, the customer gets reverse charge from the next invoice on, and a note is written on their record.

I did not change old invoices. A wrong VAT charge on an issued invoice needs a credit note and a new invoice, and that is a decision for Ines. I listed the four invoices with amounts for her; the VAT involved is 211.40 in total.

I ran the job on staging with a stubbed VIES client that fails twice and then succeeds. The customer moved from unknown to valid on the third night, as intended. After five failed tries the status becomes check_failed, and support gets a message.

A test also covers the case where VIES says the ID is invalid. Then the customer stays with VAT and receives an email asking to correct the number.

Next step is to wait for Ines's answer on the four invoices.

summary: Ines decided to credit the VAT on the four wrongly taxed invoices; I generated the credit notes and corrected invoices and checked the totals.
body:
Ines replied about the four invoices from the VIES case. She wants credit notes for the full amounts and new invoices with reverse charge, since the customers have valid tax IDs and asked for it.

I wrote a one-time script for it. For each invoice it creates a credit note with the same lines and a new invoice with the VAT rate zero and the reverse charge text. Both documents get numbers from the allocator.

The documents fall into the current open period, because the original quarter is closed. The lock logic accepted this without a change, since the credit note date is today.

On the Stripe side, the money for the VAT has to go back. The script does not move money. It prints a list of the amounts, and Ines will refund the VAT through the refund endpoint, so the finance role is involved and the action is logged.

I ran the script on staging with copies of the four invoices. The sums checked out:
- original gross 1,326.40, credit note gross 1,326.40, new invoice net 1,115.00
- the difference of 211.40 is the VAT to refund

The script is safe to run twice. It marks each invoice as corrected and skips marked ones. I tested that second run, and it created nothing.

On production I ran it once, and verified the eight new documents in the admin screen. The PDFs rendered fine. Ines has the list for the refunds.

summary: Answered Mara's question about why webhook events sometimes arrive out of order and made the invoice sync tolerate an older event after a newer one.
body:
Mara saw an invoice that went from paid back to open in our database and asked if Stripe had reversed it. It had not.

I looked at the event log. Two events for the invoice, invoice.paid and invoice.updated, were delivered in the wrong order. The updated event carried the state from just before the payment, and our handler applied it after the paid event, so the status fell back to open. Stripe says in its docs that the order of events is not guaranteed.

The nightly comparison would have caught and fixed it, but only after up to a day. In that time a dunning mail could have gone out for a paid invoice. In this case the reminder had not yet been due.

I changed the sync to compare the created time of the event with the last event time stored on the invoice. An event older than the stored one is acknowledged and logged but not applied. For the same second, the status with higher rank wins, where paid ranks over open.

I added the column last_event_at to the invoices table. A migration filled it from the event table for existing rows. It ran in a few seconds on staging, and on production I ran it in a quiet hour.

Tests cover:
- two events in the right order
- two events in the wrong order
- the same timestamp with different statuses
- an event for an invoice we do not have yet

The last case existed before and still creates the invoice from the fetch of the current Stripe object.

I also searched for other handlers that apply a state from an event without this check. Subscription updated has the same pattern. I applied the same rule there with the field on the subscription row. That is covered by two new tests.

The event table already stores the raw payloads, so I could replay the last week of events in the wrong order on staging. The end state matched Stripe for all invoices.

summary: Wrote the month-end checklist script that runs the checks Ines asked for before she starts her review and sends her one summary.
body:
Before each month end, Ines checks the invoices by hand, and she asked if we could prepare some of it. I built a script, monthEndCheck, that runs the day before her review and sends her a summary by email.

What it checks:
- invoices still in draft after their billing date
- invoices open longer than the dunning schedule allows
- customers with usage above the plan but no overage line
- invoices without a VAT rate on a line
- gaps in the invoice number sequence of the year
- differences between Stripe and our paid totals for the month

Each check is a SQL query in its own file, with a name and a short text for what it means. The script runs all of them, counts rows, and writes the summary. A check with zero rows is shown as ok, others with the first ten rows and a link to the admin screen.

The gap check was the most interesting. The allocator uses a sequence, so a rolled back transaction leaves a gap. I looked at last year and found three gaps, all from rollbacks in the first weeks. Ines says that gaps need an explanation for the accountants, so the check lists them, and I added a table where an explanation can be stored once and then the gap is not reported again.

The totals check compares the sum of paid invoices per currency in Stripe, from its balance transactions, with ours. It paginates through the Stripe list with the shim we have for the older SDK. For the month it took 40 seconds for about 6,000 objects, which is fine for a nightly job.

I ran the script on last month's data. It reported:
- 0 drafts
- 2 late open invoices, both from a customer with a payment plan
- 1 usage without overage line, which turned out to be a wrong test customer
- 0 missing VAT rates
- 0 gaps not explained
- a difference of 0.00 in EUR and 3.12 in USD

The USD difference is the interesting one, so I looked at it. It comes from a Stripe fee refund on a disputed payment, which is not an invoice difference. I excluded refunds of fees from the comparison and wrote a test for it.

It is scheduled through pg-boss on the second to last day of the month at six in the morning. I sent a first summary to Ines as a test and asked her what is missing.

summary: Ines found the month-end summary useful and asked for two more checks; I added a check for credit notes without a reason and for customers with an invalid billing email.
body:
Ines read the first month-end summary and sent her answers. She liked the layout and wanted two additions.

The first is credit notes without a reason text. The accountants ask for a reason on each one, and the API did not require it for credit notes created by the refund flow. I added the check, and it found 5 old ones from the first refund tests. I set a reason, refund test, on those after checking that they belong to the test customer of that time.

Because a check after the fact is the weaker protection, I also made the reason required in the credit note service. The refund endpoint now passes the reason from the request, or falls back to the text refund requested by finance with the user's name. The tests for the endpoint changed accordingly, and one new test checks that an empty reason is rejected in the service.

The second check lists customers whose billing email is marked invalid after a bounce and who have an invoice due in the next ten days. This is a real problem: the receipt or the reminder goes nowhere. The cleanup of bounced addresses, which I wrote earlier, marks the address but nothing follows it up. The list shows 7 customers today.

I gave the list to Mara so support can contact them in another way. The summary now has a section for this, with the count and the names.

I ran the whole script again on staging, and it took 52 seconds. The longest part remains the Stripe totals. I do not plan to change that.

Not done: Ines also asked to see the revenue per plan in the summary. I said that it belongs to another report and not to a check, and she agreed to wait.

summary: A customer's usage showed 0 for a whole day because nebula's count endpoint timed out; the meter now records the gap and asks again instead of storing zero.
body:
Mara noticed on the usage screen of a large customer that one day showed 0 events, between two days with about 2 million each. The customer had not stopped using nebula, so I looked for the cause.

The meter reads counts from the nebula API once per hour. For that customer, the call at 02:00 timed out after 10 seconds, and the error handling caught the exception, logged a warning and wrote a count of 0 for the hour. The next hours were fine, but one hour of the day was lost. The day showed 0 because the daily view in the screen took the hour with the maximum of events, and this was a different bug: the query took the value of the last row, which was the later hour that had been written first by a retry.

So two problems came together:
- a failed read was stored as a real zero
- the daily view depended on the order of rows

For the first, I changed the meter to store nothing on a failed read, and to write a row in a new table, meter_gaps, with customer, hour and the error. A second job runs every hour and tries the open gaps again, up to 24 times. When it succeeds, it writes the count and closes the gap.

For the second, the daily view now sums the hours of the day. I wrote a test that inserts hours in a random order and checks the sum.

The customer's missing hour, 2 AM, was filled by a manual run of the gap job. The count was 83,114. The invoice for the month is not yet made, so no correction of a document is needed.

I also checked all customers for gaps in the last 60 days. There were 31 hours with a zero for 12 customers, and for 19 of those, the neighbors show high usage. I can not tell which zeros are real. I asked nebula's side for a raw count query by hour so that I can compare. Mara says she will ask the nebula team.

The important point is that no invoice from the last 60 days has a lower overage than it should have, as far as I can tell, because none of the 19 hours fall on customers whose monthly total is near the plan limit. I wrote the list of those customers with their margins into the notes.

Open: the comparison with the raw counts. I will continue when Mara has an answer.

summary: Added an alert for meter gaps older than six hours, so a failing nebula read shows up before invoice time and not after.
body:
This follows the zero-hour problem of this morning. The gap job retries, but if the nebula API stays down, nobody would know until the month-end check.

I added a small check that runs after each retry round. If any gap is open for more than six hours, it posts a message to the team channel with the number of gaps, the oldest one, and the last error text. A repeated message for the same gap is limited to once every six hours, so the channel does not fill up.

I wrote the threshold into the config file as meterGapAlertHours with the default of 6. Mara asked whether that could be too tight, since nebula has maintenance windows. I looked at the history: the longest outage I can see in the logs was 3 hours and 20 minutes, so 6 is above it, and we can change it later.

The tests simulate a failing client with a fake clock. They check that:
- no message comes before six hours
- one message comes at six hours
- no second message comes within the next six hours
- the message stops once the gap is closed

I also added the number of open gaps to the month-end summary for Ines. If a gap is still open at the time of invoicing, the invoice job for that customer waits and tries again an hour later. Before this, the job would have made the invoice with a missing hour. I wrote a test for that path too.

One case needed a decision. If a gap cannot be closed in 24 tries, the customer's invoice must still be made, or it would be late forever. In that case the job makes the invoice with the known counts and adds a note on the customer record for finance. I think this is the safer way, because Ines can issue a correction later, and the note tells her where to look. I told Mara about this choice, and she agreed.

I ran a drill on staging: I blocked the nebula endpoint for a test customer for 7 hours of simulated time. The alert came once, the invoice waited, and after I opened the endpoint the gap closed and the invoice was created with the full count.

summary: Mara got the raw hourly counts from nebula and 17 of the 19 suspicious zero hours were real gaps; the two others were correct zeros during a maintenance window.
body:
The nebula team gave Mara a raw count query by hour. I compared its output with our stored counts for the 19 suspect hours.

In 17 cases, nebula had events in that hour and we had 0, so those were timeouts that the old error handling stored as zero. In 2 cases, nebula also reported 0, because the customer had paused ingestion during a planned maintenance on their side.

I filled the 17 hours with the real counts, using the same code path as the gap job so they are marked as recovered. The total is 1.9 million events across 11 customers.

I checked the effect on invoices. Two customers had an invoice in that time, and the added events did not push either above their plan limit. So no overage was missed and nothing has to be corrected.

The list of customers with small margins goes to Ines anyway, as a record. The investigation is closed.

summary: Reduced the Stripe list calls in the sync after hitting the rate limit during the month-end check; the check now uses a date filter and a page size of 100.
body:
The month-end check hit Stripe's rate limit on the test run this afternoon: the log shows 429 responses with the message about too many requests, and the SDK retried until the check took four minutes instead of one.

The cause was in my own totals check. It listed all balance transactions of the month with a page size of 10, which is the SDK default for the version we use. That gave about 600 calls for 6,000 objects. Together with the nightly invoice sync running at the same time, we passed the limit.

I made three changes:
- the page size is now 100, the maximum, which makes it about 60 calls
- the list uses created filters for the month, so a rerun for the same month does not read the other months
- the check now starts at 05:00 and the sync at 03:00, so they do not overlap

The pagination goes through our shim, which wraps the older SDK's autoPagingEach. I looked at it again, since I was changing the calls. It works, but it hides the page size, so I added an option that is passed through to the list call. A test with a fake Stripe client checks that the option arrives.

I measured on the test account with a generated load of 6,000 balance transactions. The check took 38 seconds, with no 429. The sync took the same time as before.

I also read how the SDK handles retries. By default it retries twice on 429 with a short wait. For our jobs, it would be better to wait longer, because they are not user-facing. I set maxNetworkRetries to 4 on the client used by the jobs, and left the one for the API requests at 2, so a customer is not left waiting too long.

The shim stays for now. The next SDK upgrades will probably change the list helpers, and I will look at it again at that time.

I wrote a short note in the repo docs about the limits and the times of the jobs, so that new jobs are not planned at the same time as the others.

summary: Looked at receipts for SEPA-like delayed payments and found that our receipt email assumes instant payment; listed what changes when payments can stay pending for days.
body:
Several EU customers asked whether they can pay by bank debit instead of card, which has come up more than once. Before anyone builds that, I read through our code to see what assumes that a payment finishes at once.

The receipt email is sent when the invoice is paid, which is right. But the checkout page shows a payment succeeded message right after the customer submits, and the invoice status becomes paid only when Stripe says so. With a delayed method there would be days in between, and the message would be wrong.

The list of things that assume instant payment:
- the success message on the billing page
- the dunning schedule, which starts counting from the due date and would send a reminder while a debit is still pending
- the retry logic, which treats a failure as a decline code of a card
- the month-end check, which counts open invoices as late
- the access rules, since a customer in a pending payment state must not lose access

I also looked at the states in Stripe. A payment intent can be processing for several days, and can fail afterwards with a reason such as insufficient funds, or a returned debit weeks later. Our status table has no processing state for invoices.

So this is bigger than adding a method. I wrote the list as a short plan with the effort per item, about a week of work in total, and gave it to Mara. She will talk to the customers who asked and to Ines about the accounting side of a payment that can be returned.

I did not change code in this entry. The plan is only a basis for the decision.

One small thing I did fix: the dunning job already skips invoices with an open payment intent in state processing, but only because of an accident in a query condition. I added a test so this stays that way.

summary: Split the invoice status into open and processing in the code and tests, which prepares delayed payments without changing what customers see today.
body:
Mara read the plan from this morning and said that the processing state is needed anyway and can be done first, because it changes nothing visible. So I started with it.

The invoice status is an enum in the code and a text column with a check constraint in Postgres. I added the value processing to both. A migration changed the constraint, and it ran in a moment since it only changes the rule, not the rows.

The sync from Stripe now maps a payment intent in the state processing to the invoice status processing. With cards this almost never happens, but Stripe does send it for some payments, and until now it left the invoice as open.

I went through every place that reads the status. There were 23 hits. Most were fine because they compare to paid or to void. These needed changes:
- the dunning job treats processing like paid for the purpose of not sending reminders
- the access check keeps access for customers with a processing invoice
- the month-end check lists processing invoices in their own section, not as late
- the admin screen shows a grey label for processing
- the VAT summary and ledger export ignore processing invoices, because revenue counts when the payment is complete

The last point is a choice that Ines should confirm. The accountants book on the invoice date, not the payment date, in our current export, so I asked her whether a processing invoice should appear. I kept the old behavior for the time being, where all invoices of the period are in the export regardless of payment, and wrote the question into the notes.

Tests: I added a status transition test, with processing to paid, processing to open on failure, and open to processing. The invalid ones, such as paid to processing, are rejected by the transition function. I also replayed webhook events of a processing payment on the test account and the invoice followed.

The full suite passes, 412 tests. The only flaky test was the one for the retry schedule that depends on the clock, and I fixed it by setting a fake time.

Nothing customer-facing changed, and a deploy is safe. The next step would be the payment method itself, once Mara has the decision.

summary: Built the first version of delayed payment handling: an invoice can now stay in processing for days, and the receipt email waits for the payment to settle.
body:
Following the split of open and processing last week, I made the processing state real. When a payment intent reports processing, the invoice moves to processing and no receipt is sent. The receipt job now fires only on the succeeded event.

The old receipt code assumed that the charge succeeded in the same request. I moved the send into a pg-boss job named send_receipt, keyed by invoice id, so a duplicate webhook cannot send two receipts. The job reads the invoice again before sending and skips it if the status is not paid.

I added a status field to the customer billing page: processing invoices show 'Payment in progress' instead of 'Open'. The dunning logic had to change too. Before, an invoice that stayed unpaid for three days started the reminder sequence. Now invoices in processing are excluded from the sequence, otherwise a customer with a pending debit would get a reminder for money that is already on its way.

I wrote eleven tests. They cover processing to paid, processing to failed, a failed payment that goes back to open, and a duplicate succeeded event. One test failed at first because the failed transition did not clear the processing timestamp. That is fixed.

Not done yet: a timeout for invoices that stay in processing too long, and the wording of the failure email for delayed payments. I will ask Ines how many days she wants before we treat a pending payment as lost. The PDF still shows 'Due' for processing invoices, which is also open.

summary: Added a stuck-processing check that lists invoices in processing for more than seven days, so a payment that never settles does not stay invisible.
body:
A pending payment that never resolves would sit in processing forever, and nothing would warn us. I added a query for invoices in processing for more than a configurable number of days, with seven as the default until Ines decides.

The query is part of the month-end checklist script, in a new section next to the credit note and billing email checks. For each stuck invoice it prints the invoice number, the customer, the amount, the Stripe payment intent id and the number of days in processing. I also made the script ask Stripe for the current status of each intent. That showed whether the payment is really pending or whether we missed a webhook.

I tested it with a staging invoice that I forced into processing and aged by changing its timestamp. It showed up in the list with the right intent id. A second invoice that was one day old did not appear, as expected.

One detail: the Stripe call is made one by one, and with many stuck invoices that could hit the rate limit again, as in the month-end check last week. I capped the check at fifty intents per run and the output says when it was cut. That is enough for now because there are no processing invoices in production yet.

I wrote the result into a note for Ines. She decides the real number of days.

summary: Ines chose ten days as the limit for a pending payment; after that the invoice goes back to open and the dunning emails can start again.
body:
Ines answered the question about stuck payments. Her accountants want a pending payment treated as unsettled after ten days, and the customer should then be asked to pay again. I set the default of the stuck-processing limit to ten days.

I also added a job that runs nightly and moves invoices older than the limit from processing to open, with an audit line that says 'processing timeout'. It does not cancel the payment intent in Stripe, because the payment might still settle. If it does settle later, the succeeded webhook moves the invoice to paid as usual, and the receipt goes out then.

This created a case that I had not planned: the invoice is open again, the dunning sequence starts, and then the payment settles. The customer would get a reminder for an invoice that was just paid. I made the dunning job read the invoice status again directly before it sends, so a paid invoice is skipped.

Tests added: timeout moves the status, a late success after the timeout ends paid, and the dunning job skips a paid invoice. All pass. The audit entry text is not final yet; Ines wants the reason in plain words in her export.

summary: Changed the audit line for the processing timeout to plain words and checked that it appears in the ledger export as Ines wanted.
body:
Ines said that the text 'processing timeout' means nothing to the accountants. The audit line now says 'Payment still pending after 10 days, invoice returned to open'. The number comes from the setting, so it stays right if the limit changes.

I ran the ledger export on staging with two timed-out invoices. The new line appears in the notes column next to the invoice. The CSV escaping of the comma in the text was correct. I also checked that old audit entries are unchanged.

Nothing else changed in the export. I sent Ines a sample file to look at.

summary: Investigated why some receipts show the amount before the credit note, found that the receipt template reads the gross total, and made it use the net total.
body:
Mara forwarded a customer mail: the receipt for an invoice showed 120.00 EUR, but the customer had a credit note of 20.00 EUR and paid only 100.00. The customer asked which number is right.

I looked at the receipt template. It reads invoice.total, the gross value. The net total function that I built for the invoice list and the VAT summary a few weeks ago was never used in the email. The customer paid correctly; only the receipt text was wrong.

I changed the receipt to show three lines when credit notes exist: the invoice total, the credits, and the amount paid. When there are none, the receipt looks the same as before. The paid amount comes from the net total function, so all views use the same number now.

While I was there I searched for other places that use invoice.total directly. I found four. Two are in the PDF template and the admin export, where the gross value is right and a separate net column exists. One is in the dunning email, where it is a bug: the reminder would ask for the gross amount of a partly credited invoice. The fourth is in a script that is no longer used.

I fixed the dunning email to ask for the net amount and added a test with a credited invoice. I added a snapshot test for the receipt with and without a credit note.

I listed the receipts sent in the last month that had credit notes at the time. There were nine. Ines can decide whether the customers need a corrected receipt. I did not send anything. The dunning case had no affected customers because no credited invoice had gone into dunning.

Open question: partial refunds in Stripe produce a similar difference, and I need to check how those are shown. That comes next.

summary: Checked how partial refunds show on receipts and invoices: the refund is stored but the receipt ignores it, so I listed the gap and kept it for a later change.
body:
After the credit note fix I checked refunds. A refund made through the API creates a refund row and a Stripe refund, but it does not create a credit note. So the net total function does not know about it.

I looked at what customers see. The invoice page lists the refund as a separate line in the payment history. The receipt does not mention it, which is acceptable because the receipt was sent when the payment was made. The invoice PDF does not mention it either, and that matches what Ines said earlier: a refund after the period close must be a credit note for the accountants.

So the real question is whether refunds should always create a credit note. I wrote down the two options for Ines. Option one: the refund endpoint creates the credit note itself. Option two: finance creates the note by hand when needed. Option one is safer for the books but needs a reason field in the refund request.

I did not change code. Three refunds in the last month had no credit note, which I listed with their amounts for Ines.

summary: Ines wants every refund to create a credit note, so the refund endpoint now requires a reason and writes the note in the same transaction.
body:
Ines chose option one. A refund without a credit note leaves the books wrong, and the accountants dislike manual fixes.

The refund endpoint now takes a required reason string, up to 200 characters. In one database transaction it inserts the refund row and creates a credit note linked to the invoice with the same amount and reason. The Stripe refund call comes first. If it fails, nothing is written. If it succeeds and the database write fails, the error is logged with the Stripe refund id, because that case needs a manual repair. It has not happened in tests.

The net total function now sees the refund through the credit note, so the invoice list shows the right net value. The VAT part of the credit note is computed from the invoice's tax rate, proportionally to the refunded amount.

I added tests: full refund, partial refund, a second partial refund that would exceed the total (rejected with 422), and a missing reason (400). The three old refunds without notes were left for Ines to handle by hand.

A risk remains: a client that sends the request twice could create two refunds. I noted it but have not changed it.

summary: Generated the three missing credit notes for old refunds with a one-off script and checked that the quarter VAT summary changed by the expected amount.
body:
Ines asked for the three old refunds to get credit notes. I wrote a one-off script that takes refund ids, creates the credit note with the reason 'Backfill: refund without credit note' and prints the result. I ran it first as a dry run on a copy of the data.

One of the refunds fell into a closed quarter. The period lock rejected the credit note, as it should. Ines used the finance role to reopen the period with a written reason, I created the note, and she closed it again. The audit table has both entries.

After the run I recalculated the VAT summary for that quarter. VAT went down by 4.87 EUR, which is the tax part of the three refunds. Ines compared it with her sheet and it matched.

The script stays in the scripts folder with a comment that says it is single use.

summary: Wrote a failure email for delayed payments, so a customer whose debit was rejected after days gets a clear message and a link to pay again.
body:
The existing failure email says 'your payment failed' and assumes the customer just tried to pay. For a delayed payment that fails after several days, this is confusing because the customer may have forgotten the attempt.

I wrote a second template. It names the invoice number, the amount and the date of the first attempt in relative words like 'started on' with the real date, adds the failure reason when Stripe gives one, and has a button to the page where the customer can pay again. The text is short and does not blame the customer.

The choice of template depends on whether the invoice was in processing before the failure. The webhook handler for payment_failed reads the previous status and picks the template. I added a test for each path.

I also added a rule: a failed delayed payment does not start the dunning sequence immediately. The failure email goes out first, and the dunning timer starts from that moment, so the customer is not hit with two messages on the same day.

I checked the rendering of the email in the provider's preview and in two test mailboxes. The layout is fine. One thing remains: the translations. The current emails are English only and some customers use German. Mara said the German text can come later.

Next I want to review the dunning timer settings with Ines.

summary: Reviewed the whole dunning timeline with Ines and rebuilt it as a table of steps per payment type, so card and delayed payments follow different schedules.
body:
Ines and I went through the dunning sequence. It was written for card payments: a reminder after three days, a second after seven, a final notice after fourteen, and suspension after twenty-one. With delayed payments this does not fit, because ten days may pass just in waiting.

We agreed on a table. For card payments nothing changes. For delayed payments the clock starts at the failure or at the processing timeout, not at the invoice date, and the steps are: failure email on day zero, reminder after four days, final notice after ten, suspension after seventeen.

I moved the schedule into a table in the code, keyed by payment type, with the offsets in days and the template of each step. Before it was spread across three functions with the numbers written inline. The dunning job now looks up the schedule by the payment type of the last attempt and the start date of the clock.

The invoice needs a field for when the clock started. I added dunning_started_at with a migration, filled from the old rule for existing open invoices so that nobody's schedule changes. I checked this on a copy of production data: 63 open invoices got their value and the next step for each is the same as before the change.

I wrote tests for both schedules with a fake clock, including a case where a payment settles between two steps and the sequence stops. Total 14 new tests, all green.

A case that I found while testing: a customer who switches from card to debit during dunning. The clock is kept, and the schedule of the new payment type applies to the remaining steps. Ines accepted this.

It is not shipped yet. I want one more look at the suspension step, because suspending a customer who has a pending debit would be a bad result.

summary: Wrote the first test pass for the new dunning table: card and delayed payment schedules each send the right email on the right day, with two edge cases still open.
body:
Slot 10 rebuilt the dunning timeline as a table of steps per payment type, and this evening I wrote the tests that pin it down. The test helper moves a fake clock forward day by day and records which emails the job runner would send for one invoice. For a card payment the expected sequence is a first reminder after three days, a second after seven and a final notice after fourteen. For a delayed payment there is no reminder at all while the invoice is in processing, and the schedule only starts when the invoice goes back to open after the ten-day limit.

The first run failed in four cases. Two of them were mistakes in my expected values, because I had counted the days from the due date and the table counts from the moment the invoice became open. The other two were real: an invoice that switched from a card to a delayed payment method in the middle of dunning kept its old card schedule. The table lookup read the payment type once when the invoice was created and never again. I changed it to read the type of the last payment attempt, and those two tests passed.

I also added a test that a payment arriving between two steps cancels the queued reminders. It passed at once, which fits the answer I gave Mara earlier about the reminder that was skipped correctly.

Two edge cases are still open. The first is an invoice with a credit note that brings the net total to zero. It currently gets a reminder, and it should not get one. The second is a customer with an invalid billing email, where the job logs a failure each day and does not stop. I wrote both as skipped tests with a short comment each, so they show up in the test report. Tomorrow I will fix the zero-total case first, because Ines is likely to see it at month end. The full suite takes 41 seconds and is green apart from the two skipped tests.

summary: Shipped the delayed payment and new dunning schedule to production behind careful checks, and watched the first night of jobs without finding any wrong email.
body:
After the suspension fix I deployed the whole set: processing status, receipt job, timeout job, the dunning table and the new failure email. The migration for dunning_started_at ran in two seconds.

Before the deploy I ran the dunning job in dry run mode against production data. It printed 6 planned emails for the next day, and I compared them with the old logic: all six matched.

After the deploy I watched the job runner. The nightly timeout job ran and found no processing invoices, which is right because delayed payments are not enabled for customers yet. The dunning job sent four reminders and one final notice, and I opened each in the provider's activity view to check the template and the amount. The amounts are net values after credit notes, as intended.

One warning appeared in the logs: the stuck-processing query in the checklist script used a column name from an old draft, and it failed on production while it had worked on staging. The staging schema had the column from my forced test. I corrected the name and ran the checklist by hand. The summary for Ines came out complete.

I also checked the alert for meter gaps and the Stripe sync; both were quiet.

What is open: no customer can use delayed payments yet, so the new paths have only seen tests and staging. The next feature step is the payment method itself, and I expect Mara to say when it starts. Until then the code is dormant but harmless.

summary: Answered Mara's question about why an invoice was both paid and in dunning: the reminder had been queued before the payment and was skipped correctly.
body:
Mara saw a dunning entry in the admin screen for an invoice that showed as paid and asked if a reminder had been sent by mistake.

I looked at the job table. The reminder job was queued two days earlier. The customer paid the same morning. When the job ran, the status check that I added last week found paid and the job ended as skipped, with no email. The admin screen shows queued jobs by creation time, which is why the entry looked active.

Provider activity confirmed that no email left for that address that day. I suggested to Mara that the admin screen should show the final job state. I added the state to the list as a small column.

summary: Started the work on invoice PDFs with many lines: measured render time by line count and found that time grows faster than linearly past about 150 lines.
body:
The new plain table layout helped, but some customers have invoices with several hundred usage lines. I measured on staging with generated invoices of 50, 100, 150, 200, 300 and 400 lines, five runs each.

Median times were 2.4, 3.5, 5.1, 8.3, 17 and 31 seconds. Up to 150 lines the growth is almost linear. After that it bends upward. For 400 lines the render is more than twelve times slower than for 50, while it has eight times the lines.

I looked at the browser's performance trace for the 300 line case. Most of the time is in layout and in the page break calculation, which has to place the repeated header on every page. Memory of the worker grew to about 900 MB during the render.

Two ideas to test: render long invoices in chunks of lines and merge the pages, and group usage lines into one summary line per metric with the detail on a second attachment. The second is a product change and needs Ines and Mara. The first is a technical change.

I wrote the measurements and the two ideas in a note. The real customers affected are few: seven invoices last month had more than 200 lines, and the queue time for these blocked other jobs for up to half a minute each.

Next step is to try the chunking idea in a branch-free test script and compare the page output.

summary: Tried rendering long invoices in chunks of 100 lines and merging the PDFs; time dropped to 9 seconds for 300 lines but page numbers and totals broke.
body:
I wrote an experiment in the PDF worker: split the lines into chunks of 100, render each chunk as a separate document with its own header, and merge the PDFs.

The time for a 300 line invoice fell from 17 to 9 seconds, and memory stayed under 400 MB. The cost is in the output. Page numbers restart for each chunk, so the footer says page 1 of 3 three times. The totals block appears only on the last chunk, which is right, but its position leaves a half empty page after the last chunk when the lines end near the page bottom.

I tried to fix the page numbers by passing an offset into the template, but the total page count is unknown until all chunks are rendered. A second pass would need the count before the footer is drawn, so I would have to render twice or stamp the numbers afterwards on the merged file.

Stamping afterwards seems to work in a quick test with the merge library, but the font of the stamp differs a little from the template font. I did not finish this.

Result: the chunking is promising for speed but needs the stamping step. I stopped here and left the experiment uncommitted in a scratch file. The alternative with one summary line per metric would avoid all this, so I will ask Ines how the customers use the detail lines.

summary: Looked at how customers and finance use detail usage lines, found that only a few customers ever open them, and drafted a summarized layout for invoices over 150 lines.
body:
Before choosing between chunking and summarizing, I wanted to know who needs the detail lines. I asked Ines and looked at the data.

In the access log of the invoice download endpoint, 19 customers have more than 150 line invoices. For those, the PDF is downloaded about once per invoice, so it is not opened often, but I cannot tell from the log what the customers read. Ines said two of them send the PDF to their own accountants who book each metric separately. The others only look at the total.

The usage detail is already available as a CSV through the usage endpoint. So a summarized PDF with a pointer to the CSV does not remove information.

I drafted the layout. For invoices over 150 lines, the PDF shows one line per metric and per plan with quantity and amount, then the tax and total block, and a sentence saying that the full detail is in the usage export, with the link. The sum of the summary lines must equal the sum of the detail lines, so I added a check that fails the render when they differ by even one cent. This matters after the rounding problems that Ines found before.

I built the draft with the template and rendered the 300 and 400 line test invoices. Times were 3.2 and 3.4 seconds, which is far better than the chunk idea. The PDF is two pages.

Problems: the summary line for a metric with different unit prices during a month (after a price change) needs to show the price range or split in two lines. I chose to split by price, so the lines stay exact. Another problem is that the threshold of 150 lines is arbitrary. I made it a setting.

I sent the drafts to Ines and Mara. Ines wants to show them to the two customers who book by metric before we decide. I did not touch the production template.

summary: Ines asked the two metric-by-metric customers about the summarized invoice; both accept it if the CSV is attached to the invoice email, so I added the attachment.
body:
Ines talked to the two customers. Both said a summary is fine as long as the detail is easy to get. One asked that the CSV come with the invoice email instead of being found in the product.

I added an option to the invoice email job: for invoices that use the summarized layout, the usage detail CSV is attached. The CSV is built by the same function as the usage export, so the numbers are the same. I added a test that the sum of the CSV amounts equals the invoice subtotal.

The attachment limit of the email provider is 10 MB. A 400 line CSV is about 40 KB, so there is no problem. I added a guard that sends a download link instead if the file would pass 5 MB.

I also made the threshold of the summarized layout a per-customer override, with the global default of 150 lines. The two customers can be set to never summarize if Ines changes her mind, although then their invoices stay slow.

While testing the email I found that the attachment name was 'usage.csv' for every invoice. I changed it to include the invoice number so that accountants can sort the files.

Still open: the decision to ship. I want to run both layouts on a week of real invoices in staging and have Ines compare totals. That needs the staging copy to be refreshed with last week's data.

summary: Ran the summarized layout on a copy of last month's real invoices and compared totals: all 41 long invoices matched to the cent, and render time at month end fell sharply.
body:
I refreshed the staging copy with last month's data and rendered all invoices with more than 150 lines in both layouts. There were 41 of them.

The check of sums passed for all 41. The summary lines add up to the same subtotal as the detail lines, and tax and total are identical. Ines took a sample of eight and compared them with her spreadsheet; no differences.

Render times: the old layout needed 6.8 seconds on average and 29 seconds at most. The summarized layout needed 3.1 seconds on average and 3.6 at most. For the whole month end run of those 41, the old way would take about 4.6 minutes of worker time, the new way about 2.1.

I found two invoices with a line that had a negative amount from a manual adjustment. The summary grouped these with the metric of the same name and the line showed a lower amount than the customer might expect. I changed the grouping so that adjustments get their own line named 'Adjustments'. The totals stayed the same.

Another invoice had a plan with a very long name, and the summary line wrapped to three lines. The cap of two lines that I added after the footer problem applies to the footer, not to table cells. I applied the same cap to the cells.

I looked through ten PDFs by eye for overlaps, broken page breaks and missing footers. None found after the two fixes.

I am ready to ship this, and I asked Mara for the okay because it changes what some customers see.

summary: Mara approved the summarized invoice layout; shipped it and checked the first invoices rendered with it, with no errors in the render queue.
body:
Mara agreed to ship. I deployed the template change and the email attachment together in the morning, before the usual afternoon invoice run.

I watched the queue. The first batch had 12 invoices over the threshold. All rendered, with times between 2.9 and 3.7 seconds. I downloaded four of them and checked the sum line against the CSV attachment from the email. They matched.
