I also checked that invoices below 150 lines look exactly as before. I compared three of them byte for byte in the text layer with the earlier renders, and the text is identical.

One small problem: the sentence about the usage export contained a link with the old admin domain in the staging config. The production config is right, but I checked the actual link in a rendered PDF to be sure, and it points to the correct page.

The email provider's activity page showed the attachments delivered with sizes between 18 and 52 KB.

I told Ines in a short note which invoices used the new layout today, so that she knows what to expect in the month-end review. I will look at the queue again later today and at the night run.

summary: Checked the night run after the summarized layout: all long invoices rendered, queue time stayed under a minute, and one customer asked why their PDF lost the detail lines.
body:
This morning I looked at the night run. 29 invoices over the threshold were rendered, all successful, with the longest at 3.8 seconds. The queue never held more than six jobs at once, and the longest wait was 52 seconds. Last month the same kind of run had waits above five minutes.

One customer wrote to support that their invoice no longer shows the usage lines. It is one of the 19 big customers that were not in Ines's talks. Mara forwarded the mail to me.

I looked at what the customer received: the summary PDF and the CSV attachment. Their mail may have shown the attachment as a small icon that they did not notice. I drafted an answer for Mara that explains the change in two sentences and says where the detail is, and offers to switch the customer to the full layout. For this customer the full layout would need about 20 seconds per render, which is acceptable for a single case.

I set nothing for them yet. If they ask for the full layout, the override setting exists. I checked that the override works: I set it for a test customer and the full layout rendered, and clearing it brought the summary back.

I also added a line at the bottom of the summarized PDF, in the sentence about the export, that the CSV is attached to the invoice email. The first version only mentioned the export page. This helps customers who read the PDF and not the mail text.

The change to the sentence is small and affects only text. I tested it with the 300 line invoice and the page count stayed at two. It will go out with the next deploy.

Nothing else unusual in the logs. The Stripe sync and the meter gap alert had no new entries.

summary: The customer chose to keep the summarized PDF after reading the explanation, so no override was set; the added sentence about the CSV attachment went to production.
body:
Mara answered the customer with the explanation I drafted. They wrote back that the summary is fine and that they had simply not seen the attachment. No override is needed.

I deployed the small text change: the PDF sentence now says that the full usage detail is attached to the invoice email as a CSV and is also in the usage export. I rendered the 300 line test invoice in production mode first and the page count stayed at two.

I checked three real invoices from the afternoon run. The new sentence appears and nothing else moved. The footer is intact.

I closed the note about long invoices. The chain of work is done: measurements, the chunking experiment that I dropped, the summary layout, the email attachment and the checks. I deleted the scratch file of the chunk experiment, because the stamping approach is not needed now.

The remaining question is the 400 plus line invoices that must show full detail by contract; none exist so far.

summary: Reviewed the Stripe SDK version and its changelog for the next upgrade, listed the breaking changes that touch our code, and planned the upgrade in two steps.
body:
We are still on the older major version of the Stripe SDK, and the next major is out. Before touching anything I read the changelog and searched our code for the affected calls.

I found these points that affect us. First, the type of the webhook event object changed, and our handler has a cast that will not compile. Second, the list methods return a slightly different type, and our pagination code in the sync depends on the old shape of the auto-pagination helper. Third, one parameter of the payment intent create call was renamed, and we use it in the delayed payment path. Fourth, the default API version of the SDK moves forward, so I would pin the version explicitly to keep the behavior stable during the upgrade.

I counted the usages. There are 38 calls to the SDK in 14 files. Of these, 9 are list calls with our own pagination code, 6 are in the webhook handler, and the rest are plain creates and retrieves.

Plan: step one is to pin the API version in the client and add tests around the pagination code and the webhook handler, so that the behavior is fixed before the change. Step two is to bump the package, fix the compile errors and run the whole suite with the Stripe mock server.

I also noted a risk. The pagination code was written as a workaround for an older bug in the SDK, and I am not sure it is still needed. I will test without it, but not remove it in the same change.

I wrote the plan and the list of files into a note. I will start with step one next, and I do not expect production changes from it.

summary: Upgraded the Stripe SDK from v13 to v14 on a test branch of the code in main, fixed three type errors, and all payment flow tests pass against the Stripe test mode.
body:
This was step one of the two-step upgrade planned last week. I bumped stripe in package.json to v14 and ran the TypeScript build. It gave three type errors, all in src/stripe/customers.ts and src/stripe/subscriptions.ts, where the changed types of expanded fields made our code read a field that could now be a string or an object.

I added a small helper, expandedId(), that returns the id whether the field is expanded or not, and used it in the three places. The changelog also mentioned a different default API version for the SDK. We pin the API version in the client constructor, so nothing changes there, and I checked that the pin is still read from config.

Then I ran the unit tests: 212 pass, 0 fail. The integration tests against Stripe test mode create a customer, a subscription, a card payment and a refund. All of them passed, but the refund test was slow, about 40 seconds, because test mode was slow this morning. I ran it twice to be sure that it was not a new timeout.

I also read through the webhook handler. The event types we handle have the same shape in v14, and the signature check function was not touched. I replayed ten stored webhook payloads through the handler in a test and the results were the same as before.

One thing I did not do is look at the pagination calls. The list calls with autoPagingToArray are used by the shims, and the plan says to leave the shims alone until the later upgrades. The pagination tests still pass, so nothing is broken for now.

Next is a day on staging with real webhook traffic before production. If the staging logs show no new error classes, v14 goes out tomorrow. After that the second step is v15, which has the bigger changes to error handling.

summary: Staging ran the v14 SDK for an hour with test webhooks and showed no new errors, but one log line about a deprecated option shows up on every Stripe call.
body:
I deployed the v14 build to staging after lunch and let the test-mode webhooks run for an hour. About 300 events came in, covering invoice, payment_intent and customer events. All were accepted with a 200 and none went to the retry queue.

The only new thing in the logs is a warning that one client option is deprecated. It is the telemetry option, which we set to false in src/stripe/client.ts. I checked the changelog and the option still works in v14, so the warning is harmless, but it fills the log. I removed the option since the default is acceptable to us. The warning is gone after a restart.

I also compared the response times of Stripe calls in the logs with the numbers from last week. They are the same within noise, a median of about 250 ms for a customer retrieve.

Decision: v14 goes to production tomorrow morning, before the daily invoice job at noon, so that I can watch the job. Nothing else is open on this step.

summary: Prepared the Stripe v14 upgrade for production after a clean hour on staging, and checked how the evening payment retry job would be affected.
body:
Staging had run the v14 build for an hour with test webhooks and showed no new errors. The one thing left over was a log line about a deprecated option on every Stripe call, so I looked at where our code sets that option. It is in the client setup, passed once, and the changelog says the new default does the same thing. I wrote the removal as a small separate change, so it does not get mixed into the upgrade itself.

I did not deploy in the late afternoon. The retry job runs in the evening and gives the best test of real card traffic, so I decided to release the v14 build in the morning, when there is time to watch the whole day, instead of changing the payment code just before the job. I wrote down what to check after the release: the health endpoint, one test customer lookup, the log for the words error and deprecated, and the webhook endpoint answering with 200.

I also looked at the last few runs of the retry job to have numbers to compare with. It usually picks up about twenty failed payments, most of them succeed on the retry, and the rest fail again with the card_declined and insufficient_funds codes. The dunning emails for those go to the queue and I can see them in the job table. If tomorrow's run shows another mix, that is the first thing to look at.

I will do the release tomorrow morning and check the numbers after the invoice job. Then I will start reading about v15.

summary: Read the v15 changelog and found that error classes changed, so our catch blocks that test the error type string must switch to instanceof checks.
body:
I started the second step of the upgrade by reading the v15 notes and grepping our code. The main change for us is in the errors: the SDK now exposes distinct error classes and the old type string checks are less reliable. We have 14 places that read err.type or err.code in the catch blocks of the payment, refund and customer code.

I listed them in a note in the repository with the file and the behavior that each one expects. Eight of them handle card errors and decide whether to send a dunning email. Three are in the refund endpoint. Three log and rethrow.

I wrote a small function, classifyStripeError(), in a draft that maps an error to one of our own categories: card, rate_limit, connection, invalid_request and unknown. The idea is to change the 14 places to use our categories, so that the next SDK changes touch one file only.

I did not change any caller yet. Tomorrow I will write tests for the function using the error objects that the SDK itself builds, and then switch the callers one file at a time.

summary: Wrote tests for classifyStripeError with real SDK error objects and found that connection errors were classified as unknown, so the mapping was fixed.
body:
I wrote 18 tests for the classifier. They build the errors with the SDK's own classes, so the tests follow the SDK and not my idea of it. The card, rate limit and invalid request cases passed at once.

The connection case failed. A network failure in the SDK is a connection error class with no code, and my first mapping looked at the code only. I changed the function to test the class first and the code second. The tests now pass.

I also added a case for an error that is not from Stripe at all, such as a TypeError. It maps to unknown and keeps the original error as the cause, so nothing is hidden in the logs.

The callers are still unchanged. That is the next piece of work.

summary: Switched all 14 catch blocks to the new error categories and upgraded to Stripe v15; the full test suite passes and the dunning decision is unchanged.
body:
I changed the callers in four commits, one for each area: customers, subscriptions, payments and refunds. Each commit kept the old behavior. For example, the dunning code sends an email only for the card category, and the refund endpoint still returns 402 to the client for a declined card and 502 for connection problems.

After that I bumped stripe to v15. The build had one new type error, in the code that reads the last payment error of an invoice, where a field was renamed. I fixed it by reading the new name.

The unit tests passed with 230 tests, and the integration tests passed against test mode. I also ran a replay of the stored webhooks again, with the same results.

I deployed to staging at the end of the morning. The rate limit case I could not test against the real API, so I only trust the unit test for it. I will watch staging until tomorrow and then decide on production.

summary: Wrote a short plan for the Stripe v16 upgrade and checked which of our calls it touches; the work was left open until the v15 retry job proves stable over a few more nights.
body:
After the v15 upgrade closed, I read the v16 changelog and compared it with how billing-api uses the SDK. The first thing I did was grep for every import from the stripe package, which gave 31 files. Most of them only use the customers, subscriptions and invoices resources, and none of those changed in a way that matters for us.

The breaking changes that touch our code are few. One is a changed default for the API version pinned by the client, which would silently change the shape of some webhook objects if we did not pin it ourselves. We already set the apiVersion option in src/stripe/client.ts, so this has no effect today, but I added a test that fails if the option is ever removed.

The second is the pagination helper: autoPagingToArray now requires an explicit limit. Our sync uses it in two places, the customer sync and the month-end check, and both already pass a limit of 10,000, so they stay as they are. The deprecated-option log line that showed up on every call after v14 is gone in v16, which is a small plus.

I did not change any code. The plan has three steps: bump the version on a test branch of main, run the payment flow tests against Stripe test mode, and then run staging for a day with test webhooks before production. I wrote this plan into the upgrade notes file next to the earlier one for v14 and v15.

I chose to wait because the v15 change to the error classes only went out recently, and I want a few more evening retry jobs without surprises before another SDK change goes on top. If something odd shows up in the dunning decisions, I would not know whether v15 or v16 caused it. Mara agreed with waiting when I asked her in the chat.

Next is the proration work for plan changes, which Ines asked for, and the v16 upgrade follows when the retry job has been quiet for about a week.

summary: The evening retry job on v15 behaved like before, so the Stripe upgrade work is closed for now, with v16 left for later.
body:
The retry job picked up 17 failed payments, 14 succeeded and 3 were declined again, which fits the usual pattern. The three dunning emails were queued with the right template.

I checked the logs for error categories. There were three card errors, as expected, and nothing else. No unknown category errors appeared.

I wrote a short note in the repository docs about classifyStripeError, so that the next upgrade starts from it. v16 is on the list, but the changelog suggests that it is smaller. I will do it in a few weeks.

summary: Ines asked why one customer's invoice total differed from the plan price; the cause was a coupon with a repeating duration that was applied for one month too long.
body:
Ines sent me an invoice of a customer who paid 20% less than the plan price for a fourth month, although the coupon should have ended after three. She wanted to know whether it was a mistake in the data or in the code.

I looked at the coupon in the database. The coupon is defined as repeating for 3 months, and the subscription of the customer started on the 31st of a month. Our code counted the months by calendar month and not by billing period, and a period that started late in a month was counted as part of the previous one. So the customer got four invoices with the discount.

I wrote a test with a subscription that starts on the 31st and a coupon with 3 months. It failed with four discounted invoices, which proved the cause. I changed the counter to count invoices that were made with the coupon, stored in a column on the redemption, instead of calendar months.

I checked all active redemptions with a query. Five more subscriptions had the same problem and would get one invoice too many with a discount. For those I set the counter by hand through a script, after printing the old and new values and checking them with the counts of past invoices.

The customer in question was already invoiced. Ines decided to leave this one as a goodwill discount and not to bill the difference. I added that decision to the internal note of the customer.

The fix is covered by the test, and the five subscriptions are corrected. Ines will check the next invoices of these five customers during the next month review.

summary: Ines asked why a customer's invoice total differed from the plan price; a coupon with a repeating duration was applied for one month too long, and the coupon end check is now fixed.
body:
Ines wrote that one customer's invoice showed 71.00 EUR where the plan price after discount should have been 79.00 EUR, and she wanted to know which of the two was right. I started from the invoice id and read its lines, then the subscription and the coupon attached to it. The coupon was a repeating one with a duration of three months, 10 percent off.

The invoice in question was the fourth one after the coupon was applied, so it should have been at full price. Our discount code computes the end of a coupon from the start of the subscription period, and it compared with less-or-equal instead of less-than. That gave the coupon one extra period whenever the invoice period started exactly on the boundary.

I checked that the Stripe side did the right thing. Stripe had already ended the discount on its own invoice object, so the number we stored and the number Stripe would charge disagreed. That means the customer was charged the Stripe amount, 79.00 EUR, and only our invoice PDF showed the lower total. So no money was taken wrongly, but the document was wrong.

The fix is one comparison in src/billing/coupons.ts, plus a test with a three-month coupon that checks each of the first five invoices. The test failed before the change on the fourth invoice and passes now. I also wrote a query that finds all invoices where our discount differs from the discount Stripe reports.

The query found 9 more invoices over the last year, all for customers with repeating coupons, all with the same off-by-one cause. For 7 of them the difference was under 5 EUR; two were larger, at 14.20 and 21.50 EUR. I did not touch any old invoices, because they went to the accountants already.

I sent Ines the list with the cause and amounts, and asked whether she wants credit notes or corrected PDFs. She will talk to the accountants first. Until then the fix is in main and ships with the next deploy.

summary: Ines reviewed the proration table and agreed to the seconds-based calculation, with a request that the invoice line text show the number of days used.
body:
Ines opened the CSV and went through about twenty rows with the accountant's view. She agreed that the exact calculation is the right one and that the old differences were small errors in our favor in some months and against us in others.

She asked for one change: the line text on the invoice should say how many days the amount covers, such as 'Upgrade to Pro, 21 days'. Customers have asked why the line is not a full month, and this answers it. I added the days, rounded to whole days, to the line description. The calculation itself still uses seconds.

I switched the invoice builder to the new function and updated the tests. Eleven tests changed their expected amounts. For each I checked by hand that the new number is the exact one, so I did not just copy the output.

The change is not shipped yet. I still want to run it on a copy of last month's data and compare the totals.

summary: Ran the new proration on a copy of last month's invoices: 41 invoices changed by 0.01 to 1.40 EUR, and the net change over all of them was under 6 EUR.
body:
I restored last month's invoice inputs into the scratch database and ran the invoice builder with the old and the new proration code. Of 1,180 invoices, 41 had a proration line, and all 41 changed. The other invoices were identical to the cent.

The change was between 0.01 and 1.40 EUR for each invoice. The sum over all 41 was +5.72 EUR, so the new code bills slightly more in total, because last month had 31 days.

I made a report with the old and new amount for every invoice and sent it to Ines. She said that the amounts are small enough that no customer notice is needed, but she wants the change to start at the beginning of a month so that one month is not mixed.

I set the release for the first invoice run of the next month, and put the switch behind a config value, PRORATION_MODE, with the values legacy and exact, so that I can go back without a deploy. The default stays legacy until then.

summary: A customer reported two receipt emails for one payment; the cause was the Stripe webhook being delivered twice and our handler not checking whether the receipt was already sent.
body:
A customer wrote to support that they got the same receipt twice, a few seconds apart. Mara forwarded it to me this morning and asked whether it is a one-off.

I searched the webhook log for the payment. Stripe delivered the invoice.paid event twice, 4 seconds apart. The first delivery took 6 seconds to answer because the database was busy, and Stripe sent it again, as it does after a slow answer. Both runs of the handler passed the check for the paid status, since the first one had not yet committed.

The handler already stores event ids, but the check and the insert are two steps, and in this case both ran at the same time. I changed the insert to be the first step, with a unique constraint on the event id and ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING. If the insert adds no row, the handler returns 200 and does nothing else.

I wrote a test that starts two handler calls with the same event at the same time. Before the change it sent two emails and after the change it sends one.

I also counted how often this happened. Over the last 30 days, 9 events were processed twice, and 6 of them sent a second receipt. Support had heard of only this one.

The fix goes out with the next deploy. I did not touch the slow answer itself, but I noted that the handler does too much work before it answers. Moving the email to a job would make the answer fast, and that may be the next step.

summary: Moved the receipt email from the webhook handler into a pg-boss job, so the handler answers Stripe in under 100 ms and a slow email cannot cause a redelivery.
body:
After the duplicate receipt fix, I wanted the handler to answer faster. It used to build and send the receipt email inside the request. Now it stores the event, queues a job named send-receipt with the invoice id, and returns 200.

The job loads the invoice, checks that no receipt is recorded for it, sends the email and records it. The record has a unique key on the invoice id, so a retried job cannot send twice either.

I measured the handler on staging with 200 test events. The median answer was 38 ms and the slowest 91 ms, against a median of 700 ms before.

The job has three retries with a backoff of one minute. If all fail, the job stays in the failed state and the existing alert for failed jobs picks it up. I tested that by making the email call throw once, and the second try sent the email.

I deployed it in the morning and checked the first few real receipts, which arrived after 2 to 3 seconds. That is fine.

summary: Mara asked what happens to the usage meter when a customer's plan changes in the middle of a day, and I traced it: usage is split at the change time, by the hour.
body:
Mara asked this while planning the new plan catalog. I read the meter code to answer exactly and not from memory.

The meter stores counts per customer and per hour, read from nebula. When a plan changes, the subscription row gets a new plan id and a valid_from timestamp. At invoice time the builder sums the hourly counts for each plan period of the subscription.

Because the counts are hourly, a change at 14:20 cannot split the 14:00 hour exactly. The code assigns the whole hour to the plan that is valid at the start of the hour, which is the old plan. So up to 59 minutes of usage can be billed with the old price.

I checked how much that matters. I took the plan changes of the last three months, 52 of them, and computed the usage in the hour of the change. In total it was 0.4% of the usage of those customers in that cycle, so the money effect is a few euro.

I see no reason to change it now, but it should be written down, because Ines may be asked about it. I added a paragraph to the docs of the meter, with the rule and the example.

I told Mara the answer. If the plan catalog gets plans with a very high unit price, the rule may need a finer meter, which would mean a different read from nebula, not a change to our code alone.

summary: Wrote the first part of the new plan catalog change: a plan can now have a price valid from a date, so a price rise does not touch running subscriptions.
body:
Mara wants to raise the price of one plan next quarter and keep the old price for existing customers for six months. Today the price table has one row per plan and currency, so a change would hit everybody.

I added a table, plan_prices, with plan id, currency, amount, valid_from and valid_to. A migration copies each existing price with valid_from set to the plan's creation time. The subscription stores the price id it was started with, in a new nullable column.

The invoice builder now looks up the price by the subscription's price id when set, and by the plan, currency and current time otherwise. All old subscriptions have the column filled by the migration, so they keep their price.

I wrote 9 tests for the lookup: a price change in the future, a change in the past, two currencies, and a subscription pinned to an old price. All pass.

The migration ran on staging in 2 seconds. I did not run it in production. I want to review the rollback first, which is just dropping the new column and table, since the old table is untouched.

summary: Reviewed the plan price migration with a rollback test and ran it in production; all 1,420 subscriptions got their price id and the next invoice dry run matched.
body:
First I tested the rollback on a copy of the staging database. I ran the migration, made an invoice, ran the down migration, and made the same invoice with the old code. The totals were the same.

Then I ran the migration in production in the quiet hour. It took 3 seconds and filled the price id for 1,420 subscriptions. A check query found no subscription with a missing id and none whose pinned price differed from the old price table.

I ran an invoice dry run for all active subscriptions with the new lookup and compared the totals with the old code. All 1,420 matched to the cent. The proration mode is still legacy, so the two changes do not mix.

The old price table is not used for new invoices now, but I left it in place for one more month. The price rise itself is up to Mara, who will add the new row when the date is decided.

One small point: the admin script that creates a subscription still sets no price id, so the lookup by time is used. I added the id there too and a test for it.

summary: The first month-end run with exact proration matched the table sent to Ines, and she signed off the review, with one 0.01 EUR difference against the Stripe dashboard still to be understood.
body:
The first invoice run of the month started at six in the morning with PRORATION_MODE set to exact. I set the value the evening before and checked it in the running config.

The run made 1,203 invoices. I compared the 44 invoices with proration lines against the report I had sent Ines earlier, adjusted for the real usage. All lines used the seconds formula, and the line text showed days, for example 'Upgrade to Pro, 17 days'.

I ran the month-end checklist script that Ines uses. All checks passed, and the new ones for credit notes and billing emails showed nothing. The summary mail went to her at eight.

The PDF renderer handled the long invoices with the summarized layout. The queue time was under a minute, and I saw no failures.

In the middle of the morning Ines asked about one invoice with a downgrade. The proration there is a credit line, and the sign was right, but she wanted to know why the credit was 3.11 EUR and not a round number. I explained the seconds and showed the calculation with the period start and end. She accepted it.

She then checked a sample of ten invoices against the Stripe dashboard. Nine matched exactly. One differed by 0.01 EUR, and I looked at it. Stripe rounds its preview once at the end, while we round each line half up, so the sum of the lines can differ by a cent. This is the same kind of cent difference that she has seen against the tax report before, and I have not changed anything about it. I only noted the case, and we agreed to look at the rounding of totals separately, since she wants the totals to follow the accountants' method.

I wrote a short note for Ines on this difference so that she can answer the same question the next time.

Nothing else is open. I will remove the legacy proration mode from the code next month if no problem shows up.

summary: A late alert showed that 6 SEPA-like pending invoices were not moved back to open after ten days; the timeout job had been skipped because of a failed deploy restart.
body:
The stuck-processing check sent its report in the evening with six invoices that had been in processing for more than ten days. By the rule that Ines chose, they should have gone back to open.

I looked at the job table. The timeout job is scheduled by the worker at start. At the last deploy the worker restarted, and the schedule call failed with a connection error to the database for a few seconds. The error was logged but the worker kept running without the schedule.

I ran the job by hand. The six invoices went back to open, the audit lines were written, and the dunning emails were queued for the next morning's window and not sent at night.

Then I fixed the cause. The scheduling now retries up to five times with a pause, and the worker exits with an error if it still fails, so the process manager restarts it.

summary: Added a startup check that all expected scheduled jobs exist, after the lost timeout job showed that a silent scheduling failure can go unseen for days.
body:
The lost timeout job had one more lesson: nothing told us that a schedule was missing. The only sign was a report of the stuck check, and that check is itself a scheduled job.

I made a list of all scheduled jobs in the code: the invoice run, the payment retries, the dunning run, the processing timeout, the meter sync, the month-end checklist, the stuck-processing check and the alert for meter gaps. There are eight. I put them into one file, schedules.ts, with the name and the cron expression, so that the worker and the check read the same list.

The worker now creates the schedules from that list at start, and then reads the schedule table of pg-boss and compares. If a name is missing, it logs an error and exits.

I also added a small endpoint for the health check, /health/schedules, that returns the number of expected and existing schedules and the last run time of each. The monitoring can alert if a job has not run for twice its interval.

I wrote tests for the comparison with a fake schedule table: all present, one missing, and one with a changed cron. The first passes, and the other two are reported as errors.

On staging I deleted a schedule by hand and restarted the worker. It put the schedule back at start as it should, and the health endpoint showed eight of eight.

I then deleted the schedule while the worker was running. The endpoint showed seven of eight at once. The monitoring rule with the twice-the-interval limit still needs adding on the monitoring side, and I wrote that into the open points.

In production the deploy went well. The worker started, created the schedules, and the endpoint shows eight of eight with the right last run times.

I told Mara about the missed jobs in the log and the six invoices, so that she knows what happened and that the invoices are fine. I will add the monitoring rule tomorrow.

summary: Added the monitoring rule for schedule health, so an alert fires when a job has not run for twice its interval, and tested it by pausing one job on staging.
body:
I added the rule to the monitoring config. It reads the /health/schedules endpoint every five minutes and alerts if any job's last run is older than twice its interval.

For the daily jobs that means 48 hours, which is long. I changed the limit for the invoice run and the dunning run to 30 hours, because they are the most important ones and a day plus a margin is enough. The values are in schedules.ts now, next to each job.

To test it, I paused the meter sync on staging, which runs every hour, and waited. After two hours and five minutes the alert came to the channel with the job name. I resumed the job and the alert cleared.

This closes the open point from the missed timeout job.

summary: Looked into a slow query on the customer usage page of the admin tool: a sequential scan over the meter table, fixed with a composite index that cut it from 2.3 seconds to 12 ms.
body:
Mara said that the usage page of a single customer takes several seconds in the admin tool for large customers. I ran EXPLAIN ANALYZE on the query behind it.

The query selects the hourly counts of one customer for a period, ordered by hour. The meter table has an index on the customer id alone and one on the hour alone. The planner chose a sequential scan, because the table has grown to about 14 million rows and the customer id index was not selective enough for large customers. It took 2.3 seconds.

I created a composite index on customer id and hour, with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY so that the meter writes were not blocked. It took about four minutes to build in production.

After the index, the same query used an index scan and took 12 ms. I also checked the invoice builder, which reads the same data for the sums. Its query is a range sum and it improved from 380 ms to 40 ms for a large customer.

The old customer id index is now covered by the new one, since the new index starts with the same column. I did not drop it yet, because I want to see the table statistics for a week to be sure that nothing else uses it.

I also checked the size of the new index, which is 420 MB. That is acceptable for now, but it is another sign that the meter table will need a cleanup or a cut of old rows. I put a note in the list of later work.

I told Mara that the page is fast now. She tried the biggest customer and agreed.

summary: Wrote a plan for archiving old meter rows: counts older than 25 months can move to a daily summary table, since invoices never read old hours again.
body:
After the index work, I looked at what the meter table is used for. The invoice builder reads the current and previous cycle. The admin page reads up to 13 months. Finance has asked for old numbers only as invoice totals, which are kept in the invoices.

I queried how old the rows are. Of 14 million rows, 9.1 million are older than 13 months, and 6.2 million older than 25 months. The oldest are from the first version of the service.

My plan has three steps. First, create a table meter_daily with customer id, day, metric and count, and fill it from the hourly rows older than 13 months, so that the admin page can still show a chart with daily values. Second, delete the hourly rows older than 25 months in batches of 50,000 rows with a pause, so that the database and the replication are not stressed. Third, make the delete a monthly job.

I checked what could break. The usage dispute tool, which Ines uses rarely, reads hourly rows. Disputes are accepted for 12 months only, as the terms say, so 25 months leaves a large margin.

I wrote the aggregation query and ran it on a copy for a sample of 100 customers. The daily sums matched the sums of the hourly rows exactly in all cases.

The risk I see is the delete, which cannot be undone. I will take a dump of the affected rows into cold storage first, and keep it for a year.

I sent the plan to Mara for review. I did not change anything in production today.

summary: Mara approved the meter archive plan with a longer 30-month retention, and I wrote the daily summary migration and checked it on staging, with nothing run in production yet.
body:
Mara read the plan and approved it, but she wants the hourly rows kept for 30 months and not 25, since the cost of storage is small compared to the cost of a dispute that we cannot check. I changed the limit in the plan and the job config to 30 months. She also asked for a six-month wait before anything is deleted, and I added that to the plan as a separate step with its own check.

I then built the first step only. The migration creates meter_daily with a unique key on customer id, day and metric, and a script fills it from the hourly rows older than 13 months, using INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING, so that it can run again without double counting.

I ran the script on staging. It took 40 seconds and created 380,000 daily rows from 9.1 million hourly rows. I compared the totals per customer between the two tables with a query, and the difference was zero for all customers.

I did not touch production today. The plan for it is to run the script in the quiet hour in batches by month, watch the load on the database so the invoice builder is not slowed, and run the same comparison query afterwards. I wrote that comparison into a small script so Mara can run it too.

I also started on the admin page, which should read daily rows for periods older than 13 months. The query is drafted but not yet connected, and I want to test it with the biggest customer, where 24 hours should collapse into one point per day.

Nothing is deleted, and nothing will be for a long time. The rows older than 30 months are the delete candidates, and that is about 4.4 million rows. The step after the production fill is the dump into cold storage, and the delete job in batches comes last.

summary: The meter archive job ran its first full night on rows older than 13 months and the daily summary totals matched the raw counts for every customer checked.
body:
The summary step I started yesterday ran overnight through pg-boss. It processed about 38 million meter rows and wrote 412,000 rows into meter_daily_summary. I compared the sums per customer and per day against the raw table for a sample of 60 customers, and every figure matched.

The job took 41 minutes and ran in batches of one day, so it never held a long lock on the meter table. Query load on the admin usage page did not change during the run.

One thing I noticed: customers whose plan changed during a day have two partial hour splits, and the summary keeps them as separate rows by plan id. That is correct, but the admin tool needs to sum them. I wrote that down for the admin page.

Nothing has been deleted. Mara asked for a six-month wait, so the raw rows stay for now. Next I will add a check job that compares summary and raw sums each week until the deletion step is allowed.

summary: The meter archive job ran its first full night on rows older than 13 months, and the daily summary totals matched the raw counts for every customer checked.
body:
The archive job from the plan of three days ago ran its first full night, starting at 02:00 and finishing in 41 minutes. It read the hourly meter rows older than 13 months, wrote one row per customer and metric and day into the daily summary table, and marked the source rows as summarized. It did not delete anything, as agreed with Mara: the raw rows stay for six months before any delete step exists.

This morning I checked the result in three ways. First, I took 30 customers, a mix of small ones and the largest ones, and compared the sum of the raw hourly counts with the sum of the daily summary for each metric. All 30 matched exactly. Second, I ran a query over all customers that compares the total of raw counts with the total of summary counts per metric, and the difference was zero for every metric. Third, I counted the rows: about 6.2 million raw rows turned into roughly 310,000 summary rows.

I also looked for edge cases. Days where a plan changed in the middle of the day are split by the hour in the meter, and the daily summary keeps the plan id with the count, so those days produced two rows and the totals still matched. Customers who were deleted last year have summary rows too, which is what the invoices history needs.

The job is safe to run twice, because it writes with an upsert on customer, metric and day, and I ran it a second time on staging to confirm that the row counts did not change. The next night run will only handle the rows that became older than 13 months since, so it should take a few minutes. Next I will add a check to the schedule health rule so an alert fires if the archive job skips a night, and write down the date from which the delete step may be planned.

summary: A customer asked why the VAT line on their invoice was zero; the cause was a valid reverse charge VAT id, and the invoice text was correct but too short.
body:
Support forwarded a question from a German customer who saw 0.00 EUR VAT on the last invoice and feared a mistake. I looked at the invoice and the tax record. The customer had added a VAT id three weeks ago, the VIES check passed, and the reverse charge rule applied.

The totals are right. The PDF only says 'Reverse charge' without a sentence about it, which is what confused the customer.

I drafted a longer line: 'VAT reverse charge, tax is due by the recipient'. Ines said the accountants want this text on all such invoices. I added it to the template for the current renderer and ran the tests for the reverse charge case. The answer to the customer went out through support.

summary: Wrote tests for the reverse charge invoice text across the EU countries in our table and fixed one country where the text fell back to English.
body:
After the small text change this morning I wanted all reverse charge cases covered. I added a test that renders the invoice for each of the 27 country codes with a valid VAT id and checks that the line exists.

The test passed for 26 countries. For one country the locale lookup returned nothing and the template used an empty string, so the invoice had no line at all. The cause was a missing key in the locale map, not the tax logic; the VAT amount was still zero and correct.

I added the key and a default so a missing locale falls back to English text, never to nothing. A second test checks that no invoice with zero VAT and a VAT id lacks the line.

I looked in production for invoices made in the last three months for that country with reverse charge. There were two, both missing the line. Ines will tell the accountants, and I will regenerate the PDFs of those two once she agrees, because the invoice number must stay the same.

The full test suite passes.

summary: Regenerated the two PDFs that lacked the reverse charge line, with the same invoice numbers and totals, and sent them to the customers after Ines approved.
body:
Ines agreed to the regeneration this afternoon. I wrote a small script that renders an existing invoice again from its stored data, without creating a new number or changing the totals.

I ran it for the two invoices in dry mode first. It printed the totals before and after, and both were identical. Then I ran it for real. The new PDFs have the reverse charge sentence and the old files are kept in storage under a suffix, so nothing is lost.

The corrected copies went out through the normal email path with a short note that only a text line was added. Ines put the same note in her accounting folder.

I checked the render queue afterwards; two jobs, both fine. The script stays in the scripts folder with a comment about when to use it. I did not touch any other invoice.

summary: Planned the upgrade to Stripe v16 by listing the calls it touches and found that only the pagination helpers and one webhook type need changes.
body:
The v15 retry job has been stable for several nights, so I read the v16 changelog and compared it with our code. I searched for each changed method and type in src.

Three areas are touched. First, list calls where we use autoPagingEach: the behavior is the same, but one type for the result changed. Second, the webhook event type for invoice events has a renamed field that our handler reads in one place. Third, the API version pin, which the SDK now sets by default.

There is a small risk with the pinned API version. If we move it, the shape of some objects can change. I decided to keep our explicit pin in the client setup for now and move it in its own step.

Our two pagination shims, which wrap list calls for the old cursor behavior, are still needed with v16. I checked the code and the tests for them and they still pass on a scratch install.

Plan: upgrade on a branch of the main checkout, fix the types, run the payment tests against test mode, run staging for a day with test webhooks, then production before the evening retry job. I wrote this in the notes file. Mara will read it tomorrow.

summary: Upgraded to Stripe v16 and fixed the invoice event field and the list result types; payment tests pass in test mode and staging shows no new errors.
body:
Mara approved the plan, so I did the upgrade today. The package change itself was one line. The compiler then reported 9 type errors.

Seven were in the pagination shims and the code around them, where the list result type had moved. I changed the shim signatures to the new type and kept their logic. The other two were in the webhook handler, where the invoice event field was renamed. I changed the read and added a test with a stored real event.

The payment flow tests ran against Stripe test mode: create customer, subscribe, pay, fail, retry, refund. All 64 tests passed. The classifyStripeError tests from the v15 work also passed without changes, which was the part I worried about.

I kept the API version pin as it was, as planned. A test confirms that the client sends the pinned version header.

Staging ran v16 for three hours with test webhooks and the usual sample of failed payments. No new error types, and the deprecated option log line is gone, since I removed the option.

I have not shipped it yet. I want to watch one more staging cycle of the dunning job in the morning. Production comes before the evening retry job, so a bad result would show in a small run of retries.

Open: the shims remain and will need a separate cleanup later.

summary: Shipped Stripe v16 to production and watched the evening payment retry job: 31 retries ran, 26 succeeded, and no new error type appeared.
body:
The dunning job on staging this morning looked normal, so I deployed v16 at the start of the afternoon. I checked the logs of the first webhooks: invoice.paid and payment_intent events were processed with the renamed field.

The evening retry job ran 31 retries. 26 succeeded, 5 failed with card declined, which is the usual share. The dunning email decision for those 5 did not change. No error landed in the unknown category.

I also looked at the response times of Stripe calls in the metrics. They are the same as under v15, around 250 ms for creating a payment intent.

Nothing else needed a change. I added a line to the upgrade notes with the order of steps, since it worked well for v14, v15 and now v16. The version of the SDK in the staging and production images is the same.

summary: Ines found a customer whose receipt email arrived but whose invoice PDF link returned an error; the signed link had expired after one day.
body:
Ines forwarded a mail from a customer who clicked the PDF link in an old receipt and got an access error. I checked the link: it is a signed storage URL with a lifetime of 24 hours, set when the email is made.

That is too short for a receipt that people open weeks later. Receipts should link to our own endpoint, which checks a token and then creates a fresh signed URL on each click.

I wrote the endpoint, GET /invoices/:id/pdf with an opaque token stored per invoice, and changed the receipt template to use it. Old emails with the expired links cannot be repaired, but the customer can use the link in the new template, and I sent them the invoice again.

Tests cover a valid token, a wrong token and a token for another invoice; the last two return 404 so that nobody can probe for invoices. The token has no expiry, but it can be revoked by deleting it.

I will check the log in a week for 404 spikes on this route.

summary: The PDF link endpoint ran for a few days: 212 clicks, 3 not found, all from a customer who mistyped the token when copying it by hand.
body:
I looked at the logs of the new PDF link route as planned. There were 212 requests since the change. 209 returned the PDF, and 3 returned 404.

All 3 came from one customer address within a minute, with tokens that differed from real tokens in the last characters, so they had copied the link by hand. That is not an attack or a bug.

The response time of the route is about 40 ms plus the storage call. The fresh signed URL is created on each click, which costs one call to storage and is fine.

I added a rate limit of 30 requests per minute per address to be safe, using the Fastify rate limit plugin that other routes already use. A test checks the 31st request.

The item is closed. The old 24 hour link code is removed from the receipt job.

summary: Investigated why the month-end render run takes longer each month and found that invoices with many lines grow with usage; measured the browser time per invoice.
body:
Mara asked why the render queue at month end now needs about 25 minutes. I took the timings from the render job logs for the last run and grouped them by the number of lines in the invoice.

Invoices with up to 10 lines take about 1.1 seconds. Invoices with 100 to 200 lines take 6 to 9 seconds. The few with more than 300 lines take 15 seconds. The headless browser spends most of its time in layout, not in start-up.

The summarized layout from earlier shortened the longest ones, but customers on per-metric plans still have long lists for other reasons, such as several workspaces on one invoice.

I tried two quick things on a copy. A single browser reused for several invoices instead of a new one each time saved about 0.4 seconds per invoice. Turning off web fonts loading from the network saved about 0.3 seconds. Together, the month-end run in the test fell from 25 to 19 minutes.

The browser reuse needs care, since a crash would affect the next job. I want to restart the browser after every 50 pages and on any error.

I did not ship anything today. The plan is to put the fonts in the image first, which is a safe change, and then do the reuse with the restart rule.

A bigger change, a different renderer, is in my mind but not decided. Mara agreed to look at the fonts change first.

summary: Put the invoice fonts into the render image so the browser no longer fetches them from the network, which saved about 0.3 seconds per invoice.
body:
I added the two font files to the image and changed the template to use local font-face rules. The previous version fetched them from a CDN on every render.

I rendered 200 invoices on staging before and after. Median time fell from 1.9 to 1.6 seconds. The PDFs look the same; I compared five of them side by side, and the page count did not change for any of the 200.

There is a side benefit: renders no longer fail when the CDN is slow. Two failures in last month's log came from that.

Shipped it after the tests. Next is the browser reuse with the restart rule.

summary: Built browser reuse in the render worker with a restart after 50 pages or any error; the month-end test run fell from 19 to 16 minutes.
body:
The worker now keeps one headless browser and opens a new page for each invoice. After 50 pages, or after any render error, it closes the browser and starts a new one.

I wrote tests that force an error in the middle of a batch and check that the next invoice renders correctly. They pass. I also checked memory in a 500 invoice run: it stayed under 700 MB, where the old worker used about 500 MB at peak but started and stopped many times.

On the copy of last month's invoices the run fell from 19 to 16 minutes in total. Together with the fonts change this is about a third faster than before.

I will ship it for the next month-end and watch the queue time.

summary: Shipped the browser reuse for the render worker and watched the first batch of night invoices: no errors, and only one restart for the page limit.
body:
I deployed the worker change in the evening. The night run created 188 invoices. The log shows 3 browser starts for the page limit and none for errors.

Average render time was 1.4 seconds. The longest, an invoice with 280 lines, took 11 seconds, down from 15.

I compared the PDF sizes with the day before for the same customers where I could. They are within a few percent of each other, which is normal because of timestamps in the file.

No customer complained, and the queue was empty by the early morning. I will look at the real month-end numbers in a few days.

summary: Month-end run with the faster worker took 15 minutes instead of 25, and Ines checked a sample of the invoices; the remaining slow part is the very long invoices.
body:
The month-end run finished today. Queue start to last PDF was 15 minutes for 1,390 invoices. Last month it was 25 minutes.

Ines took her usual sample of 30 invoices and compared the PDFs with the data. She found no differences in totals or text. She also asked that I keep the browser restarts, as a crash in the middle would be hard for her to see.

I looked at the slowest 20 invoices of the run. They all have 150 or more lines, and they account for about 4 of the 15 minutes. These are the customers with many workspaces. The summarized layout applies only when the customer's lines are all metric lines, which these are not.

Options I wrote down:
- Group the lines by workspace in the summarized layout, with a CSV attached.
- Paginate the table with fixed row heights so the layout step is cheaper.
- Use a different renderer that does not use a full browser.

The first is cheap but changes what customers see, so Ines and Mara need to agree. The second I can test quickly. The third is large and I will only note it for later.

I tried the second option on a copy with the 20 slowest invoices. Fixed row heights cut the time per invoice by about 25 percent. The text wraps on a few long plan names, so I need a rule to cut them.

I did not ship anything. Mara wants to see the grouped layout draft before deciding. I will make a mock of it from one real invoice and send it to her and Ines.

summary: Made a mock of the workspace-grouped invoice layout from a real 210-line invoice; Ines accepts the grouping and asks to keep the workspace names in full.
body:
I took one real invoice with 210 lines and 7 workspaces and rendered it with a grouped layout. Each workspace gets one line with its name, the total count, and the amount. The detail goes into the attached CSV, as in the summarized layout.

The PDF fell from 9 pages to 2. Render time on staging was 1.2 seconds.

I sent the mock to Ines and Mara. Ines said the grouping is fine for the accountants because the totals per workspace are what the customers pay and ask about. She asked that the workspace names are never cut, even when long, so the customer can match them. Mara agreed with the idea but wants the rule to be clear: only invoices with more than 100 lines switch to the grouped layout.

I wrote the rule as a threshold in the config, 100 lines, so we can change it without a deploy. The layout choice is saved on the invoice, so a regenerated PDF looks the same as the original.

To be careful, I checked what happens with a credit note for a grouped invoice. It must show the same grouping, otherwise the customer sees two different views. I found that the credit note template does not use the layout switch. I added it to my list.

Tests so far: grouping totals equal the sum of the lines, and a workspace with a zero amount still shows. Both pass.

Next: credit note template, the CSV with workspace column, and a run on last month's data to compare totals.

summary: Added the grouped layout to credit notes and a workspace column to the CSV, then compared the line sums with the stored totals on last month's long invoices: all 23 matched to the cent.
body:
The credit note template now uses the same layout choice that is stored on the invoice. A credit note for a grouped invoice shows the same groups with negative amounts.

The CSV got a workspace column as its first field, and the file name now includes the invoice number. I checked that the CSV opens correctly with commas and quotes in workspace names, because one real name has a comma in it.

Then I ran the whole thing on a copy of last month's invoices. 23 invoices were over the threshold of 100 lines. For each one I compared the sum of the group amounts, the sum of the lines and the stored total. All matched exactly, and no difference of a cent appeared.

Render time for these 23 went from 8 seconds on average to 1.3 seconds, which would take about 3 minutes from the month-end run.

One point to watch: Ines asked about this kind of case in the past, since some totals were once 1 cent off the tax report and she found them by hand. The current rounding is not something I touched here. The group amounts are only a regrouping of the existing line amounts. Here the sums match, but I added a test that fails if a group total differs from the sum of its lines, so a future change to how lines are rounded will show up at once.

The code is ready for review. I will ask Mara tomorrow.

summary: Mara reviewed the grouped invoice layout, asked for the threshold to be shown in the admin tool, and I shipped it after adding that.
body:
Mara read the diff and had two comments. One was a naming issue in the layout function, which I fixed. The other was that support cannot see why an invoice has the grouped layout.

I added a field to the invoice page in the admin tool: layout (detailed, summarized, grouped) and the line count. A support person can now answer a customer without asking me.

I deployed after the tests. The first invoices rendered with the grouped layout were two that were created in the early afternoon for customers with trial ends. Both rendered in about a second and the CSV was attached to the email.

I checked the render queue and the logs and found no errors. I will look at the month-end numbers in a few weeks and tell Ines when the next big run happens.

summary: Looked at a customer's complaint about a failed card payment that the dunning email described as a bank decline; the Stripe code was an expired card and the mapping needed a new text.
body:
Support passed on a customer who got a dunning email saying the bank declined the payment, while the card had simply expired. I checked the payment in Stripe. The decline code was expired_card.

Our dunning text map covers generic declines, insufficient funds and a few others. For expired_card it fell back to the generic text. That is accurate but unhelpful, because the customer needs to update the card.

I added a text for expired_card with a link to the billing page, and one for incorrect_cvc. The map now has a test for every code that has its own text, and one test for the fallback.

I also counted the last two months of failed payments by code. Expired card was 18 percent of all failures, which makes it the second most common reason after insufficient funds. That is a good reason to make the text clear.

The change went out with the next deploy. The customer was told through support.

summary: Wrote a script to list subscriptions whose card expires within 30 days, as a first step toward a reminder email before the payment fails.
body:
Because of the expired card cases, I looked at whether we can warn customers before the payment fails. Stripe gives the expiry month and year on the payment method, and we can read them in the list call.

I wrote a script that goes through active subscriptions with a card and prints those that expire within 30 days. For the current data it found 64 subscriptions out of 1,400.

The script reads with the paging helpers, 100 at a time, and it took about 40 seconds. That is fine for a nightly job.

I did not send any emails. Before that, Ines should say whether the customer notice is allowed to be a marketing-like message or only a service message. I wrote a short question for her.

Next step is a pg-boss job that records who was warned, so nobody gets two emails for one card.

summary: Built the card expiry reminder job with a record of sent notices, and ran it on staging test customers, where each got exactly one email.
body:
Ines answered that this is a service message about the customer's own payment, so it can go out with the other transactional emails. That decided the question from last week.

I created the job card-expiry-reminder. It runs once a night, reads the active subscriptions with cards that expire within 30 days, and checks a new table, expiry_notices, that holds the payment method id and the expiry date. If a row exists, no email is sent. Otherwise the job queues the email and writes the row in the same transaction.

The email uses a new template with the last four digits, the expiry month and a link to the billing page. It goes through the same send job as receipts, so the retry rules and the logging are the same. The old provider is still the one behind that job, and some customers still find those mails in their spam folder, so I noted that the reminder may land there too.

I wrote tests for these cases:
- a card that expires in 20 days gets one email
- the job running twice sends one email
- a customer who updates the card and later gets a new expiry gets a new notice
- a subscription that is cancelled gets nothing

On staging I made 5 test customers with cards that expire soon, using Stripe test cards. I ran the job twice. 5 emails were queued and the second run queued none.

I also thought about the customers who pay by invoice. They have no card and are skipped because the payment method type is not card. A test covers it.

One detail: the job runs at 06:00 UTC, which is early morning for most of our customers in Europe. That seemed good.

The schedule health rule covers the new job automatically, since it reads the list of expected jobs. I added the job to that list and the startup check.

It is ready for review. After Mara looks at it, I will ship it and read the first night's log.

summary: Mara reviewed the card expiry reminder job and asked for a dry-run flag; I added it and planned the first production check, with nothing sent yet.
body:
Mara's review found one useful point: the first production run would email all 64 customers at once, and she wanted to see the list before anything is sent. I added a config flag, dry run, that logs the planned emails and writes nothing to expiry_notices and nothing to the send queue.

I tested the flag on staging with the test customers. With the flag on, the log listed the planned emails and the table stayed empty. With the flag off, each test customer got one notice row, as before. The flag is on by default, so a fresh deploy cannot send anything by accident.

I also ran my listing script against production to compare it with what the job would plan. The script shows 64 subscriptions with a card expiring within 30 days. I expect the job to list a few fewer, because some cards may have been replaced since the script first ran, but I have not checked that yet. I will look at the difference when the dry run log exists.

The notices still go out through the old email provider, since that is the only one the send job knows. Some customers have complained that receipts end up in spam, so I am not sure these reminders will reach people. I wrote that down as a worry on the plan list and did not change anything about it today.

For the next step, I will deploy with the flag on and let the job run once at its scheduled time. Mara wants to read the log and check a sample of lines before I turn the flag off. I will also group expiry_notices on payment method id after the first real run to look for duplicates.

The item is not finished. It waits for the dry run and Mara's reading of the list. I also noted the baseline for later: about 18 percent of payment failures are expired cards, to compare once the reminders have run for a while.

summary: Ines asked for a monthly report of invoices by status and total per currency; I wrote the query and a CSV export for her to use in the month-end review.
body:
Ines said that she builds a table by hand every month from the admin tool: how many invoices are paid, open, void and uncollectible, and the sum for each currency. She asked if the service can produce it.

I wrote a query that groups invoices by month, status and currency, and sums the totals in minor units. The output is converted to decimals only at the end, to avoid float problems.

The table is large now, but the query uses the existing index on created_at, and it ran in 0.8 seconds for one month.

I added a CLI command, report:invoices --month, that writes a CSV with the columns she described. I ran it for last month and sent it to her. She compared it with her manual table and found the same numbers except for one void invoice, which she had counted as open by mistake.

I added a test with a fixture of 12 invoices in 3 currencies that checks each group. The command is documented in the README with an example.

Next time she can run it herself or ask me. She may ask for a column for tax later.

summary: Looked at the growth of the invoices table and measured query times at the current size, to decide when partitioning becomes necessary.
body:
Mara asked how long we can wait before the invoices table needs special treatment. I measured the current state.

The table has 2.1 million rows, including the line items stored as JSON, and takes about 6.4 GB with indexes. About 70,000 rows are added each month, and the growth of the size is a bit faster than that because invoices have more lines.

I ran the most common queries with explain analyze: list by customer, list by status for the month-end run, and the new report. List by customer takes 4 ms, the month-end query 90 ms, and the report 0.8 seconds. All use indexes and none is a problem today.

The cost that will grow is maintenance. A vacuum on the table now takes 11 minutes, and an index rebuild would need a long lock if we ever needed it.

I estimated the numbers for two years: about 4 million rows and 12 GB. The queries would still be fine, but the maintenance would be slower, and old invoices, which never change, would share pages with new ones.

My recommendation was to not do anything this quarter, but to plan a split by period when the table passes 3 million rows. I wrote that in the notes with the measurements so that we can compare later.

Mara agreed to revisit it then. A related question, the retention of old rows, is for Ines, since invoices must be kept for the legal period.

summary: Checked the legal retention period for invoices with Ines, who confirmed that all invoices must be kept for ten years, so the table can never be pruned.
body:
I asked Ines about retention, since it decides whether partitioning is only for speed or also for archiving. She asked the accountants and came back with the answer: invoices and credit notes must be kept for ten years in a readable form.

That means we cannot delete old rows, unlike the meter rows, which are only inputs. Any plan for the invoices table has to keep old data, but it can move it to cheaper storage if it stays readable.

I wrote this in the notes next to the size measurements. I also noted that the stored PDFs are part of the record, so they must be kept as well, with the files from the regeneration script that I made earlier.

The storage bucket for PDFs has a lifecycle rule that moves files to a cold class after one year. I checked that the rule does not delete anything, and it does not.

Nothing needs to change now. The decision on partitioning stays open until the table is closer to 3 million rows.

summary: Ines found three invoices a month where the PDF number sequence had a gap; the cause was a rolled-back transaction that had already taken a number from the sequence.
body:
Ines noticed in her month-end check that the invoice numbers jumped from 4417 to 4419 and asked whether an invoice had been lost. I looked at the invoices table and found no row for 4418, then searched the render worker logs and found a transaction that had taken the number and then rolled back because the Stripe customer lookup timed out.

The numbers come from a Postgres sequence, and a sequence does not give back a value after a rollback. That is normal database behavior, but the accountants want numbers without gaps, so a gap needs an explanation each time.

I went through the last six months and found three more gaps with the same cause. In each case the invoice was created again a few seconds later with the next number, and no customer saw a wrong document.

I considered two fixes. The first is a separate counter table locked inside the transaction, which gives gapless numbers but serializes invoice creation. The second is to take the number only after the Stripe lookup succeeded, as the last step before commit. The second one shrinks the window a lot and is cheap, but it does not remove it.

I wrote the notes for both in the repo docs and did not change code yet. I will ask Ines whether gaps with a logged reason are acceptable to the accountants, since that decides which fix we need.

For now I wrote a small query that lists missing numbers in a range, so she can run the check herself each month. It printed the three known gaps and nothing else on last month's data.

summary: Ines said the accountants accept a gap only if it is explained, so I moved the number assignment to the last step before commit and added a log line that records every skipped number.
body:
Ines asked the accountants about the invoice number gaps, and the answer was that gapless numbers are the rule, but a documented gap is tolerated if no document was ever issued with that number. That removes the need for the counter table with its lock, which I did not want on the invoice creation path anyway.

I changed the create-invoice function so the number is taken from the sequence only after the Stripe customer lookup and the line calculation are done. The insert and the commit follow right after it. The window where a rollback can waste a number is now only the insert itself.

I also added a log line, written when a transaction fails after the number was taken, with the number and the error. Ines can then look up the reason for any gap. A test forces a failure on the insert and checks that the log line appears and that the next invoice gets the next number.

I ran the whole invoice test suite, 214 tests, and all pass. On staging I created 300 invoices in a loop with random failures injected on 10 percent of the inserts, and the log showed 31 skipped numbers, all of which matched the gaps in the table.

The real production gaps from before stay as they are. I wrote a short note for Ines with the three old numbers and their causes, so she can pass it to the accountants.

summary: Wrote integration tests for the payment retry job against Stripe test mode, after finding that its tests only used mocks and never saw a real decline code.
body:
While reading the retry job for the dunning flow I saw that every test used a hand-written mock of the Stripe client. The mocks return the error shapes we remembered, not the ones Stripe sends, so a change in the real responses would pass all our tests.

I added a test file that talks to Stripe test mode with the special card numbers: one that always declines, one for insufficient funds, one for an expired card, and one that needs authentication. Each case creates a customer, a subscription and an open invoice, and then runs the retry job once.

The tests found one real difference. For the authentication card the job treated the failure as a normal decline and scheduled another retry, while the right action is to email the customer a link to confirm the payment. The mock had never returned that code. I fixed the mapping and added the case to the dunning email choice.

The tests take about 40 seconds because of the calls to Stripe, so I put them in a separate script, test:stripe, that runs in the nightly build and not on every push. The first nightly run was green.

I cleaned up the test customers at the end of each run with a tag, so the test account does not fill with old objects. Next I want to do the same check for the webhook events, which also only use sample payloads.

summary: Replayed recorded Stripe webhook payloads from the test account against the handler and found that the handler assumed a field that is missing on one event type.
body:
After the retry job tests I did the same for the webhook handler, which had only sample payloads that we wrote by hand. I used the Stripe CLI to trigger the events for the invoice and payment flows in test mode and saved the real payloads as fixtures.

I ran each fixture through the handler with the signature check on. Eleven of twelve event types worked. The invoice.payment_action_required event has no charge field on the invoice object when the payment is still waiting for authentication, and our handler read invoice.charge.id without checking it. It threw a TypeError, the endpoint answered 500, and Stripe would have retried the event for three days.

In production this did not show up yet because the event is rare for our customers, who mostly pay by card without extra authentication. Still, it would have made noise in the retry queue.

I fixed it by reading the field with a check, and the handler now logs the event and sends the customer the authentication email. I added the real fixtures to the repo under tests/fixtures/stripe, with the customer ids replaced. The handler tests now run on those files, and all pass.

summary: Looked into a customer question about why their usage on the invoice differed from the nebula dashboard, and found that the dashboard counts in the customer's time zone while the meter counts in UTC.
body:
A customer wrote to support that the event count on their invoice was 1.8 percent lower than the number on their nebula dashboard for the same month. Support passed it to me, and Ines asked for an answer she could send back.

I first checked that the meter had no missing data. The hourly rows for the customer were all present, 744 rows for the month, and the sum matched the invoice line exactly. So the invoice was consistent with the meter.

Then I looked at how the dashboard counts. It groups events by the day in the time zone that the customer set in their workspace, which was Pacific time for this customer. The meter and the invoice period use UTC. The billing month therefore starts eight hours after the dashboard month starts and ends eight hours later, so about 16 hours at the edges are counted in different months.

I recomputed the dashboard figure from the raw hourly rows by shifting the window by eight hours, and it came to the dashboard number within 12 events. That was enough to show that both numbers were right for their own window.

There is a real question behind this. Customers see one number in the product and another on the invoice, and the difference is largest for customers far from UTC. I did not change anything in the meter. A change of the billing window would alter existing invoices and the contract text says the period is in UTC.

I wrote a clear reply for Ines that explains the two windows with this customer's numbers. She sent it with one change of wording and the customer accepted it.

I also asked in the plan notes for a line on the invoice that states the period is in UTC with its exact start and end. That is a small change in the template and it would prevent most questions of this kind. Mara has not seen it yet, so I only wrote it down as a proposal.

One check is left: how many customers have a time zone more than five hours from UTC. I wrote the query and the answer is 37 of 410 active customers, which is enough to justify the line on the invoice.

summary: Added the UTC period line to the invoice template after Mara agreed, with the exact start and end of the billing window on every invoice.
body:
Mara read the proposal from the time zone question and agreed that the invoice should state its period in UTC. I added a line under the invoice header that reads, for example, Usage period: 1 to 31 in UTC, with the start and end times.

The line is in the template for invoices and for credit notes, and the CSV export has two new columns with the same times. I checked the long grouped layout too, because it has a different header block, and the line appears there as well.

I rendered the five sample invoices and looked at the PDFs by eye. The line fits on one page and does not push the table down on the long invoices. The tests for the template pass with the new text. I shipped it in the evening, and the next month-end run will be the first with the line.

summary: Measured how long each step of the month-end run takes and found that the email step is now the slowest part, because it sends one message at a time.
body:
With the render step faster, I looked at the full month-end run to see what is the longest part now. I added timing logs for each step and ran it on staging with a copy of last month's 410 invoices.

The numbers were: total 14 minutes, render 9 minutes, upload to storage 1 minute, and email sending 4 minutes. The email step sends each receipt in a loop, waits for the answer from the email provider, and then goes on. About 0.6 seconds per message.

The provider allows several requests at once, so the loop can be parallel. I wrote a version that sends with a limit of 5 at once and handles an error per message, so one failure does not stop the others. The staging run for 410 mails fell from 4 minutes to 58 seconds.

I did not ship it yet. I want a test for the case where the provider answers with a rate limit in the middle of a batch, because I do not know what the code does then. That test is the next step.

summary: Wrote the test for a rate limit answer in the middle of an email batch and fixed the parallel sender so that the message is retried after the wait the provider names.
body:
