The test used a fake provider that answers 429 with a wait time on the 20th request. The first version of the parallel sender marked that message as failed and went on, so 5 receipts would have been lost for the month.

I changed the sender to read the wait time from the answer, pause all workers for that long, and try the message again up to three times. After that the message goes to the failed list that the job already reports.

The test now passes with all 60 messages sent and a pause that matches the wait time. The full suite is green.

summary: Shipped the parallel receipt sending and watched the first real batch of 96 receipts: all sent in 21 seconds with no failures and no rate limit answers.
body:
I shipped the parallel sender with the retry after a rate limit in the morning, before the batch of receipts for the customers that bill on a day other than month end. There were 96 of them.

I watched the job logs while it ran. The whole batch took 21 seconds, compared to about a minute before. The provider answered every request with success, and no 429 came, so the pause code was not used in production this time.

I checked the sent list against the invoice list and found 96 on each side. Ines had asked me to confirm that no receipt is sent twice, so I also grouped the sent records by invoice and found no duplicates.

One thing I noticed is that the logs show the sending order is no longer the order of the invoice numbers. It makes no difference for the customers, but it makes the logs harder to read. I added the invoice number to each log line, which fixed that.

The larger test is the month-end batch with more than 400 mails, and I will watch that one in the same way.

summary: Answered Mara's question about how many invoices have more than 100 lines by running a count on the last six months: 23 on average each month.
body:
Mara asked in passing how many invoices are long enough for the grouped layout each month. I ran a count of invoices with more than 100 lines for each of the last six months.

The counts were 19, 20, 22, 23, 25 and 28, so the number grows by about one or two each month. The longest invoice has 231 lines and belongs to one customer with many workspaces.

The threshold in the admin tool is 100 lines, as we set it. At the current growth about 40 invoices a month would be grouped in a year. I told Mara that the render time follows the same growth and that no action is needed now.

summary: The month-end run with parallel emails finished in 10 minutes in total, and Ines found no problem in her sample of receipts and invoices.
body:
This was the first month-end run with the parallel receipt sender and the UTC period line on the invoices. I started the run at its usual time and followed the logs.

The render step took 8 minutes for 412 invoices, the upload 1 minute, and the emails 52 seconds. The total was 10 minutes, down from 15 minutes in the run before. The provider gave 2 rate limit answers, both handled by the pause and a retry, and every message was sent in the end.

Iines asked, and I mean Ines did ask, for a check on a sample, so I gave her a list of 30 random invoice numbers with the PDF link and the receipt status. She opened the PDFs and looked at the period line, the totals and the VAT lines. She found no problem.

One customer with a long invoice wrote that the PDF was larger than usual, at 1.4 MB. The reason is the embedded fonts that we put into the render image. It is still small enough for email links, since we send a link and not the file.

The parallel sender is now the normal way, and I removed the old loop code. Next I will look at the retry of failed receipts for customers whose email bounced, because the failed list is still read by hand.

summary: Built a bounce handling step for receipts: hard bounces from the email provider now mark the customer contact as invalid and open a task for support instead of staying in a list.
body:
The failed list of the receipt job had grown to 17 entries, and all of them were addresses that bounce. Nobody looks at the list except Ines at month end, so customers with a wrong address do not get their invoices for months.

I first read what the provider sends for bounces. It has a webhook for bounce events with a type that separates a hard bounce, which means the address does not exist, from a soft bounce like a full mailbox. I added a route for the webhook with a signature check, like the Stripe one.

For a hard bounce, the handler sets a flag on the billing contact, writes the reason, and creates a row in a table of support tasks. For a soft bounce it only counts, and after three soft bounces in a row it is treated as hard.

The receipt job now skips contacts with the flag and uses the fallback address of the account owner, if there is one. If there is none, it writes a task for support, too. That was the case for 6 of the 17 customers.

I wrote tests with sample bounce events, one for each type, and a test for the fallback choice. They pass.

There is a risk that I thought about. A wrong flag would stop receipts for a good address, for example after one unlucky hard bounce from a mail server problem. To limit that, the flag is cleared when the customer changes the address in the portal, and support can clear it by hand in the admin tool. I added a button for it.

I ran the handler on staging with the provider's test bounce events and the flag was set and cleared as expected. In production I will start with a dry run that only writes the tasks and does not change the receipt job, so Ines and support can see what it would do before it acts.

summary: The bounce handler ran in dry mode for a day and created 4 support tasks, all for addresses that are really wrong, so I switched on the flag for receipts.
body:
The bounce handler had been running in dry mode since yesterday. It wrote support tasks and flag candidates but the receipt job did not use them.

In that day the provider sent 9 bounce events. Four were hard bounces and five were soft ones, three of them from the same mailbox that was full. The handler created 4 tasks, and the soft bounces were only counted.

I checked each of the 4 addresses with support. Three had a typo in the domain, like gmial.com, and one belonged to a person who left a company. So no good address was marked.

I turned the dry mode off, and the receipt job now skips flagged contacts. For the three typos support wrote to the customers and asked for the right address.

The admin tool shows the flag next to the contact with the reason from the provider. I also added a line in the daily report that I send to Ines with the number of open bounce tasks, so the list is no longer something nobody reads.

I will check the numbers again after the next month-end, when the volume is much higher.

summary: Looked at the Stripe SDK deprecation warnings in the logs and listed the three calls that will break in the next major version, to plan the next upgrade.
body:
After the v16 upgrade I turned on the SDK's warning output in staging to see what it complains about. Over a normal day it logged three kinds of deprecation warnings.

The first is the pagination helper that we wrapped in our own function, the second is a way of expanding fields that the next version will not accept, and the third is a method for listing balance transactions that has a new name.

I listed the file and line of each use. There are 4 uses of the pagination wrapper, 2 of the old expand style and 1 of the balance method. None breaks today.

I wrote the list in the docs folder as the starting point for the v17 upgrade, which is not planned for a date yet. The warnings stay on in staging.

summary: Added a daily check that compares the sum of paid invoices in our database with the Stripe balance transactions, and it found one payment that was recorded twice.
body:
Ines asked whether there is a way to know that our records and Stripe agree, since she does the check by hand each month with exports. I wrote a job that runs every night and compares, for the day before, the paid invoices in our table with the charges Stripe reports for the same day, per currency.

The first run on the last 30 days gave one difference. On one day, the euro total in our database was 49.00 higher than Stripe's. I looked for the invoice and found two payment rows with the same Stripe charge id, written within one second of each other.

The cause was a webhook that Stripe delivered twice. Our handler inserted the payment without checking whether the charge id was already there, and the table had no unique constraint on it. The invoice status was fine, since it was set to paid twice, but the payment sum was wrong, and so was the revenue report.

I fixed three things. I added a unique index on the charge id, I changed the insert to do nothing on a conflict, and I removed the duplicate row after Ines approved the change. A test sends the same event twice and checks that there is one row.

The nightly check also writes its result to the log and sends a message to the alert channel if any currency differs by more than one cent. I tested the alert by changing one row on staging.

For the 30 days I checked, everything else matched to the cent, which is good news for the month-end review. Ines will use the log lines as a proof for the accountants and she asked for a monthly summary of them, which I will add to the report.

summary: Planned the work to reduce the PDF render time for the longest invoices further, comparing three options by measuring a 231-line invoice with each.
body:
The long invoices are still the slowest part of the render step, even with the grouped layout. The 231-line invoice takes 11 seconds, while a normal one takes under 2 seconds. I wanted to know where the time goes before deciding on a change.

I used the browser's tracing on that one invoice. Layout took 5.2 seconds, the page load with the HTML and the styles 1.1 seconds, and the PDF print itself 4.1 seconds. So most of the time is layout and printing, not the network.

I tried three options on the same data. The first was to simplify the CSS for the tables, removing nested flex containers inside the table cells. Time fell to 8.4 seconds. The second was to split the invoice into several smaller HTML pages and merge the PDFs, which gave 7.9 seconds but made page numbers and the total line hard to place. The third was to render the table without the browser, from a PDF library that draws text and lines directly. A rough test gave 0.6 seconds.

The third is by far the fastest, but it means a second implementation of the whole layout, with fonts, the logo, and the reverse charge texts in each language. That is a large piece of work and every change of the invoice text would then need to be done in two places for a time.

The first option is cheap and safe, so I will do it now. The third one needs a decision by Mara, because of the size. I wrote the numbers down in a page of notes that compares them, with the risk and the effort for each.

I also noted that any new renderer must produce the same totals and the same lines as the old one, and that the check for that is already available: the comparison script that I used for the grouped layout, which compares the totals of a whole month to the cent.

I changed the table CSS in the branchless main checkout, rendered the five sample invoices, and compared them by eye with the old PDFs. The look is the same, only the cell structure changed.

summary: Shipped the simpler table CSS for long invoices; the month's 23 long invoices rendered 28 percent faster and every total matched the old PDFs.
body:
I ran the comparison script on last month's data with the new CSS. It renders all invoices with both versions and compares the totals and the line counts from the text of the PDFs.

For the 23 long invoices, the render time fell from a total of 3 minutes 40 seconds to 2 minutes 38 seconds, which is 28 percent. Normal invoices did not change in a way that I could measure. All the totals and line counts matched, and there was no change in the number of pages.

I looked at the longest invoice page by page. One thing was different: the border under the group header was 1 pixel thinner in the new version. I fixed it with an explicit border width. After that I could not see any difference between old and new when I laid the two PDFs next to each other.

Mara reviewed the change in the evening. She had one question, whether the simpler CSS works for the credit notes, and I showed her the render of three credit notes, which look right. She approved it.

I shipped it after the evening job finished, so that no render was running at the time of the restart. The first night render of 14 invoices had no errors.

The notes about the PDF library option stay in the docs. Mara said she wants to think about it, and that it is not for this quarter, since the current speed is acceptable. I will take the topic up again when the long invoices become the bottleneck of the month-end run.

summary: A customer asked for a refund of a double payment, and I found that the first payment went through Stripe, the second through a retry after our server timed out.
body:
Support forwarded a customer who was charged twice for the same invoice, 129.00 in euros each time. Ines asked me to find out how that happened before she approves the refund.

I looked at the payment rows and the Stripe charges for the invoice. There were two charges, 4 minutes apart. The log of the retry job showed that the first call to create the payment timed out on our side after 30 seconds, and the job did not know whether Stripe had taken the payment, so it scheduled a retry. The first charge had in fact succeeded, and the retry created a second one.

This is a real gap in how we call Stripe for payments. The calls do not carry an idempotency key, so Stripe cannot recognize that the second call is the same attempt as the first one.

The fix for payments is straightforward: use a key made from the invoice id and the attempt number, and keep the same key when the call is repeated after a timeout. I wrote the change for the payment creation in the retry job and a test that simulates a timeout with a charge that succeeded in the background.

The test sends the same key twice to a fake Stripe, which returns the first result, and the job ends with one payment. It passes.

I did not touch the refund endpoint in this change. Refunds are a separate call that the support tool uses, and I noted for later that they should be looked at in the same way.

For the customer, Ines approved the refund of the second charge. I did that in the Stripe dashboard by hand and noted the refund id on the invoice. The customer was told by support.

I shipped the payment change in the afternoon and will watch the retry job for the next few evenings.

summary: Watched the evening retry job after the idempotency key change: 27 retries ran, 22 succeeded, and one timeout produced a repeated call that Stripe answered with the first result.
body:
The evening retry job ran for the first time with the payment idempotency keys. I followed the logs from the start of the run until the end.

It retried 27 failed payments. 22 succeeded and 5 failed again with a decline, which is in line with the earlier evenings, where about 80 percent of retries succeeded.

One call timed out after 30 seconds, as it sometimes does when Stripe is slow. The job repeated the call with the same key, and Stripe returned the result of the first attempt, which was a success. In the database there is one payment for that invoice. Before the change this would have been a second charge, so this was the proof that the fix works in practice.

I looked at the Stripe dashboard for the request log of that call and saw both requests with the same key, the second one marked as a replay of the first.

I also thought about the key rules. Stripe keeps keys for 24 hours, and our retry schedule has attempts that are days apart. Each attempt has its own attempt number in the key, so a later retry is a new request with a new key, as it should be. Within one attempt, the key stays the same.

One case I checked is a payment that is changed between attempts, for example after the customer updates the card. The attempt number is the same if the job repeats after a timeout, but the card is a parameter of the request, and Stripe returns an error when a key is reused with different parameters. I made a test for it and the job handles the error by creating a new attempt number. This case is rare, but a stuck invoice would have been confusing.

I added a line in the daily report for Ines with the number of replayed calls, so that she and I can see how often timeouts happen. Today it was 1 of 27.

The topic is done for payments. Next is the Stripe SDK part: I want to see whether the SDK has a setting for automatic keys, but I will decide that during the next upgrade.

summary: Wrote a plan to reduce the invoice table query times with better indexes first, listing the five slowest queries from the logs and the index each one needs.
body:
The invoices table has about 1.9 million rows and it grows by roughly 60,000 a month. After the measurements from the last weeks, I wanted to see whether indexes can help before partitioning is needed.

I took the slow query log of the last 30 days and listed the five queries that take the most total time. First is the list of invoices by customer, sorted by date, used by the portal. Second is the monthly status report for Ines. Third is the lookup by invoice number. Fourth is the search of open invoices for the retry job. Fifth is the admin tool search by email.

I ran EXPLAIN ANALYZE for each. The customer list uses an index on customer id but sorts the rows afterwards, which takes 180 ms for large customers. A composite index on customer id and created date removes the sort. The status report reads the whole table by design, at 2.4 seconds, and an index will not help, but a monthly summary table could.

The lookup by number is fast already, at 0.4 ms. The open invoices search uses a partial index that was set up in the first version and is fine, at 6 ms. The admin email search joins the customers table, and an index on the lowercase email would turn a sequential scan of 90 ms into 1 ms.

So two indexes are useful now: the customer and date index, and the lowercase email index. Both can be created without locking writes, with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY.

I wrote the plan with the expected size of each index, about 85 MB and 40 MB, and the time to build, which I estimated on a copy of the data at about 30 seconds each.

The partitioning question stays open. The numbers say that today a single table with good indexes is fine, and the table would have to be about five times larger before the queries become a problem. The retention period of ten years means the table only grows, so the decision will come, and I put that into the plan too.

Mara has the plan to read. I will build the indexes after her answer.

summary: Mara approved the index plan with one addition, a check of the index sizes after a week, and I created both indexes on staging first and measured the queries.
body:
Mara read the plan and approved it. She asked only for a check of the index sizes after a week, to compare with my estimates, and I added a reminder for that in the notes.

I created the two indexes on staging with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY on a copy of the production data from last night. The customer and date index took 34 seconds and ended at 88 MB. The lowercase email index took 21 seconds and 41 MB, close to the estimates.

Then I ran the queries again. The customer list for the largest customer fell from 180 ms to 4 ms, and the admin email search from 90 ms to 1.1 ms. The other three queries did not change, as expected.

I also checked that the writes did not slow down, with a loop that inserted 10,000 invoices on staging before and after. The time went from 14.2 seconds to 15.0 seconds, which is about 5 percent more and acceptable.

One detail: the first attempt to create the email index failed with an error because the query uses the lower function and I had written the index on the plain column. I had to drop the invalid index that the failed concurrent build left behind. After that it worked, and the planner uses it.

The production run comes next, in a quiet hour.

summary: Created both indexes in production in the evening, saw the portal invoice list drop from 180 ms to 5 ms for large customers, and checked that the table writes stayed normal.
body:
I created the indexes in production in the evening, when the write load is low. Both used CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, so the invoice creation and the payment updates continued during the build.

The customer and date index took 52 seconds, because the production table is larger than the staging copy, and ended at 91 MB. The lowercase email index took 29 seconds and ended at 43 MB. I checked pg_indexes for the validity flag and both were valid, so no cleanup was necessary this time.

Then I looked at the numbers. The slow query log for the portal invoice list shows the largest customers at 5 ms instead of 180 ms. The admin email search takes 1.3 ms. I ran EXPLAIN on both with real parameters and the planner chose the new indexes in each case.

For the writes, I looked at the insert time of invoices in the application metrics for the hour after the build and compared it to the same hour of the days before. The median was 3.1 ms against 2.9 ms, which is within the normal range of variation. No lock waits were logged.

The retry job and the render job ran in the evening as usual, with no change in their durations. The month-end status report is still 2.4 seconds, as I said it would be. I wrote the idea of a monthly summary table into the notes for when Ines asks for something faster, but she says that she reads the report only once a month, so it is not needed now.

I updated the plan document with the real numbers: build times, sizes, and the query times before and after. The reminder to check the sizes after a week is set.

The partitioning of the table is not needed for now. I added the measurement of the query times to the weekly checks, so that the day when it becomes needed will not come as a surprise.

summary: Checked the index sizes after the first days and found that the customer and date index grew faster than planned, because the month-end run adds many rows at once.
body:
The reminder from the index plan came up earlier than a week, because I wanted to see what the month-end run did to the new indexes. I read the sizes with pg_relation_size before and after the run.

The customer and date index was 91 MB before and 97 MB after, which is a growth of 6 MB in one night. The estimate in the plan was about 5 MB a month, based on 60,000 new rows. The reason is that the month-end run creates most of the monthly invoices in one burst, and the page splits of the index leave it less dense than a normal build.

I looked at the bloat with the pgstattuple extension on staging, after copying the run there. The leaf density of the index fell to 71 percent, against 90 percent right after the build. That is not a problem for the query times, which stayed at 5 ms, but it means the index will be larger than the pure row count suggests.

There are two options. One is to do nothing and accept some growth. The other is to rebuild the index every few months with REINDEX CONCURRENTLY, which is available in our Postgres version and does not block writes. I tried it on staging and it took 40 seconds and brought the density back to 89 percent.

The cost of doing nothing is small today, at a few tens of MB. I decided against a scheduled rebuild for now and put a line into the weekly checks that prints the index sizes and the density. If the density falls below 60 percent, I will rebuild by hand.

I also checked the email index. It grew by 0.3 MB, as expected, since new customers are added slowly and not in bursts.

I wrote the findings in the plan document and told Mara in the notes. She does not need to act. The topic of the invoice table is now at a quiet point: the indexes work, the numbers are watched, and partitioning is a decision for a later time, when the size makes it necessary.

summary: Traced why the customer and date index grew faster than planned and decided to keep it, since the month-end bulk insert is the cause and the read gain is large.
body:
Followed up on the index size check of a few days ago. The customer and date index had grown to about 1.6 times the estimate. I looked at pg_stat_user_indexes and at the bloat estimate to see if the growth was real data or wasted space.

The bloat estimate showed only 6 percent waste, so the size is real data. The month-end run inserts roughly 9,000 invoice and line rows in a few minutes, and each row adds a key to the index. My estimate in the plan had used the average daily insert rate, which hid this peak.

I tried a lower fillfactor on a staging copy to see if page splits were the issue. It made the index larger, not smaller, so I dropped that idea. I also tested a partial index that leaves out voided invoices. It saved only 2 percent, and it would make the portal query planner choose differently for the support view, so I did not pursue it.

The portal invoice list still answers in 5 ms for large customers, and the write time of the month-end insert did not change in a measurable way. I compared the insert step in the last two runs: 41 seconds before the index and 43 seconds after.

My decision was to keep both indexes as they are and to correct the sizing numbers in the plan document. Mara read the note and agreed. I added a line to the plan that says the size should be measured after a month-end run, not in the middle of a month.

What is left: a second size check after the next month-end run, to see whether growth is linear. If the index doubles every few months, the partitioning question will come back sooner than planned.

summary: Wrote a test that fails when an invoice total differs between the PDF, the API and the stored value, after a support case showed a mismatch in a rarely used currency.
body:
A support case this morning asked why a customer in a currency with no minor unit saw a total in the portal that differed by a small amount from the PDF. I reproduced it with an invoice of 14 lines in that currency. The stored total and the API total matched each other, but the PDF template formatted the number with two decimals and divided by 100 again.

The cause was in the template helper. It assumed that every currency has two decimal places. For zero-decimal currencies, Stripe amounts are already in whole units, so the helper made the number 100 times too small in the PDF only. The customer had in fact been charged the right amount.

I wrote a test first. It builds invoices in five currencies, including two zero-decimal ones, renders the PDF text, and compares the total in the PDF to the API value and to the stored value. The test failed for both zero-decimal currencies, as expected.

Then I changed the helper to read the number of decimals from a small currency table instead of assuming two. I used the Intl.NumberFormat resolved options for the check and kept the table as the source for the amounts we send to Stripe. The three-way test passes now for all five currencies.

I ran a query over all invoices from the last year in zero-decimal currencies. Eleven PDFs had the wrong display, all for the same two customers. I did not regenerate them yet. Ines needs to decide if the old PDFs are replaced or if a note goes to the customers.

I wrote the list of the eleven invoices and sent it to Ines with a short explanation. Next step is her decision, then a regeneration script if she wants one.

summary: Ines chose to regenerate the eleven PDFs with a correction note, so I wrote the script and ran it for the two affected customers without changing any stored totals.
body:
Ines answered the question about the eleven PDFs. She wants them regenerated, and the invoice must carry a line that says it replaces an earlier PDF, because the accountants want the trail. The invoice numbers stay the same.

I added an optional correction note field to the invoice template. It prints a line under the number with the text and the original issue date. The data only gets this field when the regeneration script sets it, so normal invoices look the same as before.

The script takes a list of invoice ids and runs in dry mode by default. In dry mode it renders the PDF into a temporary folder and compares the total text to the stored total. All eleven matched. Then I ran it for real, and it stored the new PDFs next to the old ones in the bucket, with the old ones kept under a suffix, since invoices have to be kept for ten years.

The script does not send any email. Ines said she will write to the two customers herself, and I gave her the links to the new files. I checked one of them by opening it, and the number and total were right.

I also added the zero-decimal test to the normal test run so that the template cannot regress. The full suite takes 2 minutes 40 seconds.

summary: Looked at why the Stripe list calls for subscriptions were slow in the nightly sync and found the code fetched one page at a time with a page size of 10.
body:
The nightly subscription sync had grown to 14 minutes. I looked at the logs and saw about 900 calls to the Stripe list endpoint, each returning only 10 objects. The page size was never set, and the default of the SDK call we used is 10.

In the code, a small pagination helper loops over the pages with the starting_after parameter. It was written for the first version of the SDK and does not pass a limit. I set limit to 100, which is the maximum, and the number of calls dropped to about 90.

I ran the sync on staging with the new limit and compared the result with the old one. The same 8,950 subscriptions came back, in the same order, and the diff of the local table was empty. The run took 2 minutes 10 seconds.

I also checked the Stripe rate limits to be sure that 100 per page did not push us near the read limit. The sync now makes fewer calls, so it is safer than before.

One detail: the helper stops when has_more is false, but it also stops when a page comes back empty. I left that as it is. A comment now explains why the helper exists, since the next SDK upgrade might bring a built-in auto pagination that we can use instead.

Shipped it this afternoon. The next night run will be the real test, and I will read its duration tomorrow.

summary: A customer got two dunning emails in one day because the retry job and the webhook both scheduled one, and I fixed it with a unique key on invoice and attempt number.
body:
Support forwarded a complaint from a customer who received two payment failed emails within an hour for the same invoice. I started with the email log, which showed two sends with different job ids. One came from the retry job, the other from the handler of the invoice.payment_failed webhook.

Both paths call the same function that queues the dunning email. The function checks if an email for this invoice was sent in the last 24 hours, but it checks at queue time, not at send time. When the webhook arrived within a few seconds of the retry job, both saw nothing sent yet and both queued.

I reproduced it in a test by calling the function twice in parallel. Two emails were queued, as in production. The check was a plain read followed by an insert, so there was a classic race.

The fix is a unique index on the notice table over invoice id and attempt number, and the queue function now does an insert with ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING and only queues the email when the insert created a row. The check and the claim are now one statement. The parallel test sends exactly one email.

I had to clean the existing data before the index could be created. There were 17 duplicate rows from the past three months. I kept the first of each pair and kept the removed ones in a backup table, in case Ines asks.

The migration ran on staging first and then in production without locking problems, since the table is small. I want to watch the next dunning round for any missing email, because a wrong attempt number would suppress a legitimate one. I will check the counts against Stripe's failed payments tomorrow.

summary: The evening check of dunning emails matched Stripe's failed payments exactly, then I used the quiet time to write the first draft of the notice text for SEPA-style delays.
body:
I ran the comparison I promised after the unique key change. For the last evening round, Stripe had 19 failed payment events, and the notice table had 19 rows with 19 emails sent. No duplicates and no missing ones.

I also looked at the 3 invoices where the attempt number was 2. They each got their second email at the planned interval, so the key does not block later attempts. That was my main worry, and it is now settled.

After that I read through the dunning texts once more. Several customers have asked in support about what happens when a payment is pending and not failed. Today the texts only know two states, paid and failed. Some payment methods, like bank transfers, stay pending for days, and the customer sees nothing in between.

I wrote a draft for a third state called payment pending. It says that we have started the payment, that the bank needs a few days, and that no action is needed. It does not promise a date, since banks differ. I kept the text short, with the invoice number and amount at the top, as in the other templates.

I did not wire it into the code. The webhook handler does not yet map the processing status to a notice, and I want Mara to review the wording first. I put the draft in the repository under a docs folder with a note on which Stripe statuses it would map to.

I also noticed that the handler logs an error for unknown statuses instead of a warning, which makes the alert channel noisy. I changed that log level and added a test. It is a small change, but the channel had three false alarms last week.

Open: Mara's review of the pending text, then the mapping in the handler. I wrote both in the task list so that tomorrow's session starts from it.

summary: Mara reviewed the pending payment text and asked to drop one sentence about timing; I changed it and left the wiring for later.
body:
Mara read the draft of the payment pending notice this morning. She liked the short form but asked to remove the sentence that says that banks usually need two to four days. Her reason is that we do not know the bank, and a customer who waits five days will feel misled.

I removed the sentence and replaced it with a plain line that says we will send another email when the payment is confirmed or when it fails. That is true in both cases, since the handler already sends the receipt and the failure notice.

She also asked that the subject line contain the invoice number, so that customers can find it in their mailbox. I changed the template subject to use it, as the receipt does.

I rendered the text with a test invoice in the preview tool and checked it in plain text and in HTML. Both read well, and the amounts used the right currency format.

The wiring in the handler stays open. Mara said it should wait until the EU customers' payment topic is clearer, since the pending state matters most for them. I noted that in the task list.

summary: Investigated a slow month-end run for one big customer with 40 subscriptions and found that the usage meter queried nebula once per subscription instead of once per customer.
body:
The month-end run took 3 minutes longer than usual, and the log pointed to one customer. That customer has 40 subscriptions for different teams, and the usage step for them took 2 minutes 50 seconds alone.

I read the meter code. For each subscription it calls the nebula usage endpoint with the subscription's workspace id. For most customers that is one call, so it was never visible. For this customer it makes 40 sequential calls, each taking about 4 seconds, since nebula aggregates the counts on request.

I asked in my notes whether nebula supports a batch call. It does: the endpoint accepts a list of workspace ids and returns the counts for each in one response. It was added after our first version and nobody switched the meter to it.

I changed the meter to group the subscriptions of one customer and make a single call per customer. The response is mapped back to the subscriptions by workspace id. I added a guard that fails the step if a requested id is missing in the response, because a silent zero would underbill.

I compared the output on staging with a copy of last month's data. The counts for all 8,900 subscriptions were identical to the old method. The big customer's step now takes 6 seconds.

The batch call has a limit of 50 ids per request, so I split larger groups into chunks of 50. A test covers a group of 120 ids and checks that three calls are made.

I deployed it this morning. The month-end run is in a few weeks, so I will watch the total run time then. I also told Mara about the finding, since two other large customers are near 30 subscriptions, and they would have hit the same slowness soon.

summary: Numbered the open questions about invoice numbers after Ines asked for the numbering to carry the year of issue, and wrote down what it would change.
body:
Ines asked whether the invoice number could include the year, because the accountants sort by it. Today the number is a plain sequence. I looked at what depends on the format.

The number is used in the PDF template, in the email subject, in the portal, in the Stripe metadata and in the CSV report that Ines uses. The database column is text, so a prefix would fit. The sequence itself is a Postgres sequence that never resets.

There are two options. One is a prefix with the year and the same running number, which keeps the sequence unbroken and only changes the display. The other is a sequence that restarts every year, which looks cleaner but needs a counter table with locking and makes the gap explanation harder.

I recommended the first option. It keeps the logic we fixed after the gap problem, where the number is taken at the last step before commit. The second option would bring back the risks we just removed.

I wrote this in a short note with an example of the format and sent it to Ines. I did not change any code. Her answer will decide it, and I expect it after her meeting with the accountants.

summary: Ines accepted the year prefix with the unbroken sequence, so I added it to the display format and kept the stored sequence value unchanged.
body:
Ines replied that the accountants are fine with a year prefix and an unbroken running number, as long as old invoices keep the number they were issued with. That matches my first option.

I added a function that formats the number for display from the issue date and the sequence value. The stored value stays the plain sequence, and the old invoices render exactly as before, since the function only adds the prefix for invoices issued from the change onward. A cutoff on the sequence value decides it, not the date, to avoid time zone edge cases at the turn of the year.

The template, the email subject, the portal and the CSV all call this function now. I searched the code for places that printed the raw number and found two more, in the dunning text and in a log message. Both use the function now.

I wrote tests for an invoice before the cutoff, one after, and one issued at the last minute of the year in UTC. All three give the expected text.

The Stripe metadata still carries the plain sequence value. I left it, so that reconciliation scripts keep working. I noted this in the code with a comment so that nobody wonders about the difference.

summary: Several EU customers wrote to support that they would rather pay by direct debit than by card, and I collected how many and what they said, as input for the payment methods work.
body:
Support has forwarded a growing number of messages from EU customers who ask for direct debit. I went through the support folder for the last three months and counted them: 23 customers, of whom 14 are in Germany and 5 in the Netherlands.

The reasons are mostly the same. Their finance teams do not like company cards for recurring bills, some cards have low limits that make large invoices fail, and a few customers had payments declined by their bank for cross-border charges. Of the 23, 9 had at least one failed payment in the last quarter.

I checked the failure numbers in our data to see if this is only a feeling. For EU customers on cards, the share of invoices that needed a retry was 7.1 percent, against 3.8 percent for the rest. The difference is real, though the sample is small.

I also read what Stripe offers for these countries. Several bank debit methods exist, with different rules for mandates and for how long a payment stays pending. I only took notes and did not start any design. I do not know yet what our webhook handler and the dunning logic would need to change.

I wrote the numbers and the quotes in a note for Mara, without personal data, only the customer ids. I also listed the questions that finance should answer, such as who holds the mandate records and what happens at a failed debit.

Next I will wait for Mara's view on priority. The note stays in the repository docs so that the task list can point to it.

summary: Fixed a slow query in the portal's usage page that scanned the whole usage table, by adding the workspace id to the filter that had been left out.
body:
A customer reported that the usage page of the portal took 9 seconds to load. I found the query in the log with a sequential scan over the usage table, which has about 30 million rows.

The query filtered by date range only and then joined to the subscription. A recent refactor had moved the workspace filter to the application layer, so the database returned all customers' rows for the period and the code threw most away.

I put the workspace id back into the SQL where clause. The existing index on workspace and day is then used, and EXPLAIN shows an index scan with 4,100 rows. The page now loads in 120 ms for the same customer.

I added a test that checks the query plan does not contain a sequential scan on that table, using a small seeded dataset. The test is a bit fragile in theory, but it would have caught this regression.

I deployed the fix in the early afternoon and asked support to confirm with the customer.

summary: Wrote down a short checklist for reading a Stripe webhook failure, because the last three incidents each started with ten minutes of looking in the wrong place.
body:
After the last webhook problems I wrote a checklist in the repository docs so that the next investigation starts faster. It is not code, only a list of steps in the order that worked best.

First, find the event id in the Stripe dashboard and see the delivery attempts and the response code our server gave. Second, search our logs for the event id, which the handler logs at the start. Third, check if the signature step passed, since it logs a separate line. Fourth, see if the event is in our processed events table, which tells if the handler finished.

I added the two SQL queries I always type and the command to replay an event from the Stripe CLI against staging. I also noted that the handler answers 200 for unknown event types on purpose, so that Stripe does not retry them.

Mara read it and added a line about checking the time of the event against our deploys. I will keep the file short and update it when something new comes up.

summary: Wrote tests for the coupon expiry edge case where a coupon ends in the middle of a billing period, after a customer asked why the discount stopped early.
body:
A customer asked why their discount was missing on the second half of a long invoice. The coupon had a redeem-by date in the middle of the billing period, and I checked how our code applies it.

The coupon logic looks at the coupon end date when the invoice is created and applies the discount to all lines or to none. The customer's invoice was created after the end date, so no discount. By the rules we wrote down, the coupon should apply to usage inside its validity, and the customer's usage before the end date should have been discounted.

I wrote three tests: a coupon ending before the period, one ending inside it, and one ending after it. The middle case fails today, as it gets no discount at all.

I did not fix it yet, because the correct behavior needs a decision. A proration by days is one way and applying it by usage timestamps is another, and they give different cents. I wrote both options with an example for Ines and left the test marked as pending.

summary: Ines chose the usage timestamp approach for coupons that end inside a period, and I implemented it with per-line discount windows and a test for each edge.
body:
Ines picked the second option for the coupon case: the discount applies to the usage that falls inside the coupon's validity, using the usage timestamps. Her reason is that it is the easiest to explain to a customer and to the accountants.

The usage meter returns daily counts, so a day is the smallest unit. I defined that a day counts as inside the validity if its start in UTC is before the coupon end. That is stated in the code and in the invoice text, which now shows the end date of the coupon on the discount line.

I changed the invoice builder to split a usage line into two lines when a coupon ends inside the period: one discounted and one at full price. Each line carries its own quantity and amount. The percentage and fixed amount coupons both work this way, but a fixed amount is applied only once, to the first line, to avoid double discounts.

The pending test now passes, and I added tests for the fixed amount coupon, for a coupon that starts inside the period, and for a coupon that starts and ends inside the same period. The last one gave a wrong result at first, with an overlap on one day, and I fixed the boundary comparison.

I ran the new builder against the last three months of invoices with coupons, 212 invoices, and compared totals. 207 were identical. Five differed, all of them with coupons ending inside the period, and the differences were between 1 and 14 euros in the customers' favor, since the old code gave no discount at all.

That is a point to discuss. The five invoices were already issued and paid. I did not touch them and listed them for Ines so that she can decide if a credit note is wanted.

The new builder is merged and runs from the next invoice created. I will check the next batch of coupon invoices by hand.

summary: Checked the five affected invoices with the new coupon builder and prepared the credit note data for Ines, with totals that match the difference to the cent.
body:
Late in the day I went back to the five invoices from this morning's comparison. Ines had answered that she wants credit notes for them, since the customers were charged more than the rules say.

I calculated each credit with the new builder. For every invoice I took the new total, subtracted it from the paid total, and wrote the result in a table with the invoice number, customer, currency and amount. The five credits are 1.20, 3.75, 6.00, 9.10 and 14.00 in euros.

To be sure, I recomputed by hand two of them from the usage rows. The daily counts before the coupon end, times the unit price, times the discount percentage, gave the same cents. I also checked that rounding happens on each line, as the invoices do today.

The credit notes themselves are created by the existing endpoint that Ines uses in the admin. I did not want to create money movements from a script without her check. So I produced a CSV with the five rows and a column with the reason text: discount applied to usage before coupon end.

I also asked myself whether other invoices could be affected that did not have coupons in the last three months. The coupon feature is older than that. I ran the comparison for the six months before and found 9 more invoices with a difference, 3 of them with the same cause and 6 where the coupon ended exactly at midnight of the period start. The 6 are fine, since the discount rightly does not apply.

The 3 extra invoices were added to the CSV, so there are 8 rows now. I sent the file to Ines with the explanation of both groups.

I also wrote a short note in the code near the builder about the day boundary rule, with a link to this reasoning. When Ines answers, the next step is the credit notes and a closing note in the task list.

summary: Replied to a customer who asked why a VAT number change did not alter an issued invoice, and documented the rule that issued invoices stay unchanged.
body:
A customer added their VAT number a week after the invoice was issued and asked us to change it to reverse charge. Support asked me what we can do.

I checked the rules we implemented. An issued invoice cannot be edited, because the numbers must stay as they were. The way to fix it is a credit note for the whole invoice and a new invoice with the right tax treatment. That is also what the accountants expect.

I looked at whether the admin tool supports this in one step. It does not. Ines has to create the credit note and the new invoice separately, and the new one gets a new number. I wrote the steps for support, with the warning that the VAT number must pass the validation before the new invoice is made.

I added the same text to the support docs under tax questions, so the next case does not need me.

summary: Started the Stripe SDK upgrade from v13 to v14 by reading the changelog and fixing the type errors, with the three deprecated calls listed earlier as the guide.
body:
I began the upgrade to the next major version of the Stripe SDK, using the list of three deprecated calls that I wrote some time ago. I created the upgrade in the main checkout and ran the TypeScript compiler first.

The compiler showed 11 errors in 6 files. Seven came from a changed type for the expanded fields: where we expand a customer on an invoice, the type is now a union of a string and an object, and our code assumed the object. I added a small helper that throws a clear error if the value is a plain id when we expected an expanded object.

Two errors were about the API version string. The SDK pins a version, and I had to decide whether to move our account's version too. I kept the account version as it is and set the pinned version in the client, so that the webhook payloads do not change under us. That is the safer order.

The last two errors came from a renamed parameter in the list call for balance transactions, which our daily reconciliation uses. I fixed both and read the changelog entry to see if the behavior changed. It did not.

The unit tests passed after the type fixes, 412 of 412. The integration tests in Stripe test mode are slower, and 2 of them failed. One failure was a changed error message text that a test compared as a string, which I loosened to check the error code instead. The other was a real problem: the payment retry test relied on a field that is now optional.

I fixed that code to handle a missing field and added a test for it. Then all integration tests passed, 58 of 58.

I did not deploy. The next step is a staging run with the webhook replay, since the handler reads the event objects, and the types of the events changed too. I will do that tomorrow and ask Mara to review the diff.

summary: Replayed the recorded webhook payloads against the upgraded SDK on staging and found that one event type parsed differently, which I fixed before asking Mara to review.
body:
Today's work was the staging run of the v14 upgrade. I started with the webhook replay, since the handler reads Stripe event objects and the upgrade changed some of their types.

I used the set of recorded payloads from the test account, 140 events of 22 types. The handler processed 139 correctly. One event, a charge refunded event, failed with a type error at runtime, because the refunds list on the charge is no longer included by default in the new version and the handler read from it.

I looked at the handler. It used the list to find the latest refund for the receipt email. With the new version, the field is missing unless it is expanded. Webhook payloads are fixed by the API version, so I checked which version the payloads have. They carry our account version, which I did not change, so the payload itself was the same as before. The error came from the SDK typing and a parsing step, not from the payload.

To be careful I fetched the refund by id with an explicit call, instead of reading the embedded list. It costs one extra API call per refund event, which is rare, and it does not depend on the shape of the embedded data. I added a test with the recorded payload.

Then I ran the nightly jobs on staging: the subscription sync, the card expiry reminder in dry mode, the reconciliation and the retry job. They all finished, and the sync result was identical to production for the 8,950 subscriptions.

I checked the logs for new deprecation warnings. There was one for a method that the next major version will remove. I wrote it in the upgrade note so that the following upgrade does not start from zero.

Mara reviewed the diff in the afternoon. She had two comments: the helper for expanded fields should log the object type in its error, and the pinned API version should be a named constant in one file. I made both changes.

The deployment is planned for tomorrow morning, when the load is low, with a watch on the webhook error rate for an hour.

summary: Deployed the Stripe SDK v14 upgrade in the morning and watched the webhook error rate and payment retries for the first hours without any new errors.
body:
I deployed the v14 upgrade at the start of the working day, when the traffic is low. Before that, I wrote down the current webhook error rate, which is 0.3 percent, nearly all from unknown event types, and the retry success rate of the last week, 81 percent.

After the deploy, I watched the logs for an hour. 212 webhook events came in, and all of them were answered with 200. The handler logged no errors, and the signature step passed each time.

The refund event path with the explicit fetch ran 3 times, and each receipt had the right amount. I opened one of the emails in the Postmark activity view to be sure about the text.

In the late morning the retry job ran with 14 retries, of which 11 succeeded. That is 79 percent, close to the usual rate, and the three failures were real declines with decline codes that the dunning mapping knows.

I also checked the daily reconciliation after its run. The sum of paid invoices and the balance transactions matched without a difference, which is a good sign that the changed list call works.

One small surprise was a new warning in the startup log about an old option in the client config, which the SDK now ignores. I removed the option and shipped that as a separate commit.

The upgrade is done. The remaining item from my notes is the pagination helper, which the new SDK might replace with a built-in auto paging feature, but I decided to leave it for the later upgrades, since the helper works and a change now would mix two topics.

summary: Looked into receipts that Postmark-less customers did not get at all because their stored email was empty, and added a check at signup plus a report for support.
body:
Support noticed that some customers never get any receipt. I looked at the contacts table and found 31 active customers with no billing email stored. All of them were created by the sales team through the admin tool, which did not require the field.

The receipt job skipped these customers silently. It logged a debug line, which nobody reads. So the invoices were issued and paid, but the customers had no mail at all. Some of them had written to support asking for their invoices, which is how the problem showed.

I made three changes. First, the admin tool now requires a billing email and validates the format. Second, the receipt job logs a warning with the customer id and increments a counter when it skips a customer for this reason. Third, I wrote a report for support that lists the active customers without a billing email, so that they can ask the customers.

For the 31 customers I checked whether another contact in the account has an email. For 19 of them the account owner has an address, which I put in a file for support to confirm before use. We should not copy the address without asking, since it might not be meant for billing.

I also looked back to see how many receipts were lost. In the last 3 months it was 44 invoices. They are still available in the portal, but the customers did not know. I prepared a list of the invoices, so that Ines or support can send them by hand if they want.

I wrote tests for the validation and for the skip warning. The tests passed, and the change is merged.

The open point is the old data. Support will fill in the missing addresses over the next week. After that I will make the database column not null, but only when the report is empty, since the migration would fail otherwise.

I added a line to the task list to run the report again in a week and to do the migration then.

summary: Answered Mara's question about how long failed payment retries take to resolve by measuring the time from first failure to paid for the last quarter.
body:
Mara asked how long it takes until a failed payment is resolved, because she wants to judge if the retry schedule is too long. I wrote a query over the last quarter that joins the first failed attempt of each invoice with its paid time.

Of 640 invoices with at least one failure, 71 percent were paid within 3 days, 12 percent after 4 to 7 days, and 5 percent later. The rest, 12 percent, were never paid and ended as uncollectible. The median is 1 day, since many cases are expired cards or temporary bank problems that the first retry solves.

I also split by the payment attempt that finally worked. The first retry resolves 58 percent of the cases, the second 19 percent and the third only 4 percent. So the third retry has little value in our data, though it is also cheap.

I told Mara my reading: the schedule is not too long, and the gain would come from earlier contact with the customer rather than from changing the retry days. The card expiry reminder already helps there. I put the query and numbers in the docs for later use.

summary: Started the review of how invoice totals are summed across lines, after Ines found a few invoices that were one cent off, and wrote a script that lists them with the line values.
body:
Ines wrote that in her monthly sample she found invoices where the total was 1 cent different from what her spreadsheet gives for the sum of the lines. I started to look at it today, without changing any logic yet.

First I wrote a script that recomputes the sum of the line amounts for every invoice of the last two months and compares it with the stored total. Out of about 18,000 invoices, 37 had a difference, and each differed by exactly 1 cent.

All 37 had something in common: they are in the invoices with a percentage tax. The tax is computed on the net sum of the invoice, then rounded once. Ines's spreadsheet computes tax per line and rounds each line, then sums. The two ways give different cents in some cases.

I picked three invoices and calculated by hand. For one with 9 lines at a 19 percent tax rate, per-line rounding gave 0.01 more than the single rounding. So both numbers are defensible in themselves, but they are not the same.

I also checked the lines themselves. The line amounts use the unit price times the quantity, rounded when stored, and the quantity can be fractional for prorated items. That is a second place where rounding happens, and I wondered if it adds to the difference. For the 37 invoices, the line amounts were consistent between the database and the PDF, so the difference comes from the tax step.

I wrote the results into a table with the invoice number, the sum of the lines, the tax by our method, the tax by the per-line method and the difference. I added a column for the currency, since the rounding is the same in all of them but Ines might want to filter.

Nothing is changed in production. I need to know from Ines and the accountants which method is the rule, because the choice affects every invoice from now on and the explanation for past ones.

I sent the table to Ines with a short note on the two methods and a request for a decision. Meanwhile, I will look at where in the code the tax and the rounding steps are, so that a change would be small when the decision comes.

summary: Found the invoices that were one cent off came from summing already rounded line amounts with tax computed per line, and listed the 14 affected ones with both totals.
body:
I continued from the script of this morning that lists invoices whose stored total differs from a recomputed one. Of the last six months of invoices, 14 differed by exactly one cent, all with three or more lines and a VAT rate above zero.

The cause is the order of operations. Each line gets its tax rounded to cents, and the invoice total then adds the rounded tax values, while the Stripe invoice and the PDF footer compute tax on the net sum. The two methods agree most of the time and differ when several lines end on a half cent.

I wrote down the three possible fixes: round once at the invoice level, round each line and sum the lines, or keep the current method and show the rounding line. I did not choose yet, because that choice belongs to the accountants. The script now prints for each invoice the line values, the tax per line, and the total by each method, so Ines can see the cases herself.

I also checked that none of the 14 invoices has been paid with a wrong amount: the charge in Stripe equals the stored total in every case, so customers paid what the invoice says. Only the PDF footer differs in four of them.

I added a column for the invoice currency to the output, because two of the cases were in a currency with no decimals and I wanted to rule them out. They are not related.

Next I send Ines the list and ask which method the accountants want. I change no code before that answer.

summary: Sent Ines the list of 14 one-cent invoices with three rounding methods side by side, and she will ask the accountants which rule they follow.
body:
In the evening I turned the output of the totals script into a small sheet with one row per invoice. The columns show the line amounts, the tax per line, and the total under each of the three methods.

I added a short note on top that explains the difference in plain words. Ines does not need the code, she needs to see that method A gives the stored total, method B gives the Stripe total, and method C changes 9 of the 14 cases.

While writing it I noticed that the cases cluster around prices like 12.50 and 33.33 with a 19 percent rate. That is useful for the accountants, since they can try a few examples by hand.

I did not touch the code or the stored totals. Ines answered that she will ask the accountants tomorrow and come back with a rule. Meanwhile I leave the script in the repository under scripts, with a comment on what it reads and that it only reads.

summary: Asked the accountants' question through Ines and in the meantime wrote a script that applies each of three rounding rules to the 14 one-cent invoices and shows the totals side by side.
body:
Ines asked yesterday which rounding rule the accountants follow, and until she has the answer I did not want to touch the code. So I prepared the comparison that she can show them. The script reads the 14 invoices from the list and recomputes each total from the stored line values. It does this three times, once for each rule: round each line and sum the rounded lines, sum the raw lines and round once at the end, and round the tax per line and the net sum separately.

The result is easy to read. The first rule gives a total that always equals the sum of the amounts printed on the PDF. The second rule matches the Stripe amount on 11 of the 14 invoices. The third rule matches the current stored total on all 14, which is the reason the problem exists: it computes tax per line from already rounded net amounts and then rounds again.

I also checked how the three rules behave on lines with a half cent. Out of 212 lines in the 14 invoices, 19 end exactly on a half cent, and those lines are where the rules differ. Because of that, the choice also matters for the future, not only for the 14 old invoices. One invoice with 31 lines and a 19 percent VAT rate shows the biggest spread, with 3 cents between the highest and the lowest total.

The output is a plain table with the invoice number, the customer, the three totals, and the amount Stripe charged. I added a column that marks where the PDF total and the charged amount differ, since Ines will be asked about the customer's payment too. Two of the 14 customers paid by card, so for them Stripe holds a different amount than the PDF shows, and I noted that a credit note or a small refund could follow depending on the answer.

Nothing was changed in the invoice code or in the database. The script only reads, and I ran it against a copy of the data from staging first, then against production with a read-only role. Next step: wait for Ines and the accountants, then implement the chosen rule and update the rounding tests that fix the old behaviour.

summary: Reviewed the Stripe error handling after the v14 upgrade and found that card errors and rate limit errors were both logged as generic failures, so I split them.
body:
While reading the logs of the last week I saw that many payment failures show only the text payment_failed, with no reason. The cause is in the wrapper around the Stripe calls: it catches any error and logs its message, but the v14 SDK has separate error classes for card errors, rate limits and connection problems.

I changed the handler to look at the error type. A card error now logs the decline code and is handed to the dunning logic as before. A rate limit error is logged as a warning with the retry-after value. A connection error is marked as retryable.

I checked the rate limit case with a small script that sends 120 list calls in a burst on the test account. Stripe answered with 429 after about 100 calls, and the new log line showed it correctly.

The dunning code expected one error shape, so I added three tests, one per class. One old test relied on the generic message text, and I changed it to check the class.

The change is small, 60 lines. Mara reviewed it in the afternoon and asked for the decline code to be kept in a separate field of the log, not inside the message, so we can count by code. I did that and merged it.

Next week I count the decline codes from the logs for a month, to see which ones dominate.

summary: Counted the decline codes of the last month and found that insufficient_funds is 41 percent of all failed card payments.
body:
With the new log field I could finally count the declines. Of 318 failed card payments in the last month, 130 were insufficient_funds.

The next ones were expired_card with 52, generic_decline with 49, and card_declined with 31. The rest was spread over small codes.

The result matters for the dunning emails. The text for an expired card tells the customer to update the card, which fits, but insufficient_funds may need a different text, since a retry in a few days often works.

I checked the retry success: 58 percent of the insufficient_funds payments were paid after a retry, against 12 percent for the expired cards. I wrote the numbers in the journal for Mara and proposed to split the dunning text by code later.

summary: Ines brought the accountants' answer on totals: round each line to cents and sum the lines, so the invoice total is always the sum of what the PDF shows.
body:
Ines wrote that the accountants prefer a total that a reader can check by adding the printed lines. That is method B from my sheet, round each line and sum.

It differs from the Stripe computation in 9 of the 14 cases, so the amount we charge can differ from the one Stripe computes from its own tax logic. I asked how we send the amounts to Stripe, and I confirmed in the code that we send our own total as the amount of the invoice items, not letting Stripe compute tax.

That means the change stays on our side and we do not depend on Stripe's tax setting. I wrote this down as a reason for the choice.

One open point is the rounding mode of the half cent itself: Ines said the accountants will tell us in a separate answer, since they want to check the rule for half cents. I will wait for this before I change the code. The test file from last week will show the effect.

summary: Looked into why the invoice PDF renderer takes 9 seconds for an invoice with 400 lines and found that every line row triggered its own layout pass in the headless browser.
body:
A customer with many small usage lines complained that the PDF for the month took too long to appear in the portal. I took the largest invoice of the last quarter, 412 lines, and rendered it locally. It took 9.2 seconds, against 1.1 seconds for an invoice of 20 lines.

First I measured where the time goes. The data load is 80 ms and the HTML template is built in 150 ms. The remaining 8.9 seconds are in the browser page, between the load of the content and the print call.

The template puts each line in its own table row with a small script that measures the description cell and shrinks the font if the text is too long. That script reads the element width after each row is added, which forces a layout pass each time. With 412 rows this is 412 full layouts of a growing table.

I changed the script to read all widths first and write the font sizes after, so the browser lays out the table twice and not 412 times. The render time went to 3.4 seconds.

That is better but still slow. The page also loads a web font from a local file and a logo as a large PNG. I resized the logo from 1800 pixels to 360, which saved 0.3 seconds, and the font load is cheap.

The remaining time is mostly the print step for a long table, with the page break logic. I tried turning off the repeat of the table header on each page, which took 3.4 down to 2.6 seconds, but the header on each page is wanted by finance, so I left it.

I compared the output of the old and the new render page by page for the 412 line invoice and for five others. The text and totals were identical, only the font size of 7 long descriptions differed by half a point, because the measure is now taken before the font change of the earlier rows. I accept this.

I have not deployed it. Tomorrow I run the comparison on 50 real invoices and then ask Mara for a review.

summary: Compared 50 real invoices between the old and the batched-layout PDF renderer and found identical text on all of them and a median speed-up of 2.6 times.
body:
I rendered 50 invoices of the last quarter with both versions, chosen by line count: 10 small, 20 medium, 15 large and the 5 largest.

The extracted text was equal for 49. One invoice differed, because a description with a very long word without spaces broke on another place. I looked at both PDFs and the new break is actually cleaner, but it is a change, so I noted it for Ines.

The timings: small invoices 1.0 against 0.9 seconds, medium 2.1 against 1.1, large 5.8 against 2.4, and the five largest from 8.5 to 11 seconds before, to 3.1 to 3.6 after. The median ratio is 2.6 times.

I checked memory too, since the browser holds the whole table. The peak for the 412 line invoice was 410 MB before and 380 MB after, so no worse.

Mara reviewed the change in the evening and asked for one thing: a test that renders a 300 line invoice and fails if it takes longer than 8 seconds, as a guard against a return of the slowness. I wrote it with a wide limit, since CI machines are slow, and marked it so that it does not run in the fast unit test group.

summary: Deployed the faster PDF layout in the evening and watched the first generated invoices; render times for long invoices fell from about 8 seconds to under 4.
body:
I deployed the batched layout change at the quiet time after the evening jobs.

The job runner renders the PDFs for new invoices in the background, so I watched the queue. In the first hour 31 PDFs were made, none failed, and the longest one, 188 lines, took 2.9 seconds.

I also asked the portal for the PDF of an old large invoice, which is rendered on request. It came after 3.3 seconds.

I compared the page counts of ten of the new PDFs with the stored ones from the old renderer, and all counts were equal. The stored totals were unchanged, since the change only touches layout.

I checked the error log for browser crashes and timeouts, and there were none. The browser pool of 2 processes was not full at any time.

I will look again tomorrow morning, when the month-end run for the big customers starts, since that is the real test of the change.

summary: The month-end run produced 1,240 PDFs without a failure and the longest took 3.8 seconds, so the layout change holds under real load.
body:
This morning I looked at the numbers of the month-end run. The run made 1,240 invoices and PDFs, and the job queue was empty after 26 minutes, where last month it took 41 minutes.

No PDF failed and no job was retried. The longest render was a 390 line invoice with 3.8 seconds.

I also checked the memory of the browser pool during the run. The peak was 1.1 GB for the two processes, a bit lower than last month's 1.3 GB.

For Ines I made a short check that the totals on the PDFs match the stored totals for all 1,240, and they do, with the test from before running over the whole set. The 14 off-by-one invoices are not in this month, since the cases had to do with half cents and none came up.

I think the topic is finished for now. The rest of the render time is in the print step, and a bigger change would be a different renderer, which I do not want to start without a reason. I leave a note in the journal that the next slowness will probably need that.

summary: Implemented the line-sum total rule from the accountants and updated the 22 rounding tests; nine expected values changed, all by one cent as predicted.
body:
Ines brought the answer on the half cent: the accountants want it handled in the same way for each line, with the same rule as the line amounts. For the moment I implemented the line-sum rule with the current rounding of the half cent and kept the mode in a single function, so it can change in one place.

The code change is in the invoice builder. Before, tax was computed per line, rounded, and then the total was built from the net sum plus the tax sum. Now each line gets net and tax rounded, the line total is their sum, and the invoice total is the sum of the line totals.

I ran the test file from three weeks ago. Nine of 22 examples failed, and each failed by exactly one cent in the direction that my sheet had shown. I changed those nine numbers and checked each by hand.

The comparison test between PDF, API and stored value passes. The amount sent to Stripe comes from the same function, so the charge matches the invoice.

The change only applies to invoices created from now on. Issued invoices stay as they are, in line with the rule that I documented after the VAT number question. For the 14 old invoices Ines decides if she wants credit notes of one cent, and I think she will not.

Mara reviewed it and asked me to add the case of a negative line, such as a credit, since rounding of negative halves goes the other way in some languages. I added three examples, and they pass.

What is left is the half cent mode, which is waiting for the accountants.

summary: Found that the nightly Stripe sync created a duplicate customer record for two EU companies because their VAT number was written once with spaces and once without.
body:
Ines asked why two companies appear twice in the customer export. I looked at the records. Both pairs had the same Stripe customer id but two rows in our table, with the VAT numbers DE 123 456 789 and DE123456789.

The sync matches on the VAT number when the Stripe id is missing, and the first row had been created before the Stripe id was stored. The VAT number comparison was a plain string comparison, so the spaced and the unspaced version were seen as different.

I checked how many customers are affected with a query that normalizes the numbers: remove spaces, dots and dashes, and upper-case the letters. Two pairs came out, no more, and in both cases the older row has no invoices.

Before I fixed anything I looked at the references. The older rows have no subscriptions and no usage. The invoice rows all point to the newer rows. So the merge is a delete of two empty rows.

I wrote the normalization as a small function and used it in the sync and in the signup form. I also stored the normalized number in a new column, with a unique index that ignores empty values, so the problem cannot come back silently.

The migration is in two steps. First the column and the filling, then the unique index after the two old rows are deleted. Running the first step on staging gave 3 conflicts and not 2, since a test customer had the same number as a real one. I removed the test row on staging.

The tests check six formats of the VAT number, including lower case and a number with a country prefix and dots. One more case is for numbers of countries where the format has letters in the middle.

I ran the migration in production in the morning and deleted the two old rows by their ids, after I saved them to a file. The unique index was created without a problem, and the sync of today found no duplicates.

I told Ines that the two pairs are cleaned up. The signup form now also strips the spaces before it checks the number against the validation service, which had rejected a few spaced numbers last month.

summary: Read the Stripe v14 changelog entry on pagination again and found that our manual page loop breaks when a list ends exactly on a page boundary.
body:
After the VAT cleanup I looked at the nightly sync again, since it lists subscriptions page by page with a manual loop and the page size of 100 that I set a month ago.

The loop stops when a page has fewer items than the page size. I checked how Stripe's list answers carry a has_more flag, and the loop ignores it. When the number of items is an exact multiple of 100, the last page is full and the loop asks for one more page, which is empty. That works but costs a call. The other case is worse: a page with fewer items than the size, while has_more is true, can happen when objects are deleted during the listing.

I do not think this happened in production, but the logic is wrong. I changed the loop to use the has_more flag and the id of the last item as starting_after.

To test it, I wrote a fake list function that returns pages of configurable length, with a case of a short page that still has more. The old loop fails that case and the new one passes.

There are two copies of the loop, one in the subscription sync and one in the invoice import. I moved both to one helper in src/stripe/list.ts, so there is a single place for it. This helper is a shim for the old SDK's missing auto-pagination for our use, and I noted that in a comment.
