Mara has to review it, since the sync is critical. I ran the sync on staging with the new helper and the counts matched the old run: 2,914 subscriptions both times.

summary: Mara reviewed the pagination helper, asked for a limit on the number of pages as a safeguard, and I added it with a logged warning.
body:
Mara read the helper and liked that there is one copy now. Her concern was an endless loop: if Stripe ever returned has_more as true with the same last id, the sync would run forever and use up the rate limit.

I added a maximum of 500 pages, which at 100 per page is 50,000 objects, much more than we have. When the limit is reached the helper throws an error that names the endpoint and the last id, and the sync job logs it as failed and not as a success.

I also added a check that the last id changes from page to page. If two pages end with the same id, the helper stops with an error too.

Two tests cover these cases with the fake list function: one that always returns has_more true with the same page, and one that returns 501 pages.

After the change Mara approved it. I deployed it before noon and ran the sync by hand once. It took 38 seconds for 2,914 subscriptions, with 30 calls.

The old version needed 292 calls at page size 10 a month ago, so the sync is much lighter on the rate limit now.

Nothing else is open for the sync, only the nightly check of the counts, which I look at tomorrow.

summary: Wrote an answer for support on why a German customer saw a SEPA-like pending status for a card payment, which turned out to be Stripe's processing state for 3D Secure.
body:
Support forwarded a question from a customer who saw the word pending next to a paid invoice in the portal for about two minutes, and was afraid that the payment had not worked.

I looked at the events for the payment. The payment intent went from requires_action to processing and then to succeeded, with 94 seconds between the first and the last event. The customer did a 3D Secure check with the bank, and the bank's answer took some time.

Our portal shows pending for the intent status processing. For cards that is a short state, and for the debit payments we expect later it will be a long one. The word is correct, but it alarms people.

I checked how often it happens. In the last month 211 card payments went through processing, and 187 of them lasted less than 3 minutes. The other 24 were up to 20 minutes, mostly cards of one bank.

I wrote a reply for support that explains the state in two sentences and says that the invoice becomes paid by itself and that no second payment is needed.

I also looked at the portal text. I did not change it, but I wrote a proposal: show Payment is being confirmed for card payments in processing, and keep pending for the debit ones. It costs a small change in the status mapping.

I asked Mara if the change should be done now or together with the work for direct debit. She said she wants to look at it together with that work, so I put the proposal in the notes for it.

Support sent the reply to the customer, who answered that all is clear.

The numbers on processing times are in the notes as well, with the query.

summary: Checked the failed webhook deliveries of the last two days and found only retries of an already handled event, no lost events.
body:
Stripe's dashboard showed 6 failed deliveries and I wanted to know if any event was lost. All six were deliveries of invoice.finalized that our handler had answered with a timeout of 10 seconds during a slow database moment.

Stripe retried them, and each was handled on the second try. Our table of handled event ids shows each event once, so the handling is correct.

The slow moment fits the month-end run. I did nothing but write the result down for the checklist.

summary: Planned the work to move the heavy webhook work to the job queue so the handler answers Stripe within a second and the slow database moments cannot cause timeouts.
body:
The six timeouts of two days ago show a weakness: our handler checks the signature, writes the event, and then does the full work (update invoice, send email, schedule dunning) before it answers. When the database is slow, Stripe sees a timeout and retries, and we depend on the event table to avoid double work.

I wrote down a plan. The handler should check the signature, insert the event id and payload into a table with a unique key, put a job in pg-boss, and answer 200. The job does the real work.

The pieces: a webhook_events table with columns for id, type, payload, status and received time; a job named process-stripe-event; and a worker that marks the event as done or failed. A unique key on the event id means a repeat insert is ignored and still answered with 200.

I listed the risks. Order of events can change, since jobs run in parallel, for instance invoice.paid before invoice.finalized for the same invoice. I checked the current handlers, and three of them assume an order. For these the worker should fetch the object from Stripe and not trust the payload, or use a lock per invoice id.

The second risk is a job that fails forever. I plan 5 attempts with growing delays, then status failed and an alert in the channel we use for the other jobs.

I also looked at the volume: about 9,000 events in the last month, peaks of 40 per minute at month end. The queue handles that easily.

The plan has four steps: the table and the insert, the worker with the old logic moved over, the lock per invoice, and the switch with a flag so we can go back to the old way.

I sent the plan to Mara. She agreed with the flag and asked me to start with the three event types that have no order problem, and to do the others later.

summary: Built the webhook events table and the queued processing for the first three event types behind a flag, and replayed 400 recorded events on staging without a difference in the result.
body:
I started the plan with Mara's order. The migration adds webhook_events with a unique key on the Stripe event id and an index on status.

The handler has a new path behind the flag webhook_queue. When the flag is on and the event type is in the list of the first three (customer.updated, payment_method.attached, charge.refunded), it does this: check the signature, insert the row, enqueue process-stripe-event, answer 200. All other types use the old way, even with the flag on.

The worker reads the row, calls the same handler function as before, and sets the status. I did not copy the logic, I moved the three handler functions into a module that both paths call. That kept the diff small and avoids two versions.

One thing I had to fix was the signature check. It needs the raw body, and the new path stored the parsed payload in the table. That is fine, since the signature is checked before, but I keep the raw text in the row too, for a later replay.

For the test I replayed 400 recorded events of those types on staging, once with the flag off and once on. I compared the database state after both runs with a query over customers, payment methods and refunds. The two states were equal.

I also tested the failure path. I made the handler of customer.updated throw, and the job retried 5 times with the delays and then set failed, and the alert came. After I removed the error, I re-queued the row by hand with a small script and it finished.

A duplicate delivery of the same event inserted nothing and answered 200, as planned.

The time for the handler to answer fell from a median of 120 ms to 18 ms.

I have not switched the flag in production. Tomorrow I ask Mara for the review, and the switch on for the three types follows after.

summary: Switched on the queued webhook path in production for three event types, watched it through the afternoon, and found one stuck job caused by a missing index on the status column.
body:
Mara had reviewed the change with two small remarks on names, which I fixed. After lunch I turned the flag webhook_queue on in production for the three event types.

For the first hour I looked at three numbers: the webhook answer time, the status counts in the table, and the queue length. The answer time was 15 to 25 ms. All rows went to done within 2 seconds, and the queue was empty most of the time.

At about the end of the second hour one job had stayed in the state active for 7 minutes. The row was in the status received, and the worker log had no error. I looked at the worker query that picks up stale rows and saw that it scans the table by status without a usable index. The index I wrote in the migration was on status alone, but the query also sorts by received time, and the planner chose a sequential scan, since the table was small then and a scan is cheap.

That was not the cause of the stuck job, only a point to watch. The real cause was in the job: the event was charge.refunded for a refund that was created through our API a second earlier, and the handler waited for a database lock that the refund request still held. After the request finished, the lock was released, but the job had a timeout of 30 seconds only for the fetch and none for the lock.

I set a lock timeout of 5 seconds in the worker transaction, so the job fails fast and retries. With the delays of the retry, it would have succeeded at the second attempt after 10 seconds.

I re-queued the stuck job by hand and it was done at once. I also changed the index to cover status and received time together, and created it concurrently, so the table was not blocked.

I then watched another hour. 112 events of the three types came in, all were done, and the longest time from receipt to done was 3 seconds. The lock timeout fired once and the retry worked.

I wrote the sequence of the stuck job down for the next steps, because the other event types touch the same invoice rows and will have the same problem. The lock per invoice that I planned has to take care of this.

summary: Added an advisory lock per invoice to the queued webhook worker so events for the same invoice run one after the other, and tested the order problem with shuffled events.
body:
The next step of the webhook plan was the order of events for one invoice. I used a Postgres advisory lock taken in the worker transaction, with a key made from the hash of the invoice id. Events for the same invoice wait for each other, and events for different invoices still run in parallel.

The lock is taken with the transaction variant, so it is released at commit or rollback, and a crashed worker cannot hold it. The wait is limited by the lock timeout from the last entry, and a job that cannot get the lock fails and retries with its delay.

For the test I took the recorded events of 60 invoices that went through the full path of created, finalized, payment_failed and paid. I shuffled the order in each group 20 times and enqueued all of them at once with 4 workers. The final state of every invoice was paid, as in the original order.

But the shuffle showed one real problem: invoice.paid arriving before invoice.finalized leaves the local status at draft for a moment, and then finalized overwrites it with open. The worker should not move a status backward. I added a rank for the statuses and the update only runs when the new rank is higher. With this, all 1,200 shuffled runs ended in the correct state.

I added the rule as a unit test with the six status pairs, and the shuffle test stays in the suite with a fixed seed.

The invoice event types can now move to the queue. I put them behind the same flag with a list in the config, and deploy only the list tomorrow.

summary: Moved the invoice event types to the queued webhook path in the morning and saw median handler time stay at 20 ms with every event done within 4 seconds.
body:
I added invoice.finalized, invoice.paid and invoice.payment_failed to the list of types that use the queue and deployed it early, before the busy part of the day.

In the first two hours 186 invoice events arrived. The handler answered in 17 to 30 ms, and the longest time from receipt to done was 3.9 seconds, when a payment_failed event waited for the lock of an invoice that was just being paid.

The status rank rule blocked 4 updates that would have moved an invoice backward, and I saw them in the log lines that I added for it. All four invoices have the right state.

No job failed, no alert came, and the dunning emails matched the failed payments of Stripe, as in the check I do each evening.

I left the other event types on the old path for now. Of the remaining ones only subscription events matter, and they need a look at their own order rules. That is the next topic.

summary: Invoice PDF rendering took over 9 seconds for invoices with 200+ lines; profiling showed the headless browser waiting on a web font fetch per page.
body:
Ines forwarded a complaint from a large customer whose monthly invoice PDF timed out in the download link. I reproduced it with a fixture of 240 usage lines and measured 9.4 seconds from the job start to the finished file.

The first guess was the HTML template, but building the HTML took only 80 ms. The time went into the browser: every page break re-triggered a font load from a remote stylesheet, and the render waited for network idle each time. I counted 11 requests to the font host for one invoice.

I bundled the font file into the repo under assets/fonts and pointed the template at it with a local @font-face rule. I also replaced the wait for network idle with a wait for document.fonts.ready. The same fixture then rendered in 3.1 seconds.

The remaining cost is mostly layout of the long table. I tried splitting the table into chunks of 50 rows, which saved about 400 ms but broke the repeated table header on page breaks, so I reverted it. The header repeat matters to Ines, because the accountants print these invoices.

I added a test that renders the 240-line fixture and fails if it takes more than 6 seconds. It is a loose limit because CI machines are slower than mine. The font change is merged in the main checkout.

Next I want to see whether the browser launch per job is a large part of the rest. A pooled browser is the obvious idea, but I have not measured it yet. For now the customer can download the invoice again and gets it in a few seconds.

summary: Checked why one customer's invoice number skipped from 1043 to 1045: a rolled-back transaction had consumed the sequence value, which is harmless but needs a note for Ines.
body:
Ines noticed the gap while checking the month and asked if an invoice had been lost. I looked in the invoices table and the job log. Invoice 1044 was allocated inside a transaction that failed on a tax lookup and was rolled back.

Postgres sequences do not give values back after a rollback, so the number is simply gone. No invoice was sent or stored under 1044, and no payment refers to it.

I wrote this up for Ines in plain words. Some accountants dislike gaps in invoice numbers, so she will ask them whether it is acceptable. If not, we would have to allocate the number at the moment of finalizing, in a short locked step, instead of at creation.

I did not change any code. I only added a comment on the number allocation in src/invoices/numbering.ts that explains the gap. I will wait for her answer before deciding.

summary: Replaced the slow per-customer usage query in the monthly invoice run with one grouped query, cutting the run from 14 minutes to under 2 on the staging copy.
body:
The monthly run was slow enough that Mara noticed it holding up the job queue for other work. I used EXPLAIN ANALYZE on the usage query and saw that it ran once per customer, each time scanning the usage_events table with a filter on the period.

There were about 2,300 active customers on the staging copy, so 2,300 scans. The table has an index on (customer_id, occurred_at), but the planner did not use it for the period filter because the query cast occurred_at to a date. The cast defeated the index.

I made two changes. First, the filter now compares occurred_at against two timestamp bounds, with no cast. Second, one grouped query now gets the sums for all customers in the batch, keyed by customer_id and meter, instead of one query per customer.

On the staging copy the run went from 14 minutes to 1 minute 50 seconds. I compared the produced totals for every customer between the old and the new code, and all 2,300 matched to the cent. That comparison was the main reason I trusted the change.

One edge case needed care: customers with no usage in the period no longer appear in the grouped result, so the code now defaults them to zero. A test covers a customer with no events and one with events only on the last second of the period.

I left the batch size at 200 customers. A larger batch gave no gain and made the memory use less even. Mara will review it tomorrow, and then the change can go in before the next run.

summary: Answered a customer question about why a trial ended a day early: the trial end was stored in UTC while the customer expected their local midnight.
body:
A customer wrote that their trial ended on the evening before the day shown in the signup email. I checked the subscription in the database and in Stripe. The trial_end was set to exactly 14 times 24 hours after signup, in UTC.

The email showed the date in the server's timezone, which made it look like a full day later than the customer's local time, as they are far to the west. So the charge came when the customer was still on the previous day.

Nothing was billed wrongly, the trial was 14 days long as promised. But the display is confusing. I suggested to Mara that the email should show the exact time with a timezone, and not only a date.

I replied to the customer with the exact end time and offered to move it by one day as a courtesy. Mara agreed to that. I extended the trial in Stripe and recorded the reason in the subscription notes.

I added a ticket for the email text. No code changed today.

summary: Upgraded the Stripe SDK from v13 to v14 and fixed the two typing breaks; webhook and payment intent tests all pass on the test account.
body:
The upgrade was small on paper, since v14 mostly changed the pinned API version and a few types. I bumped the package and ran the type check first. It showed two errors.

The first was in src/stripe/customers.ts, where we passed an old field name in a customer update that the typings no longer accept. I switched to the current field. The second was in the webhook code, where a type for the event object had been narrowed and our cast no longer fit.

I then ran the integration tests against the Stripe test account. All the subscription, invoice and payment intent tests passed. I also did a manual check of a failed card payment with the 4000 0000 0000 0341 test card, to see that the dunning email path still fires.

One thing I watched for was the API version. The SDK now sends a newer default version, but we pin the version in the client constructor, so the responses we parse did not change. I left the pin as it is. Moving it is a separate step that needs a look at each field we read.

Mara reviewed the diff and had no comments. I merged it in the main checkout. The pagination helper that we wrote for v13 is still needed, so it stays for now.

summary: The webhook handler processed a few invoice.paid events twice after a Stripe retry; made the handler record event ids in a table and skip ones it already handled.
body:
Ines asked why one customer got two receipts for the same payment. I found two rows in the email log with the same invoice id, about 40 seconds apart. In the webhook log there were two deliveries of the same invoice.paid event, with the same event id.

Stripe retries a delivery when it does not get a 2xx in time. Our handler had answered slowly that day, because the receipt PDF was rendered inside the request. The first call took 31 seconds, Stripe considered it a failure, and sent it again, so both ran.

There were two parts to the fix. First, a new table webhook_events with the Stripe event id as primary key. The handler inserts the id at the start with ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING, and if no row was inserted, it returns 200 and does nothing more.

Second, the handler no longer renders the receipt inside the request. It now enqueues a pg-boss job and answers at once. The job does the PDF and the email.

There was a subtle issue with the order. If the insert succeeds but the enqueue fails, the event is marked as handled and lost. I put the insert and the enqueue in one transaction, since pg-boss can use the same connection. A test forces the enqueue to throw and checks that no row remains.

I also added a test that sends the same signed event twice and expects exactly one job. It passes.

I checked how many past events were affected. In the last two months, 17 events had been duplicated, and 9 of those had sent two receipts. I listed the 9 customers for Ines, and she decided that no apology was needed because the receipts were identical.

The old events table cleanup is not done yet. It will grow by a row per event, so a job to delete rows older than 30 days is next.

summary: Added the cleanup job for the webhook_events table, keeping 30 days, plus a metric of how many duplicate events were skipped each day.
body:
This was the open end from the duplicate receipt fix. The table stores one row per Stripe event, and with about 6,000 events a day it would reach millions of rows in a year.

I wrote a pg-boss scheduled job that runs at 03:10 and deletes rows older than 30 days in batches of 5,000, so that a long delete does not lock the table for the inserts of the handler. Stripe stops retrying after three days, so 30 days is far more than we need. I kept it that long in case of an investigation.

I also added a column skipped_count, which the handler increments with an UPDATE when it sees a conflict. It is cheap and gives us a number to watch. On the first day on staging, the count was zero, which is fine because staging has little traffic.

The test for the job inserts 12,000 old rows and some recent ones, runs the job, and checks that only the recent ones remain. It runs in under a second.

One thing I looked at was an index on created_at. Without it the delete scans the table. I added the index in a migration. The table is small today, so the migration is instant.

Mara looked at the batching and asked why not a single DELETE. My answer was the lock time on a busy day. She accepted it. The change is merged.

summary: Wrote the first version of the refund endpoint: it validates the invoice, calls Stripe refunds.create and records a credit note, with no retry protection yet.
body:
Support had been doing refunds by hand in the Stripe dashboard, and Ines then had to enter the credit notes by hand. The aim of this step was a POST /invoices/:id/refunds endpoint that does both.

The handler checks that the invoice is paid and that the amount is not larger than what is left to refund, that is, the paid total minus earlier refunds. It then calls refunds.create on the payment intent and, when Stripe answers, writes a credit_notes row with the same amount and a reference to the invoice.

Partial refunds work. A full refund sets the invoice status to refunded, and a partial one leaves it paid but shows the refunded amount in the PDF footer.

I wrote tests with a stubbed Stripe client for the happy path, the over-refund case, the unpaid invoice case, and a Stripe error. For the Stripe error, the endpoint returns 502 and writes no credit note.

I noticed a weak spot while writing the error test. If Stripe succeeds but our database write fails, the money is refunded and we have no record. I put a log line with the refund id at error level so that someone can repair it by hand. A cleaner solution needs more thought.

The endpoint is behind the internal API key only. It is not yet used by any screen. Mara wants to review the amounts logic with Ines next.

summary: Dunning emails went out for invoices already paid by bank transfer; traced it to the retry job reading a stale status and added a status re-check just before sending.
body:
A customer who had paid by bank transfer got a third reminder about a failed payment. Ines sent me the invoice number and asked what happened. The invoice showed paid, with a payment recorded the day before the reminder.

The dunning job loads all invoices in status open at the start of its run and then works through them one by one, sending the email and scheduling the next retry. This run had 1,800 invoices and took more than an hour. The transfer was matched by Ines in that time. Our job had the old status in memory.

I fixed it in two places. First, the job now re-reads the invoice row with a SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED right before it sends the email, and skips the invoice if the status is not open any more. Second, the code that records a manual payment takes the same row lock, so the two cannot interleave.

I wrote a test that starts the job on a fixture of three invoices and marks the second as paid from a hook in between. The test expects two emails, not three. It failed before the change and passes now.

I also looked for other past cases. A query over the email log for dunning emails sent after a payment date found 6 cases in two months. I sent the list to Ines, so that she could decide whether to write to those customers.

One more point is that the retry on the Stripe side is a different path, since Stripe does not retry a payment for an invoice that is marked paid out of band. We mark such invoices through the API, and I checked that this call is made in the same code path.

The fix is merged. The dunning job still runs in a single process, and I would like to make it process invoices in chunks of 100 later, so that it is easier to follow.

summary: Planned the partition-free first step for the large invoices table: measured the size, the slowest queries and which ones the monthly run depends on.
body:
The invoices table is now at 4.1 million rows, and Mara asked me to collect the facts before anyone decides on a design. This entry is only the measuring, with no change to the schema.

The table and indexes together take 6.3 GB. The line items table is the larger part of it, at 21 million rows. Autovacuum runs often on it, and one run took 40 minutes last week.

I took the 10 slowest queries from pg_stat_statements. Three of them stand out. The customer invoice list, filtered by customer_id and sorted by issued_at, has a mean time of 180 ms. The monthly finance export scans by period and takes 22 seconds. The dunning job scan by status takes 900 ms.

The first one needs only a composite index on (customer_id, issued_at desc), which does not exist. I will add that at once because it is cheap. The other two are range scans over time, so they would be helped if old data could be skipped.

I also checked how old data is read. Over 95% of the reads touch invoices from the last two quarters. Only the finance export and a few support lookups go further back.

I wrote the numbers into a note in docs/invoices-growth.md so that the later steps can refer to it. The decision is open, and I told Mara that I would not suggest anything radical before the composite index shows its effect.

summary: Added the missing composite index on invoices (customer_id, issued_at desc); the customer invoice list went from 180 ms to 6 ms.
body:
This was the cheap part of the growth analysis. I created the index with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY in a migration, so that writes were not blocked. On the production-size copy it took 4 minutes and added 310 MB.

I ran the customer invoice list query before and after with EXPLAIN ANALYZE. Before, the planner used the customer_id index and sorted 700 rows for a large customer. Now it reads the first 25 rows from the new index in order.

The mean time dropped from 180 ms to 6 ms in my test. In production, the pg_stat_statements numbers will show the real result after a day or so.

The old single-column customer_id index is now almost redundant, but a few other queries use it, so I left it. Dropping it would save space and is something to revisit later.

The migration is merged and applied on staging.

summary: Reviewed the refund endpoint with Mara: found that the remaining-amount check races with two parallel requests, so both can pass and refund more than was paid.
body:
Mara read the refund handler and asked what happens if two support agents press the button at nearly the same time. I wrote a test to find out, firing two requests of 60 percent of the total in parallel on a paid invoice.

Both passed the check, because each read the refunded total before the other had written its credit note. Stripe itself refused the second refund in my test, since it knows the payment intent has only 40 percent left. So the money was safe, but the second request returned 502 and left the user confused, and in a case with two partial refunds that together fit, both would be fine but the order of credit notes might differ from the order at Stripe.

We talked about the fix. Locking the invoice row with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE inside a transaction covers the check and the credit note write, but a Stripe call inside a transaction holds a lock during a network call. Mara said that is acceptable here because refunds are rare and the lock only concerns one invoice.

I changed the handler to take the row lock, check, call Stripe, write the credit note and commit. If Stripe fails, the transaction rolls back and nothing is recorded. The parallel test now gives one success and one clean 409 with a message that a refund is in progress or the amount exceeds the rest.

Mara also asked about a client that repeats a request after a timeout. With the lock, a repeat after a success is rejected as over-refund only when the amount no longer fits, and otherwise it would refund again. That case is not solved by this change. We noted it as a known gap and will handle it later.

summary: Postmark-era check of bounce handling: hard bounces now mark the customer email as invalid and notify Ines instead of retrying the receipt forever.
body:
Looking at the email log, I found one address that had received 14 receipt attempts that all bounced. The job treated every failure as temporary and kept retrying with a growing delay.

The provider webhook for bounces already stored events in an email_events table, but nothing read them. I added a small step in the receipt job. Before sending, it checks whether the address has a hard bounce in the last 90 days, and if so it does not send.

The customer record now gets a flag billing_email_invalid, and a daily digest lists the flagged customers for Ines so that she can ask for a new address. Soft bounces, such as a full mailbox, still retry three times.

I wrote tests for three cases: a hard bounce, a soft bounce, and an address that bounced over 90 days ago. All three pass.

One open question is what to do with the invoice itself when the email cannot be delivered. For now it stays available in the customer portal, and the digest tells Ines which ones need a manual step.

summary: Upgraded the Stripe SDK from v14 to v15 and found that list calls changed their auto-pagination behavior, which broke our pagination helper in two places.
body:
After the v13 to v14 step, v15 looked like another small upgrade, but the changelog mentioned a change in how list results are iterated. I bumped the package and ran the type check, which was clean, then the tests, where four failed.

All four failures were in src/stripe/pagination.ts, our own helper that loops over starting_after cursors for the invoice sync. It relied on the has_more flag and the last id of each page. In v15 the SDK returns a list object whose async iteration already follows the pages, and our helper then fetched each page twice, once by its loop and once through the iteration inside.

I had two options: use the SDK's auto-pagination and drop the helper, or keep the helper and call the page-level method. Dropping the helper is cleaner, but the helper also carried a rate limit pause and a cap on the pages for the sync job. I kept the helper and made it call the single-page method, so its behavior stays as before.

The second place was the customer export script, which used for await on a list and also our helper. I simplified it to use only the helper.

I then ran the nightly sync against the test account with 1,200 test invoices. The number of API calls was 12, as expected for pages of 100, where the broken version had made 24. The synced rows were identical to the run before the upgrade.

I also checked the webhook path with the Stripe CLI, sending invoice.paid, invoice.payment_failed and charge.refunded events. All were handled. The error classes changed their names a little, so I updated the error mapping in the payment code to catch StripeCardError and StripeInvalidRequestError by the type field and not by the class name, which is steadier across versions.

Mara reviewed it and asked if this meant we would need the helper forever. I said that it is a shim for the older behavior and that we should look at removing it when the SDK is further along. The upgrade is merged.

summary: Wrote the first partitioning sketch for invoices on a scratch database; range partitions by issued_at work, but the unique invoice number needs the partition key in it.
body:
Mara asked for a proof of concept, no production change. I restored a copy of the invoices table with 4.6 million rows into a scratch database and tried a partitioned table with range partitions per quarter on issued_at.

The first problem showed up at once. Postgres requires the partition key in every unique constraint. Our invoice number is unique on its own, and the primary key is the id. Both would have to include issued_at. For the primary key that is fine, but then foreign keys from line items and credit notes to invoices would need the issued_at column too, which is ugly.

I tried three options. One: add issued_at to the foreign keys, which means copying the column into 21 million line rows. Two: drop the foreign keys on the partitioned table and keep the integrity by application code and a check job. Three: keep a small separate table invoice_numbers with the unique constraint and the id.

Option three kept the uniqueness guarantee with the smallest change, and the number allocation already goes through one place. Option one is the most correct but the heaviest. I did not decide. I wrote the pros and cons into docs/invoices-growth.md.

The query side was good. The finance export for one quarter touched one partition and went from 22 seconds to 3. The dunning scan by status still needed an index per partition, and a partial index on open invoices helped it.

The data move is the next worry. Copying 4.6 million rows into the new table took 11 minutes on the scratch machine, but the live move must happen while payments come in. I have not planned that. I will think about a backfill with a short switch at the end.

No production changes yet.

summary: Fixed a VAT display bug in the PDF: reverse-charge invoices showed the note in English for German customers because the locale was read from the billing country, not the customer language.
body:
Ines saw a German invoice with the English reverse-charge sentence and asked if it was a template issue. The template had both texts, so the choice was wrong.

The code picked the locale from the billing country field. This customer is in Germany but chose English in the portal, so the language and the country disagree, and the PDF header used the language while the VAT note used the country.

I changed the note to use the same locale as the rest of the document. A test renders two invoices, one German customer with English and one with German, and compares the note text. I regenerated the affected invoice and sent it to Ines.

summary: Retried-payment logic now stops after the card issuer returns a hard decline such as stolen_card, instead of using all four scheduled retries and annoying the customer.
body:
Support forwarded a complaint from a customer whose card had been reported lost. Our job had tried it four times over nine days, and each failure triggered a dunning email with wording that suggested a temporary problem.

The retry schedule treated all declines the same. Stripe returns a decline_code with the error. Some codes, like insufficient_funds, can heal with time, but others, such as stolen_card, lost_card, pickup_card and fraudulent, will never succeed on the same card.

I added a small map in src/payments/declines.ts with the hard codes. When a failed charge has one of them, the retry is cancelled and the invoice moves to a state called needs_new_method. The email for that state asks the customer to add a new payment method and does not promise another attempt.

I needed a new email template for it. I wrote the text with Ines, who wanted it to be short and calm. Postmark sends it with the same layout as the other billing mails.

Tests cover the hard codes, a soft code, and an unknown code. An unknown code falls back to the normal schedule, because a wrong cancel is worse than one extra retry.

I also went through the past three months for cases. There were 23 invoices with hard declines that were retried anyway. Ines will take the list to see if any customer was lost because of it.

The subscription itself is not canceled by this. It follows the existing grace period. I left that part alone, because it is a business rule and Ines owns it.

The change is merged and the template is live in the Postmark account.

summary: Rendered the invoice PDF with a pooled browser instead of a fresh launch per job; mean time for a 20-line invoice fell from 2.4 to 0.9 seconds, with a leak to watch.
body:
After the font fix, the next suspect for the rest of the render time was the browser start. I measured it: launching the headless browser took 1.3 seconds of the 2.4 total for a normal invoice.

I built a small pool in src/pdf/browser-pool.ts that keeps two browser processes and gives each job a fresh page, which is closed after the job. The pool replaces a browser after 200 pages, because long-lived browsers had grown by over 400 MB in my test.

The mean for a 20-line invoice went from 2.4 to 0.9 seconds. For the 240-line fixture it went from 3.1 to 2.6, since layout dominates there. So the pool helps the common case but not the one that started this work.

I had to handle a crash. If the browser process dies, the page call rejects with a protocol error. The pool now notices the disconnect event, drops that browser, starts a new one and the job is retried once by pg-boss.

I ran 2,000 renders in a loop on my machine. Memory stayed flat after the recycling, and no page was left open. I will keep an eye on the memory graph of the worker for the first days.

Mara thought that the real answer for long invoices might be a different renderer, one that does not use a browser. That is a bigger topic. I made a note of it but did not start.

summary: Wrote the SEPA-free groundwork for payment methods: a payment_methods table, a mapping from Stripe objects, and a migration that fills it for 3,100 existing customers.
body:
So far each customer had one card id stored on the customer row, and everything read it from there. EU customers keep asking about other ways to pay, and Mara wanted the data model ready before anything new is added. This entry is only about the model.

The new table payment_methods has id, customer_id, stripe_id, type, last4, brand_or_bank, is_default, and created_at. A customer can have many, and exactly one default, enforced by a partial unique index on customer_id where is_default is true.

I wrote a mapper in src/payments/methods.ts that turns a Stripe PaymentMethod into our row. For now it knows only the card type. For other types it throws an explicit unsupported error rather than guessing, so that nobody adds a type by accident without a mapping.

The migration reads the old card id from each customer, asks Stripe for the card details and inserts a row. With 3,100 customers and the rate limit, I ran it as a pg-boss batch job with 25 requests a second. It took about 2 minutes on the test account data and finished with 3,094 rows. Six customers had a card id that Stripe no longer knows, and I wrote them to a report for Ines instead of failing.

The payment code now reads the default method from the new table. I kept the old column in place and still write it, so that a rollback needs no data work. A test checks both stay in step.

A webhook for payment_method.detached now removes the row, and if it was the default, the customer gets none and the next charge attempt goes to the needs_new_method path from last week.

I looked at the customer portal API, which returned the card as a flat object. I kept its shape the same, filled from the default row, so that the front end is not affected.

The remaining work is in the dunning code, which still reads the old column in one place. I have a ticket for it. Mara reviewed the schema and asked for an index on stripe_id, which I added.

summary: Upgraded the Stripe SDK from v15 to v16; it needed a change in how we construct webhook events and a new null check on expanded fields, after one test exposed a crash.
body:
This was the third upgrade of the series. I read the changelog first and saw that v16 changed some response fields to nullable and that the webhook construction method had a changed signature for the raw body.

The type check found 9 errors, almost all of one kind: fields such as invoice.customer or charge.payment_intent are a string, an expanded object or null, and the types now say so honestly. Earlier versions let us treat them as strings in some places.

I wrote a helper idOf(x) in src/stripe/ids.ts that returns the id for a string or an object and throws a clear error for null. Then I replaced the unsafe casts with it. One of the nine was in the refund code, where a missing payment intent on an old charge would have thrown an unclear error. Now it gives a message that names the charge.

The webhook part was a different story. The tests passed, but when I replayed three real recorded payloads from the test account with the Stripe CLI, the signature check failed for one of them. The cause was our body parser: Fastify had already parsed the JSON, and the raw body was rebuilt from the object, so spacing differed. This was present before the upgrade, but older versions of the check had been more lenient about it in the cases we saw.

I fixed it by keeping the raw buffer in a content type parser for the webhook route only, and passing that to constructEvent. All three payloads now verify.

I also ran the full integration suite and the nightly sync against the test account. The call counts and the stored rows matched the run before the upgrade. Mara asked whether the sync pagination helper could now go; I said not yet, since it still carries the page cap.

The upgrade is merged. One thing I want to add later is a test that replays recorded payloads in CI, since this problem would have been found sooner by one.

summary: Answered a finance question about why the monthly export total differs from the Stripe balance report: fees and refunds are in Stripe's number, but our export holds invoices only.
body:
Ines compared the export total for last month with the Stripe report and found a difference of about 3,900 in the main currency. She asked if invoices were missing.

I went through the difference in parts. Stripe's balance report is net of fees, which were about 2,700. Refunds booked in the month for invoices of earlier months were about 1,100, and our export shows them in the month of the invoice, not the month of the refund. The rest, about 100, was one invoice paid late in the evening that falls into the next month in UTC and into this one in her local time.

So nothing was missing. The two reports answer different questions. I wrote the three parts into a short table for her, with the invoice ids behind each part.

She asked for a column for the refund month in the export. That is simple, since the credit_notes table has a created_at. I will add it next time I touch the export. No code changed today.

summary: Added a refund_month column and a credit notes sheet to the monthly finance export, so refunds can be matched to the month Stripe booked them.
body:
This follows the question from two days ago about the difference between our export and the Stripe report. Ines wanted to see refunds by the month they were made.

The export had one sheet with a row per invoice. I added a second sheet with a row per credit note: credit note id, invoice number, original invoice month, refund month, amount, currency and the Stripe refund id. The refund month comes from the created_at of the credit note, converted to the finance timezone, which Ines asked for after the late evening case.

I also added the same finance timezone to the invoice sheet as a column paid_month, so that the late-evening payments are visible. The old columns stay as they were, so her existing spreadsheet formulas still work.

The export query joins credit_notes to invoices. For a quarter with 600,000 invoices it took 4 seconds, which is fine.

I tested with the previous month's data and checked the sums by hand: the credit note sheet totalled 1,104, which matches the refunds I found in the Stripe report. Ines will try it for the next close.

One detail: amounts are written as decimal numbers with two places and not as cents, which matches the other sheet. I used the same formatting function, so rounding is consistent between the two.

summary: Started the dunning chunking change: the job now processes open invoices in chunks of 100 with a fresh status read per chunk, and a crash resumes from the last chunk.
body:
The stale status bug from earlier showed that the single long loop was fragile. I took the planned change of splitting the dunning run into chunks.

The job now selects 100 open invoices ordered by id, processes them, and records the last id in a job_state row. The next chunk starts after that id. If the process dies, pg-boss starts the job again and it continues from the stored id and does not start over. Before, a crash meant sending reminders again to everyone in the first half.

Each chunk reads the statuses again when it begins, so the window for stale data is now a few seconds, not an hour. The row lock check before each email stays as the final guard.

I tested with 450 invoices and a forced crash after the second chunk. The restart sent the emails for chunks three to five only, 250 in total, and none twice. A second test checks that an invoice paid between chunks is skipped.

The chunk size is a config value. I tried 500 and saw no gain, so I kept 100. It is not merged yet, since I want to run it against the staging data once with the real email provider in sandbox mode. Mara will look at the diff after that.

summary: Finished the dunning chunking change: crash resume from the last chunk works, and a 6,000-invoice staging run now keeps memory flat instead of growing with the open invoice count.
body:
The chunking change started two days ago was missing its resume logic, so I finished it. The job now writes the id of the last processed invoice into a dunning_runs row after each chunk of 100. When the job restarts after a crash, it reads that row and continues from the next id instead of starting over.

I tested the resume by killing the worker process in the middle of a staging run with 6,000 open invoices. The restarted job picked up at chunk 31 and finished the run without sending any email twice. I checked this by counting rows in the email log per invoice and found no duplicates.

Memory was the other reason for the change. Before it, the job loaded every open invoice into one array, and the process grew to about 900 MB on the staging copy. With chunks, it stays near 140 MB for the whole run. The run time is about the same, roughly 40 seconds.

One edge case needed care. If an invoice is paid after its chunk was read but before the email is sent, the fresh status read per chunk is too early to catch it. I left the status re-check just before sending in place, so the two checks cover each other. A run that is marked finished is never resumed, which I covered with a test.

I also added a test where the last chunk holds fewer than 100 invoices, since the first version of the loop skipped it. Two further tests cover an empty run and a run that crashes twice. All of them pass.

What is left is a metric for the invoices that are skipped mid-run, and a note in the runbook on how to clear a stuck dunning_runs row by hand. Mara will review the migration for the new table tomorrow.

summary: Added a dunning metric for invoices skipped because they were paid mid-run; staging shows 3 to 5 per run, so the fresh status read is doing real work.
body:
After the chunking fix this morning I added a counter, dunning_skipped_paid, that increments when the fresh status read finds an invoice no longer open. It is exported with the other job metrics and graphed next to the number of reminders sent.

I replayed the last three monthly runs on the staging copy. Between 3 and 5 invoices per run were paid while the job was working, mostly bank transfers booked in the morning. Before the status re-check these would have received a reminder after paying.

I also wrote a short note for Ines that explains the counter, so she does not read it as a failure number. The note says that a skip means a customer was spared an unneeded email. Nothing else changed in the job today.

summary: Answered Ines: an invoice total differing by 1 cent from her spreadsheet comes from per-line rounding in our code versus rounding the sum in the sheet.
body:
Ines sent three invoices whose totals were 1 cent off from her spreadsheet check. I recomputed them from the stored lines. Each line is rounded to cents in our code and then summed, while her sheet sums the unrounded lines and rounds once.

For an invoice with 12 usage lines at fractional unit prices the two methods can differ by a cent or two. All three invoices fit this pattern, and the stored totals match the sum of the displayed lines, which is what the customer sees on the PDF.

I told her that the invoices are internally consistent but that the rounding rule is not defined anywhere in writing. She will ask the accountants which rule they want. I did not change any code. I listed the affected invoice numbers so they can be checked once the rule is known.

summary: Traced a spike of failed receipt emails to the receipt template choking on customers with no billing name; added a fallback to the company name and a test, and resent 41 receipts.
body:
Ines forwarded a complaint from a customer who never got a receipt, and a look at the email log showed more than one. Over the past three days, 41 receipts had failed with the error 'Cannot read properties of null (reading trim)'. All of them belonged to customers whose billing_name field was empty.

The cause was in the receipt template helper. It trimmed the billing name to build the greeting line and assumed the field was always set. That held for customers who signed up through the web form, which requires a name. It did not hold for customers created through the sales import, which only fills in the company name.

The failures were not visible because the send job caught the error, logged it at debug level and marked the job as completed. That is the real bug, so I changed it. A render error now fails the job, pg-boss retries it, and after the last retry a row goes into a failed_emails table and a counter goes up.

For the template, the greeting now uses billing_name, then the company name, then the plain word 'customer'. I added three tests, one for each case. I also searched the other templates for the same pattern and found it in the dunning email too. That one is fixed the same way.

To repair the damage I wrote a one-off script that selected the 41 invoices, rendered the receipts again and queued them. I ran it first in dry-run mode and read ten of the rendered emails by hand. Then I ran it for real, and all 41 were accepted by the email provider.

I told Ines which customers were affected, so that finance knows who may have asked about a receipt in the last days. The new counter has an alert threshold of five failures per hour. I will look at the failed_emails table again tomorrow morning to make sure it stays empty.

summary: Added a check that fails the build when a new email template uses a customer field without a fallback, so the null billing name bug of earlier today cannot come back through another template.
body:
After the receipt fix earlier this evening, I wanted a guard against the same mistake in templates that do not exist yet. The check is a test that renders every template with a fixture customer where all optional fields are null. If any template throws or prints the text 'null' or 'undefined', the test fails and names the template.

It found one more problem right away. The payment failed email printed 'undefined' in the line that shows the last four digits of the card when the customer paid by bank transfer. That line is now left out when there is no card.

The fixture lives in test/fixtures/customer_minimal.ts. It has only the fields that Stripe and the signup form always set. Everything else is null.

The test runs in about 300 ms for the nine templates we have, so it adds nothing noticeable to the build. I ran the whole suite twice to check it was not flaky, and it passed both times.

I wrote a short paragraph in the contributing notes explaining that new templates are picked up automatically, because the test reads the template directory. Nothing else is open on this topic.

summary: Wrote a script to list Stripe customers whose stored email differs from ours; it found 58 mismatches, mostly from customers changing their email in the Stripe portal.
body:
Mara noticed that a few receipts went to old addresses, so I looked at how the email gets synced. We store the customer email on our side and copy it into Stripe at signup. When a customer edits it in the Stripe billing portal, the customer.updated webhook arrives, but our handler ignored it.

I wrote a read-only script that pages through all Stripe customers with the pagination helper and compares the email with our customers table. Out of about 3,100 customers, 58 differ. Forty-four of those are changes made in the portal, nine are case differences only, and five look like typos on our side.

The script prints a CSV with the customer id, both addresses and the date of the last Stripe update. I did not change any data. I sent the CSV to Ines, because finance should decide for the five unclear cases, and a wrong guess would send invoices to a stranger.

The next step is to handle customer.updated in the webhook handler and to copy the email when it changed. Stripe is the source of truth for that field, since customers edit it there. Case differences will be ignored by comparing lowercase.

I also noted that the sync should mark the old address in the audit log, so that a bounce on the old address can be understood later. That goes into the same change.

summary: Handled customer.updated webhooks so email changes made in the Stripe portal now reach our customers table, with an audit row for each change and the 44 stale addresses fixed.
body:
This is the follow-up to this morning's mismatch script. The webhook handler now has a case for customer.updated. It reads the email from the event, lowercases both values for comparison and writes the new address only when they differ.

Each change goes into a customer_email_changes table with the customer id, the old and the new address, the event id and the time. The table is small and has no cleanup job for now. The update and the audit row are written in one transaction, so there is never one without the other.

The handler already records event ids to skip duplicates, so a retried event cannot write twice. I checked that with a test that sends the same event two times. Only one audit row exists afterwards.

One case needed a decision. Stripe sends customer.updated for many reasons, such as a changed default payment method, and the email is then unchanged. In that case the handler does nothing and logs at debug level. A test covers this too.

For the existing data, I ran the mismatch script again and applied the 44 portal changes through the same code path, so that they have audit rows as well. The nine case differences were left alone. For the five unclear ones, Ines answered that three are typos on our side and two are real changes, so I fixed all five by hand and wrote the reason in a comment on each audit row.

After that, the script reports zero mismatches. I put it into the nightly checks next to the paid invoice comparison, so a new difference is reported the next morning. The webhook tests all pass on the test account, and I triggered a real email change there to see the whole path once.

summary: Looked into why the Stripe v16 test account showed card payments stuck in requires_action; the cause was our test cards, not the SDK, and the fixtures now use a card without 3D Secure.
body:
A few payment tests started to fail intermittently after the upgrade to v16, and I first suspected the SDK. The failures showed payment intents in the status requires_action where the test expected succeeded.

I compared the requests before and after the upgrade and found no difference in how we call paymentIntents.create. So I looked at the cards used by the fixtures. Two of them were the Stripe test numbers that always demand 3D Secure authentication. They had worked before only because the test account had an older setting that skipped the challenge.

That setting had changed on the Stripe side, which explains why the failures looked random. They appeared whenever one of the two cards was picked by the shuffled fixture order.

I replaced both cards with the plain test card pm_card_visa and added one dedicated test for the authentication path. That test uses the 3D Secure card on purpose and expects requires_action, then confirms the intent with the test helper.

The suite ran ten times in a row without a failure. I also wrote a line in the test readme about which test cards behave how, so the next person does not repeat this search. No production code changed. The SDK upgrade stays as it is.

summary: Investigated retried payments that charged customers on the wrong day: the schedule used the server time zone, now it uses UTC offsets stored per run.
body:
A customer asked why their card was charged at 1 in the morning, a day before they expected. I looked at the retry schedule for failed payments. The next attempt time is computed with date arithmetic that adds days in the server's local time zone.

On the server this is UTC, but the test machine of Mara uses a different zone, so the tests passed locally and hid the issue. In production the attempt was correct in UTC but the email said a local date that did not match the customer's.

The email text used the server date. I changed it to use the customer's stored time zone for display, falling back to UTC when none is set.

The retry job itself now stores the exact timestamp of the next attempt in a timestamptz column instead of computing it from a day count. This removes the arithmetic from the job.

I wrote tests for three zones, including one with a daylight saving change inside the retry window. The dunning email templates were checked for other date uses, and two more were changed. The customer was told what happened. No payment was charged wrongly in amount.

summary: Added a per-plan breakdown to the monthly usage report for Ines, after she asked why one plan's revenue looked low; the cause was a trial plan with many free customers.
body:
Ines asked why the revenue line for the Team plan in the monthly report looked about a fifth lower than she expected. The report only showed totals per plan and not how many customers were behind them.

I added three columns to the report query: the number of active customers, the number on a trial and the number with a coupon. The numbers explained it. Of 412 Team customers, 83 were still in their trial and 29 used a coupon with a full discount for the first months.

So the revenue was correct. The expectation came from multiplying the price by all customers, which included those who do not pay yet. I sent her the new report with that explanation and the three counts for each plan.

While I was in the query, I noticed that customers who cancelled in the middle of the month were counted as active for the whole month. I changed the count to use the cancellation date, so a customer is active only up to that day. That moved the Team count from 412 to 405.

The query still runs in under a second on the production replica. I added a test with a small fixture that has one trial, one coupon and one cancelled customer, and expects the counts for each. Ines will check next month's report against her own list before we trust the new columns fully.

summary: Routed the two unchecked Stripe list calls through the pagination helper; one of them had been silently dropping customers beyond the first 100 in a report.
body:
Following the plan from yesterday I fixed the two direct list calls. The first one is in the monthly reconciliation report, which lists payouts. The second lists payment methods for a customer.

The payouts call asked for 100 results and used them as the full set. On the staging account there are 130 payouts for the test period, so the report was missing 30 rows. In production the count is lower, but the last month had 96, which is close to the limit.

Both calls now use the helper, which follows has_more until the end. I added tests with a mocked Stripe that returns three pages.

I also wrote a lint rule in the form of a test that scans the source for .list( calls outside the helper file and fails when it finds one. It found nothing else.

The report was rerun for the last three months. The numbers did not change, since no month had passed the limit yet, but the next busy month could have.

summary: Fixed the pg-boss email job so that a Postmark outage no longer fills the queue with retries; failed sends now back off exponentially up to a limit of six attempts.
body:
During a short Postmark API error period this morning, the email queue grew to about 2,000 waiting jobs. Each failed job retried every 30 seconds, so the retries themselves kept the queue busy and slowed the other jobs, such as the PDF rendering.

The retry settings were the pg-boss defaults that we never changed, with a fixed delay and a limit of 20. I changed the email job to six attempts with exponential back-off, starting at 30 seconds and doubling each time. The last wait is about 16 minutes, so a short outage is covered without spamming the API.

I also gave the email jobs their own queue. PDF rendering and webhook jobs do not share it any more, so a problem with emails cannot delay them.

For jobs that are still in the old queue, I wrote a small migration that moves the waiting ones over. Of the 2,000, about 1,700 were in a retry state. They were moved and sent normally once the provider was back, and no customer got a mail twice because the jobs carry a dedupe key per invoice and template.

I tested the back-off by pointing the client at a local server that returns 503 for the first three calls. The job succeeded on the fourth attempt, with the expected waits. Next I want an alert when the email queue is older than ten minutes.

summary: Wrote the retry for soft email bounces: two further attempts over two days, then a mark on the customer so finance can follow up.
body:
This implements the note from the morning. When a receipt or reminder produces a soft bounce, the job now schedules a second attempt after 12 hours and a third after 36 hours.

If the third attempt also bounces softly, the customer gets a flag email_unreachable and Ines gets one notification. A later successful send clears the flag.

The attempt count is kept in the email_attempts table, one row per message, with the bounce type and the time. I wrote a migration for it and a test for each step of the schedule using the injectable clock.

One issue came up: the old email provider reports a full mailbox with a code that is not labeled soft, so the mapping needed an extra case for that code. I added it with a comment and a test with the sample payload.

I ran the job against the staging data with a fake provider. It made the expected number of attempts and no more. Duplicate sends were not seen.

summary: Reduced the PDF render time for 200-line invoices from 4 seconds to 1.7 by rendering the line table as plain HTML without per-row flex layout.
body:
The 200-line invoices were still the slow case after the pooled browser. I profiled one with the browser's tracing and found that most of the time went to layout, not to fonts or network.

The line table used a flex container per row, with four nested elements per cell. For 200 rows this produced several thousand layout boxes and a long layout pass of about 2.4 seconds.

I rewrote the table as a normal HTML table with fixed column widths and table-layout: fixed. The visual result is the same, and I compared 30 sample PDFs pixel by pixel. Two differed by a one pixel shift in the right border, which I fixed by changing a border rule.

Times on staging after the change:
- 20 lines: 0.8 seconds, before 0.9
- 200 lines: 1.7 seconds, before 4.0
- 600 lines: 4.9 seconds, before 14

The page breaks needed a second look. With the fixed layout the header row now repeats on each page, which it did not before, and Ines liked that. A long invoice that breaks in the middle of a row was found once, and I added break-inside: avoid for rows.

The change is in the template and the CSS only. Tests for the renderer pass. I left a note that a completely new renderer may still be worth it, since 600 lines is still slow.

summary: Wrote a runbook page for the monthly invoice run covering the order of steps, how to check each one, and how to restart safely, because only Mara knew it by heart.
body:
The monthly invoice run has grown to several steps over the last months, and the order lives mostly in Mara's head. I wrote it down while she was available to correct me.

The page lists the steps in order: the usage snapshot from nebula, the price calculation, the invoice creation through the numbers side table, the PDF rendering, the receipt emails and finally the Stripe charges. For each step it says which table to look at to see that it finished and which number to compare against.

The restart rules took the most time. The usage snapshot and the invoice creation are safe to repeat, because they skip what exists. The charges are not repeated for paid invoices, since the job checks the status first. The emails are protected by the dedupe key. Mara confirmed all three, and corrected me on the PDF step, which does overwrite files and therefore must not run while customers download.

I added the usual problems from the past months with their fixes, such as the stale status in the retry job and the slow usage query. Each has a link to the journal entry that describes it.

I also listed the commands, for example the script that shows run progress and the one that clears a stuck dunning_runs row. Ines will read the page next, because she wants to know when in the month her checks can begin.

summary: Built the first version of partition planning for invoices: a script that estimates row counts per quarter and flags which queries lack the partition key.
body:
Before any partitioning work, I wanted facts about the data. I wrote a script, scripts/partition-plan.ts, that reads the invoices table and prints rows per quarter, size per quarter and the share of rows in the last two quarters.

Results on the production snapshot: 2.8 million rows in total, with the last two quarters holding 31 percent. The oldest quarters are nearly never read.

The second part of the script parses the list of queries from pg_stat_statements and flags those on invoices that have no condition on issued_at. There were 9 such queries.

Of the 9, four are the lookup by invoice number, which does not know the date. Two come from the admin search. Two are in the monthly run and use the customer id only. One is a count for a dashboard.

The invoice number is the hard one. A unique constraint on a partitioned table must include the partition key, so a number alone cannot stay unique across partitions by the database. I looked at putting the year and quarter into the number itself, which would make the constraint work, but that changes the format that customers and Ines know.

Another option is a small separate table that holds number and issued_at with a normal unique index, and keeps the guarantee outside the partitioned table. I wrote both options with pros and cons in a document for Mara.

No decision was made. The script and the document are committed.

summary: Diagnosed a double charge complaint: the customer had two subscriptions from a retried signup request, so the signup endpoint now checks for an existing one.
body:
A customer wrote that they were billed twice for the same plan. I looked up the account and found two active subscriptions created 3 seconds apart, both for the same plan.

The logs showed that the signup request was sent twice by the browser, probably a double click on the pay button. Both requests passed the check for an existing subscription, because the check ran before either one had written its row.

I fixed this in two layers. First, a partial unique index on subscriptions (customer_id) where status is active or trialing, so the database rejects the second. Second, the endpoint catches the unique violation and returns the existing subscription instead of an error.

The Stripe side is a problem too, since the second subscription was already created in Stripe before our insert failed. I changed the order: we insert a pending row first, with the unique index in force, and only then call Stripe. If the call fails the row is deleted.

I wrote a test that sends two parallel signup requests and checks that exactly one Stripe call is made. It used a mock with a short delay so the race shows up reliably. Before the fix the test failed in 9 of 10 runs.

The customer got a refund of the second charge, done by hand in the Stripe dashboard since our refund endpoint has no protection yet. Ines was told. I also looked for other accounts with the same pattern and found 4 from the past year, which I passed to her.

summary: Added a nightly check that compares our paid invoices with Stripe charges and reports any mismatch; the first run found two invoices marked paid without a charge.
body:
To catch drift between our records and Stripe I wrote a nightly job. It lists the charges of the last 3 days through the pagination helper and compares them with the invoices we hold as paid.

The job reports three kinds of problem: paid in our database but no charge in Stripe, charge in Stripe but invoice open, and amount differing.

The first run on production found two invoices of the first kind. Both were paid by bank transfer and marked paid by hand by Ines, so they have no Stripe charge. That is legitimate, so the job now skips invoices whose payment method is bank transfer.

After that change the run was clean. No charges without an invoice were found and no amounts differed.

The result is written to a table reconciliation_runs and a summary is sent to Ines as an email when anything is found. On clean runs nothing is sent, only a metric is set.

I wrote tests with a mocked Stripe for each kind of mismatch. The job takes 12 seconds in production.

summary: Checked the Stripe webhook retry behavior against our handler: a 500 response triggers retries for three days, so the handler now returns 200 for known unrecoverable events instead of failing them.
body:
Reading the Stripe docs on delivery, I confirmed that any non-2xx answer makes Stripe retry an event with growing delays for up to three days. Our handler returned 500 for every error, including events it can never process, such as an invoice.paid for an invoice id that we do not have.

That produced noise. On the production logs of the last week, 14 events had been retried more than 20 times each, all for invoices created by a test integration that does not exist in our database. They filled the error log and hid real failures.

I split the errors into two kinds. Temporary ones, like a database timeout, still return 500 so that Stripe retries. Permanent ones, such as an unknown invoice or an event type we do not handle, are logged at warning level with the event id, stored in the webhook_events table as skipped, and answered with 200.

The split lives in one small function, classifyError, with a test for each known case. Unknown errors count as temporary, which is the safe default, because a lost event is worse than a retried one.

I added a metric for skipped events by reason. After the change on staging, replaying the 14 old events produced 14 skipped rows and no more retries. The signature check was not touched. The next step is to look at the alert thresholds for the error log, now that it should be quieter.

summary: Decided with Mara to keep the invoice number unique through a side table for now, leaving the number format alone, and started the migration for it.
body:
We read through the two options for the invoice number from the partition plan. Mara preferred not to change the format, since customers quote the numbers in support requests and the accountants know them.

So the choice is a side table, invoice_numbers, with number as the primary key and the issued_at date and the invoice id as columns. A number is inserted in the same transaction as the invoice, and the unique index on the table does the guarantee.

The migration creates the table and fills it from the 2.8 million existing invoices. I ran it on the staging copy in batches of 50,000 rows and it took 4 minutes. The check afterwards compared the count of both tables and found no difference.

The code change for the invoice builder is small: one more insert in the transaction. The lookup by number can now use the side table to find the issued_at date first, and then query the invoices with the date, which is a way to keep that query working after partitioning.

One problem came up in the tests. The test that rolls back a transaction now also rolls back the side table row, which is right, but the sequence still has a gap. That matches the documented behavior.

The migration is not run in production yet. I want Ines to see the staging result first.

summary: Ines confirmed the accountants want the rounding rule in writing; I drafted a one-page description of how lines, discounts and VAT are rounded today.
body:
Ines came back with the answer from the accountants: they want to know exactly how rounding is done and will then say which rule they prefer. I wrote a one-page description for them.

It covers four steps. Unit price times quantity is rounded per line. The discount is spread in proportion over lines. VAT is computed on each line's discounted net and rounded per line. The total is the sum of the rounded lines.

I added three worked examples with real numbers from the invoices that were 1 cent off. The page is plain text so she can paste it into an email. No code was changed.

summary: Prepared the invoice_numbers migration after Ines checked the staging result, with the production run planned for the next quiet night.
body:
Ines looked at the staging result and agreed with it, so the migration is ready to go. I went through the staging run again to be sure about the plan: 2,812,440 rows in the invoices table, and the same count in the side table after the copy, with no invoice left without a side table row. I also compared the highest number in each table and they matched.

The plan for production is to run the migration in batches of 50,000 rows during the night, when the load is low. On staging the same batch size finished in about 6 minutes, so I expect a similar time on production, but I will watch the lock times on the invoices table during the first batches and stop if they grow.

I also finished the builder change on a branch-free checkout and tested it locally. A new invoice takes its number and creates its side table row in the same transaction. I forced a failure after the number was taken and no orphan row was left. I have not deployed it yet, because it should go out only after the migration has filled the side table.

The lookup by invoice number will go through the side table first. On staging its time was 3 ms, the same as before, and I will measure it again on production after the run.

I wrote the checks I will run after the migration: counts in both tables, no invoice without a side table row, and the highest number in each. Next step after that is the real partitioning, which needs a plan for moving the data. I will start on it once the monthly run has passed with the new table.

summary: Started the credit note feature for partial refunds: a credit_notes table and a numbering scheme, because finance wants a document for every refund they book.
body:
Ines asked last week for a proper document for each refund, since the accountants only had the Stripe refund id. I started with a credit_notes table holding invoice_id, amount_cents, currency, reason and a number. The number comes from the same side table approach as the invoice numbers, with its own prefix CN so the two sequences never mix.

The first migration ran on staging and created the table with a unique index on the number. I wrote the model and a function that builds a credit note from a refund object, copying the VAT rate of the original invoice line. Partial refunds are the awkward case: the refund does not say which lines it covers, so for now the credit note is split across lines in proportion to their amounts.

The proportional split leaves a cent or two over on some invoices. I added a test with a 3-line invoice refunded for 10.00 and it produced a total of 9.99 before I put the remainder on the last line. That is a hack and I noted it in the code, since the rounding rule is still being written for the accountants.

Not done yet: the PDF for a credit note and the email. Next is a short template that reuses the invoice layout with the lines negated. I will ask Mara whether the remainder rule is acceptable before building on it.

summary: Mara accepted putting the rounding remainder of a credit note on the last line for now; the credit note PDF reuses the invoice template with negated amounts.
body:
Mara looked at the remainder rule in the credit note split and said it is fine as long as the sum always equals the refund, which the test checks. She wants it revisited once the written rounding description is signed off by the accountants.

I then built the credit note PDF by passing a flag to the invoice template that switches the title to Credit note and prints amounts with a minus sign. The reverse-charge note and the locale logic carry over unchanged, which saved a lot of work. One catch was the footer, which printed the payment due date. For a credit note that is meaningless, so it is hidden when the flag is set.

Rendering a 5-line credit note took 0.8 seconds on the pooled browser, in line with invoices. I generated samples for a German reverse-charge customer and a French one with VAT and checked them by eye. Both looked right.
