Next step is the email that attaches the PDF, and the link from the refund endpoint so the note is created at refund time.

summary: Wired credit notes into the refund endpoint and sent them by email; a refund now creates the note and queues a mail in one transaction, and a failed mail no longer blocks the refund.
body:
The refund endpoint now calls the credit note builder after Stripe confirms the refund. The credit note row and the pg-boss email job are written in one database transaction, so there is never a note without a mail job or the other way round. The Stripe call itself is outside the transaction, of course.

The first version sent the mail inline and a Postmark timeout made the endpoint return 500 even though the money had already gone back. That was wrong, so the endpoint answers 200 as soon as the refund and the note are stored, and the job does the sending with the usual backoff.

I added three tests: a full refund, a partial refund with two lines, and a Postmark failure that leaves the note stored and the job in retry. All pass. A small problem appeared in the email template check from last month: the new template used customer.billing_name, and the build failed until I added the company name fallback. The check did its job.

What is left is the note appearing in the monthly export. Ines will want a column for the credit note number next to the refund month.

summary: Added the credit note number to the monthly finance export and checked it against last month's refunds; 17 refunds matched, 2 old ones have no note and are marked as such.
body:
The export already had refund_month and a credit notes sheet. I added a credit_note_number column to both and joined on the refund id. For refunds made before the feature there is no note, so the cell says legacy instead of staying empty, which Ines had asked for so she can tell a missing note from a bug.

I ran the export on last month's data. Of 19 refunds, 17 had no note either, because they predate the feature, and 2 had one from testing in staging copied by mistake. Wait, the staging copy was the issue: the production database has no credit notes yet, so all 19 show legacy as expected. The two I had worried about came from my staging run reading the wrong connection string.

I fixed the script so it prints the database host at the start, to prevent that confusion. Then I ran it again against production and the output was all legacy rows, which is correct.

Next is a backfill question. Ines does not want credit notes for old refunds, only for new ones, so no backfill. I recorded that decision in the runbook page for the monthly run.

One more item for tomorrow is a test that the export totals still match the invoices after adding the join, since a join that multiplies rows would inflate sums silently.

summary: Found that the new join in the finance export could double count invoices with two credit notes, and fixed it by aggregating notes per refund before joining.
body:
The check I planned yesterday found a real problem. An invoice with two partial refunds, each with a note, appeared twice in one sheet and its amount was counted twice in the total. In the test data this showed as a total 12.40 too high.

The join was on invoice id in one query, not refund id. I changed the query to aggregate credit notes per refund in a subquery first, so every refund yields exactly one row, and I joined on refund id everywhere. After that, the sum of the invoices sheet equals the sum of the invoices table for the month again.

I added a test that creates an invoice with two refunds and asserts the row counts of both sheets. It failed on the old query and passes now. I also ran the export for the last three months in staging and compared totals with the previous output byte for byte except the new column. They matched.

I let Ines know that the earlier draft of the export, which I had sent her as a preview, was wrong for invoices with several refunds. She had not used it yet. The new file is the one to use.

Remaining for this topic: documentation in the runbook, and a short note to the accountants once Ines has seen one real credit note.

summary: Looked at why the Stripe v16 SDK logs deprecation warnings for the charges list call and decided to move the report to payment intents next week.
body:
After the upgrade to v16 the logs show a deprecation warning each time the nightly reconciliation job lists charges. Nothing is broken, but the warning fills the log with about 400 lines per run.

I checked the call sites. There are three: the nightly check, the double charge report and one old script. The first two can use the payment intent list with expanded latest_charge, which gives the same data. The script I will delete, since nobody has run it since the backfill.

I did not change code today. The reconciliation compares our paid invoices with charges, and I want to make that change with a good test around it, not in a hurry at the end of a day. I wrote down the plan in the task list: replace the list call, keep the pagination helper, compare old and new output on one month of data.

Also noted that the v16 types make latest_charge a string or an object, so the new code needs the null check pattern from the upgrade.

summary: Moved the nightly reconciliation from listing charges to listing payment intents with expanded latest_charge; output matches the old job on a month of data except for 3 rows.
body:
I made the change planned earlier. The job now lists payment intents created in the window, expands latest_charge, and builds the same comparison rows as before. The pagination helper is used for the list, as every Stripe list call should be.

To check it I ran the old and the new version on the same month in staging and diffed the results. Of about 2,900 rows, 3 differed. Two were payments that had been retried: the old job saw two charges for one invoice, the new one sees one intent with the latest charge only. That is actually closer to what finance means by a payment, so I accept the difference.

The third row was a failed first charge, then a success. Same cause, same acceptance. I wrote the three cases into the test as fixtures so the behavior is documented.

The deprecation warning is gone from the logs for this job. The double charge report still uses the old call. I changed it too, using the same approach, and its output was identical on last month's data.

The unused script is deleted. One thing to watch: expanded fields increase response size, and the job took 41 seconds instead of 29 in staging. That is fine for a nightly run but I will keep an eye on it.

Next I want to look at the webhook handler for payment_intent events, since the data model is now closer to what the handler sees.

summary: Wrote the plan for splitting the PDF render queue into a fast lane for small invoices and a slow lane for big ones, after a 600-line invoice blocked the monthly run for ten minutes.
body:
During the monthly run yesterday, one customer's invoice with about 600 lines occupied a render worker for close to ten minutes, and the small invoices queued behind it. The run finished late and Ines noticed the receipts arriving in the afternoon.

I looked at the numbers. Render time grows with the line count, but not linearly: 20 lines take 0.9 seconds, 200 lines 1.7, and 600 lines over 90 seconds when the page count passes about 15. The browser pool has four pages, so one such job takes a quarter of the capacity for a long time.

The plan has three parts. First, the job gets a lane by line count: up to 150 lines goes to the fast queue, anything above to a slow queue. Second, the slow queue has one worker with its own browser, so it can never take pages away from the fast one. Third, a timeout of 3 minutes with a clear error, so a stuck render fails instead of hanging.

I considered a different approach, rendering large invoices in chunks of pages and merging the PDFs. That would fix the speed too, but it needs a merge library and changes in page numbering, and it is much larger. I noted it as a later idea.

For pg-boss this means a second queue name and a small change where the job is created. The line count is known at creation time, so no extra query is needed. I also want a metric for the queue depth of each lane.

I have not written the code yet. Mara agreed with the plan and asked that the threshold be a config value. I will start tomorrow with the queue split and test it with a generated 600-line invoice in staging.

summary: Implemented the two render lanes with a config threshold of 150 lines; in staging a 600-line invoice no longer delays 300 small ones.
body:
I did the queue split. There are now two pg-boss queues, pdf-render and pdf-render-large, and the creation code picks one by comparing the line count to PDF_LARGE_THRESHOLD, which defaults to 150. The large queue has a concurrency of one and its own browser instance.

The browser pool code assumed a single shared pool. I changed it so a pool is created per lane, with the page count as a parameter: four for the fast lane and one for the slow. Closing the pools on shutdown needed a loop instead of a single call, and I missed that at first. The test run hung at the end until I fixed it.

The timeout is set to 3 minutes for the slow lane and 30 seconds for the fast one. A job that times out throws a RenderTimeout error and pg-boss retries it twice with backoff. After that it is marked failed and an alert goes to the log.

Test in staging: I created 300 invoices of 20 lines and one of 600 lines, and queued them together. The small ones finished in 41 seconds in total. The large one took 94 seconds on its own lane and did not influence the others. Before the change the same mix took a bit over 11 minutes for the small ones.

Memory of the slow browser grew to about 700 MB while rendering the big invoice and fell back after. That is acceptable but I noticed that the leak I watched earlier on the pooled browser is still possible. The browsers are restarted after 200 jobs on the fast lane, and I gave the slow lane a restart after every 10 jobs.

I added the two queue depth gauges to the metrics. Next is to deploy this before the next monthly run and add a line to the runbook.

summary: Deployed the render lanes to production and ran a canary batch of 50 invoices; all rendered, the slow lane handled two big ones in 2 minutes.
body:
I deployed the render lane change this morning. Before the full run I created a canary batch from 50 real invoices of last month with the render only, no emails, and put them through the new queues.

All 50 finished. Two had more than 150 lines, 210 and 340, and they went to the slow lane and finished in about 25 and 60 seconds. The remaining 48 were done in 19 seconds. The gauges showed the depths rising and falling as expected.

I checked the output PDFs against those stored from the original run by comparing page counts and text content with a small script. They were identical in all 50. Pixel level was not compared, as the renderer is the same.

One detail came up: the large queue name is not in the dashboard of queue sizes that Mara uses, so a backlog there would be invisible. I added it to the dashboard definition file and she will load it.

The runbook now has a paragraph on the two lanes and on how to see which one a stuck job is in. The next monthly run will be the real test.

summary: Answered Ines: a customer's invoice shows VAT of zero because the customer entered a valid VAT id after the invoice was created, and invoices are not recalculated.
body:
Ines asked why an Italian business customer was charged no VAT on one invoice and VAT on the one before. I checked the customer history. The customer saved a VAT id three days before the second invoice, and our VAT check marked it valid on that day, so reverse charge applied.

The earlier invoice was created before the id was saved, so it correctly had VAT. Invoices are not recalculated after creation by design, because they are legal documents once sent.

If the customer wants the first one changed, the way to do it is a credit note for the full amount and a new invoice with reverse charge. With the credit note feature this is now possible without a manual step. Ines will talk to the customer.

I wrote the explanation to her in plain words and attached the two invoice ids and the date of the VAT id check. She replied that this was what she suspected.

summary: Replaced the expiry guess for Stripe webhook event dedupe with a stored event id table, after a retried payment_intent.succeeded event sent a receipt twice.
body:
A customer got two receipts for one payment. I traced it to the webhook handler. Stripe delivered payment_intent.succeeded, our handler took 11 seconds because of a slow query, and Stripe retried. Both deliveries passed the check, because the dedupe was an in-memory set that was empty on the second server instance.

There are two instances in production, so an in-memory set cannot work. I made a table webhook_events with the Stripe event id as primary key and a received_at column. The handler now inserts the id first with ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING and checks the affected row count. If zero rows were inserted, the event was seen and the handler returns 200 without doing the work.

There is one problem with insert first: if the handler crashes after the insert and before finishing, the retry is dropped and the work is lost. To avoid that, the insert and the handler work run in one transaction for the database parts, and the email is queued inside it. If anything throws, the insert rolls back and the retry works again.

I wrote tests for the double delivery, for a crash in the middle with a retry, and for two parallel deliveries of the same id. The parallel test was the interesting one: with a real Postgres, one of the two waits on the lock, then sees the conflict and returns. Good.

The table will grow, so I added a cleanup job to delete rows older than 30 days. Stripe retries for three days at most, so that is a wide margin.

I checked how many of the old duplicates had happened. The logs of the last month show 6 events delivered twice and handled twice. Of those, 2 were receipts. I sent an apology to nobody, as the customers had not complained, but I listed the invoice ids in the task for Ines.

The slow query that caused the 11 seconds is a separate topic. It is the lookup of the customer by Stripe id without an index on a new column. I have not fixed it yet.

summary: Added the missing index on customers.stripe_customer_id, which took the webhook lookup from 2.8 seconds to 3 milliseconds on the production copy.
body:
This is the slow query behind the webhook retry from earlier. The customers table has a stripe_customer_id column that was added in the payment methods work, but the migration did not create an index, and the webhook handler looks up customers by it on every event.

On a copy of production the lookup did a sequential scan over about 41,000 rows. Alone, that is fast enough, but under load with parallel events it reached 2.8 seconds in the slow cases.

I created the index with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY so that writes were not blocked. On the copy, it took 0.4 seconds. The same query now takes 3 milliseconds according to EXPLAIN ANALYZE.

I also checked other columns that are used for lookups and found two more without indexes: payment_methods.stripe_id and credit_notes.invoice_id. I added both in the same migration file, each concurrently. The migration tool does not run concurrent statements inside a transaction, so the file needed a no-transaction marker, which I added after the first run failed with the expected error message.

Deployed to production in the evening. It ran for less than two seconds in total.

summary: Planned the removal of per-run dunning email duplicates: a customer with three overdue invoices got three separate reminders, and finance wants one combined mail.
body:
A customer with three overdue invoices got three reminder emails in the same hour. Ines forwarded the complaint and agreed that one mail listing all open invoices is better.

Currently the dunning job creates one email job per invoice. The change is to group the open overdue invoices by customer inside each chunk and create one job per customer with the list of invoices. The chunking from earlier lets me do this safely only if all invoices of a customer fall in the same chunk. They may not, because chunks are by invoice id.

Options I considered. One: sort the open invoices by customer id before chunking, so that a customer's invoices are adjacent, and move the chunk boundary to the next customer change. Two: do the grouping in a second pass after all chunks. The second loses the crash resume simplicity. I prefer the first.

The resume point would then be a customer id instead of an invoice id. That changes the stored cursor, so a run in progress at deployment time would resume wrongly. I will deploy outside the run window, which is at night.

The email template needs a table of invoices with number, due date, and amount, and a total per currency. A customer with invoices in two currencies exists in the data, so the total cannot be a single number.

The dunning stages, first reminder, second, final, are per invoice. A combined mail needs a rule: I will use the most advanced stage among the invoices for the tone of the text, and mark every listed invoice as having received that stage. Mara agrees but wants the final notice never to include an invoice that is only at the first stage. I need to think about that, since mixing is exactly the case here.

The simplest rule that respects it: group by customer and stage, so a customer may get up to three mails, but only one per stage. This is still better than one per invoice. I will implement that.

summary: Decided to group dunning mails by customer and stage, and wrote the test cases before the code.
body:
Following the plan, a customer gets at most one dunning email per stage. I wrote the test cases first so the rule is clear.

Case one: three invoices, all at the first stage, give one mail with three rows. Case two: two at the first stage and one at the final stage give two mails. Case three: invoices in euro and in dollars at one stage give one mail with two totals. Case four: a run that crashes after the first customer and resumes must not send the first customer's mail again.

The fourth case depends on the resume cursor being the customer id. I wrote the test against the planned interface and it currently fails, as intended. Implementation comes next.

summary: Shipped the grouped dunning mail to production behind a setting; a customer with three overdue invoices now gets one reminder with a table of all three.
body:
Slot 16 sits between the grouping decision and the subject line fix, so this entry covers the first real implementation of the grouped reminder. The dunning job now collects the open invoices of a customer per stage and builds one email context with a list of invoices, instead of one mail per invoice. The grouping key is the customer id plus the dunning stage, so an invoice that moved to a later stage is not folded into an earlier reminder.

The test cases written beforehand helped. Five of the eight passed on the first run; the failing ones were about the order of lines in the mail and a customer with two currencies. We decided that a customer with invoices in two currencies gets one mail per currency, because a combined total would mean nothing. The invoice lines in the mail are sorted by due date, oldest first.

The Postmark template got a new block that loops over the invoices and shows number, due date and amount, plus a total line. The fallback check for template fields passed, since every field in the loop has a default. The single-invoice case still uses the same template with a loop of one, so there is only one template to keep.

On the staging copy of production data the job produced 412 mails instead of 689 for the same set of overdue invoices. One thing to watch is the retry of a failed send: it now retries the whole group, and the sent marker is written per invoice only after Postmark accepts the mail. I checked this by killing the send halfway in staging, and no invoice was marked twice.

The subject line still reads awkwardly for groups, and the German wording is not yet approved by Ines. Next I will fix the subject and send both language versions to her.

summary: Fixed the grouped dunning subject lines and got Ines to approve the wording of the multi-invoice reminder in German and English.
body:
The subject for a single invoice stays as before. For several, it is now N open invoices on your nebula account, with the German version translated by me and checked by Ines, who corrected one phrase about payment deadlines that sounded too harsh.

I rendered the mails for both languages with three invoices and with one, and sent them to a test inbox. The table looks fine in the main clients I tried, and the plain text part lists the same rows.

I noticed that the final-stage text mentions that the account may be suspended. Ines confirmed this is still the policy for final notices. Nothing changed there.

The change is deployed outside the run window. I watched the next dunning run in the logs: 212 open invoices, 148 mails, no errors. One customer received two mails because of two stages, as designed.

What remains is a note in the runbook about the cursor now being a customer id, so that anyone restarting a run by hand uses the right value.

summary: Investigated a Stripe error rate rise: 429 rate limit responses during the monthly run because the usage sync made parallel calls; added a concurrency limit of 8.
body:
The logs of the monthly run showed 190 responses with status 429 from Stripe. The SDK retried them, so nothing was lost, but the run was slower, and a few calls failed after the SDK retry limit of two.

The source was the usage sync, which updates a usage record per subscription and used Promise.all over all subscriptions of a chunk, up to 100 at once. Stripe's limit in live mode is 100 reads and 100 writes per second, and other jobs ran at the same time.

I replaced Promise.all with a small pool that allows 8 calls in flight. In staging against the Stripe test mode, which has lower limits, 1,000 updates now take 38 seconds without any 429. Before, the same test produced 60 of them.

I also raised the SDK maxNetworkRetries from 2 to 4 for this job only, through a client instance with its own option. The default client for other code stays unchanged.

The 14 calls that had failed in the last run were identified from the logs. I made a list of the subscription ids and ran the sync for them by hand. All succeeded. The customers affected had their usage recorded late but before the invoice, so no invoice was wrong.

To make this visible I added a counter for 429 responses to the metrics, read from the error type in the catch block. Next month's run will show whether the limit of 8 is right or too careful.

summary: Made the monthly invoice run resumable per step, after it stopped halfway because of a database failover and Mara had to restart it by hand from the runbook.
body:
Last night the managed database failed over during the monthly run. The run process lost its connection, crashed after the usage sync, and before invoice creation. Mara restarted it in the morning following the runbook, which worked, but it took her an hour to find out which steps had completed.

The run is a sequence: usage sync, invoice creation, PDF rendering, email sending, and the export for finance. Each step is idempotent in itself, but nothing records the progress of the whole. I added a table run_steps with run_id, step name, status, started_at and finished_at.

The runner now writes started before a step and finished after it. On start, it looks for an unfinished run in the same month. If it finds one, it skips the finished steps and continues with the first unfinished one. A step that is marked started but not finished is run again, which is safe because each step handles existing results.

I checked that claim for each step. Usage sync: it sets absolute values, so repeating is fine. Invoice creation: it checks for an existing invoice for the period and customer. PDF rendering: it overwrites the file. Emails: it checks a sent flag per invoice. Export: it writes a new file.

The emails step had a gap. The sent flag is written after Postmark accepts the message, so a crash in between could mean a duplicate mail. The window is small, a few milliseconds per mail, and I decided to accept it, but I noted it.

I wrote a test that kills the runner after each step in turn, restarts it, and checks the final state. The five cases pass. A sixth case with a crash in the middle of invoice creation, after 50 of 100, passes too, with exactly 100 invoices at the end.

The runbook page is updated: restart is now the same command as start, and there is a query that shows the step status. The old manual instructions are removed, as keeping both would confuse.

I also added a log line with the run id at each step so that the logs can be filtered. Next I want a way to alert when a run has not finished two hours after start.

summary: Added an alert for a monthly run that is unfinished two hours after its start, based on the run_steps table, and tested it with a stuck step in staging.
body:
With the step table in place, an alert is simple. A small job runs every ten minutes and looks for a run whose last step has status started and a started_at more than two hours old, or a run that has no finished_at after three hours.

When it finds one, it writes an error log with the run id and the step name, which the existing log alert sends to Mara. I did not build a separate notification channel, as the log alert already works.

I tested in staging by making the PDF step sleep forever. After two hours of simulated time, I shortened the thresholds through config for the test, the alert fired with the right step name. I then released the step and it cleared on the next check.

One false positive source: the large render lane can take a long time for huge invoices. A step of 2 hours is far longer than any render I have seen, so I left the threshold.

Thresholds are config values, RUN_STUCK_MINUTES, default 120. Deployed this evening.

summary: Answered a question from Mara about whether SEPA mandates will need their own reminder emails; not yet, but the mandate data model should leave room for it.
body:
Mara asked whether SEPA direct debit, which is coming, needs its own emails, such as a pre-notification before each debit. The rules require customers to be told the amount and date in advance, normally at least 14 days before, unless agreed otherwise in the mandate.

So yes, in practice there is a need for a pre-notification mail, and the invoice email itself can serve if it states the debit date and the mandate reference. That means the invoice template should be able to show those fields without breaking for card customers.

The payment_methods table I built earlier has a type column and a JSON field for details, so a mandate reference fits there without a migration. A debit date would be computed from the due date.

I wrote this up in a short note for the SEPA work and did not change code. The template fields come later, once the payment method itself exists. Mara agreed and put the note in the planning document.

summary: Wrote a script to compare the Postgres invoices table size per quarter and estimated 35 million rows in two years, which makes the partitioning plan more urgent.
body:
The partition planning script from last month estimated row counts per quarter, but only from invoice dates. I extended it to include the invoice_lines table, which is the real growth driver, as each invoice has on average 14 lines, with the big ones in the hundreds.

Today's numbers on a copy of production: invoices has 1.9 million rows and 1.1 GB with indexes. invoice_lines has 27 million rows and 9.4 GB with indexes. Growth over the last four quarters was about 22 percent per quarter for lines, because customers use more metered items.

If that rate holds, invoice_lines reaches around 35 million rows in two years, and the table around 25 GB. That is not extreme for Postgres, but the pain is in the queries. I ran the ten most frequent queries from the slow log through EXPLAIN. Four of them filter by customer and date range and use an index. Three scan by invoice id only, which will be fine after partitioning only if the partition key is part of the lookup.

The script's second function flagged the queries lacking the date column. There are six in the code base, mostly in the finance export and the credit note lookup I wrote last month. Credit notes find the invoice by id without a date, and that would hit every partition.

Options for handling this. One: add the invoice date to such lookups, which requires callers to know it. They mostly do, since the date is in the row they come from. Two: keep a small lookup table from invoice id to quarter. That is another table to maintain. I prefer the first for new code and the second only if a caller cannot know the date.

I also thought about what to partition. Partitioning invoices alone would not help the lines table, and partitioning lines by the invoice date needs the date copied into the line rows. That denormalization is a migration of 27 million rows. Estimated by a test on the copy: 14 minutes in batches of 100,000, without blocking writes.

No decision yet. I wrote the numbers and the six flagged queries into a planning note, and Mara will read it before we talk. The question for her is whether we partition both tables together or only invoices first.

As a side benefit, the dropped-partition approach would make data retention easy later, as old quarters could be detached and archived, but finance needs seven years, so this is not urgent.

summary: Met with Mara on the partition plan: partition invoices and invoice_lines together by quarter, copy the invoice date to lines first, and fix the six lookups before any move.
body:
Mara read the planning note and we went through it. We agreed to partition both tables, since partitioning only invoices would leave the biggest table untouched and the lines are always read together with their invoice.

The order of work we decided on has four steps. First, add an invoice_date column to invoice_lines and fill it in batches. Second, change the six lookups that lack a date so they pass it. Third, create the partitioned tables next to the old ones and copy the data. Fourth, switch over in a short window and drop the old tables later.

We discussed whether the partition key should be the invoice date or the creation time. The invoice date is what finance thinks in and is stable, while the creation time can differ at month borders because the monthly run starts late in the evening of the last day. Mara pointed out that this has caused confusion in the export before. We chose the invoice date.

Another point was primary keys. In Postgres a unique constraint on a partitioned table must include the partition key. So the primary key of invoices becomes the id together with the invoice date. Foreign keys from other tables, credit notes and payments, then need the date too, or have to be dropped and replaced by checks in code. That is a bigger change than I had assumed.

For the foreign keys, we decided that credit notes get the invoice date column, as they are new and small. For the payments table, which references the invoice by id, we will keep the id and drop the database foreign key, replacing it with a nightly check that finds orphaned rows. The nightly reconciliation job already exists, so adding a query is easy.

The invoice number side table was built for uniqueness, and it stays outside the partitioning, so the number remains unique across all quarters. That was the reason for building it that way.

I started the first step right away. The migration adds a nullable invoice_date to invoice_lines. The fill script updates in batches of 50,000 rows ordered by invoice id, with a short pause between batches so that the replication lag stays low. On the copy, the fill took 16 minutes. I will run it on production in the night.

After the fill, a second migration sets the column not null. Setting not null on a big table scans it, so I will add a check constraint as not valid first, validate it separately, and then set not null, which is quick in recent Postgres versions when a valid check exists.

I wrote the whole sequence into the planning document with the commands, so that each step can be repeated or checked by someone else.

summary: Ran the invoice_date backfill on production overnight in batches; all 27 million lines are filled, the check constraint is validated and new lines get the date from code.
body:
I started the backfill at the end of the afternoon with the batch size of 50,000 and a 200 millisecond pause. It ran for about 19 minutes in total and the replication lag stayed under two seconds the whole time.

After it finished I counted lines with a null invoice_date. The count was 312, all of them created during the run. The code did not set the date yet for new lines, so they came in with null. I deployed the change that copies the date from the invoice when a line is created, and ran the fill again for the 312 rows. Then the count was zero.

The next step was the check constraint, added as not valid and then validated. The validation took 38 seconds and did not block writes. Setting the column not null afterwards was instant.

I verified the data with a query that joins the lines to their invoices and compares the dates. Zero mismatches in 27 million rows. The query ran for about a minute on the replica.

One snag: the credit note builder from last month copies lines from the invoice and did not set the date either. The test caught it after the constraint was in place, and I fixed the builder before the deploy completed, so no row failed in production.

The next entry for this topic will be the six lookups. I listed them in the task so they are done one by one with a test each.

summary: Checked the six invoice lookups that the partition plan says must be fixed first, and found that four of them filter only by invoice id without a date.
body: After the backfill finished last night I went through the six lookups listed in the partition plan. Four of them select invoice lines by invoice id alone, which would scan every partition once the table is split. The other two already carry the invoice date: the monthly export and the dunning query. I wrote the list into the plan document with file names, for example src/invoices/lines.ts and src/pdf/loadInvoice.ts. The fix for each is to pass the invoice date along with the id, since every caller already has the invoice row loaded. Nothing was changed in code yet. Tomorrow I will start with the PDF loader, because it is the hottest path.

summary: Changed the PDF loader and the receipt email job to query invoice lines with the invoice date, so they can use partition pruning later; tests pass.
body: Two of the four lookups are done. loadInvoice in the PDF code now takes the invoice row instead of an id and filters lines by invoice_id and invoice_date. The receipt email job did the same thing through its own query, so I replaced it with the shared helper. I added a test that fails if a lines query is run without a date, using a small wrapper around the query function in the test setup. EXPLAIN on the production copy shows the same index scan as before, which is expected because the table is not partitioned yet. Two lookups remain: the credit note builder and the refund endpoint. Both read lines from a route that only gets an id from the client, so they need to load the invoice first. That is for the next session.

summary: Fixed the last two lines lookups in the credit note builder and refund endpoint by loading the invoice first, which completes the list from the partition plan.
body:
The credit note builder and the refund endpoint were the awkward two, because the client sends only a payment or invoice id. Both now load the invoice row by primary key and take the invoice_date from it. The invoice row lookup is cheap, one index hit, so the extra query costs almost nothing.

In the refund endpoint I kept the flow the same: load invoice, load lines, compute the refundable amount, call Stripe, write the credit note and queue the mail in one transaction. I only changed how the lines are loaded. The credit note builder had a second place that summed lines for the rounding remainder, and I changed that too, since it used a subquery on lines without a date.

I ran the full test suite, 412 tests, and all passed. I then ran the guard test that fails on undated lines queries. It found one more query in a script under scripts/, an old repair tool that nobody uses. I fixed it instead of excluding it, so the guard stays strict.

I also searched for raw SQL strings that mention invoice_lines in migrations and reports. The finance export has a join from invoices to lines, and the join already includes the date column through the foreign key, so it is fine. One report in reports/ageing.sql joins lines by invoice id only. I added the date there.

With this, all six lookups from the plan are changed, plus two extras found by the search. Next the partition migration itself needs a design: how to move 27 million lines and the invoices without a long lock. I will write that as a proposal and show it to Mara before anything runs.

summary: Wrote the first design for moving invoices and lines into quarterly partitions: create new partitioned tables, copy in batches, then swap names in a short lock.
body: The proposal has four steps. First create invoices_p and invoice_lines_p as partitioned tables by range on the invoice date, with partitions for every quarter from the first invoice up to two quarters ahead. Second, copy rows in batches of 50,000 by id, oldest first, with a job that can be resumed. Third, keep both tables in sync during the copy with a trigger on the old tables. Fourth, swap the names in one transaction with a short lock, which should take under a second. The risk I see is foreign keys: credit_notes, payments and invoice_numbers point to invoices, and a partitioned table needs the partition key in its primary key. That means the key becomes (id, invoice_date), and the referencing tables need the date too. I listed those tables in the document. I did not decide yet whether to add the date to them or drop the foreign keys; that is a question for Mara.

summary: Went through the partition design with Mara and decided to add invoice_date to the referencing tables and keep the foreign keys, with a rehearsal on the production copy first.
body:
Mara read the proposal and had two concerns: the foreign keys, and the trigger sync during the copy. On the keys, we compared two options. Dropping them is simple but we lose protection against orphan payments and credit notes, and finance relies on those links. Adding the date to credit_notes, payments and invoice_numbers costs a backfill, but the backfill pattern worked well for the lines, so we chose to add the column.

On the trigger, Mara was worried about write load during the monthly run, when thousands of invoices are inserted. I measured it on the production copy with a synthetic load of 5,000 inserts and the trigger added about 12 percent to the insert time. That is acceptable, and the copy would not run during the monthly run anyway.

We agreed on this order:
- add invoice_date to the three referencing tables and backfill in batches
- create the partitioned tables with composite keys
- rehearse the whole copy and swap on a fresh copy of production
- schedule the real run for a quiet period

Mara also asked what happens to the invoice number side table, because the unique number is enforced there. It has a foreign key to invoices as well, so it gets the date column like the others, and the unique index on the number stays unchanged.

We also talked about retention. Nobody wants to delete old invoices, finance must keep them for years, but partitions make it possible to move old quarters to cheaper storage later. I noted it as a possible follow-up and not part of this work.

I wrote the three migrations as drafts and ran them against the copy. The column additions took a few milliseconds because they are nullable without default. The backfill on payments, the largest of the three, will take longer; I estimated about 40 minutes from a sample.

Tomorrow I will finalize the backfill script by reusing the batch runner of the lines backfill, and run it on staging first. I left a note for Ines that no invoice data changes in this work, only structure, so the monthly check should look the same.

summary: Backfilled invoice_date on payments, credit_notes and invoice_numbers in production overnight; counts match and the check constraints are validated.
body: I reused the batch runner from the lines backfill. It updates 20,000 rows per batch, sleeps between batches and records its position, so a failure can be resumed. Payments took 38 minutes, credit_notes a few seconds, invoice_numbers about 6 minutes. After each table I ran a count of rows where the date is null and got zero, and a second check that the date equals the date on the invoice row. Both returned zero mismatches. Then I added the check constraints as NOT VALID and validated them, which does not block writes. New rows get the date from the code path, and I added tests for the payment webhook and the credit note creation to confirm it. One thing I noticed: payments created by the nightly reconciliation repair job did not set the date, and the constraint caught it in staging. I fixed the job. The referencing tables are ready for the composite keys.

summary: Rehearsed the partition copy on a fresh production copy: 27 million lines moved in 94 minutes, but the swap failed on a sequence ownership error that I fixed.
body:
I restored last night's backup into a scratch database and ran the full rehearsal. The partitioned tables were created with quarterly partitions from the first invoice to two quarters ahead, 14 in total.

The copy ran in batches of 50,000 ids. Invoices took 11 minutes and lines took 94 minutes. The trigger on the old tables kept the new ones in sync while I ran a loop of inserts and updates against the old tables to simulate live traffic. At the end, row counts matched exactly and a checksum over id and total per quarter matched as well.

The swap failed. The rename transaction ran, but the sequence for invoices.id was still owned by the old table column, so after the swap the new table had no default for id and inserts failed with a null value error. In production that would have stopped all invoicing. I fixed it in the script: before the swap, set the default of the new id column to nextval of the existing sequence and change the sequence owner to the new table.

I also found that the old table's indexes keep their names, so renaming the tables produced name clashes with the new indexes. I now name the new indexes with a _p suffix and rename them after the swap.

After fixing both, I reran the swap alone on the scratch database. The lock time was 400 milliseconds. I ran the application test suite against the swapped database with 412 tests and all passed. I also ran the monthly invoice run for a small sample of 200 customers, and the invoices, lines and numbers were created correctly.

The query plans are the part I wanted to see. The invoice list for one customer in one quarter now scans one partition. The PDF loader with the date prunes to one partition. The ageing report scans only the recent partitions for open invoices. The finance export for a full month touches one or two partitions as expected.

Open points: the rollback script needs a test, because after the swap the old tables stay under another name and the sync trigger would have to run in reverse. I will write that tomorrow and rehearse the rollback too.

summary: Wrote and rehearsed the rollback for the partition swap; renaming the old tables back works within a second if no new invoice was written in between.
body:
The rollback script has two cases. If something is wrong within minutes of the swap, I rename the tables back and the old tables are used again. For that to be safe, rows written to the new tables after the swap must also exist in the old ones. So after the swap I keep a reverse trigger on the new tables that copies inserts and updates into the old ones. I wrote that trigger and tested it on the scratch database with 2,000 writes after the swap.

The second case is a problem found later, when the reverse trigger has been dropped. Then rollback means copying the new rows back, which I described in the runbook but do not plan to automate.

I rehearsed case one: swap, run 500 inserts through the application, rename back, and check that all 500 invoices are in the old tables. They were. The rollback took 700 milliseconds of lock time.

One detail needed care: the sequence default has to move back as well. I added it to the script.

The runbook now has a checklist with steps for before, during and after, and the commands for each. Mara will review it. I also listed the checks to run right after the swap: row counts per quarter, a test invoice, a test refund and a test credit note.

I will propose a quiet period for the real run to Mara and Ines, since the monthly run must not overlap.

summary: Answered Ines on why a customer's receipt shows a total one cent different from the invoice: the receipt rounded the sum, the invoice rounded each line.
body:
Ines sent an example of a customer where the receipt email says 119.04 and the invoice PDF says 119.05. I took the invoice and looked at its lines. There were seven lines with VAT, and each line total carries fractions of a cent in the calculation. The invoice rounds each line and adds them. The receipt template computes the sum first and rounds once. With these seven lines the two methods differ by one cent.

This is the same type of problem Ines has found in the monthly check before: totals that are 1 cent off. It is not new data corruption, it is two code paths with different rounding rules. I looked for others and found three places that compute totals: the invoice builder, the receipt template and the credit note builder. Only the invoice builder is the reference, because the PDF is the legal document.

I told Ines that the invoice figure is the right one and that the receipt will be corrected, but I did not change anything in the rounding rules yet because the accountants have not decided on the rule. I opened a task to make the receipt read the stored total instead of computing it. That is a safe change on its own, since it shows exactly what the invoice says. I checked the last month of receipts: 41 of 6,200 differ from their invoice by one cent, so it is rare.

summary: Made the receipt email show the stored invoice total instead of computing it again, and checked a month of receipts against invoices with no differences left.
body:
The receipt template had its own function that summed the line amounts and applied VAT. I removed it and made the template use invoice.total, invoice.vat_total and the stored line amounts. The credit note builder stays as it is for now, since it has its own rule about the remainder on the last line, accepted by Mara earlier.

I wrote a test with the seven line invoice from Ines' example. Before the change the receipt showed 119.04 and after it shows 119.05, the same as the PDF. I also added a test that renders the receipt for ten random invoices from a fixture and compares the total string with the invoice total.

Then I ran a check over the production copy: render the receipt data for every invoice of last month and compare with the stored totals. Of 6,200 invoices, zero differ now. Before the change there were 41.

I deployed it to staging, sent a test receipt to a Postmark sandbox style address and looked at the result. The email provider does not matter here, since only the template data changed. After that it went to production in the afternoon deploy.

I told Ines in the finance channel. She asked whether receipts already sent will be corrected. They will not be resent, because the customer already has the right invoice PDF, and I think sending a second receipt would confuse people. She agreed and will tell the accountants.

The larger question remains how each line should round. That depends on the accountants' answer, and I will not touch the invoice builder before it comes.

summary: Chose a quiet window for the partition swap with Mara and Ines: after the monthly run is verified and before the next usage sync starts.
body: Mara and I looked at the load graphs for the last three months. The quietest time for the API is early morning on the second day after the monthly run, when finance has finished their checks. Ines confirmed that her check of the invoices will be done by then and that she will not export data during the swap. The plan is to start the copy the evening before and do the swap at the quiet time. I will watch the run myself. I also decided that the usage sync job will be paused for the swap, which only takes a few minutes, because it writes to invoices through the draft invoice path. Mara will be on call in case the rollback is needed.

summary: Upgraded the Stripe SDK from v15 to v16 in a branchless step on main, fixing two typing changes in the webhook handler and one in the customer sync.
body:
The upgrade had little in it. The changelog of v16 changes some types for expanded objects and moves a few deprecated fields. I bumped the package, ran the type check and got eleven errors, all in three files.

In the webhook handler, event.data.object for invoice events is now typed more strictly, so I added narrowing by event type before reading fields. In the customer sync, the default_source field was typed as possibly an object, and I added a check for the string id case. In the refund code, the charge field on a refund may be an id or an expanded object, and I wrote a small helper to get the id in both cases.

The pagination shims stay in place. They wrap the old auto-pagination calls, and the new SDK still works with them. I wrote a note in the shim files that they are needed because of the way list calls return pages, so nobody removes them by accident.

I ran the whole test suite, which uses recorded Stripe responses, and all 412 passed. Then I ran the webhook tests against the Stripe CLI in test mode, with events for payment_intent.succeeded, invoice.paid, charge.refunded and customer.subscription.updated. All were processed.

The warnings about the charges list call are gone, since the reconciliation already uses payment intents.

I deployed to staging and left it for the afternoon. A trial signup and a payment with a test card worked. Production will follow after the swap, because I do not want two risky changes in the same week.

summary: Prepared the production partition swap of invoices and lines, with the final checks and the go/no-go list written down but nothing swapped yet.
body:
I spent the evening getting ready for the partition swap and did not run it. The rehearsal on the production copy showed that the copy and the swap work, so this session was about the checks around them.

I wrote the verification script that I will run right before the swap: row counts per quarter, a checksum over id and total, and a comparison of the three referencing tables with their date columns. I ran it against the rehearsal copy and everything matched. I also made it print a short summary that I can paste to Mara and Ines.

Then I wrote the swap runbook as a numbered list. Pause the usage sync, wait until the job runner is idle, run the swap script, rename the indexes, check the sequence default, and create a test invoice, a test refund and a credit note for an internal customer. Each step has the command and the expected output next to it. The rollback from the previous entry is the last item, with the condition that it only works within a second if no new invoice was written in between.

I looked at the query plans on the rehearsal copy for the main lookups. The customer invoice list and the PDF loader with a date each scan one partition. The dunning query and the ageing report scan the two newest partitions, which is what I expected.

Things I noticed:
- autovacuum settings on the partitions use the defaults, which is fine for old partitions but the newest one will get many updates
- the partition creation for future quarters is not automated, so I need a job and an alert for it
- pg_dump will take a bit longer because of the number of tables, not a problem

Nothing in production changed today. Next I will agree the exact start of the copy with Mara and ask Ines to keep last month's export for comparing after the swap.

summary: Prepared the follow-up work for the partition swap: a job to create future invoice partitions, an alert for missing ones, and checks of the old and new tables, with the swap itself still ahead.
body:
Overnight nothing odd happened. The error log has no database errors, and the monthly reconciliation of invoices against Stripe payment intents found no mismatch. I used the quiet morning to prepare what has to be ready before the partition swap, which has not happened yet. The invoices table is still one big table, and the partitioned copies exist only as a design and a staging test.

I wrote the partition job as a small pg-boss task named ensure_partitions, scheduled to run on the first day of each month. It checks the latest partition end date and creates quarters until there are four ahead. The create statement uses IF NOT EXISTS, so running it twice does no harm. I wrote it for both invoices and invoice_lines. It is not scheduled on production yet, only in staging.

The alert checks the same thing from the other side: it reads the partition list from the catalog and fires when fewer than two future quarters exist. I tested it in staging by dropping a future partition by hand, and the alert fired within a minute of the check running.

I also tested what happens when an invoice with a date beyond the last partition is inserted into the staging copy. Postgres raises an error that no partition was found. In the application that would be a failed monthly run, so the alert matters. I added a test that the error is logged with the invoice id so it can be found.

For autovacuum, I drafted a fillfactor and a lower scale factor for the current quarter partitions, to be set through the same job, since the newest partitions are updated the most when invoices go from draft to paid. The older ones keep the defaults.

I checked sizes in the staging copy: the biggest partition has about 4.5 million lines, and queries on it are fast. The total size on disk is the same as before, as expected.

I put a note in the task list for after the swap: keep the old tables under the names invoices_old and invoice_lines_old for a week, then drop them. Next: agree the quiet window for the swap with Mara and Ines.

summary: Deployed the Stripe v16 upgrade to production and watched webhooks for two hours; no handler errors, and one test refund went through.
body:
With the partition work settled, I released the SDK upgrade that had waited on staging. The deploy was in the late morning. I watched the logs for webhook errors, the rate of Stripe API errors, and the job runner failures.

In two hours the handler processed about 340 events with no errors. The usage sync made its calls with the concurrency limit of 8 and got no 429 responses. A customer paid an invoice with a card and the invoice.paid event came through and sent the receipt.

I made a test refund of 1.00 on an internal invoice. The refund helper that handles the charge field as id or object worked, and the credit note and its email were created in the same transaction as before.

One thing to remember: the SDK now logs a warning for an API version mismatch, because our account is pinned to an older API version. The SDK works with it, but this should be looked at in a later upgrade. I wrote it down in the notes for the next one.

The pagination shims are still in use and work with v16. Nothing to do there for now.

summary: Investigated slow invoice PDFs for invoices with many lines: rendering time grows faster than linearly, and a 600-line invoice takes 38 seconds mostly in the browser layout.
body:
After the render lanes the big invoices no longer block small ones, but a customer with a 600-line invoice still waits long, and Ines asked whether it can be faster. I measured rendering for invoices of 50, 100, 200, 400 and 600 lines on my machine, using the same headless browser and template as production.

The times were 2.1, 3.4, 7.9, 19 and 38 seconds. That is clearly worse than linear. I took a profile of the 600-line case. About 30 seconds are spent in layout, not in our code or the database. The database part, loading the invoice and lines, is 80 milliseconds.

I tried three things with the template to see what changes:
- removing the box shadow and border radius on the line rows: 38 down to 35 seconds, small effect
- replacing the table with fixed row heights: 38 down to 17 seconds
- splitting the lines into pages in our code, one table per page, and letting the browser print them: 38 down to 11 seconds

The page splitting gives the best result, because the browser no longer calculates the page breaks for one huge table. But it changes where page breaks fall, and the invoice has a header and a repeated column header on each page. I would need to reproduce those by hand.

I also looked at memory: the browser process grows to 1.4 GB during the 600-line render. In production the render workers have a limit, and I saw two out-of-memory restarts in the log for last month, which probably were big invoices.

There is a different approach: a new renderer that does not use the browser for the table at all, only for the header, or a native PDF library. That is a bigger project, and I will write it as an option, not as a decision.

For now I think the page-splitting change is the quickest improvement. I did not change the production template. I wrote the numbers and the three experiments in the notes, and I will ask Mara which of the two directions she prefers before spending more time.

To reproduce: scripts/render-bench.ts takes a line count and writes the time per stage.

summary: Decided with Mara to try page splitting in the existing template first, and implemented it behind a config switch; a 600-line invoice now renders in 12 seconds.
body:
Mara looked at the benchmark numbers and agreed that page splitting is the cheaper first step, and that a new renderer should wait until we know whether it is needed. We decided to put the change behind a setting, pdf_split_pages, off by default, so we can compare output.

The implementation chunks the lines into groups of 40 per page for invoices above the lane threshold of 150 lines. Each chunk is rendered as its own table with the column header repeated. The first page has the full header with customer address and invoice number, the later pages have a short header. The totals block goes on the last page.

The difficult part was the page count in the footer, "page 2 of 9". With separate chunks I know the number of pages in advance, so I compute it in our code and write it into the footer, which removes the dependency on the browser counter.

I tested with 150, 151, 400 and 600 lines. Times were 4.5, 4.7, 8 and 12 seconds with the setting on. Memory in the 600-line case went from 1.4 GB to 600 MB.

Then I compared the output visually. I rendered 20 large invoices from the production copy with and without the setting and put the PDFs side by side. The differences are the page breaks, which were uneven before. Amounts, numbers and totals are identical. I also extracted the text of both versions and diffed the numbers: the same.

Two small problems came up. A line with a very long description wraps to three rows and a 40-line page can overflow, so I added a rule that counts wrapped rows by description length. The second is the credit note, which uses the same template; it works, since it goes through the same code.

I added unit tests for the chunking, including the empty case and the exact multiple of 40.

The setting is off in production. Next I plan to enable it for the slow lane only on a canary and watch the timing.

summary: Enabled pdf_split_pages for the slow lane on production; the first monthly run with it rendered 31 big invoices, the longest in 13 seconds, with no failures.
body:
I turned the setting on for the slow lane just before the monthly run. The run created 6,300 invoices, and 31 of them were above the 150-line threshold. The slowest was a 640-line invoice that rendered in 13 seconds, where earlier a similar invoice needed about 40.

The slow lane finished in under 4 minutes in total. There were no out-of-memory restarts of the render workers this time. I checked the PDF sizes and they were similar to before, within 5 percent.

I asked Ines to look at three of the big invoices. She said the layout looks fine and that she likes the repeated column header on each page, which the old one lacked on some page breaks. She will tell me if the accountants complain.

I saved the benchmark results to the notes. A new renderer is not needed for now, but I kept the idea in the task list because the browser dependency remains the heaviest part of the service.

summary: Answered a customer support question about a failed SEPA-style payment retry: the customer had a card declined three times and the dunning stopped after the third attempt by design.
body:
Support forwarded a question from a customer whose invoice stayed open although he had added a new card. I looked at the payment attempts for the invoice. There were three failed charges, with decline code insufficient_funds, spread over seven days, which is our retry schedule. After the third failure the invoice goes to the final dunning stage and no more automatic retries run.

The new card was added after that, so nothing tried to charge it. The customer can pay through the link in the dunning mail, or we can trigger a retry by hand. I used the admin endpoint to retry the invoice with the new card, and it was paid on the first try. The receipt was sent right away.

This showed a gap: adding a payment method does not trigger a retry for open invoices that are in the final stage. I wrote a task for it, with the proposal to retry once when a new default payment method is attached and the customer has overdue invoices. It needs a limit so that it cannot loop.

I replied to support with the explanation and the steps for the customer.

summary: Implemented a single retry of overdue invoices when a customer attaches a new default payment method, guarded so it runs at most once per invoice and method.
body:
The webhook for customer.updated tells us when the default payment method changes. I added a handler that checks whether the customer has overdue invoices and queues a retry job for each one. The job charges the new method and records the attempt with the method id.

The guard is a table, retry_on_new_method, with a unique key of invoice id and payment method id. The insert fails if there already was an attempt with that method, so the same method is never tried twice for the same invoice. That also covers the case where Stripe sends the event twice, together with the event id table I added earlier.

I wrote tests for four cases: new method with one overdue invoice, with three, with none, and a repeated event. In the Stripe test mode I attached a card that works and watched the invoice become paid, then a card that is declined and saw the attempt recorded but no loop.

The dunning stage is not changed by the retry. If it fails, the invoice stays where it was. If it succeeds, the normal paid path runs and cancels the next reminder.

I deployed it behind a setting, off for now. I will turn it on after Ines has seen the wording of the receipts it may trigger.

summary: Prepared the move of the invoices table to partitions by checking the table, its readers and a rehearsal plan, without moving anything yet.
body:
The invoices table is still a single unpartitioned table, and the old and new layouts do not exist side by side yet. Today I only prepared the partition move and changed nothing in production.

I first checked what reads from invoices and invoice_lines. pg_stat_user_tables shows a steady stream of sequential scans from the monthly finance export and the reconciliation job, and index scans from the API. I also searched the code for direct references to the two table names and listed every query that filters by date, because those are the ones that will benefit from reading a single partition. Several referencing tables, such as the payment attempts and the credit notes, do not carry the invoice date, so a partition key of (id, invoice_date) will need that column added to them. I wrote that down as a separate step.

I wrote the plan for the move. It creates the partitioned tables with one partition per quarter, adds a helper function that creates upcoming partitions ahead of time, and copies the rows quarter by quarter in a job that runs at night. The current quarter comes last, together with a short write pause. A test copy of the lines table into a scratch database took a little over an hour, and the new tables would need about 38 GB of extra room on the database volume, which fits. The rollback section of the runbook is still a stub, and I drafted a note saying that until the swap the old tables stay untouched, so a rollback is only a rename.

I ran the reconciliation job and the finance export against the scratch copy as a dry check. The export for the last month matches the one from production, row for row.

I also looked at index sizes. Some secondary indexes, for example the one on status, are rarely used on old rows. For closed quarters all invoices are paid or void, so a partial index could be smaller. I did not change anything and noted it as possible savings.

I started a docs page about the partition scheme, covering the key and why every referencing table needs the date. It is not finished yet. I will talk to Mara about the date of the move before I do anything.

summary: Reviewed the dunning and receipt emails after a month of Postmark-free spam complaints still trickling in, and found that the links in the reminder mail point to a domain without SPF alignment.
body:
Support keeps getting a few reports a week that reminders and receipts land in spam, even though most receipts arrive. I took ten reported cases and looked at the headers the customers sent us. Eight were mails from the dunning flow, two were receipts.

In the headers, the SPF check passes for the sending domain, but the DKIM signature uses the domain of the email provider and not ours, so DMARC alignment fails in strict mode for some receivers. That is a setup problem of the sending domain and not of the code. The receipts are less affected because they have fewer links and less marketing wording.

I also read the reminder template. The reminder mail has a large red button, three links to the same payment page, and a subject with the word URGENT in the final stage. These things hurt reputation with the filters. I counted the links: five in total, with a tracking redirect on each.

I listed what could be done:
- set up our own DKIM key for the sending domain at the provider
- turn off click tracking for transactional mails
- remove the word URGENT from the subject of the final stage
- reduce the links to one payment link and one link to the invoice

The first needs DNS changes that Mara or the ops side makes. The others are in the templates and the settings, so I can do them.

I checked the tracking setting in the provider account: click tracking is on for the stream used by billing. That means every link is rewritten to a tracking domain, which is a known cause for spam scoring. I wrote this down with the sample headers as the main suspect.

I did not change anything yet. First I want the wording of the subject approved by Ines, since she approved the existing German and English texts, and I want Mara to decide about DNS.

summary: Turned off click tracking on the billing mail stream and reduced the reminder mail to two links; test mails to three mailbox providers landed in the inbox.
body:
Mara agreed with the plan for the quick parts and said she will handle the DKIM records herself this week. I disabled click tracking for the billing stream in the provider settings and removed the extra links from the reminder template. It now has one payment link, the button, and one link to the invoice PDF.

I sent test reminders in both languages to test accounts at three large mailbox providers. All three arrived in the inbox, not in spam. The links are now direct URLs on our own domain. I checked the rendering on a phone and on a desktop client and the layout was fine.

I did not change the subject yet because Ines has to approve it. I sent her the proposal: the final stage subject without the word URGENT, using the invoice count and the amount instead. She will answer after her morning check.

summary: Changed the final dunning subject lines after Ines approved them and added a test that the grouped mail contains no more than two links; a first week of data will show the effect on spam reports.
body:
Ines answered with a small change: she wants the German text to say "Zahlungserinnerung" in the final stage, and not the shorter word I had proposed. I applied her wording for both languages and kept the amount and the invoice count in the subject, for example "Final reminder: 3 open invoices, 412.50 EUR".

The template test now renders the grouped mail for one invoice and for three, and counts the links in the HTML. It fails when there are more than two, so nobody adds a tracking style link again by accident. I also added a check that the subject has no all-capital word longer than three letters, which is a bit crude but catches the case that started this.

I ran the dunning job in staging with a customer with three overdue invoices at each stage. The mail was grouped as before, with the table of three invoices, and the subject changed as intended in all stages.

Then I deployed. The next dunning run is tomorrow morning, and I will look at the delivery and complaint numbers in the provider dashboard over the next week. For comparison I wrote down the current numbers: about 4 spam reports per 1,000 reminders over the last month.

Mara has not yet set up the DKIM key, so I cannot judge the effect of the templates and the tracking change alone. I decided to wait for her change before drawing conclusions, and to compare the week before, the week after my change and the week after hers.

I also added a line to the notes about the stream settings, so the next person knows that click tracking should stay off for transactional billing mail.

summary: Checked the first day of spam-report data after the dunning mail change; reports fell from about 14 per thousand to 3, and the remaining ones come from one mailbox provider.
body:
Pulled the Postmark stream statistics for the billing stream after the click tracking change and the two-link limit. Spam complaints were about 14 per thousand sends in the week before and 3 per thousand since the change, though only a day of data exists so far.

Most of the remaining complaints come from a single mailbox provider, and they all concern the final dunning mail. I read the text of that mail again and found that it still opens with a long block of capital letters in the subject, which Ines had approved but which looks like a classic spam pattern.

I wrote down the numbers in the notes file for the mail stream and did not change any template today. The plan is to wait for a full week, then compare the final dunning mail against the first reminder per provider. If the capital letters still look like the cause, I will ask Ines for a softer subject.

I also checked that the bounce handling still marks hard bounces on the customer record. It does, and 11 addresses were flagged this week. Those customers will not get further reminders until someone fixes the address.

One open point is whether the plain text part of the mail should carry the same two links. It currently has three because the footer adds an unsubscribe-style link for the account settings page. I left it as is and noted it for the review next week.

summary: Added a test and a fix for invoice numbers that skipped a value when an invoice run rolled back, so the numbering stays gap free for the accountants.
body:
Ines asked yesterday why invoice number 20418 was missing in the last run. The cause was the invoice_numbers sequence: the number is taken from a Postgres sequence inside the step transaction, and when the step rolled back after the database failover retry, the number was lost.

Gaps in invoice numbers are a problem for the accountants, so a sequence is the wrong tool. I replaced it with a counter row per year and series that is locked with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE inside the same transaction as the invoice insert. A rollback now gives the number back automatically.

The cost is that two invoices in the same series are now written one after the other. I measured the monthly run on the staging copy: 4,100 invoices took 6 seconds more than before, which is fine.

I wrote a test that forces a failure after the number is taken and checks that the next invoice gets the same number. A second test runs 20 parallel inserts and checks that the numbers are consecutive and unique.

The existing gap at 20418 stays. Ines will note it for the accountants with a short explanation, and I added the number to a table of known gaps so the verification query does not flag it every month.

The change is deployed to staging only. Production follows after the next monthly run is verified, so no run starts on the new code halfway.

summary: Deployed the gap-free invoice numbering to production and confirmed it with a small manual run of ten invoices; the numbers were consecutive.
body:
The monthly run is verified and Ines signed it off this afternoon, so I deployed the counter row change for invoice numbers to production.

To check it, I created ten test invoices for the internal demo customer in a separate series. The numbers came out consecutive. I then killed one step in the middle on purpose with a statement timeout and the next invoice reused the number.

I also checked the lock time. The counter row was held for 2 to 3 milliseconds per invoice, so there is no visible contention with the regular invoice creation from the API.

The known gaps table now holds the one gap at 20418. The verification query that Ines uses ignores numbers from that table and reported zero gaps afterwards.

One thing remains: the credit note numbers use the same old sequence. They are less strict for the accountants, but I will move them in a later change so both series behave the same. I wrote this in the todo list.

summary: Answered Mara about whether a Stripe list call needs the manual pagination loop; with SDK v16 auto pagination works, but our shim still wraps it.
body:
Mara asked why the customer sync still has its own pagination loop with starting_after when the SDK has autoPagingToArray. I looked at the code and at the git history of the helper.

The helper was written for SDK v13, where auto pagination on some list calls hit a typing problem. In v16 the typing is fine and autoPagingEach works on customers, subscriptions and payment methods.

I tried replacing the loop in a scratch copy for the customer sync. It worked, but the shim also adds a small pause between pages to stay under the rate limit, and the SDK does not do that for us.

So the answer is that the shim is not needed for correctness any more, but the rate limit pause is still useful. I will not remove it now, because the next SDK upgrades will touch the same code anyway. I noted it in the upgrade checklist.

summary: Looked at a slow query in the usage meter report and cut it from 9 seconds to 400 milliseconds with a composite index on customer and period.
body:
The usage report page in the internal admin was taking about 9 seconds for large customers. I ran EXPLAIN ANALYZE on the query and saw a sequential scan on usage_counts, which has about 60 million rows.

The query filters by customer_id and a period range, and sorts by period. The existing index was only on period, so Postgres filtered the customer after the scan.

I added a composite index on (customer_id, period) with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY. It took 11 minutes in production and did not block writes.

After the index, the same query runs in about 400 milliseconds for the largest customer. The old period index is still used by the nightly sync, so I kept it.

I checked the disk use, and the new index adds 2.1 GB. That is acceptable for now.

summary: Reviewed the tests of the dunning flow and found that three of them depended on the real clock; they now use a fake clock and run in a fraction of the time.
body:
While waiting for the spam data, I went through the dunning tests because one of them failed on the CI machine last night and passed again on a re-run. It checked that the second reminder is sent three days after the first, and it used the real time with a margin.

I searched for the same pattern and found three tests that read the system clock: the second reminder test, the final notice test and the test for the retry after a new payment method. All three now take the time from a small clock object that the job runner already supports in its options.

The tests now set the clock to a fixed instant and move it forward by days. They no longer sleep or compare against the current time. This also removed a one-second sleep in the final notice test.

The whole dunning suite took 41 seconds before and now takes 6 seconds. The number of assertions is the same, and I added one for the case when the reminder time falls on the daylight saving change in Europe.

That case showed a real problem. The reminder was computed by adding 72 hours, so in the week of the clock change the mail came an hour early in local time. For customers it is not important, but the finance team wants the mails in the morning. I changed the calculation to add three calendar days in the customer's time zone.

I ran the suite 50 times in a loop on CI to check for flakiness and saw no failures. The change is merged on main. Next I will look at the tests for the usage sync, which use sleeps too.

summary: Investigated why one EU customer got a VAT line on an invoice despite a valid VAT id; the id was validated once and expired in the cache after the invoice was drafted.
body:
Ines forwarded a question from a customer in Austria who received an invoice with 20 percent VAT even though the company had a valid VAT id on file. She wanted to know if reverse charge had failed.

I looked at the customer record. The VAT id was stored and marked valid. The invoice was drafted at the start of the monthly run, but the tax step runs later and asks the VAT validation cache. The cache entry had a time to live of 30 days and had expired three days before the run.
