When the cache entry is gone, the tax step calls the VIES service. On that day VIES returned a timeout, and our code treated the timeout like an invalid id. The result was normal VAT.

This is wrong in two ways. A timeout says nothing about the validity of the id. And a monthly invoice should not change its tax treatment because a remote service was slow.

I changed the tax step so that a timeout or a service error keeps the last known status of the id. Only a definite answer of invalid changes it. If there is no earlier status at all, the invoice step fails and the step is retried later by the runner.

I added three tests: a valid id with a timeout, an id that was valid and is now answered as invalid, and a new id with a timeout. The second case produces normal VAT and sends a note to finance.

For the affected customer, the invoice has to be corrected. I prepared a credit note and a new invoice with reverse charge, and left them as drafts for Ines to check. I did not send anything to the customer.

I also searched the last three months for the same cause. Two other invoices had the same pattern, both for small amounts. I put their numbers in the note for Ines.

The fix is merged, and the monitoring now counts VIES errors per day so we can see if the service is often down.

summary: Ines approved the corrected invoices for the three EU customers hit by the VIES timeout, and I sent the credit notes and new invoices.
body:
Ines checked the drafts this morning and approved all three corrections. One of them needed a change of the customer address line, which she fixed in the customer record first.

I sent the credit notes and the new reverse charge invoices through the normal job, so the numbers come from the gap-free counter. The receipts were not sent again, because the payments themselves did not change.

The Austrian customer replied within an hour and thanked us. The refund of the VAT difference goes back to the card automatically through the credit note flow.

I checked in Stripe that the three refunds were created and had status succeeded. They show up in the payments table with the credit note reference.

Nothing is left open for this case. The VIES error counter shows two timeouts since the fix, and both kept the old status.

summary: Upgraded the test fixtures for Stripe webhooks so they are signed with a real signature helper, after a handler change passed tests but failed against staging.
body:
Yesterday a small change in the webhook handler passed all tests and then failed in staging with a signature error. The reason was that the tests posted events with a fake header and the handler had a test bypass, which hid a problem with the raw body.

I removed the bypass. The tests now create the signed header with stripe.webhooks.generateTestHeaderString and send the raw body exactly as it was signed.

This showed that two older tests parsed the body first and sent it again as JSON, which changes the whitespace. Those tests had been passing only because of the bypass. I fixed them to send the raw string.

I also added a test with a wrong secret and one with a body that was changed by one character. Both get a 400.

The suite runs in the same time as before. The staging webhook endpoint now accepts a replayed test event from the Stripe dashboard.

summary: Moved the credit note numbers to the same gap-free counter as the invoices, with a test for rollback and parallel inserts.
body:
The invoice numbers got the counter row change a few days ago, and credit notes still used the old sequence. I moved them to the same mechanism with their own series.

The code is shared now, so both series use one function that locks the counter row. I copied the two tests for rollback and parallel inserts and ran them for credit notes.

The current value of the credit note sequence was copied into the counter row inside a migration. I checked it against the highest number in the credit_notes table, and they matched.

The change is deployed to staging and will go to production with the next release.

summary: Looked into why the receipt PDF attachment is sometimes empty and found that the job reads the file before the upload to storage is complete.
body:
Support got two reports of receipt emails with an attachment of zero bytes. I looked at the receipt job and the PDF job in the logs for the two cases.

Both cases had the same pattern. The PDF job wrote to object storage and published a done event. The receipt job started on the event and downloaded the file, but the storage client had returned before the upload was committed, because the code did not wait for the final promise of the upload stream.

The bug is a missing await in the upload helper. It only shows when the storage is slow, which happened twice in the last week.

I added the await and a check in the receipt job that the file size is greater than zero. If it is not, the job fails and is retried by pg-boss after a minute.

I wrote a test with a storage stub that delays the commit by 200 milliseconds. Before the fix it produced an empty file, afterwards it did not.

The two affected customers need their receipts sent again. I queued them by hand, and both mails went out with a correct attachment.

summary: Planned the removal of old Stripe API version pins after the v16 upgrade and listed which calls still send an explicit apiVersion header.
body:
After the v16 upgrade, I wanted to know where the code still fixes the Stripe API version, because mixing pins is a typical source of surprises for the next upgrade. I searched the repository for apiVersion and for raw HTTP calls to api.stripe.com.

There are four places. The main client in stripe.ts sets the version that matches the SDK. The webhook endpoint in the Stripe dashboard has its own version, which is older by two releases. A small script for the monthly reconciliation uses fetch with a hard coded header. And the test helper creates a second client with the default version.

The webhook endpoint version is the most important one. Events are sent in the shape of that version, and the handler has a few lines that read old field names. If we change the dashboard version, those lines break.

I wrote a list of the event types the handler uses: invoice.paid, invoice.payment_failed, charge.refunded, customer.subscription.updated and payment_method.attached. For each one I compared the old and the new shape in the changelog.

Only charge.refunded and invoice.payment_failed differ in a way that matters. The refund object has a changed field for the reason, and the failed payment event no longer carries one nested object that we read.

The plan has three steps. First, make the handler accept both shapes. Second, deploy and watch for a few days. Third, change the version of the endpoint in the dashboard and later remove the old field handling.

I also replaced the fetch call in the reconciliation script with the SDK client, so there is one place that fixes the version. I ran the script against the test account and the output was the same as before.

The handler change is the next piece of work. I wrote tests for both shapes from saved sample events before touching it.

summary: Made the webhook handler accept both the old and the new shape of refund and failed payment events, ahead of changing the endpoint API version.
body:
This is the first step of the plan for the endpoint version. I saved sample events from the Stripe dashboard in both versions for charge.refunded and invoice.payment_failed and put them in the test fixtures.

For the refund event, the handler read the reason from one field. In the new shape it is in a different place. I wrote a small function that looks in both places and returns a normalized reason. The rest of the handler only uses the normalized value.

For the failed payment event, the handler read the error code from a nested object that is gone in the new shape. The code now takes the error from the last payment attempt of the invoice, which is available in both. For the new shape, this needs one more API call to fetch the payment intent, so I added it with an expand parameter on the invoice fetch we already make.

I checked the cost of the extra expand. It does not add a request, and the response is a little larger. The handler time went from about 90 to 110 milliseconds in the staging load test.

The tests now run every sample event through the handler and compare the resulting database changes. The old and new shape give the same result for all five event types.

There was one surprise. The dunning code checks the error code to decide whether a failure is hard, for example a stolen card, or soft, for example insufficient funds. With the new source of the code, one test case gave soft instead of hard for a card marked as lost. The reason was that the last attempt object uses decline_code and not code.

I fixed the mapping and added a test for lost and stolen cards, and for insufficient funds.

The handler is deployed to staging. I sent test events with both shapes from the Stripe CLI, and the database state was right in both cases. Production follows tomorrow, and then I wait a few days before the dashboard change.

summary: Deployed the dual shape webhook handler to production and changed the endpoint API version in the dashboard after a day of clean events.
body:
The handler with both shapes ran in production for a day with no errors in the logs. The count of processed events per type was normal, and no event ended in the retry queue.

Before changing the version, I made a new webhook endpoint in the dashboard for the new API version, pointing to the same URL with a different path suffix, rather than editing the existing one. That gives a safe way to compare and to go back.

I sent both endpoints to the handler for an hour. Each event arrived twice, once in each shape. The handler already ignores events it has seen, based on the event id stored in the webhook_events table. But the ids differ between endpoints, so I looked at what the idempotency really depends on.

It depends on the object. For invoice.paid the update is a set to paid, so a repeat is harmless. For charge.refunded the handler writes a refund row keyed by the refund id, with a unique constraint, so a repeat does nothing. I checked all five types and found that each is safe for a repeat.

After an hour I compared the database state with a query: no differences between what the two shapes caused. I then disabled the old endpoint and kept it for a week, not deleted.

The retry behavior is unchanged. A failed event is retried by Stripe for three days, and our handler returns 500 only on database errors.

The signature secret is different for the new endpoint, so I added it to the configuration as a second secret and the handler tries both for now. I will remove the old secret together with the old endpoint.

Next week I want to remove the code for the old shape, once the old endpoint is deleted. I put this on the list.

summary: Retired the leftover Stripe event shape from the retry path of failed payments, so the handler and its tests now speak only the new webhook format.
body:
After the endpoint moved to the new API version, the retry path for failed payments still carried a branch for the old event shape. I removed that branch from the webhook handler and from the helper that reads the failure reason, and deleted the two fixtures that only existed for it. The remaining tests use the signed fixtures and still cover the declined card, the expired card and the insufficient funds cases.

I also searched the logs of the last week for events that took the old branch and found none. The change is small, but it makes the handler easier to read before the next SDK work. Next I want to check the refund events the same way and then list the explicit apiVersion headers that are still sent.

summary: Removed the old webhook secret and the deleted endpoint after a week without events on it, leaving one endpoint and one secret.
body:
The old webhook endpoint had received no events since it was disabled, which I checked in the dashboard delivery log. I deleted it.

In the code, I removed the second secret from the configuration and changed the handler to verify with one secret only. The test for a wrong secret still returns 400.

I also deleted the old field handling for the refund reason and the failed payment error, since events now come only in the new shape. The helper functions are gone and the handler is about 60 lines shorter.

The saved sample events in the old shape stay in the fixtures folder under a legacy name, in case we need to replay something old from the logs. The tests no longer use them.

I deployed this to production and watched the handler for an hour: 212 events, no errors.

The Stripe API version pins are now consistent in all four places that I listed, so the next SDK upgrade has one thing less to check.

summary: Reviewed the monthly run timing and found that the PDF step now takes 70 percent of the run, mostly the big invoices in the slow lane.
body:
I looked at the run_steps table for the last three monthly runs to see where the time goes. The whole run takes about 2 hours 10 minutes now.

The PDF step takes 1 hour 31 minutes of that. Invoice creation takes 14 minutes, tax 6 minutes, emails 11 minutes and the rest is small.

In the PDF step, the slow lane with big invoices handles only 31 invoices but takes 24 minutes, because each one needs 12 to 13 seconds even with page splitting. The normal lane handles 4,000 invoices in about an hour, with 4 workers.

The headless browser is the limit. Each render starts a page, loads the template and waits for fonts. About 40 percent of the time of a normal invoice is that startup and not the layout.

I tried reusing the same browser page for several invoices in a scratch test. It brought a normal invoice from 0.9 to 0.55 seconds, but memory grew with each render and the process had to be restarted after about 200 invoices.

That is a possible small gain, but it adds a restart logic with a risk of stuck renders. The better answer may be a different renderer, which I have not started to plan. I noted the numbers for a later discussion with Mara.

For now, nothing is changed in the code. I added the step durations to the dashboard of the run so the trend is visible each month.

summary: Went through the monthly run timing after the PDF step grew to most of the run, and set out three options for the big invoices, starting with a bigger slow lane.
body:
The monthly run had been taking longer each cycle, and the earlier review showed the PDF step at about 70 percent of it. Today I measured the step per invoice size to see where the time really goes. Invoices with fewer than 50 lines render in under 2 seconds and make up almost all of the count. The 31 or so invoices with several hundred lines make up most of the time, even with page splitting on.

The slow lane currently runs with a concurrency of two. I raised it to four on the staging copy and ran the same month of data. The step dropped from 52 minutes to 31 minutes, but the memory of the worker host went up to 85 percent because each headless browser needs about 400 MB. That is too close to the limit for production without a bigger host.

The second option is to render fewer pages per browser start. Each browser launch costs about 1.5 seconds, and reusing one browser for a batch of small invoices saved about 20 percent in a quick test. It also leaked memory after about 200 renders, so it needs a restart after a fixed number of jobs. I did not write that part yet.

The third option is the new renderer that we have been thinking about, which would not use a browser layout at all. It is the real fix for the superlinear growth, but it is a larger piece of work and cannot be ready before the next runs. I wrote the numbers into a short note for Mara with the three options and my view. My view is to do the concurrency change with a bigger host now, as it is only a config change, and to keep the browser reuse as a later step.

I did not change anything in production today. Mara will read the note, and we will decide together tomorrow. Ines does not need to be involved, because the invoices themselves do not change, only the time the run takes.

summary: Deployed the retry limit for new payment methods to production and checked that the 38 earlier cases would now give at most three attempts.
body:
I deployed the guard that skips the new-method retry after three attempts in seven days.

To see that it works, I replayed the 38 invoices with four or more attempts through the guard function in a dry run against a copy of the data. In all 38 cases the fourth attempt would have been blocked.

I also replayed a sample of 200 invoices with one or two attempts and a new method, and in all of them the retry would still run.

On production, one new method was attached by a customer in the afternoon on an invoice with a single failed attempt. The retry ran and succeeded, which is the normal path.

The log line for a blocked retry now includes the invoice id and the number of attempts, so support can explain it.

It is a small change with an effect mostly on customers with a repeated card problem. I will look at the numbers again after the next monthly run.

summary: Reviewed the first full week of Postmark-stream spam data after the dunning mail changes; the final notice subject was the last real problem, and a softer one cut its reports by half.
body:
The week of data is complete. Across all mails on the billing stream, spam reports are 2.6 per thousand, from 14 before the changes.

Broken down by mail type, receipts and first reminders are below 1 per thousand. The final dunning notice stands at 9 per thousand, and almost all of those reports come from one mailbox provider.

The subject of that mail has capital letters for the words final notice. Ines had approved it, but I asked her whether a softer version would be acceptable for the accountants and the legal side.

She checked with the accountants. The legal text is in the body, and the subject can be anything that is clear. We chose a normal-case subject: Your invoice is still unpaid and service will pause on a given date.

I changed the template and the test for the subject. The test also checks that the subject has no more than 3 capital letters beyond the first of each word that is a name.

I deployed it. Because the final notice goes out only for a small number of customers each week, it takes time to get data. In the first 3 days, 14 final notices were sent and one was reported, which is 71 per thousand but a tiny sample.

I will not draw a conclusion from that. I set a reminder to look at the figures after the next monthly run, when the volume is larger.

In the meantime I checked the sending domain records. SPF and DKIM are aligned for the link domain now, and the DMARC report from the mailbox provider shows 100 percent pass.

This closes the spam investigation for the dunning mails for now. The open item is only the sample of the final notice.

summary: Started a cleanup of the usage sync because it reads counts from nebula one customer at a time; a batch endpoint call reduced a test sync from 14 minutes to 3.
body:
The usage sync that reads counts from nebula takes about 14 minutes now and has grown with each new customer. It makes one HTTP call per customer, 3,900 calls in total.

nebula has a batch endpoint that takes up to 100 customer ids and returns the counts for all of them. I had not used it earlier because the first version had only a few hundred customers.

I changed the sync to chunk the customers into groups of 100 and call the batch endpoint. The results are written to usage_counts in one insert per chunk with ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE.

In a test against staging data, the sync took 3 minutes 10 seconds, and the rows were identical to those of the old sync. I compared them with a checksum per customer and period.

One difference came up. The batch endpoint returns customers without any usage as missing, while the single endpoint returned zero. The old code stored a zero row, and the invoice step expects a row for each active customer.

I fixed it by filling in zero rows for the ids that are missing in the batch response. A test covers a chunk where 10 of 100 customers have no usage.

The error handling needed thought. If one chunk fails, the old sync failed only one customer. Now a failed chunk affects 100. I made a failed chunk fall back to the single calls for its customers, so the failure is limited again.

I added a metric for the fallback count. It should normally be zero.

The change is on main and deployed to staging. A production run of the sync is scheduled for the next nightly slot, and I will check the checksums the next morning.

summary: Checked the nightly production usage sync with batches: it took 3 minutes, matched the old counts by checksum, and used the fallback zero times.
body:
The nightly sync ran with the batch calls. It finished in 3 minutes 4 seconds, against 14 minutes earlier in the week.

I compared the usage_counts rows of the night with those of the previous night for customers with no activity changes, and also against a checksum computed by the old method for 200 sampled customers. There were no differences.

The fallback to single calls was not used. The zero rows for customers without usage were created, 412 of them, which matches the number of idle customers.

The nebula team side shows no rate limit warnings on their end, as far as the logs I can see.

The next step is to move the sync to run twice a day, since it is cheap now. Ines had asked for fresher numbers on the usage page, and I will discuss it with Mara.

summary: Discussed with Mara running the usage sync twice a day and decided on an extra midday run, with the invoice run still reading only the nightly result.
body:
Mara and I talked about the sync frequency. A second run is cheap, but the invoice step must read consistent counts, and a run in the middle of the monthly run could change numbers under it.

We decided to add a midday run only for the usage page. The monthly run will read a snapshot marked by the nightly sync, which I add as a column sync_run_id on usage_counts.

I added the column and a small table sync_runs with a start, an end and a kind, nightly or midday. The invoice step selects the latest finished nightly run and reads rows of that run id.

This means the rows are written per run and not overwritten. The table will grow, so a cleanup job deletes midday runs older than 7 days and keeps nightly runs.

I wrote a test where a midday run writes different numbers after the nightly one, and the invoice step still reads the nightly values.

The migration took 4 minutes on the production copy, because the column is added with a default of null and then filled with the id of the existing nightly run in batches.

The change is on staging. I want one more check with Ines for the usage page: it should show the time of the last run so customers understand the numbers are not live.

The midday job is not scheduled yet. I will enable it after the migration is on production.

summary: Ran the sync_run_id migration on production and enabled the midday usage sync; the usage page now shows the time of the last update.
body:
The migration ran on production in 3 minutes 40 seconds, and the existing rows were all assigned to the last nightly run. I checked that no row had a null run id afterwards.

I deployed the invoice step change that reads the latest finished nightly run. A dry run of the invoice calculation for ten customers gave the same totals as the previous month's method.

Then I enabled the midday job at 12:00. It finished in 2 minutes 50 seconds, and the usage page showed the new numbers and a line with the time of the last update.

I checked that the invoice step ignored the midday rows by running the preview for one customer right after: the usage counts used were those of the nightly run.

The cleanup job for old midday runs is scheduled for the night. I will look at the table size in a few days to see that it stays small.

It is not a change that customers will notice much, apart from fresher numbers on the usage page. Ines said she will tell the account managers.

summary: Started the work on the slow PDF lane: measured the 40 biggest invoices of last month and found that the renderer spends most time on the line table layout.
body:
Picked up the PDF options from the monthly run review. I took the 40 biggest invoices of last month and rendered each of them ten times on a staging box. The median was 21 seconds for invoices with more than 300 lines, against 2 seconds for invoices with fewer than 30 lines.

I added timing marks around the three steps of the render job: building the HTML, loading it into the headless browser, and printing to PDF. The HTML build took under 300 ms. Loading took about 1 second. Printing took the rest, and the time grew faster than linearly with the number of lines.

A trace showed the browser recomputing the layout of the whole table for every page break, because the line table has a repeated header and each row has a fixed-height detail cell. Removing the repeated header in a test copy cut the 300-line case from 21 to 13 seconds, but the header is needed by finance.

I also tried splitting the table into one table per 50 lines. That gave 6 seconds for the same invoice and kept the header on every page. The page breaks fall slightly differently, so the PDFs are not identical to the old ones.

Nothing is changed in the code of main yet. The measurements are in a notes file next to the render job. Next I will show Ines two sample PDFs with the split table, because she has to accept the new page layout.

Mara suggested that a bigger slow lane remains a fallback, but it only costs more and does not fix the growth. I will keep the layout change as the first choice.

summary: Ines accepted the split line table layout for large invoices after comparing two sample PDFs, with one change: the page total must stay on the last page only.
body:
I sent Ines two PDFs of the same 320-line invoice, one in the old layout and one with the table split into blocks of 50 lines. She went through both in the morning and checked that the sums on every page matched the invoice total.

She accepted the split layout. Her one request was that the subtotal and the tax block appear only on the last page, because the accountants once complained about a page that looked like a final page when it was not. In my sample the subtotal was repeated after each block, which was a leftover of the template.

I changed the template so only the last block has the summary rows. The other blocks end with a small line saying that the invoice continues. The test for the template now counts the summary rows and expects exactly one.

I also checked an invoice with exactly 50 lines and one with 51. The first made a single block and the second made two blocks with one line in the last block. The 51-line case looked odd, with a nearly empty last page, so I made the last block take at least 5 lines by moving lines from the block before it.

The renderer tests pass. I did not deploy yet, as I want a measured run on the full set of large invoices first.

summary: Deployed the split table layout to the PDF render job and ran all large invoices of last month through it: the slowest went from 34 seconds to 9, and no totals changed.
body:
After the template tests passed I deployed the split line table to production in the evening, when no run was active. The change only affects invoices with more than 50 lines, so the small ones are rendered as before.

To check the result I re-rendered all 212 invoices of last month with more than 50 lines into a scratch bucket, not the real one. I compared them with the stored PDFs in two ways. First I extracted the text of both and compared the total, tax and currency lines. Second I counted the pages.

All 212 totals were the same. The page counts were equal for 187 of them, and 25 had one page more or less because of the new block breaks. I looked at six of those by eye and they were fine.

Times: the slowest invoice, with 1,140 lines, took 34 seconds before and 9 seconds now. The median of the large invoices went from 14 to 5 seconds. The whole set took 17 minutes in the old layout in the slow lane and 6 minutes now.

One problem showed up. Eight invoices with very long product names had the name wrap into three lines, and in the split layout a row could be cut at a block border. I set the rows to not break inside a row, and re-rendered those eight, which then looked right.

The scratch PDFs are deleted. The stored ones of past invoices are left alone, as they are legal copies and must not be re-rendered.

What is left: watch the next monthly run, and decide whether the slow lane still needs its extra workers. I will write the numbers when the run is done.

summary: Answered a support question from an EU customer who got two receipts for one payment: the second was the receipt of a SEPA-style retry, not a duplicate charge.
body:
A customer wrote that they received two receipt emails for the same amount and feared a double charge. I looked at their Stripe customer and the invoice. There was one invoice and one successful payment.

The first email was the payment receipt. The second one was sent after the invoice was marked paid again by a webhook event that arrived twice, because the endpoint returned a timeout once and Stripe delivered the event again. Our handler recorded the event but did not check whether the receipt for that invoice had already been sent.

So the customer was charged once, and the answer to them was that no money was taken twice. I wrote that and attached the single payment line.

The real defect is in the handler: the receipt job should be unique per invoice. I added a note to the backlog and a failing test that sends the same paid event twice and expects one receipt job. The fix will follow in the next session.

summary: Fixed duplicate receipts by making the receipt job unique per invoice, so a redelivered paid event no longer sends a second email.
body:
Following the support case, I made the receipt job use a singleton key built from the invoice id. pg-boss then refuses to queue a second job with the same key while one exists, and I extended the key window to 24 hours so a late redelivery is also caught.

The test from the last session now passes: two identical paid events give one receipt job. I added a second test where the events arrive an hour apart, and a third where the invoice is paid, voided and paid again by a new payment, which should still send a receipt for the second payment. For that, the key includes the payment intent id, not only the invoice id.

I looked for the same kind of problem in the other mails. The failed payment reminder was already guarded by the dunning step number. The credit note mail was not, so I applied the same key with the credit note id.

I checked the production log of the last 30 days for double receipts. I found 11 invoices that got two receipts, all after endpoint timeouts. Ines does not need to do anything, as no customer was charged twice.

Deployed after the tests passed. I will look at the job table tomorrow to see whether any send was wrongly suppressed.

summary: Reviewed the first monthly run after the split PDF layout: the PDF step fell from 70 percent of the run to about 25, and the slow lane stayed mostly idle.
body:
The monthly run finished this morning and I went through its timing. The whole run took 41 minutes, against 2 hours 10 minutes the month before. The PDF step took about 10 minutes of that, which is 25 percent.

The slow lane, which we had sized for the big invoices, handled 190 jobs and was idle for most of the run. The normal lane did most of the work. The longest single PDF took 9 seconds, as measured in the test.

There were 3 failed PDF jobs. All three were retried by the runner and passed. The errors were browser timeouts from a page with an image of a customer logo that loaded slowly from a remote host. That is a separate issue from the table layout, and I noted it. We should not load remote images during the render.

Ines checked a sample of 20 invoices and found no problem with the totals or the layout. She mentioned one customer who asked why the invoice now says that it continues on the next page. This is the new line, and I told her it is intended.

Decision: I will not remove the slow lane yet, but I lowered its worker count from 4 to 2. If the next run is the same, the lane can go. I also opened an item to inline the logos as data when an invoice is built.

summary: Inlined customer logos into the invoice HTML at build time so the PDF render never fetches remote images, which had caused three browser timeouts in the monthly run.
body:
The browser timeouts of the last run all came from logos on remote hosts. The render job waits for the load event, and a slow host holds that back for up to 30 seconds.

I changed the HTML builder so that it fetches the logo itself with a 3 second timeout when the invoice is built, checks that the type is PNG, JPEG or SVG and the size is under 500 KB, and puts it into the page as a data URL. If the fetch fails, the invoice is built without a logo and a warning is logged with the customer id.

I also cache the logo in Postgres for a day by URL, so a run with many invoices for the same customer fetches it once. The cache table has the URL hash, the bytes and the fetch time.

Then I set the browser to block all network requests during render except the local ones, so a stray remote reference can no longer hold a job. I tested by putting a link to a non-routable address in a test template; the render finished in 1 second and the image was missing, as expected.

Tests: one for the data URL, one for a failed fetch giving a PDF without logo, one for a file too big. All pass.

I found that 14 customers have logo URLs that no longer work. Ines will ask the account owners to update them. Deployed in the afternoon; I will watch the logs for the warning count.

summary: Looked at the warnings from the logo inlining after a day: 14 customers have dead logo URLs and none of the renders failed.
body:
I checked the logs after one day of the logo inlining. There were 62 warnings for failed logo fetches. They come from 14 customers, because the same invoice is rendered again for previews.

Twelve of the URLs return 404, one has an expired certificate, and one returns an HTML page instead of an image. The type check caught that last case correctly.

No render failed and the median render time did not change. The cache hit rate for logos was about 80 percent.

I wrote the list of 14 customers with their URLs and sent it to Ines, so the account owners can be asked for new logos. Until then their invoices are rendered without a logo, which is allowed.

I think the warning should be logged once per customer per day. I will change that later.

summary: Upgraded the Stripe SDK from v14 to v15 in a branchless step on main, fixing two type errors and one changed error class used by the refund code.
body:
I started the upgrade of the Stripe SDK to v15. The changelog listed a few breaking changes, and I checked which ones touch our code with a search for the affected calls.

The package change itself compiled with two type errors. The first was in the usage invoice item creation, where a parameter type had become stricter and our code passed a number as a string. The second was in the webhook helper, where the type of the event data was narrowed.

The more important change was in the error handling. The refund code catches the error class for invalid requests and reads its code to decide whether a refund was already done. In v15 the class names for errors were reorganized, and our check on the old name would silently never match. I changed the check to look at the type string on the error, which exists in both versions, and added a test that throws a fake error of that type.

I ran the unit tests, which passed, and then the integration tests against the Stripe test mode. Two failed because of a pinned API version in the test setup, which I updated to the one that v15 expects.

The pagination shim for list calls still works with v15, and I did not touch it. It will have to be looked at once we are on a newer version.

Deployed to staging. A full run of the sample billing cycle gave the same totals as before for all 60 test customers. I will deploy to production tomorrow morning after Ines has no run planned.

summary: Deployed the Stripe SDK v15 upgrade to production and checked payments, refunds and webhooks for a few hours; no differences in behaviour were found.
body:
The upgrade went out in the evening after a quiet day. Before the deploy I made a list of what to verify: a card payment, a SEPA payment, a refund, a webhook with signature, a customer update and a list call with pagination.

After the deploy I did these checks against live mode with small amounts on our own test customer. The card payment succeeded and the receipt came through Postmark. The SEPA payment was created and stayed in processing, as it should. A partial refund of 1.00 returned the expected object and status.

For the webhooks I looked at the incoming events for two hours. There were 143 events, all with a valid signature and all handled. No unknown event types were logged.

The list call with pagination returned all 87 customers of a test filter through the shim, the same as before. I checked that the shim did not call the auto pagination of the new SDK in addition, which would double the requests. The request count in the Stripe dashboard confirmed one request per page.

I watched the error rate for the Stripe calls: 0.4 percent before and 0.4 percent after, mostly card declines, which are normal.

One more thing I checked was the user agent header, as the SDK sends its version. Stripe now shows v15 for our requests.

Nothing is open from this upgrade. The next version, v16, is planned for later, and I want to read its notes about pagination first, because the shim is the part most likely to break.

I wrote the verification list in the repository docs so that it can be reused for the next upgrade. It has the steps, the amounts to use, and what to look at in the dashboard.

summary: Planned the partitioning of the invoices table after a sizing review: 38 million rows, a few hot quarters, and queries that nearly always filter by period.
body:
Mara and I looked at the invoices table, which keeps growing and is now the largest table in the database. This entry is the sizing and the plan. Nothing is changed yet.

Numbers from production: the invoices table has 38 million rows and its indexes take 21 GB, more than the table itself. The lines table has 210 million rows. The vacuum on the invoices table now takes 40 minutes and had to be interrupted twice during the monthly run.

I looked at the queries from the last week in the statistics view. About 92 percent of the reads filter by customer and a period or by an invoice number. Reads of invoices older than two years are under 1 percent of all, mostly for the accountants and for support.

The options were these:
- Partition by period with one partition per quarter. Old partitions can be left alone, the hot one is small, and vacuum works per partition.
- Partition by hash of the customer. Reads for a customer are fast, but the period queries and the archive would touch all partitions.
- Keep one table and archive old rows into a second table with a view over both. Simple, but the view hides the plan and the writes need care.

I prefer the quarter partitions. The monthly run writes to the current partition only, and the accountants' export of a quarter reads exactly one partition.

A few hazards were found in the review. First, the primary key of a partitioned table must include the partition column, so the key becomes id plus period start. Second, the foreign keys from the lines and the payments to the invoices must be changed, because they cannot point to a partitioned table by id only in the same way. Third, the invoice number counter is a separate sequence and is not affected.

The lines table should be handled with the invoices in the same step, or the foreign key cannot hold. I will check if that is possible with a reference by invoice id and period.

Plan: build the new partitioned tables beside the old ones, copy in batches, keep them in sync with a trigger for a week, switch the reads, then the writes, and drop the old ones later. Mara wants a dry run on a copy of production first. That is the next step.

summary: Answered Ines's question why two invoices of the same customer have totals that differ by a cent from her spreadsheet: her sheet rounds the total, we sum rounded lines.
body:
Ines sent two invoices of one customer where her check spreadsheet disagreed with our total by one cent. I looked at both.

The invoice has 12 lines. Each line is quantity times unit price with the tax rate applied. In our code the tax is computed per line and rounded to the cent, then summed. Her sheet sums the net amounts first and applies the tax once to the sum, then rounds.

For the first invoice the two methods gave 1,204.37 and 1,204.38. For the second the difference went the other way. Both methods are legitimate in principle, but the rule must be the same everywhere. The invoice we send shows the lines with their tax, so the per-line method is consistent with what the customer sees.

I confirmed this with the code in the totals module. It rounds half up at the line level using a helper that works on integer cents. The sums in the PDF come from the same numbers as the database, so the PDF and the database agree.

I replied to Ines with the two calculations written out and said that I think the per-line method should stay, because it matches the printed lines. She will ask the accountants whether they accept it.

I also checked how many invoices of the last month would differ between the two methods. I ran the check on a copy: 61 of 9,400 invoices, about 0.65 percent, and the difference was always one cent.

No code change was made.

summary: Wrote the dry run script for the invoices partitioning on a copy of production and found that the copy of the 210 million line rows takes 5 hours with the default batch size.
body:
This session was the dry run that Mara asked for. I restored last night's backup to a scratch database on a bigger machine, so that the timings are not from the production box.

The script creates the new tables invoices_p and invoice_lines_p, with quarter partitions from the earliest invoice up to two quarters ahead. A function creates the next partition so that we do not depend on someone remembering to do it.

The copy runs in batches by id range. With 10,000 rows per batch the invoices took 38 minutes. The lines took 5 hours 10 minutes, which is too long for comfort but it can run in the background while the old table is still used.

I tried 50,000 rows per batch. The lines then took 3 hours 40 minutes, but the write-ahead log grew a lot and the replica lag in a test went to 90 seconds. I settled on 25,000 as a compromise and a pause of 200 ms between batches.

The sync trigger is the next piece. Inserts and updates to the old tables are copied to the new ones with an upsert, and deletes are copied too, although we hardly ever delete. I tested it by running the monthly run simulation against the old table while the copy was running. Afterwards, the row counts were equal and a checksum over the id, the total and the status columns matched for the invoices.

Problems found:
- The foreign key from payments to invoices had to be dropped on the new side and replaced by a check job, because a partitioned table needs the partition column in the reference.
- A unique index on the invoice number must include the period column. Uniqueness across partitions is no longer guaranteed by the database, so the gap-free number counter stays the guard. I added a nightly check that looks for duplicates.
- Three queries used the plain id as the key and now have to pass the period as well to use partition pruning. I counted them with a search; there are 3 in the usage code and 5 in the reports.

The plan holds. The switch of the reads would come after a week of sync. Before that I want Mara to review the script and the trigger.

summary: Mara reviewed the partitioning script and asked for three changes: a lock timeout on the trigger creation, a resumable copy and a dry run of the switch itself.
body:
Mara went through the script and the trigger in the early afternoon. Her points were all fair.

First, creating the trigger on the old invoices table takes a lock, and if a long transaction holds the table, the creation waits and blocks everything behind it. She asked for a lock timeout of 2 seconds with a retry loop, so that the step fails fast instead of freezing the service. I added it.

Second, the copy must be resumable. My script restarted from zero if it was stopped. I added a small progress table with the last copied id per table, updated in the same transaction as each batch. A kill in the middle now loses at most one batch. I tested it by killing the script three times during a run on the copy and checking the counts after the end.

Third, she wants the switch itself to be rehearsed, not only the copy. The switch is a short transaction that renames the old tables and the new ones, and she does not want to find out about a lock wait in production. I ran the rename on the copy while a load generator hit the tables with 200 requests per second. It took 40 ms, and the queue of waiting requests was cleared within a second.

I also noted that the sequences of the ids must be owned by the new tables after the switch, or the next insert might reuse an id. I added a step that sets the sequence to the maximum id plus one and a test that inserts a row after the rename.

Mara also asked whether the accountants' export needs a change. The export reads by period, and with the new layout it only needs the partition filter that it already has. I ran it on the copy for the last quarter and it was faster, 11 seconds against 70.

Status: script changed, tests pass, copy and sync rehearsed. Not yet in production.

summary: Started the production copy for the invoices partitioning: the new tables are created, the trigger is on, and the copy of the invoices rows is done, with the lines running overnight.
body:
I ran the first real steps in production in the evening, after the usage sync of the midday and before the night run. The timing was chosen so that the sync was quiet.

First I created the partitioned tables and the partitions. The function that makes the next quarter's partition was created too and I ran it once to see that it makes nothing when the partition exists.

Then the trigger on the old tables. The lock timeout of 2 seconds worked: the first attempt failed because a report query was holding a lock, the loop retried, and the second attempt got through after 3 seconds. No request was delayed noticeably. I checked the application latency in the dashboard and it stayed flat.

The copy of the invoices started right after. With 25,000 rows per batch and the pause it ran 41 minutes. I compared counts: 38.2 million on both sides. A checksum over the id, the total and the status matched in 40 random ranges of 100,000 rows each.

The lines copy started after that. It is running as a background process under the progress table. At the moment I am writing this, it has done 31 percent. The replica lag stayed under 4 seconds.

What I watch: the lag, the size of the write-ahead log disk, and the error log for the trigger. There was one error in the trigger, an upsert conflict on the invoice number unique index when an invoice was updated in the old table, because the new index includes the period and my conflict target did not. I fixed the conflict target to use the id and period and re-synced the 6 affected rows by hand.

I also wrote a small status command that prints the progress, the row counts of both sides and the oldest unsynced change. Mara can run it without knowing the details.

Tomorrow: check that the lines finished, run the full checksum comparison, and then decide whether to switch the reads at the end of the week.

summary: The lines copy finished overnight and the full checksum comparison matched on invoices and lines, so the sync stays on for a week before the reads are switched.
body:
The background copy of the lines finished in 4 hours 20 minutes. The replica lag peaked at 9 seconds and the log disk never went above 60 percent.

I ran the status command and then the full comparison. For the invoices I computed a checksum per quarter on both sides over the id, the number, the total, the status and the updated time. All 31 quarters matched. For the lines I did the same per quarter, over the id, invoice id, quantity, the unit price and the tax amount. All matched, 210.4 million rows on each side.

I also compared the rows written since the trigger was installed. The oldest unsynced change was 0 seconds in all the checks I made during the day. Over 14 hours there were about 52,000 changes, nearly all from the usage sync updating draft invoices.

One more check was for the deletes. A test invoice that I deleted on the old side disappeared on the new one within the second.

The nightly duplicate check on invoice numbers ran for the first time and found none.

I looked at the query plans on the new tables for the 8 queries that I had marked. With the period in the filter, the plan touches one or two partitions. Without the period, it touches all, as expected, and takes longer. So the 8 queries need the period passed. I changed 5 of them in a branch of the work, all in main as we do not use branches, but hidden behind a setting that selects the table names. The setting is off.

The remaining 3 are in the usage code. They look up an invoice by id from a webhook, where the period is not known. I decided to look up the period from the payment record that carries both. I wrote that and a test.

Plan: one week of sync with the setting off, daily status checks, then the read switch. If anything differs, I stop and look. I told Ines about the plan, because the monthly run is about two weeks away and she wants the switch finished before it.

summary: Looked at a failed payment case where a customer's Stripe card update arrived after the dunning email had already gone out, and added a re-check before each dunning step.
body:
A customer wrote that they had updated their card and still got the third dunning email. I looked at the timeline in the logs.

The card update happened at 09:12. The retry job for the overdue invoice ran at 09:20 and succeeded. But the dunning email for step three had been queued the evening before for 09:00 the next morning, and it was sent at 09:01 without checking the state again.

So the mail was queued with the state of the evening before. The retry itself was right, but the mail was stale.

I changed the dunning job so that it loads the invoice again when it runs and stops if the invoice is paid, voided or in a payment attempt that is not finished. The job logs why it skipped. I wrote tests for the three skip reasons, using the fake clock, and one for a mail that should still be sent.

I also thought about a payment that is in processing, as with SEPA debits which take days. A mail for an invoice in processing would be wrong, too, so processing counts as a skip reason. For that case the next dunning step is shifted by 2 days instead of being dropped, to cover the case where the debit fails.

I checked the last 60 days for similar cases: 9 customers got a dunning mail after paying on the same day. I gave the list to Ines so she can decide whether a short apology is needed. I think a sentence is enough for the two who wrote in.

Deployed in the evening. I will check next week whether skip counts look reasonable.

summary: Checked the partition sync after a week: no unsynced changes, no duplicate numbers, and the read setting is ready to be switched on tomorrow.
body:
Morning check of the invoices sync. The status command showed 0 seconds for the oldest unsynced change and equal row counts on both sides for invoices and lines.

The nightly duplicate check on invoice numbers found nothing in seven runs. The monthly sums per quarter match between the old and the new tables, including the quarter that is still open.

I re-ran the full checksum comparison on the last two quarters, since those change most. Both matched.

I also ran the 8 marked queries with the setting on in a staging copy and compared the results to the old tables. All results were equal, and the slowest query went from 1.9 seconds to 0.3.

Mara agreed to switch the reads tomorrow morning with the setting, which can be turned off again at once. The write switch comes after a week of reads.

summary: Looked at the slow monthly invoice export for the accountants and cut it from 70 to 11 seconds by reading from the new partitioned table in a test.
body:
Ines asked why the quarterly export takes more than a minute. I looked at the plan on the old table. It scanned a large index range for the quarter and then fetched rows at random from the heap, which is slow when the table is bloated.

On the new partitioned table the same query reads the one partition in order and finished in 11 seconds on the copy. This is a good side effect of the partitioning, though not the reason for it.

For now the export still uses the old table, because the reads are not switched. I told Ines that the export will be faster after the switch and that her request does not need a separate fix.

I also noticed that the export sorts in the application. Moving the sort into the query with an index on the invoice number inside the partition would save another second or two. I did not do it, since it is not needed.

The export file format is unchanged. I compared the output of the old and new queries byte by byte for the last quarter and they were the same.

summary: Prepared the switch of invoice reads to the partitioned tables: ran the shadow comparison against production and fixed a slow lookup and a raw query, with the switch itself still to come.
body:
In the evening, after the quiet time of the day, I ran the 8 marked queries against production in a shadow mode that runs both the old and the partitioned tables and compares the results. Mara was online to watch with me. For one hour, about 24,000 comparisons were made and none differed.

The latency of the invoice list for a customer in the partitioned tables was a median of 14 ms against 38 ms on the old table, and the p95 was 60 ms against 210 ms. The read setting is still off, and the application reads only from the old tables.

One call was slower: the lookup by invoice number without the period, used by support in an admin page. It touches all partitions and took 450 ms. I changed it to try the current and the two previous quarters first and only then all, and the usual case is now 20 ms in the shadow run.

The error log showed no database errors. One warning came from a report that still used the plain table name in a raw query. I fixed it, and the report gave equal numbers.

What is open:
- Turning the read setting on tomorrow, with the setting kept as a quick way back.
- A week of reads before the write switch.
- Removing the setting and the trigger after the write switch.

I will keep the shadow comparison running at low rate until then.

summary: Wrote the plan for the write switch of the invoices partitioning: a short maintenance window, the rename in one transaction, sequence fix, and a rollback that keeps the trigger reversed.
body:
A week of reads went well, with no differences in the shadow comparison over about 1.4 million checks. This entry is the plan for the write switch, so that Mara can review it before we do it.

What the switch does: in one transaction it renames the old tables to invoices_old and invoice_lines_old, and the new tables to the plain names. After this the application writes into the partitioned tables with no setting needed. The sequences are set above the maximum id.

Before the rename I stop the job runner for 2 minutes, so that no job holds a transaction on the tables. The web service stays up, and requests that arrive during the rename wait for a short time. On the copy the rename took 40 ms under load.

The trigger direction is reversed at the same moment: after the switch, changes to the new tables are copied back to the old ones, so that we can go back by renaming again if something is wrong. This is the rollback path and I tested it on the copy. After a rename back, the old tables were complete and the ids continued correctly.

We keep the reversed trigger for a week and then drop it.

Checks after the switch: insert a test invoice and see that it is in the current partition, run a small invoice run of 10 invoices, check the numbers are consecutive, and look at the error log for 30 minutes.

Risks I see: a long-running transaction that blocks the rename, handled by the lock timeout and a retry; a job that caches the table oid, which I could not find in our code; and the foreign key replacement checks, which are run by the nightly job and not by the database.

We will do the switch tomorrow before the lunch time, when the load is low.

summary: Prepared the write switch of the invoices partitioning: rehearsed the rename on staging and checked the sequence fix and the rollback path.
body:
Spent the early afternoon on the rehearsal for the write switch, with Mara reviewing the script. Nothing was changed on production. The invoices still go into the old table, and the new partitioned tables are only kept in sync by the trigger.

On staging I ran the whole script against a fresh copy. The first rename attempt hit the lock timeout after 2 seconds, because a long export query was running at the same time. The script retried and the second attempt went through in 60 ms. This showed me that the retry is needed, and that the switch should not be started while an export is running. I added a check that looks for long queries on the invoices table before the script begins, and it stops with a clear message if it finds one.

The sequences are set to the maximum plus one in the script. On staging I checked it by inserting a test invoice, which got the right id and went into the current quarter partition. I removed the test invoice afterwards. The reversed trigger removed it from the old table as well, which is the behavior the rollback depends on.

I also tried the job runner part of the plan. On staging I stopped the runner, ran the switch and started it again, then did a manual run of 10 invoices. The numbers were consecutive, the PDFs were rendered, and the receipts were queued with one job each. The totals were the same as computed on the copy.

Open points for the real switch:
- Choose a short window in the early afternoon, with a pause of about 2 minutes for the job runner.
- Keep the read setting in the code until the old tables are dropped.
- Keep the reversed trigger as the rollback path for a week.

After the switch I want to look at the nightly duplicate check on invoice numbers, the foreign key check for payments and lines, and the row counts of both sides. The vacuum time on the current partition is already a few seconds on staging, against 40 minutes on the old table, so that goal looks reachable.

I told Ines that the monthly run can use the new layout once the switch is done, and that the accountants' export should be faster. Next: write the final checklist with Mara and pick the day for the switch.

summary: Prepared the checks for the invoices partitioning write switch and wrote down what to look at in the first hours afterwards.
body:
Went through the plan for the write switch of the invoices partitioning once more and turned it into a checklist, so that the first hours after it can be judged quickly. Nothing has been switched yet; new invoices still go into the old table.

The numbers to compare are written down. I take the count of invoices created since the switch and check that their numbers are consecutive, with no gap and no duplicate. I also want the row counts of the old and the new table for the current quarter to match, and the insert time before and after, because the reversed trigger will add some cost to each insert. On staging the trigger added about 2 ms, and I want to see whether production shows the same.

For the logs I prepared a query for lock waits and deadlocks on the invoices table, and a second one that lists the slowest statements on it. The accountants' export is the one I expect at the top, so I will check that it uses partition pruning for the current quarter.

While reading the table settings I saw that autovacuum is configured for the old table, and it will keep running on it after the switch, even when only the trigger writes to it. I decided to leave it as it is and let it go away when the old table is dropped at the end of the rollback week.

Open: decide on the exact day and time of the maintenance window with Mara. Also write a short note for Ines that the invoice numbers will not change in any way, so that she is not surprised when she sees the new table names in the database. After that, look at the creation of the partition for the next quarter, because a missing partition would make every new invoice insert fail.

summary: Wrote a job that would create the invoices partition for the next quarter two weeks ahead, tested it on a copy of production, and left the deploy for later.
body:
A missing partition would make every new invoice insert fail, so I started on a job that creates the next one in time.

The quarterly partitions are still created by hand in a migration. An insert for a date without a partition fails with 'no partition of relation invoices found for row', and that would stop the monthly run. So I wrote a pg-boss job that checks the partitions every day.

The job reads the existing partition bounds from pg_inherits and pg_get_expr. If the newest partition ends less than 60 days from today, it creates the next one with the same indexes and constraints as the others. It uses a lock timeout of 2 seconds, so it cannot block invoice writes for long, and it retries on the next run if the lock was not free.

The lines table has its own partitions by the same quarters, and the job creates both in one transaction. A unit test covers the date math for the year boundary and the case where a partition is missing in the middle. Another test makes sure that running the job twice creates nothing the second time.

I also wrote a metric for the number of days until the last partition ends, and an alert for when it falls below 30. In a dry run on the copy of production, the job created the partition of the next quarter in 120 ms.

Not done yet: a default partition as a safety net. I decided against it for now, because rows in a default partition make later partition creation fail, and a loud error is better than a silent one. The job is not deployed yet; I plan to deploy it next, and then force a test creation on staging to check the indexes and the alert.

summary: Prepared the partition creation job for the invoices table and tested it on a staging copy, with the alert metric and the index checks still to be confirmed.
body:
The partition creation job was written and ran on staging this evening. Nothing was deployed to production, and the invoices table there is still a single table with its normal inserts.

The first run on staging found the newest partition ending in more than 60 days and did nothing, which is the right result. The metric showed 71 days of margin on the staging copy.

To see a real creation, I moved the threshold to 100 days on staging. The job created the next partition for invoices and lines in one transaction. Compared with the older test partitions, the indexes were the same: the number unique index, the customer and period index, and the status partial index. The constraint names followed the same pattern.

One small bug showed up: the partition name used the quarter number without a leading zero for the lines table, so the name did not match the others. It is harmless, but a later cleanup script would trip on it. I fixed the name builder and added a test for it, then dropped and recreated the staging partition.

The alert was tested by setting the threshold to 90 for a moment, and it fired and cleared as expected. After that I reset the staging settings.

Still open: the plan for how the job runs against the real table, and who gets the alert. Nothing else changed in billing behavior. Tomorrow I want to look at the reports of the customers who asked for their invoice history, to see which queries they depend on before the storage changes.

summary: Checked the invoice history endpoint against the partitioned tables and found that one query without a period filter scans all partitions and takes 4 seconds.
body:
I went through the endpoints that read invoices to find queries that cannot use partition pruning, so that I know what the plan to move the invoices table to partitioned storage would hit. I ran them against a copy of production that has the partitioned layout. Most of them filter by period or by an invoice id with a known period, so they are fine.

The invoice history for one customer, GET /customers/:id/invoices, has no period filter by default. On the copy it took 4 seconds for a customer with 900 invoices, because it visits every partition index. The current single table does this in 1.1 seconds, so this one gets slower with the new layout, and it has to be fixed before anything is switched.

The cause is the plan: Postgres appends the results of all partitions and sorts them again. The customer and period index exists in each partition, but the merge costs time. I tried adding a limit of 50 with the order by period descending, which allows the planner to use a merge append. This took the query down to 90 ms for the first page on the copy.

The endpoint already has a page size, but the cursor is an invoice id. I am drafting a change of the cursor to period and id together, so that the next pages also use the index order. The old cursor format would keep working for one release. This is only on a branch of my working copy so far and nothing is deployed.

Tests for the pagination order pass locally. I still need to look at the support tool that calls this endpoint with a very large page size, and I will ask Mara to check the list of callers.

summary: Deployed the new cursor for the invoice history endpoint and saw its p95 fall from 3.8 seconds to 120 ms.
body:
The cursor change is in production. I watched the endpoint for a few hours.

The p95 went from 3.8 seconds to 120 ms, and the heaviest customer, with 1,400 invoices, answers the first page in 150 ms. Old cursors from clients that had a page open still worked, and the log showed 6 of them.

The support tool asks for a page size of 5000. I capped the size at 200 on the server and told Mara. The tool does paging, so nothing breaks.

Next I remove the old cursor format after one release.

summary: Ines asked how the books can be checked once the invoices table is partitioned, so I planned a comparison of the old table against the planned partitions and wrote down what it should cover.
body:
Ines asked whether the quarter totals in her report would stay the same after the planned partitioning of the invoices table, as the accountants will ask. Nothing has moved yet, so I used the day to prepare a check that can prove it later.

I wrote the comparison as a query that works on any two tables with the same columns. For each quarter it gives the row count, the sum of totals in each currency (EUR, USD and GBP) and a hash over invoice number, customer, total and tax. I ran it on staging against a copy of the invoices table that I split into quarterly pieces by hand. All of the numbers matched, including the sum for last quarter to the cent in each currency. That shows the query works. It says nothing yet about production, where the partitions do not exist.

I wrote a short note for Ines with the query, so she can run it herself before and after the move. She asked if the invoice numbers would ever have gaps. I explained that the sequence is shared and that a failed insert can skip a number, as it does today. The partitioning is not meant to change that, and I will test it with a batch of test invoices when the time comes.

She will add the check to her month-end list, to run once now for a baseline and again after the move. No code change was needed today, and production was not touched.

summary: Investigated a failed dunning run that sent no emails for 40 minutes and traced it to a Postmark rate limit response that the job treated as a permanent error.
body:
Mara noticed in the morning that the dunning emails of one batch were missing. The job log shows 212 emails to send, 58 sent and then a series of failures.

Postmark answered with HTTP 429 after a burst, and our send function threw an error that the job handler classified as permanent for every non-5xx status. So the job marked the remaining emails as failed and did not retry them. Only the next dunning step the day after would have caught them, which is too late for the first reminder.

I changed the classification: 429 is now temporary and uses the Retry-After header of the response if there is one. Other 4xx codes stay permanent, for example 406 for an inactive recipient and 422 for an invalid address. For those the customer gets a note in the account and no retry.

Then a second change: the job sends at most 10 emails per second, which is below the limit of our Postmark stream. Before this, the loop sent as fast as it could.

I wrote tests with a fake server that answers 429 twice and then 200. The mail is sent once, and the attempt counter shows 3. A second test checks that a 422 does not retry.

For the 154 emails that were lost, I started a manual resend with a script that only picks invoices still unpaid and without a dunning mail for this step. It sent 149 emails, and 5 customers had paid in the meantime and got nothing, which is right.

Deploy is done, and the next dunning run is tomorrow morning. I will check the rate and the retries then.

summary: Checked the morning dunning run after the rate limit fix: all 230 emails went out in 25 seconds with no 429 responses.
body:
The run started at the usual time. The new send rate of 10 per second kept it below the limit, and the whole batch of 230 emails took about 25 seconds.

The Postmark activity page shows 230 delivered and no bounces in the first hour. The job log has no retries, so the 429 path was not used, but it is covered by the test.

I also looked at the five customers from yesterday who had paid before the resend. None got an email. The re-check before each dunning step did its work.

I consider this closed. A last small task is a log line with the count of throttled sends, which I added so that we see it if the limit comes closer.

summary: Checked the Postmark sending after the rate limit fix over a full day: bounces stayed low, the dunning batches ran clean, and the one soft bounce spike came from a single customer domain.
body:
I looked at the Postmark activity for the whole day after the rate limit fix of the dunning run. The goal was to see that the fix had not just moved the problem somewhere else. In total 1,840 transactional emails went out: receipts, reminders, dunning steps and a few invoice mails.

The hard bounce rate was 0.4 percent, which is in line with the weeks before. The spam complaint rate was zero for the day, and that is the number we watched most closely since the move away from the old provider. Open rates for the receipts are not a good signal because many clients block the tracking pixel, so I ignored them.

There was one spike of soft bounces around midday. All of them went to the same company domain, and the response text said the mailbox was full. This was a problem on the side of the customer, not ours, and the next retry by Postmark delivered the mails a few hours later. I wrote a note for support so that nobody opens a ticket about it.

The dunning batch in the morning took 25 seconds and the batch in the afternoon took 19. No job logged a 429 response. I also checked that no email job sits in the retry state in pg-boss, and the queue was empty at the end of the day.

One small finding: the Postmark message stream for the dunning mails still has a default tag value of none. That makes filtering in the Postmark dashboard harder than needed. I added a task to set a tag per template name, but I did not change it today because it touches the email client code.

Next step is to do that tagging, and then to stop watching the daily numbers and look at them only in the weekly review.

summary: Prepared the accountants' yearly export script for the planned move of the invoices table to partitioned storage, and checked the current output against last year's file.
body:
The yearly export script still names the single invoices table. Once the invoices table is moved to partitioned storage, one partition per quarter, that name would stop working, so I started preparing a version that reads by quarter. The move itself has not happened yet. The script is the last known user of the old table that I have found, and I wanted it ready before the plan goes ahead.

The script writes a CSV with one row per invoice line, sorted by invoice number. I wrote the quarter-by-quarter version on a branch of my own working copy and kept it off the main checkout's scheduled runs. To check it, I ran the current version and the new version for last year and compared the files. Both have 1.9 million rows, and the hashes of the two files are identical.

The new version is also faster in this test: 4 minutes instead of 19. It does the quarters one after another with a period filter on each, instead of one big scan. I expect this to matter more once the data is split by quarter, because each query will then read only one partition.

I added a test with a small fixture of three quarters that checks the order and the totals. The script also prints the sum of totals by currency at the end, which Ines can compare with her sheet. I will send her the output of the test run so she can see the format before the real run.

One detail: the script formats amounts with the existing rounding of the totals, and I did not touch that. The numbers match to the cent.

Before the move, I still need to look for other readers of the old table, such as ad hoc queries in the finance sheets, and agree a quiet period with Ines. Next is a written plan for the order of the steps: the new table, the job that moves the old quarters at night, and only after that the cleanup of the old table.

summary: Prepared the cleanup of the old invoices tables by checking the readers, the trigger and the backup, and planned the steps without changing anything.
body:
Today I prepared the first step of the cleanup after the move of invoices to partitioned storage is being planned. Nothing was renamed or dropped. I only looked and wrote down the plan.

First I listed everything that still touches the invoices and invoice_lines tables. I searched the code and the job definitions and looked at the pg_stat counters. The readers are the API, the webhook handler that updates invoice status after a payment event, the receipts job, and the nightly checksum job. The accountants' export script is the only one that still reads the old names, so I noted that it needs a change before any rename.

Then I looked at the reversed trigger and its function. It copies writes back to the old tables so that a rollback stays possible. I wrote down the order I want to use later: turn off the nightly checksum job, drop the trigger and its function in one transaction with a lock timeout of 3 seconds, and only after that think about renaming. I plan to do it when the load is low, in the evening.

I also tried the dump on staging. I took a compressed dump of a small part of the tables and restored it into the staging database. The restore worked and the row counts matched. The full dump will be about 41 GB compressed, and I want to keep it in the backup bucket with a retention of 90 days.

I talked to Mara about the rollback. Once the trigger is gone, a full rollback would need a copy back, and she wants one more week of checksums with no differences before we accept this. Ines will be told before the change, so she is not surprised by the table names in her report.

Open: change the export script, take the full dump, and pick the evening for the trigger step.

summary: Prepared the cleanup of the old invoices tables by checking who still reads them, taking a test backup and planning the steps, without dropping anything.
body:
I checked the places that could still read the invoices_old and invoice_lines_old tables, because the move of the invoices table to partitioned storage is still planned and has not happened yet. For now the old tables are the live ones, so this entry is about preparing the cleanup that will come after the move, not about doing it.

I went through the readers one by one: Ines's quarter report, the accountants' export script, the invoice history endpoint, the nightly jobs and the dunning code. All of them still read the old tables, and I wrote down the queries each one uses so that I can compare them against the partitions later. The scan counters on both tables show normal traffic, so nothing can be dropped yet. The list is only a map of what must be switched first.

I also made a fresh backup dump of both tables and restored it into a scratch database to check that the row counts match. The dump is about 88 GB on disk. I plan to keep a dump like this for 90 days after any later drop, so the dump location needs a retention note.

I looked at the setting that would switch reads between old and new tables. It does not exist yet, so I sketched where it would sit and estimated that the old read paths would be about 140 lines plus two tests. Removing them would go in a separate commit after any drop, so each step can be reverted by itself.

The volume is at 81 percent used, which is the reason for the cleanup. I expect it to fall well below that after a later drop, once autovacuum and file removal have finished. I will ask Mara to look over the drop statement before it is run in one transaction.

Still open: the old cursor format on the invoice history endpoint, which I want to check in the logs for a few more days, and a runbook note about the partition job. I changed nothing in the database today.

summary: Removed the old cursor format from the invoice history endpoint, since the logs show no client using it for a week.
body:
The log counted requests with the old invoice id cursor. In the last seven days there were none, so the compatibility code could go.

I deleted the parser for the old format and the test for it. A request with a cursor that does not parse now returns 400 with a clear message instead of starting from the beginning.

The support tool and the customer dashboard both use the new format. Tests pass and the change is deployed.

Nothing else is left of the cursor topic.
