summary: Went through the Stripe error handling of the refund and payment code to prepare the v16 upgrade, and listed which error classes and fields our code reads and where.
body:
Before the upgrade to Stripe SDK v16 I read through every place where our code catches Stripe errors. I searched for the error class names and for the fields that we read from the caught object. There were 11 catch sites, spread over the payment service, the refund endpoint, the webhook handler and the dunning job.

Most of them check the error type string, for example card_error or invalid_request_error. Those did not change in the release notes for v16, so I left them as they are. Two places read the raw error field on the object, and the notes say that the shape of it moved a little. I wrote a small test for each, with a fake error object in the new shape, and both tests passed.

The refund code was the most careful part, since it has to tell a real failure from an already refunded charge. It looks at the error code charge_already_refunded and then returns the existing refund. That code string is unchanged, so no edit was needed there.

I also found one catch block in the dunning job that logs the whole error object. With the new SDK that object may include more request data than we want in our logs. I changed it to log only the type, the code and the request id.

The type check of the compiler gave no errors against the v16 typings when I tried it in a scratch run, which makes the upgrade look small. The plan is to do the real upgrade tomorrow morning, when the traffic is low, and to watch payments and webhooks for a few hours afterwards.

summary: Looked at a customer whose card payment succeeded in Stripe but the invoice stayed open, and found that the webhook arrived before our invoice row was committed.
body:
A customer wrote that she paid but still got a reminder. In Stripe the payment intent was succeeded, but our invoice was still open.

The webhook log shows the event payment_intent.succeeded arrived 80 ms before the transaction that created the invoice row committed. The handler looked for the invoice, found nothing, logged a warning and returned 200, so Stripe did not retry.

The cause is the order in the payment job: we confirm the payment at Stripe inside the transaction and commit afterwards. For fast card payments, the event can be faster than the commit.

The fix has two parts. The handler now returns 404 for an unknown invoice, which makes Stripe retry with its backoff, and the webhook retries then find the row. And the payment job now commits the invoice row with the status 'paying' before it calls Stripe.

I wrote a test that delivers the event before the row exists and checks that the second delivery marks the invoice as paid. For the customer, I marked the invoice as paid by hand and cancelled the reminder.

I searched the last 30 days for the same pattern with a query on webhook warnings and found 4 more cases. Three had been paid by the next retry of dunning logic, and one more got a reminder. I wrote to that customer.

summary: Deployed the webhook retry fix and checked three hours of events: two events arrived early, were answered with 404 and applied on the Stripe retry.
body:
The change went out in the morning. I watched the webhook log for three hours.

Out of 120 events, two arrived before the invoice row was visible. Both got 404, and the retry came after about a minute. Both were applied then, and the invoices show as paid.

The new 'paying' status is shown as open in the customer dashboard, so nobody sees a change. Finance reports treat it as open as well.

One thing to watch: a 404 for an event of a deleted test customer would be retried by Stripe for days. I added a rule that events for unknown customers return 200, and only unknown invoices of known customers return 404.

summary: Answered the question of whether the Stripe SDK v16 upgrade is worth doing now: yes, because v15 loses support soon, and the changes in our code look small.
body:
Mara asked if the upgrade to v16 can wait. I read the changelog between v15 and v16 and searched our code for the things that changed.

What the changelog says that touches us:
- the type of the list results changed a bit, which affects the pagination shim we have for old list calls
- a few deprecated parameters of the invoices API were removed, and we use none of them
- the webhook helper has a stricter type for the event, which may need a cast in two places

I ran the TypeScript compiler on a branchless trial in my working copy of main, without committing, and got 7 errors. Five are the stricter webhook event types, one is in the pagination shim and one is in a test helper. None needs a change in behavior.

The API version of the account is set by us in the client, so the upgrade does not change the version Stripe uses. That reduces the risk a lot.

My recommendation was to do it this week: fix the 7 errors, run the tests with the Stripe mock, and deploy while the load is low. Then watch payments, refunds and webhooks for a few hours, as with v15. Mara agreed. I will start tomorrow.

summary: Wrote a short status and plan for the next weeks of work on invoices and Stripe, with the partitioning of the invoices table still to be planned and the order of the next steps.
body:
Mara asked for a written plan so that we both see the same list, so I took time to write a short status for the next weeks. I wrote it as a document in the repository, and this entry is the summary.

The biggest item is the invoices table. It keeps growing, and the queries that filter by period get slower each month. The plan is to partition it by quarter. I wrote down the steps in order: a copy of the data into the new partitioned table with checksums, a read switch, a write switch, a job that creates the next partition ahead of time, and a new cursor format for the invoice history endpoint. The cleanup of the old tables and the old cursor format comes last, only after some quiet days. None of this is started. I only listed the steps and put a rough size next to each one. I also noted that Ines should check her quarter totals against the new tables before the accountants' exports are switched over.

On the Stripe side, the upgrade to v16 is small and comes next, and v17 later. Our code has two shims for pagination that the older SDK needed, and they should go away when we reach v17. I do not want to remove them earlier, because the older version still depends on them.

On the email side, the dunning mails need a tag per template in Postmark. This is a small task and I put it first on the list. After that comes a look at the bounce data once a week instead of every day.

The PDF renderer is the largest open topic. The split table layout helped with big invoices, but the headless browser is still the slowest part when many invoices are rendered at once. I wrote down the idea of a second renderer, to be tried behind a flag, but I did not choose a design. The first step would be to measure what a simple template engine can do on the 40 biggest invoices.

Three smaller items are also on the list: the tax profile warnings that finance sees, a check for payment methods of customers in the EU who may want direct debit, and a cleanup of old test data on staging.

Mara will read the plan tomorrow and change the order if needed. I will start with the Postmark tags and the v16 upgrade.

summary: Deployed the Stripe SDK v16 upgrade and watched payments, refunds and webhooks for the morning: the numbers matched the days before and no new errors appeared.
body:
The deploy was at 09:30. I compared the first three hours with the same hours of the last three days.

Payments: 64 succeeded and 3 failed, which is within the normal range, and the decline codes were the same kinds as before. Refunds: 5 created, and all got their webhook event. Webhooks: 188 events handled, the signature check passed for all, and there was no event in the retry queue after the first hour.

I looked at the SDK retry log line that I had lowered to info. It appeared 4 times, all for short network errors to the Stripe API, and each request then worked on the second try. That is the SDK's own retry and works as intended.

The pg-boss jobs that call Stripe, like the usage reporting and the dunning re-check, ran at their times and finished in the usual duration. The monthly run is a few days away, and this upgrade means it will be the first one with v16.

Nothing needs to be fixed. I will add a note to the checklist of the monthly run to look at the Stripe error rate during it.

summary: A customer with a EUR invoice asked why the VAT line shows 0 although he is in Germany, and the cause was a VAT number that was marked as valid in a stale check.
body:
The customer wrote that his invoice had no VAT. His account is in Germany and has a VAT ID, but the company seems to be a German one, and the reverse charge is only for other EU countries.

I looked at the tax decision for the invoice. The code decides reverse charge if the customer has a valid VAT ID and the country differs from ours. Our country is Germany, so reverse charge should not apply. But the stored country in the tax profile was Austria, while the billing address said Germany. The profile country came from the first VAT ID check two years ago, when he used an Austrian branch.

So the logic was right, but the data was stale. The fix for the customer: I corrected the tax profile to Germany, voided the invoice and issued a corrected one with 19 percent VAT, with a credit note for the first. Ines approved this and will tell the accountants.

For the general problem, I searched for profiles where the profile country and the billing country differ and found 23. Most have a reasonable reason, like a different billing office. Six look like errors, and I gave the list to Ines to check with the customers.

I did not change the tax code. A rule to compare the countries when the invoice is made is an idea, but it needs a decision from finance first.

summary: Added a warning to the invoice job when the tax profile country and the billing country differ, so finance sees these cases before the invoice goes out.
body:
After the VAT question, Ines said a warning would help more than a block. I added the check to the invoice creation.

When the two countries differ, the job writes a row in a new table, tax_profile_warnings, with the customer, the invoice and both countries. The invoice is created as before. The monthly report for finance now has a list of these warnings.

The check ran on last month's data in a dry run and found the same 23 profiles as the query. Two had been fixed already.

A test covers the warning and the case with equal countries, where nothing is written. The change is deployed and it does not change any total.

summary: Looked into why the monthly run slowed to 48 minutes and found that the email step waits for each Postmark call one by one, which a small concurrency of 5 brings down to 12 minutes.
body:
The monthly run grew from 31 to 48 minutes over the last months. I looked at the timing of each step in the job logs.

The PDF step is about 25 percent as before, and the invoice creation is steady. The email step grew most: it sends the invoice mail with the PDF for each customer in a loop and waits for each response. With 9,800 customers and about 200 ms per call, that is 33 minutes in the worst case, and it grows with the customers.

The fix is to send with a concurrency of 5 calls at once. The dunning job already has a rate limit of 10 per second, from the earlier fix, and I used the same limiter for this step, so it stays below the Postmark limit. With 5 calls at once and the 200 ms response time, we send about 25 per second in theory, and the limiter holds it at 10, so the email step should take about 16 minutes. In a test on staging with 2,000 fake customers sending to the Postmark sandbox token, it took 3.4 minutes, which scales to about 17 for the real run.

I looked at the order of mails as well. Each mail is a separate job that records the result in the table, so a failure of one does not stop the others. A failed call is retried by the job, and the unique key per invoice stops a second mail, as in the duplicate receipts fix.

One risk I thought about is memory, since each mail holds a PDF of up to 2 MB. With 5 in flight it is at most 10 MB, so that is no problem.

I changed the loop to use the limiter and a small pool, added a test that checks that no more than 5 are in flight, and a test for the retry of a 429. Deploy is planned before the next monthly run, and I will watch the step timing in that run.

summary: Deployed the concurrent email step of the monthly run and checked it with a small batch of 300 real invoice emails: 29 seconds, no duplicates, no 429 responses.
body:
The change went out in the evening. Before the monthly run, I wanted a real check, so I sent the invoice emails of a small batch of 300 customers whose invoices were created late last month and had not been mailed because of a bounce fix.

The batch took 29 seconds, which is about 10 per second as set by the limiter. The Postmark activity page shows 300 delivered and 2 bounces for known bad addresses. There were no 429 responses and no retries in the job log.

I checked the table of sent mails for duplicates by invoice and found none. The unique key worked.

Memory of the worker stayed flat at about 380 MB during the batch. The expected time of the full run for the email step is now around 16 minutes. I will look at the real number after the monthly run.

summary: Reviewed the monthly run after the email concurrency change: the run took 29 minutes instead of 48, and the email step took 15 of those.
body:
The run finished this morning, and I read the step timing from the job logs.

Total time was 29 minutes. The email step took 15 minutes for 9,900 invoices, close to the estimate of 16. The PDF step was 7 minutes and the invoice creation 5. The remaining 2 minutes are the usage read and the checks at the end.

Postmark showed no rate limit responses, and there were 31 bounces, which is the normal level. The Stripe error rate during the run was low, and no payment job failed. Ines got her invoice report on time and found nothing odd in the totals.

The email step is now the biggest part of the run. Raising the limit would need a talk with Postmark about our stream, which is not worth it for a few minutes. I left it as it is.

summary: Wrote up the monthly run timings after the email concurrency change and found the PDF rendering step is now the biggest part, at 11 of 29 minutes.
body:
After the review this morning I split the monthly run into steps and timed each one on the staging copy. Email takes 15 minutes, PDF rendering takes 11, and the usage meter read takes 2. The rest is small.

The PDF step renders one invoice at a time in a single headless browser page. Invoices with many lines are clearly the slow ones. An invoice with 12 lines takes about 0.4 seconds, one with 400 lines takes 9 seconds. A few large customers carry most of the cost.

I looked at where the time goes for the large ones. The browser waits for a font file and for a logo image each time, and the table layout for hundreds of rows is slow. Caching the font and the logo locally cut about 0.2 seconds from every invoice, which is small for big ones.

I did not change anything in production today. I wrote the numbers into the notes file in the repo as a base for later. Next steps: measure with a pool of two browser pages, and check whether page breaks inside long tables cost much. Ines does not need anything from this yet, but I will tell her that the run time may fall again.

One open question is memory: two pages at once on the worker may push it near the limit, so I will check that before any change.

summary: Tried a pool of two browser pages for the PDF step on staging; the step fell from 11 to 6.5 minutes with memory still within the worker limit.
body:
I implemented a small pool in the PDF renderer module, with a size taken from the setting PDF_PAGES, default 1. With 2 on staging, the same 3,100 invoices rendered in 6.5 minutes instead of 11.

Memory on the worker rose from about 600 MB to 950 MB at peak, below the 1.5 GB limit. With 3 pages it went to 1.3 GB and the time was only 5.8 minutes, so the third page is not worth the risk.

I found one bug on the way: when a page crashed, the pool kept handing out the dead page and the next invoices failed with 'Target closed'. I now replace a page after any render error and retry that invoice once. A test forces a crash and checks that the next five invoices still render.

The output is the same as before. I compared the text of 200 PDFs from both versions and they matched. Not yet deployed. I will deploy with PDF_PAGES=2 after the tests run in CI.

summary: Deployed the two-page PDF pool and watched an invoice batch: 6 minutes instead of 11, no failed renders, and the memory peak stayed under 1 GB.
body:
The CI run passed this morning, so I deployed the pool with PDF_PAGES=2 around lunchtime. There was no monthly run today, so I started the weekly batch of usage invoices by hand for a test, 870 invoices.

It took 1 minute 42 seconds. Before the change the same kind of batch took about 3 minutes. No render errors, no retries used, and the logs show both pages working in turn.

I watched the worker memory during the batch. The peak was 940 MB, and it dropped back after the run. I checked that the browser processes are gone after the job and found none left.

I also checked the PDFs of the three largest customers. The biggest has 410 lines and 18 pages. It rendered in 7 seconds and the totals on the last page match the invoice row. I compared the totals of all 870 PDFs to the database values with a small script and found zero differences.

The setting can be put back to 1 without a deploy, so there is a quick way back. Next I want to look at the page break behaviour of long tables, because a few customers complained about a header that is missing on page two. Not started yet.

summary: Answered Ines's question why two invoices of one customer have different VAT rates: one was made before the customer moved to Austria and the profile was updated later.
body:
Ines saw two invoices for the same customer, one with 19 percent VAT and one with 20 percent, and asked which is right.

I looked at the tax profile history. The customer changed the billing country from Germany to Austria on the 3rd of the month, and the first invoice was created the day before. So the 19 percent was right at that time. The second invoice used the Austrian profile and 20 percent.

The VAT number was also valid in the check at the time of the second invoice. I confirmed that in the stored check result, which has a timestamp.

I told Ines that both invoices are correct for their dates and that no credit note is needed. I also gave her the profile history lines so that she can show them to the accountants if they ask.

One small thing: the invoice PDF does not show the country used for the tax. I noted it as an idea to add the country next to the VAT line later. No code change today.

summary: Fixed the missing table header on page two of long invoice PDFs by repeating the header row on each page; the 410-line test invoice now looks right on all 18 pages.
body:
A customer with many lines wrote that page two of his invoice had no column titles. I reproduced it with the 410-line invoice from the test data.

The cause was in the template: the table used a div layout with CSS grid, which does not repeat anything across page breaks. I changed it to a real table with thead and the style 'display: table-header-group', so that the headline row repeats.

This changed the layout a little. The row height was a bit larger, and the 410-line invoice went from 18 to 19 pages. I reduced the row padding by 1 pixel and it is back to 18.

I also checked that rows do not break in the middle: added 'break-inside: avoid' on each row. On page ends this works, only a very long description with 6 lines still moves as a whole to the next page, which is fine.

Render time did not change within the noise, 7.1 seconds against 7.0 before. I compared the totals on the last page to the database for 100 invoices with more than 40 lines and all matched.

I also looked at the view in two PDF readers and in the mail preview of a phone. The header repeats in all of them.

Not deployed yet. The template change is in a branch-free commit in main, behind nothing, so I want one more look at a few real invoices tomorrow in staging before I deploy it.

summary: Deployed the repeated table header for invoice PDFs after checking ten real large invoices in staging; no layout problems found.
body:
I rendered ten of the largest real invoices from last month on staging with the new template and looked at all pages of each. The headline row repeats on every page and no row is cut in the middle.

One invoice had a very long product name that wrapped to four lines. It still fit. I deployed the template at the end of the day.

I regenerated the PDF of the customer who complained and sent the link to him with a short note. The totals are identical to the original invoice, so he did not get a new invoice number.

I will check the support inbox in the next days for further layout remarks.

summary: Looked into why SEPA debit payments show as processing for five days and found our dunning job treats processing invoices as unpaid after three days.
body:
Support forwarded a case: a customer paid by SEPA debit, the invoice was still open after three days, and he got a first reminder email. The money arrived on day five.

SEPA debits take several days in Stripe, and the payment intent stays in the state 'processing' during that time. Our dunning job only looked at our own invoice status, which stays 'open' until the webhook 'payment_intent.succeeded' arrives. So it sent the reminder after three days.

I checked how many invoices were affected in the last two months. 41 reminders went to customers whose payment intent was in processing at that moment. Most of them paid a day later. None was suspended, because the suspension comes after the third reminder.

The fix: before each dunning step the job now loads the payment intent of the invoice from Stripe and skips the step when the status is 'processing'. This builds on the re-check that I added some weeks ago for card updates, so the change is only a few lines in the same function.

I wrote a test with a stubbed Stripe response in the state processing and one with requires_payment_method. Both pass. The Stripe call adds around 120 ms per invoice to the dunning run. With 230 invoices in a run this is half a minute, which is acceptable.

I did not send any apology email. I wrote a note for Ines with the list of 41 customers so that finance can decide if a message makes sense. Deploy follows after one more review of the code.

summary: Deployed the dunning fix for SEPA invoices in processing; the morning run skipped 12 invoices and sent no reminder to customers whose debit was on its way.
body:
I deployed the change after a second read of the diff. The morning dunning run was the first test.

It looked at 231 open invoices. 12 had a payment intent in processing and were skipped, which the log lines 'dunning_skip_processing' show. The other 219 were handled as before, and the emails went out in 28 seconds.

I followed three of the 12 invoices during the day. Two were paid by the debit in the afternoon, one is still processing. No reminder went out for them.

I also looked at the run time: 28 seconds against 25 seconds last week, as expected from the added Stripe calls.

The Stripe call is made one invoice after the other. If the runs grow, I can make it concurrent in the same way as the email step. For now it is not needed.

Finance has the list of 41 customers. Ines said that no message is needed, because nobody was suspended.

summary: Wrote tests for how failed SEPA debits show up in billing-api and found that a returned debit left the invoice marked paid for a few minutes.
body:
I wanted to know what happens when a SEPA debit is returned, for example because of insufficient funds. Stripe sends 'payment_intent.payment_failed' in that case, sometimes after the invoice was marked paid by an earlier success event.

I replayed recorded test events in order: succeeded, then failed. Our webhook handler set the invoice to open again, but it did not reset the paid_at column, so reports still showed a paid date. Also, the receipt email had already gone out at the time of success.

For the paid_at column I changed the handler to set it to null when the invoice goes back to open. I added a test for it.

The receipt email is harder. With SEPA, Stripe sends success only when the debit is accepted, and failures after that are rare but possible. I decided not to delay receipts, but to send the customer a short note on a failure, using the existing dunning template for failed payments. I only noted that decision for now.

I also checked the mandate handling in the same test. A failed debit because of a cancelled mandate leaves the mandate status 'inactive', and the next retry correctly asks the customer for a new mandate.

The tests are green. Next: deploy the paid_at change and write the plan for the note on failure.

summary: Deployed the paid_at reset for returned SEPA debits and checked that no existing invoice has an open status together with a paid date.
body:
I deployed the handler change this evening. Before that I ran a query over the invoices table for rows with status open and paid_at not null. It is one large table and the query took a while, but it found 3 rows from the last four months, each from a returned debit.

I cleared paid_at on those 3 rows in a transaction and wrote the ids into the notes. A second query afterwards found none.

I then replayed a succeeded and a failed event on staging with the deployed code, and the invoice went to open with paid_at null as designed.

It was a small change and the logs are quiet after two hours. The monthly report of Ines reads paid_at, so the three rows will now appear in the right period.

The note to customers on a failed debit is still to do.

summary: Added a short email to customers when a SEPA debit is returned after success, using a new Postmark template, and checked it on staging with a test account.
body:
I built the email planned last week. The template 'debit_returned' says that the debit was returned, gives the invoice number and amount, and links to the payment page where the customer can pay by card or sign a new mandate.

The handler sends it only when the invoice was paid before the failure event. In other failure cases the normal dunning flow applies, so customers do not get two emails.

I added the template in Postmark and a template file in the repo with the English and German text. The language comes from the customer profile, as with other emails.

On staging I used a Stripe test mandate that fails with the code 'insufficient_funds'. The sequence of events was succeeded, then failed after a few minutes. One email arrived in the test inbox, with the right amount and link. Postmark showed it as delivered, not in spam.

I also tested the replay of the same failed event twice, because Stripe may resend it. The second time no email was sent, because the invoice was already open. This is covered by a test now.

A review of the German text by Ines is still open, since she knows the wording the accountants like. I will send her the text and deploy after her answer.

summary: Ines reviewed the German text of the returned debit email and asked for the word 'Rücklastschrift' instead of 'zurückgegeben'; changed and deployed.
body:
Ines answered in the afternoon. She prefers 'Rücklastschrift', because that is the term used on bank statements, and customers search for it.

I changed the subject and body text in the German template. I also added the line that bank fees for the return are not charged by us, which she asked for to avoid questions.

After that I rendered the template once more with test data and sent it to my own inbox. It looked right.

I deployed this evening. Watched the logs for an hour: no events for returned debits yet, which is normal as they are rare.

This closes the SEPA return topic for now.

summary: Investigated why the invoice totals in the usage report differ by a few cents from the sum of invoice lines and found the report rounds the sum, not each line.
body:
Ines noticed that her usage report for one customer shows 1,204.37 while the invoice says 1,204.38. She wanted to know which is right.

I took the 86 lines of the invoice and summed them. The invoice rounds each line to cents and adds the lines. The report query sums the unrounded line values and rounds once at the end. With many usage lines of small unit prices, this gives differences of a cent or two.

The invoice is the legal document, so the report is what has to change. I checked how many customers are affected in the last month: 63 of 1,980 invoices differ by a cent, and 4 differ by two cents. The sum of all differences was 0.71 EUR across the month.

I changed the report query to round each line first, using the same function as the invoice code, so there is one definition of the rounding. I tried to do it in SQL with round(), but Postgres rounds numeric half away from zero, while the application function does something different at exactly half a cent. This showed up in two test lines at x.xx5.

So I did not use the SQL round. The report is now built in the application from the invoice lines, and not by a query sum. It is slower, 4 seconds against 0.6 for the month, but it is exact. Ines said that is fine for a monthly report.

I compared the new report with the invoice totals for the whole month, and all 1,980 match. I also kept the old query in the repo with a comment, to show how the difference came up. I will deploy it tomorrow after a short review.

summary: Deployed the report built from invoice lines, then reviewed how many places still sum unrounded values and found two more, in the quarterly export and a dashboard query.
body:
The report change went out this morning without trouble. Ines ran the monthly report and compared three customers by hand with their invoices: equal.

Since the cause was a different rounding between SQL and the application, I searched the repo for other sums over line amounts. I grepped for 'sum(' in the SQL files and in the query strings of the TypeScript code.

Found five places. Three of them are fine: they sum integer cents that are already rounded per line. Two are not. The quarterly export for the accountants sums numeric values of the usage lines, and an internal dashboard query shows the revenue per plan in the same way.

For the quarterly export, I compared last quarter against the invoice totals. The difference was 2.14 EUR over 5,700 invoices. This is small, but accountants check for exact equality, so it matters. I changed the export to use the invoice total column, which already holds the rounded sum.

The dashboard query is only for internal use. I changed it to the same column, as that is simpler than the line approach and nothing is lost.

Tests: one for the export with a made-up invoice with three lines at x.xx5 each, which would differ with a single rounding. It now matches the invoice total.

I wrote down in the notes that the invoice total column is the source for all money sums, and the report from lines only exists for the per customer view. Ines got a note about the 2.14 EUR difference, and said she will tell the accountants that the last quarter file was off by that amount in sum.

I also thought whether to regenerate the last quarter's file. Ines said yes, so I made a new one and sent it to her. It is identical to the invoices table totals by a check query.

summary: Ran the fixed quarterly export for the last quarter and checked it against the invoice totals, with no difference over the invoices.
body:
This evening I ran the fixed export for the last quarter and got a file with 5,712 invoice rows. I compared the total per customer with the invoice total column through a join, and there were no differences.

The old file differed on 38 customers, by one or two cents each. Together this made the 2.14 EUR that I told Ines about.

I sent the new file to Ines with the old one for comparison, and with a list of the 38 customers.

The export takes about 14 seconds on the invoices table as it is now, and it only sums one column. It is a bit slow for such a small result, and since the invoices table keeps growing, I wrote down the idea of splitting it by quarter as a topic to look at later. I did not change anything on the table today.

I marked the sums topic as done. Remaining idea: a test in CI that compares the report and the invoices on the test data, so that a drift is found early. I put it on the list for later.

summary: Upgraded the Stripe SDK from v16 to v17 on a test copy first to see what breaks, and found that the old list helpers need two shims, which is the main work of the upgrade.
body:
Before the real upgrade I wanted to see how big it is. I made a local change of the version in package.json, installed it, and ran the type check.

There were 17 type errors in 6 files. Eleven of them are caused by the same thing: the pagination. We use 'autoPagingToArray' in a few places to read all invoices or charges of a customer. In the version we run, this works with a 'limit' option as we use it. In the new version the option is named differently and the return type changed, so our code did not compile.

The other errors are small: a renamed enum for the payment method types, a field on the subscription that is now optional, and the type of the webhook event.

I checked the changelog of the SDK against our usage. The webhook signature function did not change, which was my main worry. Refund and payment intent creation are the same.

What I decided: the change is not large, but it touches payments, so it needs care. For the pagination I will write a small helper function in our own code, which takes the Stripe list call and reads all pages with the starting_after cursor, and returns an array. It is a shim between our code and the SDK, and it keeps all the call sites unchanged. A second shim is for the subscription field, which fills in a default.

I started the helper and wrote tests with a fake list that has three pages of 100 and one with 0 results. The tests pass for both the empty and the exact multiple of the page size, which is where such loops often fail.

I did not update the version on the main line yet, as v17 is only a test here. I wrote the list of the files and call sites in the notes: 9 places for pagination, 4 for the enum, 2 for the subscription field.

The plan: finish the shims, run all payment tests against the Stripe test mode, then deploy in the morning when I can watch the first payments.

One point I want to ask myself again before deploy: the timeouts. The new SDK has a different default for network retries, and I need to check that it does not double a payment attempt. Payment creation already has an idempotency key, so it should be safe, but I will read the code to be sure.

summary: Checked the retry behaviour of the new Stripe SDK for payment calls and refunds and found that automatic retries are on by default, which matters for refunds without keys.
body:
Today I looked at the network retry setting that I flagged yesterday. The SDK retries a request when the connection fails, with the setting maxNetworkRetries. In the version we run it is 1, in the new one it is 2 by default, and the SDK adds an idempotency key by itself to POST requests when it retries.

I tested this with a small local proxy that drops the first response of a request. For payment intent creation we pass our own key, and the SDK used it on the retry. One intent was created.

For refunds the picture is different. Our refund endpoint calls the Stripe refund creation without any key from us. The SDK generates a key per call and reuses it only for its own retries inside that call. So a network failure inside one call is safe. But if our own client calls the endpoint twice, for example after a timeout of its own, two refunds are created. This is not new with the upgrade, it is how it is now.

I tried it: two POST requests to our endpoint for the same payment with the same body gave two refunds in test mode, until the amount was used up, and the third request got the error 'charge_already_refunded'.

This is a gap that I want to close separately, with a key sent by the client and stored on our side. I wrote it in the notes as the next topic after the upgrade, and did not mix it with the upgrade.

For the upgrade itself I set maxNetworkRetries to 1 explicitly in our client creation, so behaviour stays the same as today. I added a test that reads the option from the client.

I also ran the whole payment test suite against Stripe test mode: 212 tests, all green with the shims in place. Two tests were flaky because of rate limits of the test mode, and passed on the second run.

The webhook tests with signed sample payloads pass as well. I also checked the one test that uses an old timestamp for the signature, and it behaves as before, which I will keep in mind as the clock matter comes up now and then.

Still open: the review of the diff, and the choice of the time for the deploy. Tomorrow evening is calmer, because the monthly run is not near.

summary: Reviewed the diff of the Stripe v17 upgrade with its two shims and found one missing case: the pagination helper did not stop when the SDK returns has_more true with an empty page.
body:
I read my own diff again with fresh eyes. It has 14 changed files, of which 5 are tests.

The pagination helper loops while has_more is true and takes the last id of the page as the next cursor. If a page were empty while has_more is true, the last element does not exist and the loop would either throw or repeat forever. Stripe should not do this, but a loop without a guard in a billing job is a risk.

I added a guard: an empty page ends the loop and writes a warning to the log with the call name. I also added a hard limit of 1,000 pages, after which the helper throws an error. For our largest customer 1,000 pages of 100 are 100,000 objects, which is far above reality.

A test now covers the empty page with has_more true, and one covers the page limit with a fake list that never ends.

I also renamed the helper file to 'stripe-list-compat.ts', so that it is clear that it is a temporary bridge, and put a comment at the top that says what it is for and when it can go.

The subscription shim is five lines. I checked it with a subscription from the test mode that has no 'default_payment_method', and the default applies.

The tests are green again, 216 now. The deploy is planned for the next days.

summary: Looked at why the invoice PDF job for one customer with 900 lines takes 40 seconds and found the cost is in the layout of one very wide description column.
body:
Support told me that the PDF download for one enterprise customer waits a long time. I rendered the invoice on staging and measured: 40 seconds, against 9 seconds for another with 400 lines.

So the time is not linear in the number of lines. I looked at the profile of the browser. Most time goes into layout, and it grows when descriptions contain long strings without spaces, in this case event source names like 'prod-eu-west-ingest-pipeline-cluster-07-region-b' repeated on every line. The table has an auto layout, and the browser measures every cell several times to find the column widths.

I tried 'table-layout: fixed' with set widths for the columns. The time dropped from 40 to 14 seconds. The long strings now wrap with 'overflow-wrap: anywhere'.

This changes how the table looks, since the columns have fixed widths now. The description column gets 45 percent of the width. I rendered ten other invoices and compared them. They look about the same, but long product names wrap earlier than before.

I did not deploy it. It is a change in the look of all invoices, and I am not sure it is the best way, since the renderer is slow in other ways too. Rendering is done by a headless browser, and a different method could be much faster. I noted the numbers as an argument for a bigger change later.

For the customer, I rendered the PDF by hand with the fixed layout and sent it to support. A proper decision about the layout change follows later.

summary: Deployed the Stripe SDK v17 test branch fixes to staging only and ran a full day of simulated payments, refunds and webhooks against it without errors.
body:
I put the upgrade on staging this afternoon and let a script run through the evening. It creates customers, subscriptions with cards and SEPA mandates, makes payments, refunds a part of them, and triggers webhooks through the Stripe CLI.

Over about 3 hours, 480 payments were made, 120 refunds, and 900 webhook events arrived. No errors in the logs. The event handling times are the same as before: p95 of 45 ms.

The pagination helper was used in 9 places. I checked the log lines of the helper and saw that the largest list had 3 pages. No warnings for empty pages.

One thing came up: a type of an event, 'invoice.finalized', has a field that the type declaration marks optional now. Our handler read it without a check. I added a check and a test, so that the handler does not fail on a missing field.

For refunds on staging, I confirmed again that two quick calls to the endpoint create two refunds. This is the known gap and not part of this work.

The upgrade is not on production yet. The plan is to go in the morning of a quiet day and to watch payments for a few hours. I wrote the list of things to watch: payment success rate, refund errors, webhook 4xx and 5xx rates, and the dunning run.

One more reason for care is that the accountants' exports use Stripe data for the payout reports, so I ran the payout report on staging and compared the result with the one from the old SDK. Same numbers.

summary: Wrote a short note on how to roll back the Stripe SDK upgrade if payments show errors: revert the commit, redeploy, and the shims stay harmless for the old version.
body:
Before the deploy I wrote down the way back. It is short, but I want it to exist before I need it.

The upgrade is a single commit plus the shims. A revert of the commit restores the old package version and the old call sites. The lockfile is part of the commit, so the install is exact.

The pagination helper works with both versions, because it only uses the plain list call and the cursor. So if I had to keep the helper while going back, it would still work, and this lets me revert in two steps if needed.

A deploy takes about 4 minutes. Payments that are in flight during a deploy are not lost, because the payment jobs are in pg-boss and are retried after the restart. Webhooks that arrive during the restart are retried by Stripe.

I listed what I would check to decide on a revert: an increase of failed payments above 3 percent against the previous week, any error 'Invalid signature' in the webhook logs, or refund errors from the SDK.

I put the note in the repo docs folder next to the notes of the earlier upgrade to v16. It follows the same form.

summary: Decided against deploying the pagination fix and layout change together: the table-layout change for PDFs waits, and instead I measured how much a rendering in another way could save.
body:
I came back to the invoice PDF speed. The fixed table layout saved 26 seconds on the worst invoice, but it changes the look of every invoice, and Ines would have to approve the new look. The gain only matters for a handful of customers.

Instead I made a rough test of a different way to render. I wrote a throwaway script that creates the PDF from the same data with a PDF library that draws tables directly, without a browser. For the 900-line invoice it took 1.8 seconds, and for the 12-line one 30 ms. Memory is a few tens of MB.

The look is not the same, of course. Fonts, the logo and the footer needed manual work, and I did not reach the same look in a few hours. The VAT block and the page numbers worked, the header on every page too.

So the possible gain is large: the monthly PDF step could fall from 6 minutes to maybe one. The cost is a new template to build and check, and a risk, because the PDFs are legal documents. Any difference in how amounts are shown must be excluded.

I did not decide the way yet. Options are the fixed layout in the browser, or a new renderer behind a flag, so that both can run side by side and be compared for a month. I like the flag option since it allows a comparison of the output on real invoices.

I wrote the numbers and the options into the notes, with the script saved in a scratch folder outside the repo. I will bring it up when the Stripe upgrade is done, as the two should not run in parallel.

summary: Measured the Stripe SDK v17 branch with its shims against the old list helpers on 3,000 payments and found no timing cost, but retries on refunds without keys remain a risk.
body:
The test branch for the Stripe SDK v17 upgrade ran against staging with a replay of 3,000 payments and 400 refunds taken from a real busy day. The goal was to see whether the two shims for the old list helpers change the timing of the calls we make. They did not: the median call took 210 ms with the old SDK and 205 ms with the branch, and the paginated customer listing took the same number of requests.

The second part was the retry behaviour found a few days ago. I forced a network timeout on 40 refund calls by cutting the connection after the request was sent. In 6 of them the SDK retried by itself and Stripe saw two requests. Stripe refused the second one in those cases only because the charge was already refunded in full, so the test showed no double refund. A partial refund would not have been protected the same way.

That means the branch looks fine for payments, where Stripe reuses its own keys, but refunds are not covered yet. Our refund endpoint has no idempotency key, and a client that retries can still refund twice, with or without the SDK. I wrote this down as an open item and did not change the SDK setting for automatic retries.

The next steps are to fix the missing pagination case and to design the key for refunds. The key must come from the client request, not from a random value made inside the call. Nothing about the upgrade goes to production until both are done, and the branch stays on staging for now.

summary: Wrote the design for idempotency keys on the refund endpoint: the client sends a key, we store it with the refund, and a repeat returns the first result.
body:
After the retry test of the last days, I wrote the design for idempotency keys on the refund endpoint. Today the endpoint takes an invoice id and an amount and calls Stripe directly. If a client sends the same request twice, because of a timeout or a double click in the admin tool, two refunds can go out.

The design has the client send an Idempotency-Key header with each refund request. The key is stored in a new table, refund_requests, with the key, a hash of the request body, the invoice id, the status and the Stripe refund id. A unique index on the key makes sure that only one request wins when two arrive at once.

If the same key comes again with the same body, the endpoint returns the stored result and does not call Stripe. If the key comes with a different body, it answers 422, because that is almost always a bug in the client. If the first request is still running, the second one gets 409 and the client can try again later.

The same key is also passed to Stripe as its own idempotency key. That way, if our service crashes after the call to Stripe but before we save the result, the retry reaches Stripe with the same key and gets the same refund back. This closes the gap that the automatic retries of the new SDK would open.

I chose to keep keys for 30 days and delete older ones in a nightly job, since Stripe forgets its own keys after a day or so and no client retries after that long. Ines asked whether the admin tool of finance can send keys. It can, once the tool makes one key per click on the refund button, which is a small change on its side.

Nothing is coded yet. The next step is the migration for the table and the endpoint change, with tests for a repeat, a changed body and two parallel calls.

summary: Reviewed the refund idempotency design against the current endpoint code and found three places where a refund is created, not just the one route.
body:
I went through the refund code to see where the idempotency design from earlier today has to apply. The HTTP route in src/routes/refunds.ts is the obvious one. The admin script that Ines uses for goodwill refunds also calls the same service function, and the dunning cancel path issues refunds when a subscription is cancelled in the middle of a period.

All three end in refundService.create(), so the key belongs there and not in the route. The route only passes the header through. The admin script will generate its own key from the invoice id and the amount, so running it twice cannot refund twice. The cancel path will use the subscription id with the period.

I did not write code yet. The next step is the migration for the keys table, with a unique index on the key and the customer.

summary: Planned the storage for refund idempotency keys and wrote down the table layout and the open cases, with nothing built or run yet.
body:
Worked on the design of how a refund request could be kept safe against a retry, and wrote it down as a plan for the next sessions. Nothing is written in code, no migration exists, and nothing is deployed.

The idea is a new table, refund_idempotency, with the columns key, customer_id, request_hash, refund_id, response_json and created_at. The unique index would be on (customer_id, key), so the same key from two customers does not clash. I checked the other migrations in the repo to see the numbering and the naming, and the table is new and empty, so I expect it to be quick on a copy of the staging database. I have not tried it.

The planned flow in refundService.create() is this. It first inserts a row with the key and the request hash and no refund id. If the insert fails on the unique index, it reads the existing row. If the hash is the same and the refund id is set, it returns the stored response. If the hash differs, it returns a 422 with the message that the key was used with other parameters.

The hard case is a row without a refund id, which means the first request is still running or crashed. For a running request, I think the second one should wait a few seconds on a row lock and then return 409. For a crashed one, the retry could continue after the lock is free, but it should first ask Stripe for refunds on the payment and look for our key in the metadata. That would avoid a double refund when the crash came after the Stripe call. This means the Stripe refund call would have to set a metadata field with our key, and I noted that as part of the plan.

Still open: how long the wait should be, and whether the Stripe SDK option for the key belongs in this step or the next one. I lean towards keeping this step only about our own storage. The tests are to be listed and written before any of the code.

summary: Planned the tests for refund idempotency and checked what the Stripe mock server can do, before any of the idempotency code exists.
body:
Wrote down the four tests I want for refund idempotency before writing the code they will cover: same key twice, same key with another amount, two parallel requests, and a crash after the Stripe call. None of them can pass yet, because the endpoint still takes no key and creates a refund on every request.

The tests will run against a real Postgres and the Stripe mock server we already use for payments. The first one sends the same refund twice with one key and checks that the mock saw one refund call and that both responses are equal. The second sends the same key with another amount and expects a 422.

The third fires two requests at once with the same key. I expect one to get 201 and the other to wait on the row lock and then return the stored result with the same refund id. Once it exists I want to run it a few hundred times in a loop to look for flakiness.

The fourth is the crash case. The mock has to throw after it has recorded the refund, so our code has no refund id stored. The retry would then have to look up the refund by metadata, find it, and write the id into the row. Today the same scenario creates a double refund, so I kept that as a plain reproduction to check later that the test fails without the lookup.

One problem came up while reading the mock: it does not support listing refunds filtered by metadata, so the crash test needs a small filter added to the mock first. I started a branch-free sketch of that change in the main checkout but did not finish it. Next I write the storage for the keys, then fill in the tests one by one. Passing the key on to the Stripe call as a second layer comes after that.

summary: Read through the refund code and the Stripe SDK retry behavior to plan how a refund request could be protected against a double refund, without changing any code yet.
body:
Started on the refund retry risk that I noticed last week. Nothing is changed in the service yet; today was reading and planning.

First I went through refundService.create() and the places that call it. The call to Stripe has no idempotency option today, and our own table has no protection for refunds either. A client that retries after a lost response would create a second refund. The Stripe SDK also retries by itself on network errors, and I wanted to know what that means for refunds. I read the v16 documentation and the SDK source: it accepts idempotencyKey in the request options, and without a key the automatic retry of a POST is not guaranteed to be safe. That is the part that worries me most.

Then I looked at the admin script. It has its own loop that retries on network errors, with no key, so it has the same weakness as the API. I wrote down that it needs a stable key as well, built from the input of each run.

I wrote a short plan in the notes. The client sends a key in a header, we store it with the refund under a unique index, and a repeat returns the first result. The key for Stripe would be derived from the client key and the customer id. Stripe keeps keys for 24 hours, which looks longer than any client retry window we have, but I want to check the mobile app to be sure.

Open questions for tomorrow: what to do with clients that send no key, how to test a crash after the Stripe call, and whether the key should be required at once or only after the clients are updated. I also want a counter for requests without a key, so that I can see how many there are before I decide.

summary: Added a log line and a counter for refund requests without a client key, and the first morning on staging showed that only the admin script and one old client send none.
body:
The refund endpoint now logs refund_no_key with the client name when no Idempotency-Key header comes in, and a counter goes to the metrics endpoint. I let staging run overnight with the usual simulated traffic.

The result was 214 refund requests, 31 without a key. All 31 came from two clients: the admin script and the nebula support tool, which has its own small refund button. The support tool is the one that matters, because a person can click it twice.

I wrote down for the nebula side what it has to send: a UUID made when the dialog opens, sent as the Idempotency-Key header, and reused when the person clicks again. I did not touch the nebula code. The note is in docs/refund-keys.md with a curl example.

The admin script is fixed on our side with a key from the invoice id and the amount. Making the key required is a later step, after the support tool sends it.

summary: Fixed the admin refund script to build a stable key and dry-run mode, then ran it on staging twice with the same input and got one refund each time.
body:
The script scripts/admin-refund.ts took an invoice id and an amount and called the service directly. I changed it to build the key from the string refund, the invoice id and the amount in cents, so the same command always has the same key. This is what Ines needs, since she sometimes repeats a command when the terminal shows no answer.

I also added a --dry-run flag that prints what would be refunded and the key, without calling Stripe. Before this, the only way to check was to run it on staging.

On staging I ran the same command twice for 12.50 EUR on a test invoice. The first run printed the new refund id and the second printed the same id with the line already refunded, key reused. The Stripe test dashboard shows one refund.

A case I considered is a deliberate second refund of the same amount on the same invoice, for example two partial refunds of 5 EUR. With this key the second would be treated as a repeat. So the script now accepts an optional --note value which goes into the key. The help text says this in one line. I think the behaviour is right but I want Ines to try it on a real case before I call it done.

summary: Looked into a customer whose invoice total was charged twice in Stripe and found a webhook retry that created a second payment record, not a double charge.
body:
Ines forwarded a mail from a customer who saw two payment lines of 148.00 EUR in his account and thought we charged him twice. I started with the Stripe dashboard. There was one charge, ch_ id ending in 7Qa, and one payment intent. So money moved once.

The second line was in our own payments table. Two rows pointed to the same payment intent, created 41 seconds apart. The customer portal reads this table, which is why he saw two lines.

The cause was in the webhook handler for payment_intent.succeeded. It first checks whether an event id was processed, then inserts the payment. The first delivery took longer than Stripe's timeout, because the database was busy with the monthly run, so Stripe sent the event again. Our check of the event id happens before the insert and the marker of the event is written after it, so both deliveries passed the check.

The fix has two parts. A unique index on payments.stripe_payment_intent_id stops a second row at the database. The handler now writes the event marker and the payment in one transaction and uses insert on conflict do nothing.

Before the index I had to find existing duplicates. A query over all payments found 6 pairs in the last year, all with the same cause and all from busy times. For each, the later row had no refund or other link, so I could delete it. I wrote the delete as a migration that first copies the rows into payments_duplicates_backup.

The invoices of these six were all marked paid once, so no amounts were wrong. Only the portal view and one report that counts payments were affected, and the report was off by those six rows over a year.

I added a test that delivers the same event twice at the same time and checks for one row. Without the index and the transaction it fails, and with them it passes in 100 of 100 runs. I answered Ines with the explanation and told her the customer can be told that only one charge happened. The deploy is planned for the evening.

summary: Deployed the payments unique index and the transactional webhook handler, and watched webhook deliveries for an hour without a duplicate or a failure.
body:
The migration ran first. It copied the six duplicate rows to payments_duplicates_backup, deleted them, and then created the unique index on stripe_payment_intent_id. I used create unique index concurrently so that the monthly tables were not locked, and it took 3 seconds on 410,000 rows.

Then I deployed the handler change. After the deploy I used the Stripe CLI to resend the last 50 payment_intent.succeeded events from the test account to the staging copy and the real deliveries on production came in as normal. For an hour I watched the logs for the handler. 163 events were processed, none failed and none logged the new conflict message.

To see the conflict path in real life, I resent one real event from the dashboard to production. The handler answered 200, the log said duplicate payment ignored, and the payments table had still one row. That is the case that failed before.

One small thing I noticed is that the handler returned 200 even when the conflict happened, which is right for Stripe because it should stop retrying. I made the log level info and not warn, since otherwise the alert for warnings would fire on every retried delivery.

The customer portal now shows one line for the customer from the mail. I wrote a reply for Ines to send. She confirmed the customer was happy.

What is left: the same pattern of check first and mark later may exist in other handlers. I listed them: invoice.paid, charge.refunded, charge.dispute.created and customer.subscription.updated. I will check each tomorrow, since only the first one touches money rows that a duplicate could break.

summary: Checked the other webhook handlers for the same race as the duplicate payment and found that charge.refunded could insert a refund row twice, so it got the same fix.
body:
I read the four handlers I listed yesterday one by one. invoice.paid only updates the invoice status and paid_at, so a second delivery writes the same values again. That is harmless. customer.subscription.updated does an upsert by subscription id, also harmless. charge.dispute.created inserts a row into disputes with a unique index on the dispute id that already existed.

The handler charge.refunded was the one with the problem. It inserts a row in refunds for each refund object in the event, and the table had no unique index on the Stripe refund id. It only checked for an existing row in code. With two parallel deliveries both could insert.

I looked in production data for duplicates and found two pairs in the last two years. In both cases one row had the refund id from our API call and the other came from the webhook, so they were created by a different path from the one I feared: the endpoint inserts the refund when the API call returns, and the webhook inserts it again when it arrives first.

That is related to the idempotency work. The endpoint and the webhook now both use insert on conflict on stripe_refund_id, and the webhook fills in fields that the endpoint does not know, like the balance transaction. I created the unique index, again concurrently, after moving the two duplicates to a backup table. The two duplicate refunds had amounts of 20.00 and 7.45 EUR, and the totals of the refunds report were too high by this much.

Tests: the endpoint and the webhook race each other in a test with a random delay, run 300 times. There is always one row and the fields from both sides are filled.

I did not deploy yet, because the change touches the refund endpoint that I am also changing for keys, and I want to ship them in order. The key work goes first, the unique index second.

summary: Prepared to make the refund idempotency key required by checking who still sends refunds without one, and wrote the docs page for the error message.
body:
The nebula side shipped its change today and its refund dialog now sends an Idempotency-Key header. I looked at the staging counter for refunds without a key over the last six hours and it was zero. On production, the counter had 3 requests in the last day, all from the admin script, which still builds no key. So the endpoint is not ready to require the header yet, and I did not touch its behavior.

I read through the refund service function to see who calls it. The cancel path calls it internally and has no client header, so it will need a derived key before the endpoint can insist on one. I wrote down the two options, a key built from the invoice id and the amount, or a key built from the cancel request id, and leaning toward the second, since a repeated cancel should give the same refund and not a new one.

I started docs/refund-keys.md. It says what the header is, that the client creates it, that it should be a random string or a UUID, and what a retry should do. I also noted the length limit, since a key that is too long would fail in the Stripe call, and I sketched three tests for later: no header, an empty header, and a header longer than 200 characters.

I asked Mara whether the admin script can be fixed this week. She said yes, and that she would also check the one old client that sends no key. Nothing was deployed today. The unique index on stripe_refund_id from yesterday is still the next thing to go out, and the required header comes after that.

summary: Deployed the unique index on stripe_refund_id and the endpoint and webhook upsert, and ran a day of refunds on staging to confirm that the two paths no longer create two rows.
body:
The order of the deploy was the migration, then the code. The migration moved the two old duplicates into refunds_duplicates_backup and created the unique index on stripe_refund_id concurrently. It took 2 seconds.

The code change makes both the endpoint and the webhook handler insert with on conflict do update, where the update only fills columns that are still null. This way whoever comes second adds the missing fields and never overwrites the other one's values. The balance transaction id comes from the webhook, and the customer note comes from the endpoint.

On staging I ran the simulated traffic with 400 refunds, with the webhook delay set at random between 0 and 3 seconds so that it arrived before the endpoint answer in about a third of the cases. The result was 400 rows, no duplicates, and no null in either of the two fields. Before the change a copy of the same run gave 37 duplicates when I tried the old code, which showed the problem was real and not just in my head.

I deployed to production and watched the refunds table. In the first two hours there were 9 refunds and 9 rows. I also compared the refunds report before and after: it dropped by 27.45 EUR, which is the two old duplicates, and nothing else changed.

I wrote a short note for Ines about this number, because the monthly refund total she compares with the Stripe balance report now matches Stripe closer than before. She has not replied yet.

Two more things I noticed while in this code. First, the refund row has no column for the idempotency key, so support cannot find a refund by key. I would like to add it but it is not urgent. Second, the test helper that creates refunds in fixtures still builds rows without a Stripe id, which will break once I make the column not null. I left both for later and wrote them into the todo file.

summary: Ines confirmed that the refund total of the month now matches the Stripe balance report to the cent, which she had not seen for two months.
body:
Ines wrote back this morning after she did her check of the previous month. For the first time in a while the refunds line in our report and the refunds in the Stripe balance report were the same. Before, she found a difference of 27.45 EUR and had listed it as an open point for the accountants.

I asked her to send the numbers so I could check them myself. I ran the report query for the month and got 3,918.20 EUR in 61 refunds, and her Stripe export showed the same amount in 61 lines. So the two duplicate rows were the whole difference.

She asked whether the same could be true for payments, as the payments report had been off by a small amount too. I told her the six duplicate payments from last week were the cause for that and the report is right now for the new month, but the old months still include them in the old exports she already sent. I offered to regenerate the old exports, and she said the accountants only need a one-line note about the difference, which I wrote for her with the six payment ids.

Nothing was changed in the code today.

summary: Added the idempotency key as a column on the refunds table so support can look up a refund by the key that a client sent.
body:
The todo from last week: support asked twice which refund belonged to a certain click in the support tool, and we could only find it by amount and time. I added the column idempotency_key to refunds as nullable text, with an index on it. The migration took one second.

refundService.create() now writes the client key into the column when it creates the row. For old rows the column stays empty, since the key table has the pairs of key and refund id, and I wrote a backfill query that joins them. It filled 214 rows, the ones from staging-like traffic since the key work began.

The admin script has a new option, --find-key, that prints the refund for a key. Ines does not need it but I did, for testing. I also added the key to the log line of the refund creation. A test checks that the column is set for a refund through the endpoint.

summary: Fixed the refund fixtures in the tests to carry a Stripe refund id and made the column not null, since the unique index alone allowed many null rows.
body:
The index on stripe_refund_id accepts any number of nulls, so a row without an id would still slip through. The test helper createRefundFixture built such rows, and about 40 tests used it.

I changed the helper to generate an id like re_test_ and a counter, and ran the suite. Eleven tests failed because they compared whole rows and now saw the new id. I fixed them by comparing the fields they care about.

Then I checked production for rows with a null Stripe id and there were none, since every refund goes through Stripe first. The migration to set not null ran in 1 second after that check.

The suite is green with 612 tests in 3 minutes 10 seconds. The refund topic is closed for now. I left the Stripe v17 upgrade deploy as the next large item, together with the removal of the shims.

summary: Looked at the Postmark bounce webhook after Ines saw invoice emails to a few customers marked as sent but never delivered, and found hard bounces were not saved at all.
body:
Ines gave me four customers who said they never got their invoice email. In our table the emails have the status sent. In the Postmark activity view, for three of them the status is hard bounce because the mailbox does not exist, and for the fourth a spam block at the receiving server.

Our code never learned this. We register no webhook for bounces, so the status stays sent forever. I checked how many sent emails of the last three months had a bounce in Postmark through the API. It was 58 out of 21,000, about 0.3 percent, which looks small but each one is an invoice a customer does not see.

I wrote the handler for the Postmark bounce webhook at /webhooks/postmark. It checks the basic auth credentials we set in Postmark, finds the email by the MessageID we store, and sets the status to bounced with the bounce type and the text. For hard bounces it also sets a flag on the customer, email_invalid, which the invoice job reads to show a warning to finance.

Tests use the sample payloads from the Postmark docs for hard bounce, soft bounce and spam complaint. The handler is idempotent in the same style as the Stripe ones, with an upsert by message id and bounce id.

A question is what to do with the 58 old ones. I wrote a script that goes through them with the API and fills the status. I ran it with --dry-run and it found 58 matches. The real run, the webhook registration in Postmark and the deploy come next. Ines asked for a list of customers with an invalid email address, so I will make it from the flag after that.

summary: Deployed the Postmark bounce handler, registered the webhook and backfilled the 58 old bounces, which gave Ines a list of 41 customers with an invalid billing email.
body:
I deployed the handler first and tested it with the Postmark webhook test button. The log showed the sample bounce, and the handler answered 200 and wrote nothing for an unknown message id, which is right.

Then I registered the webhook in Postmark for bounce, spam complaint and subscription change events, using a password stored in the secret manager. A real bounce arrived within an hour from a customer who had mistyped the domain, and the status changed to bounced as it should.

The backfill ran next. It updated 58 emails and set email_invalid on the customers behind them. Several customers had more than one bounced email, so the number of customers is 41.

I exported the 41 customers with name, billing email, the bounce text and the date of the last bounced invoice as a csv for Ines. She will contact them by phone or through the account owner in nebula, as we cannot reach them by mail.

There is one more thing I noticed in the Postmark data. For spam complaints, Postmark suppresses the address and later emails to it fail with an inactive recipient error. Our sender code treats any error from Postmark as retryable and tried the same email three times. I changed it so that error code 406, inactive recipient, is not retried and is stored as suppressed.

The tests for the new status cover this error too. After the deploy I checked the retry count in the job table and the 406 case produced one attempt. I think the topic is done unless Ines finds that the list is wrong.

summary: Showed the invoice email warning for customers with an invalid address in the finance preview, so Ines sees it before the monthly run and not after.
body:
The warning for tax country mismatch from a few weeks ago lives in the invoice job preview, which finance opens before the run. I added the second warning in the same list: customer has an invalid billing email, with the date and text of the last bounce.

The preview is built in src/jobs/invoicePreview.ts, and it collects warnings as objects with a code, a customer id and a text. I added the code EMAIL_INVALID and a link to the customer page in the admin view.

If an address is invalid, the invoice is still created and the PDF is still made, since the law needs the invoice whether or not the customer got the mail. Only the sending is skipped and the invoice is put on a list called needs_manual_delivery. Ines can download these PDFs in one zip from the admin view.

I tested with a staging customer with the flag set. The preview showed the warning and the run skipped the email, and the zip had the one PDF. When the flag is cleared, because the customer fixed the address, the next run sends normally. I added a line to clear the flag when the customer changes the billing email, as otherwise it would stay forever.

summary: Investigated a slow query behind the admin invoice search, which took 6 seconds for a customer name, and fixed it with a trigram index and a smaller select.
body:
Ines complained that searching an invoice by customer name in the admin view takes several seconds. I ran the query with explain analyze on a copy of production. It did a sequential scan over customers with an ilike on lower(name), 120 ms, and then a join to invoices that read the whole invoices table for each of the 40 matching customers, because the sort was on created_at without a useful index.

The plan said 5.8 seconds in total, most of it in the join and the sort. The invoices table now has about 1.1 million rows, which is the reason we will think about partitioning later.

The fix has two parts. First an index on invoices (customer_id, created_at desc), which let the join read only the newest rows per customer. I did not have this one, and I was surprised, since all other lookups use the customer id as well. Second a trigram index on customers.name with the pg_trgm extension, which was already installed for another search, so the ilike uses the index.

I also noticed that the query selected the pdf_cache column, which holds a base64 string and can be several hundred KB. Nothing in the list view uses it. Removing it from the select reduced the data sent from 90 MB to 400 KB for a result of 200 rows.

New time: 45 ms on the same copy. I created both indexes concurrently on production, and creating the invoices index took about 40 seconds. Afterwards I tried the search from the admin view with three names and each answered at once.

The list of things I saw in the plans and did not do: the monthly run reads the same table in a few places with similar sorts. I will look at those only if the run time becomes a problem again. The table size is the underlying issue and goes to the todo file.

summary: Answered a question from Ines whether the coupon discount is taken before or after VAT, and checked the invoice code and three real invoices to confirm that it is before.
body:
Ines asked this because an accountant wanted it written down. I read the totals code in src/billing/totals.ts. The order is: line amount, coupon discount on the line net amount, then the VAT on the discounted amount, then the rounding of each line. So the coupon is taken before VAT.

To make sure the code and the real invoices agree, I took three invoices with a percent coupon and one with a fixed amount coupon and recomputed them by hand. A 20 percent coupon on a net line of 100.00 EUR gave a net of 80.00 and 19 percent VAT of 15.20, total 95.20, and the invoice shows the same.

The fixed amount coupon is a bit different. A coupon of 10 EUR is split among the lines in proportion to the net amounts, and the last line takes the remainder so that the sum is exactly 10.00. This is why a line of a fixed coupon invoice can have a discount that looks odd, like 3.33 and 6.67 for two equal lines.

I wrote a paragraph for Ines in plain words with the one example, and I put it into docs/invoice-calculation.md so it does not depend on my memory. She said that this is what the accountants need.

summary: Wrote a draft plan for the coming Stripe v17 upgrade deploy and checked the changelog, with the refund question still open.
body:
Started on the plan for the Stripe v17 upgrade today. The upgrade branch has run on staging for a while, but it is not ready to deploy, and the refund endpoint still has no idempotency keys, so I am treating the refund concern as open and not as closed. I wrote the plan down so that the deploy can later be done in one calm morning.

The order I propose is this. First, deploy the SDK change with the two shims still in place, because they should be harmless with the new version. Second, watch for one full business day. Third, remove the two shims in a separate commit and deploy that. I prefer two steps because a problem with pagination is then easy to tell apart from a problem with the SDK, and the rollback note says the shims stay harmless for the old version.

What to watch in the first day: the error rate of payment intents, refunds and the webhook handler, the number of 4xx responses from Stripe, the retry counts in the logs, and the time of the monthly list calls for payments, which use the pagination shim. On staging, listing 3,000 payments took 8.2 seconds before and after the change.

I also read the changelog for v17 and checked two things. One is a changed type of the expand option, which TypeScript now flags, and I fixed the three places that use it. The other is that the default API version of the SDK changes. Our account has a pinned version in the dashboard, and the SDK sends its own version in the header unless we set apiVersion in the constructor. We set it, so there should be no change in behaviour.
