I checked this by logging the Stripe-Version header of a request on staging.

One case the plan must handle is the pagination helper with has_more true and an empty page, which the review found some time ago. The fix is in the branch, and I wrote a test with a mock that returns two empty pages and then a full one. It passes and stops after the last page. I also added a limit of 1,000 pages to the helper so that a bug at Stripe cannot make it loop for ever, with an error log if the limit is reached.

Things still open: for refunds I need to decide how to check the endpoint once it carries keys, and that has to come before any deploy. The webhook endpoint does not seem to change in v17, and the signature check stays the same. I will not deploy before the monthly run is over, because I do not want to touch payments in that period.

summary: Looked at how the monthly run behaved with the new email and PDF settings in a real month and found it at 21 minutes, with the invoice query now the largest step.
body:
The monthly run happened yesterday evening. I read the timings from the job logs this morning. The whole run took 21 minutes, down from 29 minutes after the email change and 48 before that.

The steps were: loading usage from nebula 2 minutes, computing the invoices 6 minutes, PDF rendering 5 minutes, emails 8 minutes. The email step is slower than I expected from the 29 second test, but that test had only 300 invoices and this run had 5,900 with Postmark limits.

The invoice computing is the largest step per invoice, and the logs show that most of it is waiting for the database, not CPU. Each invoice runs about 14 queries, and a few of them read the invoices table for the previous invoice number or the previous period of the customer.

I do not want to start a big change on this. 21 minutes is fine for a monthly job, and no one waits for it. I only recorded the numbers and put the idea of batching the lookups into the todo file.

There were two warnings in the preview this time, a tax country mismatch and one invalid email. Ines handled both before the run. No failed invoice and no retry of a job.

summary: Fixed a bug where the invoice number sequence skipped a number after a failed PDF render, which Ines noticed as a gap between two invoices.
body:
Ines found a gap in the invoice numbers from the monthly run: INV-… jumped by one between two invoices of the same batch. In many countries gaps in the numbers are a problem for the accountants, so this needed an explanation.

I looked at the job logs for the run. One invoice had a failed render with a timeout of the browser page, and the job retried. In our code the number is taken from a Postgres sequence at the start of the job step, and the retry started the step again and took the next number. The first number was lost because the sequence is not rolled back.

The fix is to assign the number only after the PDF is rendered successfully, in the same transaction that saves the invoice as final. Before that the invoice has a draft status and no number. The render uses a placeholder for the number, and the final number has to be in the PDF, so I changed the order: take the number in a transaction, render, and if the render fails, the transaction rolls back, but the sequence does not.

This is the real problem, because a sequence is not transactional. The answer is a counter table with one row per series, locked with select for update, so that the number is taken and released together with the transaction. It is a bit slower, because the invoices of one series are made one after another for the number step, but the render itself stays parallel when the number is assigned in a very short transaction at the end and the PDF is stamped with it afterwards.

That would mean rendering twice, though. So I took a simpler solution: render with the number, but reserve it with the lock held only during the render of that single invoice per worker. The two page pool of the PDF step still works, since the lock is by series and each worker uses its own series part. Hmm, that did not work with one series.

In the end I kept the sequence and added a gap filler: a failed render now records the lost number in a table invoice_number_voids, and the retry reuses the voided number first. The number stays in order and no gap appears. A test covers a render that fails once.

I could not remove the gap that Ines found, because that invoice has been sent. I wrote an explanation for the accountants. The new code is deployed after the tests pass.

summary: Wrote a repair for the invoice number void logic after review found a race between two workers reusing the same voided number, and added a test that runs 8 workers at once.
body:
When I read my change from this morning again, I saw that two workers could read the same voided number. The retry takes the lowest unused row from invoice_number_voids, and without a lock both can take it. That would give two invoices the same number, which is much worse than a gap.

I changed the query to select the row for update skip locked and delete it in the same statement, using a CTE with delete returning. A second worker skips the locked row and either takes the next void or takes a new number from the sequence. In both cases no number is given twice.

I also added a unique index on invoices.number for each series. I thought it existed already but it only existed on the staging copy, not on production. I checked production for duplicates first, with a group by having count more than one, and found none over 70,000 invoices. The index creation took 11 seconds concurrently.

The test starts 8 workers in parallel on a database with 5 voided numbers and 40 invoices to number. After the run there are 40 distinct numbers, the 5 voids are used, and the highest number is as expected. I ran it 100 times and it never failed. I also ran the older version of the logic against the same test, and it produced duplicates in 31 of 100 runs, which shows that the test finds the problem.

The next case is a worker that dies after taking a void but before saving. Then the delete is rolled back with the transaction, because both are in the same one, and the void is available again. A test kills the transaction on purpose and checks this.

One more thing: the monthly preview now shows the count of voids, so finance can see if any exist at the time of the run. The expected number is zero and a number above zero is explained in the log with the reason of the failed render.

I deployed it in the afternoon, after the staging run of 500 invoices with the browser killed at random on 5 percent of the renders. The result was 500 invoices, numbers in order, no gaps and no duplicates.

summary: Wrote the explanation for the accountants about the single gap in the invoice numbers and what has changed so that it cannot happen again.
body:
Ines asked for a short text for the accountants, which she will attach to the month. I wrote it in plain language, without the code details. It says that one number in the run was lost because the PDF of that invoice failed to render and the retry took the next number, that no invoice was created with that number, and which invoice number comes before and after.

It also says what changed. A number from a failed render is now reused for the next invoice, a database rule makes it impossible for two invoices to have the same number, and the finance preview shows when a number is waiting to be reused.

I checked the facts in the job log and the table before I wrote it, so that the numbers in the text are right. The lost number is the only one in the last twelve months, which I found by a query for gaps over the whole series. Ines read it and said she would send it as it is.

summary: Re-ran the monthly invoice run on staging after the number-void fix and found no gaps across 2,310 invoices, with the run at 19 minutes.
body:
After the repair of the void logic this afternoon I wanted proof on a full month of data, not just the 8-worker test. I copied last month's usage into staging and ran the whole monthly run with four workers. It produced 2,310 invoices and the numbers were consecutive from first to last.

I also forced 40 PDF renders to fail on purpose by killing the browser process at random. Those 40 numbers were voided and each was reused exactly once, never by two workers. The run took 19 minutes, two less than the last real one, mostly because fewer jobs were retried.

I sent the query that checks for gaps to Ines so she can run it herself after the next real run. Next is to look at the invoice query, which is still the biggest step of the run.

summary: Profiled the invoice query of the monthly run and found a per-customer usage lookup that runs 2,300 times, so it is a good target for one batched query.
body:
The monthly run spends about 7 of its 19 minutes in the invoice query step, so I started there. I turned on pg_stat_statements on staging and ran the run once. One statement stood out: the usage lookup by customer and period was called 2,311 times, with a mean of 150 ms.

The cause is in src/invoicing/collect.ts. For each customer the code loads the subscription, then the usage rows, then the coupons, in three separate queries. With the invoices table growing, the usage query scans more than it needs because the index is on (customer_id) and not on (customer_id, period_start).

I tried the new index first. On staging, EXPLAIN ANALYZE went from a bitmap scan of 38,000 rows to an index scan of 410 rows, and the mean dropped from 150 ms to 6 ms. That alone should cut about 5 minutes from the run.

The second idea is to batch the lookups per group of 100 customers with an ANY($1) query and group the rows in memory. I wrote a draft of that but did not wire it in yet. The risk is memory: a few customers have more than 900 lines of usage, and a batch with several of them gets large.

I decided to ship the index first because it is a pure addition and cannot change any invoice total. The batching waits until I have compared old and new output on a full month, byte for byte, in the totals. I wrote the index migration with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY so it does not lock the table.

Next step is to deploy the index to staging for a day and look at the plan on the production-sized copy again.

summary: Added the (customer_id, period_start) index on usage rows and the run on staging dropped from 19 to 13 minutes with identical invoice totals.
body:
I deployed the concurrent index migration to staging and let it build on the copy, which took about 90 seconds. Then I ran the full monthly run again.

The run went from 19 to 13 minutes. The invoice query step fell from 7 minutes to just under 1.5 minutes. The other steps did not change, so the PDF rendering is now the biggest part.

To be sure nothing changed in the money, I dumped invoice number, subtotal, tax and total for all 2,310 invoices from the run before the index and the run after it. A diff of the two files was empty. This is a check I want to keep for every performance change that touches the invoice code.

I also checked that the planner does not choose the new index for the small queries of the admin search, where the trigram index from last week should still be used. The plans were unchanged for the admin search.

One detail: the old single-column index is now mostly redundant. I did not drop it, since two other queries use it and I want to see the statistics for a week first. I put a note in the migration file.

The migration goes to production tomorrow morning when the load is low. I added the check of the diff as a small script in scripts/compare-run.ts so I do not have to do it by hand again.

summary: Wrote scripts/compare-run.ts, which diffs the totals of two monthly runs line by line and fails on any difference of even one cent.
body:
The manual diff from the previous entry worked, but it needed three shell commands and I would forget one. I turned it into a script. It takes two run ids, reads the invoice number, subtotal, tax, discount and total for each invoice and prints every difference.

It exits with code 1 if any invoice differs or if the sets of invoice numbers are not the same. I added a flag --ignore-pdf because the PDF hashes always differ with the creation time inside the file.

I tested it with two cases. A run against itself gives no output and exit 0. A run where I changed the tax of one invoice by one cent in a copy gives exactly one line and exit 1.

It is small, but it is the thing Ines asked for when the rounding was a topic: a way to show that a technical change did not move any amount.

summary: Deployed the usage index to production at night, no lock waits, and the next scheduled report query ran in 40 ms instead of 900 ms.
body:
I deployed the migration to production this evening instead of waiting until morning, because the load was already low. CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY took about 4 minutes on the real table and I watched pg_locks the whole time. There were no waiting queries.

After it finished I checked the plan of the usage lookup on production. It uses the new index and the mean time is 5 ms. The report query that Ines uses for the usage by plan also uses it now and went from 900 ms to 40 ms.

I left the old index in place as planned. Disk use went up by 310 MB for the new one.

The real test is the monthly run in a few weeks. For now staging says 13 minutes, so I expect about 15 in production.

summary: Looked at the PDF render step, now the biggest part of the run, and found that a new headless browser page is started for every invoice instead of reusing one.
body:
With the invoice query fixed, the PDF step takes about 8 of the 13 minutes. I read src/pdf/render.ts to see why. For each invoice the code launches a browser, loads the HTML, prints and closes the browser again.

Starting the browser takes about 600 ms on staging. For 2,310 invoices that is more than 20 minutes of work spread over the workers, which matches what I see.

A pool would be the obvious fix: one browser per worker and a fresh page for each invoice. The danger is a page that leaks memory or a browser that crashes and takes the job with it. I would need a restart after some number of renders.

I wrote down the plan but did not change code yet. First I want to measure on staging with a quick prototype of 200 invoices.

summary: Prototyped a browser reuse in the PDF worker and rendered 200 invoices in 61 seconds instead of 168, with the same output size.
body:
I changed the worker in a scratch change so that it keeps one browser and opens a new page per invoice. I rendered the same 200 invoices as the baseline.

The baseline took 168 seconds. The prototype took 61 seconds. The PDFs had the same page counts and nearly the same sizes, within 1 percent.

Memory of the browser process grew from 180 MB to 520 MB over the 200 renders, so a restart after about 100 pages looks needed. One page of a customer with 900 lines still took 40 seconds, so this does not help that case; it is the layout problem from before.

I will turn it into a proper change tomorrow with a render counter and a restart, and tests for a crashed browser.

summary: Built the PDF browser pool with a restart after 100 renders and crash recovery, and the staging run of 2,310 invoices fell from 13 to 8 minutes.
body:
I turned the prototype into src/pdf/browser-pool.ts. Each worker owns one browser. A page is opened per job and always closed in a finally block, even if the render throws.

The pool counts renders and, after 100, closes the browser and starts a new one before the next job. This keeps the memory at about 350 MB in my measurements. I made the limit a setting, PDF_BROWSER_MAX_RENDERS, with a default of 100.

Crash recovery was the part that needed care. If the browser dies, a page call fails with a disconnect error. The pool now notices the disconnected event, marks the browser as dead and starts a new one. The failing job is not retried inside the pool; it fails normally and pg-boss retries it, which keeps the retry logic in one place.

I wrote tests for this: a normal render, the restart after the limit (with the limit set to 3), a killed browser in the middle of a job, and two jobs in parallel in one worker. The last case showed that one worker handled jobs one at a time already, so a pool of pages is not needed.

The interaction with the invoice number void logic from last week mattered. A failed render still voids its number and the retry takes the next one or the same voided one. I ran the 8-worker test again with random browser kills and got no gaps and no duplicates.

Then I ran the full monthly run on staging. It finished in 8 minutes, down from 13. compare-run.ts reported no differences in the totals across all 2,310 invoices.

What is left: a look at memory on the production machine, because it has less room than staging, and a decision about the setting. I will deploy it behind no flag, since the output is the same, but I will watch the first real run closely.

summary: Reviewed the Stripe v17 upgrade branch once more against the list of calls in billing-api and found two places that still use the old auto-pagination helper directly.
body:
With the invoice work in good shape I went back to the Stripe SDK upgrade to v17 that is waiting. I listed every call into the SDK with grep and sorted them by type: customers, subscriptions, payment intents, refunds, invoices and the webhook construct call.

Most go through our own wrapper in src/stripe/client.ts, which is where the two shims live. Two calls do not. One is in the admin script that exports payments for Ines, and one is in the reconciliation job that compares our payments with the Stripe balance transactions. Both call the old auto-pagination helper directly.

This matters because the shims were written for the wrapper only. If the old helper behaves differently in v17, these two would break and the break would show up as a missing page of results, not as an error. That is the kind of failure that Ines would find at the end of the month.

I read the changelog of v17 again for the list helpers. The helper still exists, but the type of the returned object changed, and the callback form is gone in one of the overloads. The reconciliation job uses the callback form.

I changed both calls to use the wrapper and added a test for the reconciliation with three pages of fake data, with a page size of 2. The test fails on the old code under v17 types and passes on the new.

I also ran the export script against the Stripe test account with 250 payments and compared the count with the dashboard. Both were 250.

I did not remove any shim yet, since the order of removal is in the plan from earlier. This was only about making sure all calls go through one place first.

Next: run the whole test suite with the branch, then update the plan with these two findings.

summary: Ran the full test suite on the Stripe v17 branch after the pagination fixes: 412 pass, 3 fail, and all three failures come from a changed error message text, so I planned how to handle them.
body:
I rebased the v17 branch on the current main and ran the whole suite. The result was 412 passing and 3 failing.

All three failures were in tests of the dunning code. They compare the text of a Stripe error message for a declined card. In v17 the message for insufficient funds is worded a little differently, and our test asserts on the exact string.

The code under test does not depend on the text. It reads the decline code, for example insufficient_funds, and decides the email from that. So the product behavior looks fine and only the assertion is too strict. I did not change any of the tests yet. I wrote down that the three tests should check the code and the type of the error and not the message, and I left the branch as it is for now.

I also looked for other places in src where we match on a message string. I found one in the payment retry code that checks for the word expired in a message. That one is a real risk, because a changed message would send an expired card down the wrong path. I did not touch it. I put it on the list as a follow-up: it should check the decline code expired_card, with a test for a card error that has the code and one that has a different text.

I added a general rule to the upgrade plan draft: no decisions on message text, only on codes. The grep for message matching should become part of the checklist for the next upgrade. The three failing tests stay red on the branch until that follow-up is done.

summary: Answered Ines on why one customer got two reminder emails for the same overdue invoice, and found the dunning job ran twice after a worker restart.
body:
Ines forwarded a complaint from a customer who received two payment reminders within an hour for one invoice. She asked if this is a bug or a rule of the dunning schedule.

I checked the dunning rules first. The schedule sends a reminder at 3, 7 and 14 days after the due date, so two within an hour is not part of it. Then I looked at the email log in Postmark and the job table. There were two sends from two different job ids, 52 minutes apart.

The pg-boss table showed the first job as expired and not completed. A worker had been restarted during a deploy at that time, while the job was running. The job had already sent the email but not yet written the sent marker, so after the expiry pg-boss ran it again.

The cause is the order in src/dunning/send.ts: send, then write the marker. If the process stops between them, the retry sends again. I changed it to write a sending marker with a unique key of invoice and step before the send, and to mark it as sent after. A retry that finds a marker in state sending checks Postmark by the message tag before sending again.

That last check needs an extra API call, but it only happens in the rare retry case. I wrote tests for the normal path, a crash after the marker, and a crash after the send.

I also searched for other customers hit by the same problem. The log shows 6 double reminders in the last three months, all near a deploy time. I gave Ines the list of the 6 so she can write a short note to them if she wants.

The fix is not deployed yet. I want to look at whether the receipts email has the same order, since it follows the same pattern.

summary: Checked the receipt email job for the same send-then-mark order and found it is safe, because it already uses a unique key per payment.
body:
After the double reminder I read the receipt email code in src/receipts/send.ts. It was written later than the dunning code, during the busy month, and it takes a different approach.

The receipt job inserts a row in the sent_emails table with a unique key of payment id and type before it calls Postmark. If the insert fails, the job stops without sending. So a restart cannot send a second receipt for the same payment.

The weak point is the other direction: if the process dies after the insert and before the send, the receipt is never sent and nothing retries it. I looked for such cases in the table. There are 3 rows in the last three months with state pending and no Postmark message id.

I wrote a small job that finds pending rows older than 30 minutes and sends them, using the same tag check as in the dunning fix. I did not deploy it either. I want both changes to go out together so the behavior is the same in both places.

I put the three old pending receipts on a list for Ines, to confirm that the customers were not asking for them.

summary: Moved the email send-and-mark logic of dunning and receipts into one helper in src/email/once.ts, so both use the same marker and the same Postmark tag check.
body:
Two jobs had two similar solutions, so I merged them. The helper sendOnce takes a key, a type and a function that sends the mail. It writes the marker, sends, then updates the marker with the message id.

If it finds an old marker in state sending, it asks Postmark for messages with the tag of that key. If one exists it marks it as sent, and if not it sends again.

Both the dunning job and the receipts job now call it. The cleanup job for pending rows uses it as well. I ran the 11 tests of both jobs and added two for the helper itself. All pass.

I will deploy this tomorrow on staging with a forced restart in the middle of a batch of 50 mails.

summary: Deployed the sendOnce helper to staging, killed the worker in the middle of 50 reminders three times, and got exactly 50 mails each time.
body:
I started a batch of 50 dunning reminders to test addresses on staging and killed the worker process after about 20 of them. Then I started it again and let pg-boss run the expired job.

The result was exactly 50 messages in Postmark. In the first run, one marker was in state sending. The tag check found the message in Postmark and marked it sent, so it was not sent a second time.

I repeated this three times with different kill points: before the first mail, in the middle and right after the last send. Each run gave 50 mails and 50 markers in state sent.

The pending receipt cleanup also found a planted old row and sent it once.

One thing I noticed is that the tag query of Postmark is limited in how far back it looks by default, so I set the search window to 3 days. Retries older than that are not expected, since pg-boss expires jobs sooner.

I deployed it to production this afternoon. The counters for sending markers older than an hour should stay at zero, and I added an alert for that. Next is a short summary for Ines about the 6 customers with double reminders.

summary: Wrote the short note for Ines on the double reminders: cause, the 6 affected customers, and what changed so that a deploy cannot cause it again.
body:
Ines asked for something she can pass on to customer support. I wrote half a page in plain words without code.

It says that a restart of a worker during a reminder could make the system send the same reminder again. It lists the 6 customers with the invoice numbers and the times of both mails. It explains that no payment or amount was touched, only the email.

It also says what changed: each email now has a marker that is written before it is sent, and a repeat checks whether the mail was already sent. The same holds for receipts now. The three receipts that were never sent were sent yesterday.

I added that the alert will tell me if a marker stays open for more than an hour.

summary: Planned the production rollout of the PDF browser pool: a lower restart limit at first, memory watching during the run, and a quick way back to one browser per job.
body:
The pool is on staging and gave 8 minutes for the full run, but production has less memory, so I wrote down how to deploy it with a way back.

First, the memory. The production worker machine has 2 GB and runs 4 workers. At about 350 MB per browser that is 1.4 GB, which leaves too little for the Node processes. I will start with PDF_BROWSER_MAX_RENDERS at 40 and 3 workers. In my staging test a limit of 40 kept the browser near 250 MB and cost about 30 seconds more over the whole run.

Second, the watching. I added a gauge of resident memory per worker and a counter of browser restarts to the metrics. During the first real run I will look at them every few minutes. If the total goes above 1.6 GB I lower the limit again.

Third, the way back. I added a setting PDF_BROWSER_POOL with the values on and off. With off the code launches a browser per job as before. A change of the setting needs a restart of the workers but no deploy, so the way back is about a minute.

Fourth, the order. The deploy goes out on a day with no run planned. I will start a test run of 300 invoices for a test account first, with the compare script against the old path, then wait for the real run.

One open point is the customer with 900 lines. Its single page still takes 40 seconds and holds a browser the whole time. With a pool this blocks that worker for the time, but jobs are taken one at a time anyway, so other workers continue.

I also thought about whether the new PDF renderer that is still only an idea should wait for this. It does not need to. The pool helps the current renderer and the work on a layout change is separate.

The checklist is in docs/rollout-pdf-pool.md. Tomorrow I will deploy with the lower limit and run the 300-invoice test.

summary: Invoice PDF render time grew with line count, so Mara and the agent profiled a 400-line invoice and found the browser waits on web fonts for each page.
body:
Mara reported that the monthly invoices for the largest customers take almost a minute each to render. The agent built a fixture with 400 usage lines and timed the renderer: 48 seconds, against 3 seconds for a 20-line invoice. The trace showed the headless browser waiting on a web font request for every page break. The font is fetched from a CDN on each render because the template links it by URL.

The agent only measured this session and changed nothing in the template. Next step is to embed the font as a local file and compare the timings again. The profile output was saved under scripts/profile-pdf/ for reuse.

summary: Embedding the invoice font locally cut the 400-line render from 48 to 21 seconds; the rest is table layout that grows worse than linearly with rows.
body:
Following up on the profile from earlier today, the agent put the font file into the template assets and referenced it with a local @font-face rule. The 400-line fixture dropped from 48 to 21 seconds, and the 20-line invoice from 3.1 to 1.4 seconds. The font wait was real but not the whole problem.

A second trace showed that the layout step grows faster than the number of rows. The usage table has one row per meter per day, and each row has nested spans with percentage widths. The agent tried fixed column widths in a copy of the template, and the 400-line time fell to 17 seconds.

The visual diff against the old output showed one change: the description column wraps at a slightly different place for long event-index names. Mara said that is acceptable if Ines agrees. The agent kept both templates side by side and did not merge anything. It will ask Ines to look at three sample PDFs, and then decide whether to group rows by meter to cut the line count itself.

summary: Grouping usage lines by meter on the invoice cut the line count of big customers by about 90 percent, but totals must stay identical, so the agent added a check that proves it.
body:
After the layout tests, the agent looked at the cause: a customer with 12 meters and 30 days gets 360 rows, each needing its own layout. The idea was to show one row per meter with the quantity summed over the period, and keep the daily detail in a CSV attachment. This changes only the presentation, so the totals must not move.

The agent wrote a function groupLinesForDisplay in src/invoices/render-lines.ts. It sums quantity and amount per meter and price tier. It does not touch the stored invoice lines, only the list that goes to the template.

The risk is that a sum of rounded line amounts differs from the stored line totals by a cent. To catch that, the agent added a test that takes 200 real invoices from the staging copy, groups them, and compares the grouped sum with the invoice total. All 200 matched in cents.

The render time for the 400-line fixture, now grouped to 12 rows, was 2.4 seconds including the font change. That is a big gain over 48 seconds.

The agent also noticed that tiered meters needed the tier boundary kept as a separate row. Otherwise the unit price shown would be an average and confuse customers. The grouping key now includes the tier. With that change, the big fixture has 19 rows and renders in 2.9 seconds.

Not done yet: the CSV attachment and the email wording that mentions it. The agent left those for the next session and wrote the plan in the TODO file. Ines still has to approve the new layout, since she checks these PDFs every month.

summary: Built the CSV attachment with the daily usage detail for grouped invoices, and fixed a bug where commas in event-index names broke the columns.
body:
The grouped invoice hides the daily rows, so customers need the detail somewhere. The agent added src/invoices/usage-csv.ts, which writes one row per meter per day with the columns date, meter, tier, quantity and amount. The CSV is stored next to the PDF and attached in the receipt email.

The first test run showed a bug. An index name such as "logs, prod" contains a comma, and the line was split into two columns. The agent switched from manual joining to a small escape function that wraps fields in quotes and doubles quotes inside them. It added three test cases for commas, quotes and a line break in a name.

The attachment size matters for email. A 30-day, 12-meter invoice gives a CSV of about 22 KB. The largest real customer in staging gave 310 KB, which is fine for the email provider limit.

The agent also checked the amount column. It uses the stored line amount in cents, formatted with the invoice currency, so there is no new rounding path. The sum of the column equals the invoice subtotal in all 200 staging invoices.

The download endpoint GET /invoices/:id/usage.csv now returns the same file for the customer portal. It uses the same auth check as the PDF download, and a test confirms a customer cannot fetch another customer's file.

Open points: the email text says "see the attached PDF" and should mention the CSV; the file name should contain the invoice number. The agent did the file name now, as invoice-INV-number-usage.csv, and left the wording to Mara. Ines has the three sample PDFs and will answer tomorrow.

summary: Ines approved the grouped invoice layout with one change: show the tier boundary quantities, so the agent added them and the PDF now matches what finance expects.
body:
Ines answered about the three sample PDFs. She likes that the invoices are shorter, and she asked for one thing: for tiered meters, each tier row should show the range, such as "first 1M events", because the accountants compare it with the price table. The agent added a label to the tier rows from the price table data in the plan catalog. Flat meters show no range.

The label is built in render-lines.ts from the tier's from and to values. Open-ended last tiers read "over 10M events". The agent wrote tests for a first tier, a middle tier and a last tier, and for a plan with a single flat price.

Then the agent rendered all 200 staging invoices again with the new template and looked at the page count. The median went from 4 pages to 1, and the largest from 19 pages to 3. Total render time for the batch fell from 31 minutes to about 6 minutes.

One problem showed up in the batch. Three invoices of a customer with a very long company name overflowed the header and pushed the address under the logo. The agent added a CSS rule that lets the name wrap and limited its width. The three invoices now look right.

Mara reviewed the diff and asked to keep the old template file for now, so the change is behind the existing template choice in config and not a hard switch. The agent kept it that way. The default is still the old layout in production, and staging uses the new one. The plan is to run both for one billing cycle and compare. The email wording about the CSV is still open.

summary: Evening check of the nightly usage meter found that two days of counts from nebula were read twice after a restart, so the meter now keys its reads by day and index.
body:
While looking at the staging invoices, the agent saw that one customer had usage of exactly double on two days. The meter job reads counts from nebula and stores them in the usage table. A deploy restart in the middle of a run made pg-boss retry the job, and the second run inserted the same rows again.

The table had no unique constraint on customer, index and day. The agent added a migration that first removed the duplicates, keeping the row with the earliest created_at, and then added a unique index. The insert now uses ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE, so a rerun replaces the count with the newer value.

The agent checked production data read-only. Four customers were affected over the last month, with a total of 11 duplicate rows. None of those invoices were issued with the wrong amount, since the invoices of that period are still drafts. Ines will be told which four customers so she can look at them.

The tests now include a job that runs twice for the same day. The result has one row per index and day. The migration was run on the staging copy and took under a second. It will go out with the next deploy, and Mara wants to look at the cleanup query first.

summary: Reviewed Mara's Stripe SDK v14 branch notes and listed the breaking changes that touch billing-api, mostly in how pagination and error classes are used.
body:
Mara asked for a review of what the move from Stripe SDK v13 to v14 needs before anybody changes code. The agent read the changelog and grepped the source for each affected call.

Three items matter. First, the default API version is pinned differently, and we pass apiVersion explicitly in src/stripe/client.ts, so that is fine. Second, the error classes are checked by name in two places, in the payment retry code and in the webhook handler; the names are unchanged, but the agent found one place that uses error.type strings that should become instanceof checks. Third, the list helpers we wrapped in a pagination shim behave the same for autoPagingToArray, but the shim relies on a private field that is probably going to change.

The agent made a short list in docs/upgrade-v14.md with the file and line of each use, 14 call sites in all. No code changed in this session.

The next step is to bump the version on a scratch change, run the 212 tests, and see what breaks. The shim is the part the agent expects to fail, so it will look at that first.

summary: Bumped the Stripe SDK to v14 and the tests passed except for the pagination shim, which relied on a private field that no longer exists.
body:
The agent changed the version in package.json and ran the tests. 209 of 212 passed. The three failures were all in the shim tests for listing invoices and payment methods.

The cause was what the review had predicted. The shim read a private property to find the last item id for the next page, and v14 no longer sets it. The error was TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined.

The agent rewrote the shim to take the id from the last element of the returned data array, which is what the public API documents. It added a stop condition on has_more. The three tests passed after that.

The agent also changed the two error type string checks to instanceof checks on the SDK classes. Nothing else needed to change. The next step is a run against the Stripe test mode with a real subscription create, update and cancel, which the agent will do after lunch.

summary: Test-mode run of the v14 upgrade went through subscriptions, a card payment and a failed card, and the dunning flow behaved the same as before.
body:
After the unit tests, the agent ran the scripted scenario in Stripe test mode with v14. The script creates a customer, attaches a card, starts a subscription with a trial, ends the trial, and pays the first invoice. All steps passed, and the webhook events arrived at the local handler with valid signatures.

Then it used the test card that always declines. The invoice moved to past_due, the payment failed webhook created the first dunning email job, and the retry schedule was the same as under v13: after 1, 3 and 5 days. The agent compared the job rows with a saved run from last month and found no difference except the ids.

One small difference came up in the logs. v14 includes a request id in the error message, which made our log lines longer, and the log redaction rule cut one of them in the wrong place. The agent adjusted the rule so that the request id stays in and the card fingerprint stays out.

The agent also tried a cancel with proration. The credit note amount matched the amount from the old version to the cent.

The branch is ready for Mara's review. The agent noted in the pull request text that production needs no change of the pinned API version. The deploy is planned for tomorrow morning, in a quiet hour, so that any problem with webhooks shows up before the monthly invoice run.

summary: Deployed the v14 upgrade in a quiet hour; one webhook for a customer update failed on a new optional field, which the agent fixed with a lenient parse.
body:
The v14 change went out early in the morning. The agent watched the webhook handler logs for the first hour. Most events passed, but one customer.updated event failed with a validation error from our own zod schema, which did not know a new optional field called invoice_settings.rendering_options.

The schema was strict and rejected unknown keys. Stripe returned 500 for that delivery, so it was queued for retry. No data was lost, since Stripe retries for days, but the agent wanted to stop the errors at once.

The fix changed the schema for webhook payloads from strict to passthrough for the nested objects that we do not read. We only read a handful of fields, and a new field on the Stripe side should never break us. The agent also kept the strict schema for our own API input, where strict is right.

The agent wrote a test with a payload that has extra unknown keys at three levels, and it passes now. Then it replayed the failed event from the Stripe dashboard, and the handler returned 200.

A second look at the logs showed 14 more retries waiting in the queue of the same kind. They all cleared after the fix went out, about 20 minutes later.

The agent wrote down the lesson in docs/webhooks.md: schemas for incoming Stripe objects must ignore unknown keys. It also searched the other webhook schemas for the same strictness and found two more, for invoice.paid and charge.refunded, and changed them too. Mara approved the fix by message.

Nothing else odd happened in the rest of the hour. The monthly invoice run is in two days, and the v14 code will have run through two days of real events by then.

summary: Wrote the email wording for the CSV attachment and rewrote the receipt template so the invoice link, the PDF and the CSV are described in plain sentences.
body:
Mara picked the wording task for this session. The receipt email is a Postmark template with variables, and the old text said only "your invoice is attached". With the grouped PDF, customers need to know where the detail is.

The new text has three short parts. The first line gives the amount and the period. The second says the PDF shows totals per meter and the attached CSV lists usage per day. The third gives the link to the portal for the full history.

The agent changed the template in the repository under emails/receipt.html and emails/receipt.txt, since both parts are sent. It added the variable hasUsageCsv, so that invoices without usage lines, such as a flat plan, do not mention a CSV that does not exist. A test renders both cases and checks that the text part and the html part carry the same sentences.

The agent sent test emails to Mara's address and to a seed address and checked the layout in two clients. The attachment names show the invoice number as planned.

One issue came up: the subject line was too long for mobile and cut the amount. It was shortened from "Your nebula invoice for the period ending..." to "Nebula invoice INV-number, amount". Mara liked that.

Still open is the translation of the text for the German and French customers, which Ines said the accountants would like checked. The agent left the strings in the same file with a TODO for the two languages.

summary: Answered Mara's question why one customer was billed for an index they had deleted: the meter counts the day an index existed, and the rule is by design but unclear on the invoice.
body:
Mara forwarded a support question. A customer deleted an index on the 3rd of the period and still saw usage for it on the 3rd and not later. They asked if that was a mistake.

The agent read the meter code. The usage meter reads the count per index per day from nebula at the end of the day, and for a deleted index nebula returns the count up to the delete. The invoice therefore has a line for the day of deletion with the events counted before it. That is correct under the plan terms, which bill events indexed, not days kept.

The agent checked the customer's rows: 1.2M events on that day, 0 afterwards, and the amount matches the price table for their tier. Nothing needs to be corrected.

The confusing part is that the PDF now groups by meter and shows the index name only in the CSV. The agent suggested to Mara adding a short note in the support reply and to think about marking deleted indexes in the CSV. It did not change code.

summary: Added a deleted flag to the usage CSV so that rows of indexes removed during the period are marked, which answers the support question from this morning.
body:
Mara agreed that the CSV should mark deleted indexes, so the agent made the change. The meter table has no field for it, but nebula's count response includes a deleted_at timestamp for the index. The agent stored it in a new nullable column on the usage table, filled from the response.

The migration adds the column without a default, which is cheap even on the big table. The meter job writes the value on each run, and older rows stay null. For the CSV, a null shows as empty and a set value shows as the text "deleted" in a new last column.

The agent changed the CSV tests to include a deleted index and an old row with null. It also updated the column list in the docs and the customer help text.

One point to watch: adding a column at the end avoids breaking customers who read the CSV with a script that uses column positions. The agent chose the end for that reason.

The change is in review. The question from the support case can now be answered with the note that the CSV shows the deleted index and its last day.

summary: Looked at the slow monthly dunning query and found a missing index on invoices by status and due date, which turned a 9 second scan into a 40 ms lookup.
body:
The dunning job, which selects unpaid invoices that need a reminder, took 9 seconds in production and was getting worse. The agent ran EXPLAIN ANALYZE on the query and saw a sequential scan on the invoices table with a filter on status and due_date.

The table has an index on customer_id and one on number, but none that helps this query. The agent created a partial index on (due_date) where status in ('open', 'past_due'), because only a small share of rows is ever unpaid. The index is about 2 MB, against 600 MB for the table.

On the staging copy, with the same data size, the query went from 9 seconds to 40 ms. The plan now uses an index scan.

The migration uses CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, so it does not block writes, and it runs outside a transaction as the migration tool requires. The agent checked that the tool supports that setting and added a comment in the file.

One caveat is that the table keeps growing, and Mara thinks about partitioning it at some point. The agent noted that a partial index like this would need to be recreated per partition then. It put that in the TODO file so the plan does not forget it.

The change is deployed, and the next dunning run in the evening will show the real time in the logs.

summary: Wrote the German and French strings for the receipt email and the reminder emails, and fixed a Postmark template variable that printed raw braces in French.
body:
Ines had the accountants check the German and French text, and they sent back small corrections. The agent applied them to the strings files and then looked at all three emails that have translations: the receipt, the first reminder and the final notice.

The corrections were mostly about formal address. The French text used "tu" in the final notice, which the accountants did not want, so it became "vous". The German receipt had the wrong term for "period", and now uses "Abrechnungszeitraum".

While testing, the agent found a real bug. In the French reminder, the amount showed as {{amount}} with the braces visible. The cause was a typographic space that the translator had put inside the braces, so the template engine did not see a variable. The agent fixed the string and added a test that scans all translation files for variables with unusual whitespace, and for variables that exist in English but not in a translation.

The new test found a second case, a missing dueDate in the German final notice, where the sentence just had no date. That is fixed too.

The agent sent test emails in all three languages to the seed addresses. The layouts looked right, and the CSV sentence appears only when the attachment exists.

The locale of a customer is taken from the billing address country, with English as the fallback. The agent checked that rule against 30 staging customers, and the result was correct for 29. The one exception is a Swiss customer with a German address, who got English because the mapping has no CH entry. The agent added CH to German as the default and left a note that Swiss French customers might want a choice later. Mara will ask whether to add a language setting on the customer record.

summary: Mara asked whether the retry schedule for failed card payments should change, and the agent pulled recovery rates: 61 percent are paid after the first retry and only 4 percent after the third.
body:
Mara wanted to know if three retries over five days is the right schedule. The agent queried the payments table for the last six months of failed invoices, grouped by the retry attempt at which they were finally paid.

Of 1,840 failed first attempts, 1,122 were paid after the first retry (61 percent), 310 after the second, 74 after the third (4 percent), and the rest were not recovered. The third retry therefore brings little. Most of the late payments came after the customer got a dunning email and updated the card, not from the retry itself.

The agent suggested to keep the schedule, because the retries are cheap, but to move the final notice email earlier by one day, since customers act on emails. It did not change any code, since this is a business decision that Ines should see.

The agent saved the query as scripts/reports/retry-recovery.sql and wrote the numbers into the notes file. Mara will ask Ines in the next finance meeting.

summary: Started the v15 upgrade of the Stripe SDK: the review found that the changed webhook construct function and a renamed type affect the signature check, and a test branch compiled after fixes.
body:
With v14 stable for a week, Mara asked for the next step, v15. The agent read the changelog first and then grepped for each affected call.

Two changes matter for billing-api. The first is a set of renamed TypeScript types for the invoice line items, which touch eleven files but only at the import level. The second is a change in how webhooks.constructEvent takes the raw body. In v15 it needs a string or a Buffer, and no longer accepts a parsed object silently. Our Fastify route has a raw body plugin, so we pass a Buffer, but one old test used a parsed object and would have passed by accident.

The agent bumped the version and ran the compiler. There were 23 type errors, all from the renamed types. A search and replace fixed 21, and two needed a manual look because they used a union that changed shape. The code now compiles.

The tests then ran: 221 passed and 2 failed. One failure was the old webhook test with the parsed body, which the agent rewrote to send a real raw body with a computed signature. The other failure was a snapshot of a Stripe mock whose field order changed, so the agent updated the snapshot after checking the diff by hand.

The agent also checked the pagination shim again. It still works, but the changelog says that auto pagination for some list calls is more reliable, so the shim could be reduced later. The agent did not touch it now, to keep the upgrade small.

Next is the test mode run with real calls, the same scenario script as for v14. The agent expects no difference but wants to confirm the signature check with events from the Stripe CLI.

summary: The v15 scenario run in test mode passed, including webhooks from the Stripe CLI, and the upgrade went to review with a note about the rewritten webhook test.
body:
The agent ran the scenario script against Stripe test mode with v15. A customer, card, trial subscription, first invoice and cancel with proration all passed. The credit note amounts matched the saved results from v14.

For the webhooks, the agent used stripe listen with forwarding to the local server and triggered nine event types: invoice.paid, invoice.payment_failed, charge.refunded, customer.subscription.updated, and five more. All nine were accepted, and the signature check passed for each. One event, charge.dispute.created, had no handler and was logged as ignored, which is the expected behavior.

Then the agent tested the negative case: a request with a changed body and the old signature. The handler answered 400 with signature verification failed, as it should. A request with no signature header also gave 400.

One more check was the retry code for failed payments, which uses error classes. The agent made Stripe return a card_declined error and a rate_limit error, using the test helpers, and looked at the paths. The decline led to the dunning flow, and the rate limit led to a retry with backoff. Both worked.

The agent looked at response times too, since a new major version can add overhead. The scenario took 38 seconds under v15 and 39 under v14, so no change.

The pull request text now lists the 23 type fixes, the rewritten webhook test and the updated snapshot. It also says the production API version is still pinned. Mara will review tomorrow.

The only open point is the shim, which the agent wants to simplify in a later change when more is known about the pagination in v16.

summary: Mara reviewed the v15 change and asked for one fix: the raw body plugin must be limited to the webhook route, which the agent verified and tightened.
body:
Mara's review had one question. The raw body plugin in Fastify was registered globally, and she asked if that was needed. It keeps a Buffer copy of every request body, which costs memory for large uploads like the CSV import of customers.

The agent checked the setup. The plugin was global with the option global: true from the first version of the service. Only the webhook route needs it. The agent changed it to global: false and enabled it with config: { rawBody: true } on the single route.

Then it ran the tests. Two other routes had used request.rawBody for logging, and their tests failed with undefined. The agent removed that use, since logging the raw body of a payment request was also not good for privacy. The logs now keep only the content length.

The webhook tests all passed. The agent re-ran the Stripe CLI test with the nine events once more to make sure the route still gets the raw body, and all nine were accepted.

Mara approved the change and it was merged. The deploy is planned for tomorrow, again in a quiet hour.

summary: Merged v15 and prepared the deploy checklist: watch webhook error rate, the dunning job, and the evening invoice run for one hour each.
body:
After the merge, the agent wrote a short checklist in docs/deploy-checklist.md for SDK upgrades, because there have been three now. It lists what to watch and for how long.

First is the webhook error rate, with the query for the logs and the Stripe dashboard page for failed deliveries. Anything above 1 percent for 10 minutes means a rollback. Second is the dunning job, where the count of emails queued should match the unpaid invoices of the day. Third is the evening invoice run, with a check that the invoice count and the sum match the preview numbers from the morning.

The checklist also says to keep the previous image tag ready, and gives the command for the rollback. The agent tried the rollback command against staging to be sure it works, and it did.

Mara added one more line: tell Ines before an invoice run if a change touched totals. The v15 change does not, but the line is there now.

summary: The v15 deploy went smoothly: webhook errors stayed at zero, dunning counts matched, and the evening invoice run gave the same totals as the preview.
body:
The agent deployed v15 in the early hour and followed the new checklist. The webhook error rate stayed at zero for the first hour, with 212 events delivered. The Stripe dashboard showed no failed deliveries.

The dunning job ran at its normal time and queued 37 emails for 37 unpaid invoices, so the counts matched. Postmark showed all 37 as delivered, with no bounces.

For the invoice run, the agent compared the preview from the morning with the real run. Both gave 641 invoices and the same sum to the cent. The agent also spot checked five invoices in the PDF against the database. They matched.

One small thing showed in the logs: a deprecation warning from the SDK about a method that we still call, listing payment methods with the old parameter name. It is harmless today, but the agent put it in the TODO for the v16 work.

Mara closed the upgrade task. The agent also noted the numbers in the upgrade doc, for the next time.

summary: Found why the SEPA-minded EU customers keep asking about direct debit: 23 of the last 40 support tickets from EU customers mention paying by bank, so the demand is documented for planning.
body:
Mara asked for a count to back up a planning item. The agent read the support ticket export that Ines had saved in the shared folder and searched the last 40 tickets from customers with an EU billing address.

Twenty-three of them mention paying by bank transfer or direct debit. Nine of those say that card payments are blocked by their company policy. Six say that the card fee makes the total higher than their budget line. The rest ask for a general bank option.

The agent also looked at how those customers pay today. 17 of the 23 pay by card after a manual reminder, and 6 pay by sending a bank transfer that finance matches by hand. Ines spends about two hours a month on that matching, according to a note in the export.

For the failed payment numbers, the agent used the report from last week. EU customers have a higher rate of failed first attempts than others, 19 percent against 13 percent. That fits the story that company cards are declined.

The agent wrote a one page summary in docs/planning/eu-payments.md with the counts, the quotes without names, and the effect on finance work. It did not propose a design, since that is the next task. It only listed what Stripe offers for the EU and what finance would need, such as mandate records and a clear failure flow.

Mara will bring the summary to the planning talk. The agent also noted that the counts come from a small sample of tickets, so they show direction and not exact shares.

summary: Looked at invoices with a total of zero after a full coupon: they got a PDF and a payment attempt, so the agent made them skip the charge and mark as paid.
body:
Support noticed that a customer with a 100 percent coupon got a receipt for 0.00 and a payment failed notice. The agent reproduced it in test mode. An invoice with a total of zero was created, and our payment step still tried to charge it through Stripe, which refuses a zero amount.

The fix is in the invoice finalize step. If the total is zero, the invoice is marked paid with the method none and no charge is created. The receipt email is still sent, since the customer should have a record, but the subject says no payment was needed.

The agent added tests for a full coupon, for a coupon that brings the total to exactly zero after tax, and for a normal invoice. It also found 3 real invoices in production in this state in the last two months and listed them for Mara, who will mark them by hand after checking with Ines.

summary: Began the v16 upgrade review, noting that the new default pagination and the list parameter rename remove the need for part of the shim, and a test branch compiles.
body:
With v15 deployed, the agent started on v16 and read the changelog. Three changes are relevant: the old parameter name for listing payment methods is gone, which our warning from yesterday was about, a few more types are renamed, and auto pagination now handles the cursor for more list calls.

The agent bumped the version on a scratch change. The compiler gave 9 errors. Six were renamed types, and three were the old parameter name in the payment method calls. The agent fixed all nine, and the code compiles.

Then the tests ran: 226 passed and 1 failed. The failure was a mock that returned the old parameter in its expected call. The agent updated the mock.

The shim is still there. The agent compared it with the new built in auto pagination for the invoice list and found equal results for 1,500 invoices in staging, but the payment method list in the shim has a special case for detached methods that the SDK does not cover. So the shim stays for now, in a smaller form.

The agent wrote the notes in the upgrade doc with the nine fixes and the shim finding. The next step is the scenario run in test mode and the review by Mara.

summary: Finished the Stripe SDK v16 upgrade on a test branch: the shim for list pagination shrank to one helper, and the full test suite passed after three type fixes.
body:
Continued the v16 work started yesterday. The new default pagination and the renamed list parameter removed most of the old shim, so the agent deleted the auto-paging wrapper for customers and invoices and kept only the helper that collects all pages of subscription items.

Three type errors remained. The first was in the refund code, where the shape of the refund object changed a little. The second was in the dunning job, which read an optional field as if it were always set. The third was a renamed enum for payment intent status in the retry logic. All three were fixed with small edits in src/stripe/refunds.ts, src/jobs/dunning.ts and src/stripe/types.ts.

The unit tests passed after the fixes: 412 tests, no skips. The webhook test needed no change this time, because the construct function kept the v15 signature.

The agent then ran the test-mode scenarios: a new subscription with a trial, an upgrade in the middle of a period with proration, a card payment, a failed card, and a coupon that makes a total of zero. The proration lines matched the v15 results to the cent.

One thing looked odd. The list call for invoices of a customer with more than 100 invoices returned the second page in a different order than before. The agent checked the Stripe changelog and found that the order is by creation time descending in both versions, but the old shim sorted again on its own. The remaining helper now sorts explicitly, so the invoice history page of a customer stays stable.

Not done yet: the deploy checklist and the review by Mara. The plan is to put it into review tomorrow morning with a note about the ordering change, and to deploy in a quiet hour like the last two upgrades.

summary: Mara reviewed the v16 branch and asked for a test of the sorting helper with 250 invoices; the agent wrote it and it caught a missing await in the last page.
body:
Mara read the v16 change in the evening and had two comments. One asked why the helper sorts again, which the agent answered with the changelog note about ordering. The other asked for a test with more than two pages of invoices, because the old shim was never tested beyond one page.

The agent wrote a test that builds 250 fake invoices behind a stubbed list function with a page size of 100. The first run failed: the helper returned 200 invoices, not 250. The cause was a missing await on the call for the last page, so the final promise was dropped when the loop ended. In production this would have shown as an invoice history that silently lost its oldest invoices for large customers.

After the fix the test passed with 250 entries in the right order. A second case with exactly 200 invoices, where the last page is empty, also passed.

The agent also looked for other places where the same pattern could hide. The search over src found two loops that call list functions, one in the usage export and one in the reminder job, and both already awaited correctly.

Mara approved with the test added. The branch is ready to merge, and the deploy is planned for tomorrow in the quiet hour.

summary: Merged and deployed the Stripe SDK v16 upgrade; webhook errors stayed at zero and the evening invoice run matched its preview.
body:
The v16 change was merged after the morning check and deployed in the quiet hour. The agent watched three things for an hour each: the webhook error rate, the dunning job and the evening invoice run.

Webhook errors stayed at zero over 340 events. The dunning job processed 58 invoices and the counts matched the day before. The evening invoice run produced the same totals as the preview for all 212 invoices.

The only noise was a warning in the logs about a deprecated field on the customer object, which the SDK prints once per start. The agent noted it for a later cleanup but did not change anything today. The deploy checklist for SDK upgrades now has a line about checking the order of invoice history.

summary: Wrote a short guide for SDK upgrades from the v14, v15 and v16 experience, so the next upgrade follows the same steps and nothing is rediscovered.
body:
After three upgrades in a few weeks, the agent collected what repeated into docs/stripe-upgrades.md. The guide is short and in steps.

First, read the changelog and list what touches billing-api: webhook construction, pagination, error classes, types. Second, make a test branch that compiles before touching behavior. Third, run the test-mode scenarios: trial, mid-period upgrade, card payment, failed card, zero total coupon, refund. Fourth, deploy in a quiet hour and watch webhooks, dunning and the invoice run.

The guide also lists the traps found so far. The v14 pagination shim used a private field. The v15 webhook change touched the signature check. The v16 upgrade changed the order of lists in one place, so the helper sorts on its own.

There is also a note that two shims are still left in src/stripe/compat.ts and are expected to go with a later major version. Mara read it and asked to add the commands for the Stripe CLI webhook test, so the agent added those too.

summary: Looked into why the PDF render of a 60-line invoice still takes 14 seconds and found the headless browser starts fresh for each invoice; a reused browser brought it to 6.
body:
Even after grouping lines and local fonts, mid-sized invoices were slower than expected. A 60-line invoice took 14 seconds in the evening run, which adds up over 200 invoices.

The agent measured the steps with timestamps in the render function. Launching the browser took about 5 seconds, loading the HTML 1 second, the layout and print about 7 seconds, and writing the file to storage under a second.

The launch was the easy target. The code in src/pdf/render.ts started a new browser for each invoice and closed it at the end. The agent changed it to keep one browser per worker and open a new page for each invoice. A page is closed in a finally block, so a failed render does not leak.

There was a risk: a browser that lives for hours can grow in memory. The agent ran 300 renders in a row in a test and watched the process. Memory grew from 180 MB to 410 MB and then stayed flat after the page closes. To be safe, the worker now restarts the browser after 100 renders.

The same 60-line invoice now took 6 seconds in total. The numbers for the invoice run in the evening: 212 invoices went from 49 minutes to about 21 minutes in a staging copy.

The agent also checked that the output is identical. It rendered 30 old invoices with both versions and compared the extracted text of each PDF, and all 30 matched. Pixel comparison was not used because the PDF metadata has a time stamp.

One crash case was tested on purpose: killing the browser in the middle of a run. The next render noticed a closed connection and started a new browser, and the job finished with a retry. The change goes to review tomorrow.

Still open is the layout time of 7 seconds, which depends on table size and is the reason for the planned new renderer later.

summary: Mara approved the browser reuse change with one request: log the render time per invoice, so slow ones can be found without profiling again.
body:
Mara reviewed the browser reuse change and liked the restart after 100 renders. She asked for one thing: a log line for each render with the invoice id, the line count and the milliseconds, so slow cases show up in the normal logs.

The agent added a structured log entry after each render with those three fields and the worker's render count. It checked that no customer data is in the line, only ids and numbers.

A quick query over the logs of a staging run showed the spread: most invoices under 3 seconds, and four above 10 seconds, all with more than 150 lines. That confirms where the next effort belongs.

The change was merged and deployed in the evening. The first real run is tonight.

summary: The first evening run with the reused browser finished 212 invoices in 23 minutes instead of 49, with identical totals to the preview.
body:
The agent checked the result of last night's invoice run. It took 23 minutes, close to the staging estimate of 21. All 212 invoices were created and the totals matched the preview.

The new log lines worked. Four invoices took more than 10 seconds, all of large customers with 150 or more lines, and the slowest took 19 seconds. The browser restarted twice, as expected for 212 renders on two workers.

No failed renders and no retries. Memory of the workers stayed under 450 MB.

The agent told Mara the result and noted that the remaining slowness is the table layout. The slow four are the first test cases for any new renderer.

summary: Ines found two invoices where the VAT line was shown twice in the PDF; the cause was a template loop over tax lines that also included the summary line.
body:
Ines wrote that two invoices of EU customers from last night showed the VAT line two times. The totals were right, but she did not want to send these to the accountants as they are.

The agent opened the two invoices. Both customers had two tax rates on one invoice, because a plan changed in the middle of the period and the old and new rates were both valid for some lines. The invoice data had the tax lines as a list with one entry for each rate and a summary entry with the type summary.

The template in templates/invoice.hbs looped over all tax entries and printed each one, then printed the summary below. For invoices with one rate, the list had only the summary entry and the loop printed it once, so the problem never showed. With two rates the loop printed two rate lines and the summary, and the summary looked like a duplicate of the VAT line in the case that both rates were the same percentage.

The agent changed the template to loop only over entries of type rate and to print the summary once under them. It also added a snapshot test with an invoice that has two rates and one with the same rate on two lines.

The totals were checked against the stored values: the sum of the rate lines equals the summary for all 31 invoices in the last month with two rates.

The two invoices of Ines were rendered again. Since the invoice number must not change, the agent used the existing re-render command, which keeps the number and the date and only replaces the PDF. The old PDFs were kept in storage under a suffix for the audit trail.

The agent also searched for other invoices from the last 3 months with the same pattern and found 5 more, which are now re-rendered and listed for Ines to check.

A note went to Ines with the list of the 7 invoice numbers. She will confirm tomorrow that the new PDFs are fine.

summary: Ines confirmed the seven re-rendered invoices; the answer to her side question was that the credit note numbering is separate from the invoice numbering by design.
body:
Ines checked the seven invoices and confirmed that the VAT block is now correct. She did not need any more changes.

She also asked why credit notes have their own number series and not a continuing invoice number. The agent looked at the code and the early design notes. The series are separate because the accountants wanted credit notes to be clearly traceable, and some countries expect a separate series. The prefix CN and the year-free counter are set in src/invoices/numbering.ts.

The agent wrote this answer for her in plain words, with one example of an invoice and its credit note. She said that it matches what the accountants said and that no change is needed.

Nothing was changed in the code today.

summary: Added a nightly check that compares the sum of invoice lines to the invoice total for all invoices of the day and reports mismatches to a log channel.
body:
After the VAT display issue the agent wanted a cheap safety net. A new job, totals-audit, runs after the evening invoice run. It reads all invoices created that day and sums the net lines, the tax lines and the total, then compares them with the stored totals.

The first version compared in cents as integers, so there are no floating point surprises. A mismatch is written to the log with the invoice id and the three differences, and a counter is exported to the metrics.

The agent ran it over the last 30 days of staging data: 6,300 invoices, zero mismatches. To prove that it works, a test inserts an invoice with a total changed by one cent and checks that the job reports it.

One limit is known: the job checks that the numbers are consistent, not that they are right according to the price table. That is a different check and stays open.

summary: The totals audit reported one mismatch on its first real run: a zero-total invoice with a rounding line of one cent, which came from the coupon logic.
body:
The first real run of totals-audit last night reported one mismatch out of 214 invoices. The agent looked at it this morning.

The invoice was of a customer with a 100 percent coupon. The lines summed to 0.00, the tax to 0.01, and the total was stored as 0.00. So the tax line had one cent that was not in the total.

The cause was in the order of steps. The coupon is applied to the net amount and the tax is computed on the net before the coupon for one tax rate path, then the total is clamped to zero. The clamp hides the cent.

The agent changed the tax calculation to use the discounted net, which gives a tax of 0.00. A test with a full coupon on a taxed line was added next to the zero-total tests from a few weeks ago.

The invoice itself was not paid, so it was corrected before the payment run. Ines was told, since this touches the totals, and she wants to see the corrected PDF.

summary: Ines accepted the corrected zero-total invoice, and the agent checked that no earlier invoice with a full coupon carried a stray tax cent.
body:
Ines looked at the corrected PDF and accepted it. She asked whether older invoices could be affected too.

The agent ran a query over all invoices with a coupon of 100 percent in the last year. There were 47 of them. For each one it compared the tax line with the net after the coupon. All 47 had a tax of zero except the one from last night, because older invoices were created before the other tax path was used for those customers.

So only the one invoice was wrong, and it is fixed. The query was saved in scripts/audit-full-coupon.sql for later use.

The agent reported this to Ines, with the count and the result.

summary: Planned the work for partitioning the invoices table: it has 410,000 rows and grows by about 6,000 a month, and the plan weighs a partition per quarter against one per month.
body:
Mara asked whether the invoices table should be split before it hurts. The agent took the numbers: 410,000 rows, about 6,000 new rows a month, and the growth is faster since grouped invoices exist, because the CSV and the line tables grow too.

The agent measured where it hurts today. The monthly dunning query is now fast with the index from last week. The invoice history for one customer is fast. The slow parts are the yearly export for the accountants, which scans the whole table for a year, and the vacuum, which takes 11 minutes at night and competes with the invoice run.

Two options were compared. One partition per month gives 12 partitions a year, small ones, and an export of a quarter touches three. One per quarter gives 4 partitions a year, and the accountants think in quarters and in years. The agent leaned to quarters, because the tables are not so big that monthly pieces help, and fewer partitions mean fewer things to create and to forget.

There are risks to plan for. Postgres needs the partition key in the primary key, so the key of invoices becomes the id plus the creation date, and every foreign key from other tables to invoices must be looked at. The agent listed five tables that point to invoices: lines, payments, refunds, credit notes and email logs. A foreign key to a partitioned table is allowed in the Postgres version in use, but the keys need both columns.

A migration plan was written in steps. Create the new partitioned table next to the old. Copy the rows in batches by quarter. Switch the names in one short transaction during a quiet hour. Keep the old table for a week.

The invoice number must stay unique over all partitions. A unique index cannot span partitions without the key, so the number is made unique with the date, and the numbering code already gives numbers in sequence, which keeps them unique in practice. The agent proposed a separate small table of used numbers to keep a hard guarantee.

No code was changed. Mara wants to think about the number table and decide in the next days.

summary: Mara decided on quarterly partitions and a small invoice_numbers table for the hard uniqueness guarantee; the agent turned this into a task list.
body:
Mara read the plan and chose quarterly partitions. She also liked the separate table for invoice numbers, because the accountants care about gaps and duplicates more than anything else in the system.

The agent wrote the task list in docs/partitioning.md. First, create invoice_numbers with a unique number and a reference to the invoice id, and fill it from the existing rows. Second, make the numbering code write there inside the same transaction as the invoice. Third, the partitioned table and the batch copy. Fourth, the key changes for the five tables. Fifth, the switch and the clean up.

The order is chosen so that the first two steps are useful alone and can be deployed on a normal day. The agent will start with them.

summary: Created the invoice_numbers table and filled it from 410,212 existing invoices; a check found no gaps and no duplicates in the invoice series.
body:
The agent wrote the migration for invoice_numbers with a unique constraint on the number and a column for the invoice id. The backfill ran in batches of 10,000 rows and finished in about 90 seconds on staging.

After the fill, two checks ran. The count of numbers equals the count of invoices, 410,212 in both. The numbers of the invoice series run from the first to the last without gaps, and the credit note series, which is separate, also has no gaps.
