The migration is reversible. The table is not used by the code yet, so it can be deployed without any change in behavior.

summary: The numbering code now writes to invoice_numbers in the same transaction as the invoice, and a concurrency test with 20 parallel runs produced no duplicates or gaps.
body:
The next step was to use the new table. In src/invoices/numbering.ts the next number came from a sequence and was put on the invoice. The agent changed it so that the number is taken from the sequence and inserted into invoice_numbers in the same transaction as the invoice itself.

There is a subtle problem with sequences: a rolled back transaction burns a number, which makes a gap. The old code accepted this in theory, but in practice the invoice run did not roll back. The agent looked at how to be safe. The solution is to take the number as late as possible, just before the insert of the invoice, and to lock the counter row with select for update, instead of a sequence. This costs a little concurrency, but the invoice run creates only a few invoices a second, and the render is the slow part.

The agent changed the code to a counter row for each series. The invoice and credit note series each have a row with the last number. The transaction locks the row, increments it, inserts into invoice_numbers and the invoice, and commits. If anything fails, everything rolls back and no number is lost.

Then the test. Twenty parallel workers each created 50 invoices against a test database, 1,000 in total. The result was 1,000 distinct numbers with no gaps, and the time was 6 seconds, which is far above the real need.

A second test forced a failure after the number was taken, by throwing in the middle of the transaction. The counter was unchanged afterwards and the next invoice took the same number.

One more check was on the migration of the counter rows: the starting value was set from the maximum in invoice_numbers, per series, and a test compares them.

Mara reviewed the diff and asked about deadlocks if a credit note and an invoice are created in the same transaction. They use different rows, and the agent made the code always take the invoice row first if both are needed, which is written as a comment at the top of the function.

The change is ready for deploy in the evening run window, when no run is active.

summary: Deployed the counter row numbering after the evening run; the next 31 invoices got consecutive numbers and the totals audit stayed clean.
body:
The change was deployed after the evening invoice run was done, so no run was active during the switch. The agent created the counter rows with the start values taken from the maximum numbers and checked them against invoice_numbers: equal for both series.

A test invoice in staging-like conditions was not enough, so the agent waited for the first real creations. Over the next hour 31 invoices from late trials and upgrades were created. Their numbers were consecutive and each had a row in invoice_numbers.

The totals audit ran after midnight with no mismatches. The first two steps of the partition plan are done.

summary: Wrote the batch copy script for the partitioned invoices table and tested it on a staging copy: 410,000 rows moved in 7 minutes with matching counts per quarter.
body:
The agent started the third step of the partitioning plan. The new table invoices_p has the same columns, the key on id and created_at, and partitions for each quarter from the first invoice to two quarters ahead.

The copy script in scripts/copy-invoices.ts works by quarter. For each quarter it reads in batches of 5,000 ordered by id, inserts into the new table and logs the count. It can be started again after a stop, because it skips ids that exist already.

On a staging copy with all 410,000 rows the copy took 7 minutes. The counts per quarter matched the old table, and a checksum of the id and total columns per quarter matched too.

One thing came up: the default partition. Rows with a date outside the ranges would fail. The agent added a default partition on purpose so that an insert never fails because someone forgot to create the next quarter, and a job logs a warning if anything lands in it.

The five tables with keys to invoices are next.

summary: Went through the five tables that point to invoices and found that the email log joins by invoice id only, so it needs the created date too, or its queries scan every partition.
body:
The agent went through the lines, payments, refunds, credit notes and email log tables one by one, to prepare the keys for the partitioned table.

For lines, payments and refunds, the foreign key can include the created date, because the code already has the invoice row in hand when it inserts. The agent added a column invoice_created_at to each and wrote the backfill from the invoices table.

For credit notes the same works, but the credit note has its own date, so the new column is separate and filled from the invoice.

The email log was different. It stores the invoice id and the kind of mail, and the support page looks it up by invoice id only. With the new table, a lookup by id without the date has to look in all partitions. At present that is 4 to 6 partitions, which is fine, but each quarter adds one, so it would get slower over time.

The agent checked the plans with explain. A lookup by id alone on the partitioned test table went through every partition with an index scan each, 6 scans, around 2 ms in total. That is acceptable for now, but not forever.

The better way is to keep the created date on the email log as well, and to change the support page to pass the date from the invoice it already loaded. The agent changed the query function to take both values and kept a fallback by id alone for the old callers, with a warning log.

The backfills for all five tables ran on staging in under 4 minutes together. The foreign keys were created as not valid first and then validated, so that the production run does not lock for long.

The next entry will be the switch plan with a rehearsal.

summary: Rehearsed the table switch on a staging copy and found that the rename left the sequence and two views pointing to the old table; the script now fixes both.
body:
The agent did the full rehearsal of the partition switch on a fresh staging copy: copy the rows, set the keys, then swap the names in one transaction.

The swap went as planned in the sense that the names changed in 40 ms. But the first test of the service afterwards failed in two places.

The first was a database view for the finance export, v_invoice_export, which was bound to the old table by object id and not by name. After the rename, the view still read the old table, now called invoices_old. A rename does not move views. The export showed no new invoices, which would have been a silent problem. The agent recreated the view inside the swap transaction, and the same for a second view, v_open_invoices, which the dunning report uses.

The second was the sequence for the invoice id. It was owned by the old table, so a drop of the old table would have dropped it as well. The agent moved the ownership to the new table with alter sequence owned by.

After the fixes the rehearsal was repeated from the start. The copy took 7 minutes again, the swap 60 ms with the views, and the service tests passed. The tests include a full invoice run in test mode with 20 invoices, a payment, a refund and a credit note.

The agent also timed the yearly export for the accountants. On the old table, a year took 38 seconds. On the partitioned one it took 9 seconds, because only four partitions are read.

The vacuum was measured too. A vacuum on the biggest partition took 2 minutes, and the others are quicker. Old partitions are mostly static, so they will need little attention.

For the real switch, the new rows that arrive during the copy are a problem. The plan is to do the copy in the day, then in the quiet hour copy the last rows that are newer than the copy start, stop the invoice job, swap, and start again. The window should be about two minutes.

The agent wrote the steps as a checklist in docs/partitioning.md with a rollback: rename back, which works as long as no new rows came in; after that, a reverse copy of the new rows is needed, and the script for that exists as an option in the copy script.

Mara will review the checklist tomorrow.

summary: Looked at a customer report of a receipt email in French that showed the amount with a dot instead of a comma, and fixed the number format for French and German receipts.
body:
Support forwarded a message from a French customer: the receipt email said 1,234.50 EUR where a French reader expects 1 234,50 EUR. A German customer had written something similar a week ago, and it was not yet followed up.

The agent looked at the receipt code. The emails are built with Postmark templates, and the amount is passed as a ready string. The string was made with a helper that always formatted with the English locale, while the date was formatted with the customer locale. So only the date was localized.

The helper in src/emails/format.ts now takes the customer locale, with a fallback to English. It uses Intl.NumberFormat with the currency, so the symbol position and the separators follow the locale. Node had to have full ICU data, which it has in the current image, and the agent checked this with a quick test for de-DE and fr-FR.

The tests got six cases: English, German and French, each with a small and a large amount. One detail: the French format uses a narrow no-break space as the thousands separator, and the test had to compare with that character, not a normal space. In the email HTML this is fine, but in the plain text part some mail clients show a strange sign, so the agent replaced it with a normal no-break space in the plain text only.

The PDF invoices were also looked at. They use their own formatting, and the invoice text follows the customer language already, so no change was needed there. The agent checked three invoices for each language and they were right.

The reminder emails use the same helper, so the fix covers them. The agent sent test emails through Postmark to the test inbox for each language and looked at the result in the mail client: receipt, first reminder and last reminder, 9 emails in all.

Support can answer the two customers that the format is fixed from the next email. The change was deployed in the evening.

An open point is the currency code or symbol: for euro the symbol is used now, and for other currencies the code is shown, which is the Intl default. Ines said earlier that the code is better for the accountants, so the agent left a note to ask her if the emails should show the code everywhere.

summary: Mara reviewed the partition switch checklist and asked for a dry run of the rollback; the agent ran it and found that the reverse copy skipped rows with null dates.
body:
Mara read the checklist and said that she trusts the forward path but wants to see the rollback work. So the agent did the rollback rehearsal on staging.

The steps: do the switch, create 30 new invoices on the partitioned table to simulate a day, then roll back by renaming the tables back and copying the 30 new rows to the old table with the reverse option of the copy script.

The rename back worked. The reverse copy reported 27 rows, not 30. The agent looked and found that three invoices had a null in the column paid_at, and the reverse copy used a where clause that compared paid_at with the copy start time, which is false for null.

The filter was meant to select rows created after the start, but it used the wrong column. The agent changed it to created_at, which is never null, and ran the rollback again from a fresh state. This time all 30 rows were copied.

A second check followed after the rollback: the counter rows and invoice_numbers. The counter had moved on by 30, and the old table now had the 30 rows with the matching numbers, so no number was lost or used twice.

The views also needed to go back. The agent added the recreation of both views to the rollback steps. Without it the export would have read the wrong table, just as in the first rehearsal in the other direction.

Mara looked at the new steps and the test run. She approved the plan and asked to keep the old table for two weeks and not one, since the accountants do their closing in that time and may want to compare.

The agent changed the checklist to two weeks. The real switch is not scheduled yet; Mara will pick a quiet evening and the agent will prepare the final copy.

summary: Ines asked for the currency code on emails; the agent changed all receipt and reminder amounts to show the code after the number, in the same style as the invoice PDF.
body:
Ines answered the open question from yesterday. She wants the currency code in the emails, because customers forward receipts to their accountants and a symbol can be unclear, and a dollar sign is shared by several currencies.

The agent changed the format helper to use currencyDisplay code in Intl.NumberFormat. In English the result is EUR 1,234.50, in French 1 234,50 EUR and in German 1.234,50 EUR. These match what the PDF shows.

The tests were updated for the new strings: nine cases, three for each language. The snapshot of the Postmark template variables changed in the same places.

One more place used its own format: the subject line of the dunning email, which had the amount in it. The agent found it with a search for toFixed and changed it to use the helper. Two other uses of toFixed were in internal logs and were left alone.

Test emails went out for each language and the agent looked at them in the inbox. All looked right, and the plain text part had no strange signs.

The change was deployed together with the earlier format fix. Support was told, so they know what the customers will see.

The agent also noted that the amounts in the Slack-like alert for failed payments use another format, but those are for the team only, so there was no change.

summary: Answered Mara's question how many EU invoices used the reverse charge last quarter: 318 of 5,900, all with a valid VAT id checked at creation.
body:
Mara asked for the share of invoices with reverse charge in the last quarter, since the accountants asked her. The agent wrote a query on the invoices and tax lines with the tax type reverse_charge.

Result: 318 of 5,900 invoices, a bit more than 5 percent. All 318 belong to customers with a VAT id that was checked at the time of creation, and the check result is stored with the invoice. There were no invoices with reverse charge and without a stored check.

The agent also split the number by country: Germany 104, the Netherlands 61, France 47, and the rest in smaller counts. Total net amount of these invoices was about 9 percent of the quarter's net, because the business customers are larger.

The query is saved in scripts/report-reverse-charge.sql and the output went to Mara as a table.

summary: Prepared the final run of the invoices table switch to quarterly partitions and checked the plan with Mara, without doing the switch yet.
body:
Mara and the agent went through the plan for the switch of the invoices table to partitions and chose an early afternoon slot for it, because the invoice run is in the evening and there are few payments around that time. Nothing was switched today; the day was for preparation.

The agent wrote the checklist as a list of steps with a person and a check for each one. First pause the invoice job and the webhook workers for the tables involved. Then copy the rows newer than the copy start. Then compare the counts per quarter and the checksums of id and total. Then run the swap transaction: rename the tables, recreate the two views, move the sequence ownership, rename the keys. Then restart the jobs and watch.

On the staging copy the main copy of the rows took a little under 8 minutes, and the agent noted that it will probably take longer in production because of the load. For this reason the main copy is planned for the morning, well before the window, and only the small catch-up copy stays inside the window. The swap transaction on staging took 48 ms, and the agent estimated a pause of about a minute and a half including the checks.

The agent also prepared the checks for after the swap: a test invoice in test mode that is created, paid, refunded and credited, with a query to show in which partition each step landed. The finance export view and the dunning report get a quick look for new rows. The default partition should stay empty, and the job that warns about it is ready.

Mara decided that the old table stays as invoices_old for two weeks after the switch, so the accountants can finish their work. The agent will add a reminder to the task list to drop it later. Still open is the job that creates the next quarter's partition ahead of time. It exists only as a draft and is the next thing to finish after the switch.

The agent also started the totals audit script on a copy of the last quarter, to have a baseline of zero mismatches to compare with after the switch.

summary: Prepared the cleanup after the planned partition switch of the invoices table and checked the plan on a staging copy, since the switch has not happened yet.
body:
The switch of the invoices table to quarterly partitions is still ahead, so this session was about preparing the cleanup and the checks that will follow it. Nothing in production was changed.

The agent wrote the cleanup steps as a script. After the switch, the old table will be renamed to invoices_old and revoked for writes, so nothing can write to it by mistake. It will stay for two weeks as a fallback. The script was run on the staging copy only, and the rename and the revoke worked there.

The agent also wrote a query that compares row counts per quarter between invoices_old and the new partitions. On staging, all five quarters matched. The staging copy is smaller than production, so the real counts will be checked after the switch. The query will also cover invoices created since the final copy.

The five most used queries were run with EXPLAIN against the staging partitions. Four of them prune to a single partition. The fifth, the monthly finance export, reads two partitions, which is expected, because a month can cross a quarter border. The email log query that needed the created date was rewritten to filter on the date, so it should no longer scan every partition.

The agent listed the pg-boss jobs that touch invoices, the dunning job and the PDF job, and noted that both must be watched in the first evening after the switch. The first evening invoice run on the new table should be compared with its preview, and the totals audit should be run after it.

Open for later: a job that creates the next quarter partition ahead of time, so an invoice on the first day of a quarter does not fail for lack of a partition. Mara wants that before the quarter ends. A short draft note about the fallback and the drop date of invoices_old was prepared for the deploy notes.

summary: Planned a daily job that would create the next quarterly invoice partition ahead of time, and tested the idea on a staging copy.
body:
The partition switch of the invoices table was still ahead, and the main risk the agent saw was a missing partition at the start of a quarter. An insert with no matching partition fails with 'no partition of relation found for row', and the evening run would stop.

The agent drafted a pg-boss job that would run daily at 03:00. It checks whether partitions exist for the current and the next quarter, and creates the next one if it is missing, using CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS ... PARTITION OF, so it is safe to run many times. The job would also write a warning to the log channel if the next partition is still missing one week before the quarter ends.

On a staging copy the agent moved the clock to the last day of a quarter and saw that the next partition was created. Mara read the draft and asked for the indexes to be copied from the parent. The agent noted that partitioned tables do this on their own, so nothing changed. The job stays unmerged until the switch is done.

summary: Investigated a customer's complaint that a dunning email arrived twice and found that the job retry sent it again after a timeout from Postmark, so sending is now recorded before the call returns.
body:
A customer wrote to support that a payment reminder came twice within ten minutes. The agent looked in the email log and saw two rows for the same invoice and the same dunning step.

The pg-boss log showed the cause. The first attempt called the Postmark API, the call took longer than our 10 second timeout, and the job was marked failed. Postmark had in fact accepted the message. The retry after one minute sent a second one.

There were two ways to handle this. One was a longer timeout, which only makes the window smaller. The other was to make the send step idempotent on our side. The agent chose the second. Before the call, a row is now written to the email log with the state 'sending' and a unique key made of invoice id, template and dunning step. A retry that finds a row in 'sending' older than five minutes asks Postmark for the message by metadata before it sends again.

The unique key also stops two parallel jobs from sending the same reminder. A test simulates a timeout with a stub server that accepts the message but answers late; the retry then finds the message and does not send. A second test covers a real failure, where the retry does send.

The agent checked the last 30 days of the log for other duplicates and found three more, all from the same cause. Support will not contact those customers, as the amounts were correct. Mara reviewed the change and asked to log the key in each send, which was added. The change was deployed after the evening run. Next the agent will watch the duplicate count for a week.

summary: Wrote a query that counts duplicate emails per day from the email log, and it found none since the fix for the double dunning email.
body:
As a follow-up to the double reminder, the agent wrote a small query on the email log that groups by invoice id, template and dunning step and shows groups with more than one sent row.

It was run for the last 60 days. Before the fix, it showed seven groups, four of them from the timeout case. The other three had different causes: a manual resend from the support tool, which is allowed. The agent added a column to the log that marks manual resends, so they do not show up as duplicates.

The query was put into the nightly totals audit job as a second check. It writes to the same log channel and stays silent when the count is zero. Since the deploy there were 96 emails, no duplicates.

Mara asked whether the same could happen with the receipts after a payment. The receipt job uses the payment id as its key already, so it is safe. A test was added to document that. Nothing else is open on this topic.

summary: Answered Ines's question why one invoice shows 19% VAT for a German customer who moved to Austria: the VAT rate follows the country on the billing address at the invoice date.
body:
Ines asked in the evening why an invoice of a customer showed German VAT of 19% although the customer wrote that they had moved to Austria. The agent checked the customer record and the history of the billing address.

The address was changed to Austria only after the invoice was created, and the tax rules take the country from the address on the invoice date. The invoice was therefore correct for the day it was made. The next invoice, which was created after the change, used 20%.

The agent also checked that the customer has a valid Austrian VAT id, which is not used for reverse charge here because the customer is a consumer for our purposes without a business flag. Ines will ask the customer whether they want the business flag set, which would change the rule for future invoices.

No code was changed. The agent wrote the explanation and the two invoice numbers into the finance thread. It noted that the address history table is the place to look for such cases, since it keeps every change with a time.

summary: Looked at the Stripe webhook retry log and found that events for deleted customers fail with a 404 on every retry, so they are now acknowledged and logged as skipped.
body:
The webhook error rate showed a small steady number of failures, about 8 per day. The agent looked at the failed events.

All of them were events for customers that no longer exist in our database, from test accounts deleted weeks ago. Our handler looked the customer up, threw a not-found error and returned a 500. Stripe then retried for three days, so the same few events kept coming back.

The handler now returns 200 for events whose customer is unknown and writes a line with the event id and the type to the log as 'skipped, unknown customer'. For event types that create data, such as a new subscription, an unknown customer is still logged as a warning, because there it might point to a real problem.

A test for each case was added. After the deploy the error rate went to zero within an hour, and the old retries stopped. The agent also removed the three failed events from the pg-boss table so they do not appear in the dashboards.

summary: Began planning the move of PDF rendering off the main service because 100-line invoices take over 20 seconds, and measured where the time goes in the render path.
body:
The reused browser helped, but invoices with many lines are still slow. The agent measured a 100-line invoice and a 200-line invoice, ten runs each, with the render time per invoice that Mara asked to log earlier.

Results: the 100-line invoice took 21 seconds on average, the 200-line invoice 47. A 10-line invoice takes under one second. The time grows faster than the number of lines.

The agent split the time into steps with timestamps. Building the HTML from the template took 0.4 seconds even for 200 lines. Loading the HTML into the browser page and waiting for the load event took 3 seconds. The call that produces the PDF took the rest, 43 seconds. The page layout seems to be the cost: the table has a repeated header, a fixed footer on each page, and a shadow on each row.

The agent tried three quick experiments in a scratch copy of the template. Removing the shadows brought 200 lines from 47 to 31 seconds. Removing the repeated header too brought it to 24. Removing the fixed footer as well gave 9 seconds. So the three CSS features together make most of the cost. The footer is the worst, because the browser lays it out again for each page.

The finance team needs the footer for the page numbers and the company details, so it cannot simply go. One option is to render the footer through the PDF options of the browser, which has its own header and footer templates and is cheaper. Another is a different renderer, which would be a larger project.

The agent wrote this down with the numbers and the three experiments. The next step is a test of the PDF footer option, then a check that the page numbers look the same as now. Mara will decide after seeing the numbers whether a different renderer is worth planning.

summary: Tested the browser's own footer template for invoice PDFs: 200 lines fell from 47 to 14 seconds, but the page count text needed a different font setting.
body:
Following the measurements of the morning, the agent moved the footer from the HTML template to the footer template of the PDF call. The company details and the text 'Page X of Y' use the special classes pageNumber and totalPages.

Render times on the same test invoices, ten runs each: 10 lines 0.8 seconds, 100 lines 8 seconds, 200 lines 14 seconds. The 200-line case went from 47 to 14, about a third.

The first result looked wrong. The footer text came out tiny, about 3 points. The footer template ignores the page styles, and the default font size is very small. Setting an explicit font-size on the footer's root element fixed it, and the agent compared the output to the old PDF side by side. The position of the text moved by about 2 mm, so the bottom margin was increased from 18 to 20 mm.

The next problem was the logo in the footer. It was a linked image, and the footer template cannot load linked files. The agent inlined it as a data URI, which costs 4 KB per template and works.

The shadows on the rows were replaced by a thin border, which finance said looks fine. The repeated table header is kept because without it the second page is hard to read; its cost is smaller than the footer's.

A regression check rendered 40 existing invoices from last month with both versions and compared the text of each page with pdftotext. 38 matched exactly. Two differed in the footer only, in the spacing of the page numbers. The agent reviewed those and found them harmless.

The change is behind no flag yet. The agent will ask Ines to look at five sample PDFs before it goes out, since the PDFs go to the accountants too.

summary: Ines checked the five sample PDFs with the new footer and approved them, asking only that the VAT id of the company stays on every page.
body:
The agent sent Ines five sample PDFs: a short invoice, a 60-line one, a 200-line one, a credit note and an invoice with reverse charge. She looked at them in the evening.

She approved the layout. Her one request was that the company VAT id must be on every page and not only on the last one, because the accountants sometimes print single pages. The agent checked: the VAT id is in the footer template, so it is on each page. The sample with 200 lines shows it on all six pages.

She also noticed that the border between the rows is thinner than the shadow was. She said that is fine and even easier to read when printed.

The agent merged the change after Mara's quick look at the diff and deployed it after the evening run, so the next run would be the first with the new layout. The render time log will show the effect. The agent will compare the average render time of the first run to the old numbers tomorrow.

summary: The first evening run with the new PDF footer cut total render time from 23 to 11 minutes for 218 invoices, and the slowest invoice went from 52 to 15 seconds.
body:
The agent read the render time log of the run that finished in the night. 218 invoices were made, and the whole run took 11 minutes instead of the 23 of the run after the browser reuse.

The slowest invoice was a customer with 210 lines, 15 seconds against 52 before. The median was 0.9 seconds. 17 invoices took more than five seconds, all with more than 80 lines. The totals matched the preview for all invoices, and the totals audit was clean.

The agent also looked at memory use of the service during the run, because layout work in the browser can grow it. Peak memory was 610 MB, down from 720. No browser crash was logged.

There was one new warning: for three invoices the footer showed 'Page 1 of 1' correctly but the log noted a console message from the browser about a missing font weight. The font is a fallback for the bold weight, and the PDFs looked the same. The agent noted it and left it.

The remaining slow cases are customers with very large invoices. A customer with 400 lines would probably still take about 30 seconds. The usage lines of such customers come from metering and could be grouped by day or by product, which would be a change of the product itself and not only of the renderer. The agent wrote this as an idea for Mara and did not start on it.

Next, the agent wants a hard limit on render time. Today a stuck render holds a job slot until the job timeout of 10 minutes. A render timeout of 90 seconds with a clear error and a retry would protect the run. The plan is to do that in the afternoon, with a test using a page that never finishes loading.

summary: Added a 90-second render timeout to the PDF job so a stuck browser page fails fast and is retried once with a fresh browser instead of blocking the run for ten minutes.
body:
Until now a stuck render was stopped only by the job timeout of ten minutes. In the last two months this happened twice, and each time the evening run was late by that much.

The agent added a timeout of 90 seconds around the render call. When it fires, the page is closed, and if the page close does not return within five seconds the whole browser is killed and started again, since the browser is shared between renders. The job then fails with the error 'render timeout' and pg-boss retries it after a minute.

On the second failure the invoice is marked 'pdf_failed', and the job writes a line to the log channel with the invoice id and the number of lines. The invoice itself stays valid and payable, only the PDF is missing. Support can trigger a new render from the admin tool.

For the test the agent made a small HTML page with a script that loops forever and a stub that returns it for one special invoice id. The test checks three things: the first attempt fails after the timeout, the browser is restarted, and the retry works for a normal invoice that follows. A second test lets the stub fail twice and checks that the status is set.

The timeout was chosen from the data. The slowest normal render in the last two weeks was 52 seconds before the footer change and is now 15, so 90 leaves plenty of room. The value is a setting, so it can be changed without a deploy.

Mara reviewed the change and asked what happens to other invoices that wait while the browser restarts. The agent explained that renders run one at a time per worker, and a restart takes about 2 seconds, so they just wait. She asked for the restart count to be logged, which was added as a counter in the same log line.

The change was deployed before the evening run. The agent will check the log tomorrow for any timeouts.

summary: Found that the Stripe list call for charges in the refund report returned only the first 10 results after the v16 upgrade changed one default, and fixed the helper.
body:
Ines reported that the monthly refund report listed only 10 refunds for a customer who she knew had 14. The agent looked at the report code.

The report calls the Stripe list API for refunds of a payment intent through the pagination helper that is left of the shim. The helper passed the 'limit' parameter only when it was set by the caller, and this report did not set it. The default page size is 10, and the helper stopped after the first page when 'has_more' was read from the wrong field in this one code path.

The agent traced it: the helper has two ways to iterate, one with the SDK's auto pagination and one by hand for the sorted case. The report used the manual way, and the manual way read has_more from the response of the previous page instead of the current one. For lists of 11 to 20 items the second page was fetched, but the check after it used the old value, so the third page was never fetched. Here, with 14 refunds, the first page was fetched and the check was wrong too, which explains the missing four.

The fix reads the flag of the current page. A test with 25 items in pages of 10 and one with exactly 10 items, where the second page is empty, were added. The existing test with 250 invoices did not catch it because it used the sorted helper with a limit of 100.

The agent then searched for other callers of the manual path. There were two more: the dunning job, which lists open invoices, and the export of payouts. For the dunning job the effect would be that customers beyond the first page are not reminded. The agent checked the counts of the last run against the database and found that the job had missed 3 reminders last week.

Those three customers were listed for Ines, who decided to send the reminders by hand this week. The fix was merged and deployed.

summary: Ran the refund report and the dunning job against the corrected pagination helper on a staging copy and compared with the database to confirm that no list is truncated anymore.
body:
After the pagination fix of this morning, the agent wanted proof that all callers are right, not only the ones that were found.

The agent wrote a script for staging that calls each list function of the helper with a small page size of 3. It then compares the number of results with a count from our own database. The functions covered: refunds by payment intent, open invoices for dunning, payouts, charges by customer, and subscriptions by status.

First run: four of five matched. The charges by customer function returned one item too few for customers whose charge count was an exact multiple of the page size. The reason was an off-by-one in the cursor: the last item of a page was used as the 'starting_after' value but was also dropped from the page when the page was exactly full. This is a different bug from the morning one, and it had been hidden because real customers rarely have exactly 10 or 20 charges.

The agent fixed it and added a test for exact multiples. The second run matched in all five cases, with page sizes of 3, 10 and 100.

Then the production check. The agent ran the read-only counts for the last month on production with the fixed code and compared them to the database. Everything matched. For the charges function, 11 customers had been affected by the off-by-one in the past, but the function is only used by the support tool to show a customer's payment history, so no money or invoice was touched.

The agent wrote a short summary of both bugs in the upgrade guide as a section called 'list helpers to test after each upgrade', with the script path. The script will be run by the agent before each SDK upgrade from now on. Mara asked if it can be part of CI. The script needs the Stripe test mode keys, which are available in CI, so the agent will add it as an optional job that runs on changes under the stripe folder.

That job is left for tomorrow. Today's work was merged and is in production.

summary: Added the optional CI job that runs the list helper comparison against Stripe test mode when files under src/stripe change, and it passed on its first run.
body:
The job was added to the CI config as planned. It only runs when files under src/stripe or the package lock change, so normal builds are not slowed down.

The script creates its own test data in Stripe test mode on the first run of each day: 25 customers with different numbers of charges, among them 10, 20 and 30 for the exact multiple case, and a few refunds. It uses the metadata field 'ci_fixture' to find that data later and does not create it again. That way the run takes about 40 seconds and not several minutes.

The agent had to handle the rate limit of the Stripe test mode. The fixture creation does 100 calls in a burst, and one run got a 429. The SDK retries on its own, with its network retry setting at 2, and the second try passed. The setting was raised to 3 for CI only.

The first real run passed. To make sure the job can fail, the agent put the old off-by-one back in a scratch commit and ran it again: it failed with 'expected 20, got 19' for the customer with 20 charges. Then the commit was removed.

Mara asked whether the test data piles up in the Stripe test account. The agent checked, and there are 25 customers from the fixture and nothing else, because the second run reuses them. A cleanup flag was added in case someone wants to start new.

The documentation of the upgrade guide was updated with the CI job. This topic is finished.

summary: Answered Mara's question about how many receipts bounce per month: 41 of about 5,900, mostly invalid addresses, with the bounce handling working as designed.
body:
Mara asked in the evening how many receipt emails bounce, because she wants to know if address quality is a problem for the dunning flow.

The agent used the Postmark bounce data that is stored through the webhook, for the last 30 days. Of about 5,900 receipts and reminders, 41 bounced: 33 were hard bounces with invalid or closed addresses, 6 were soft bounces such as a full mailbox, and 2 were blocked by the receiving server.

For hard bounces the system marks the address as bad and shows a warning in the admin tool. The agent checked that the 33 customers have the marker. For 9 of them a reminder was due this month, and these would not reach anyone. The agent listed them for Ines, so that finance can call or write through another route.

There is no change in code. The question of whether to show a banner in the nebula product for customers with a bad billing address was written down as an idea, as that would touch the other team's code.

summary: Wrote the first test and query plan for refunds listing by customer, since the support team wants to see all refunds of a customer in the admin tool without calling Stripe each time.
body:
Support asked for a list of all refunds of a customer in the admin tool. Today the page calls Stripe live, which takes 2 to 4 seconds and fails when Stripe is slow.

The agent checked what the database already has. Refunds made through our API are stored in the refunds table with payment id, amount, reason and creator. Refunds that were created in the Stripe dashboard by hand are not stored, except through the webhook event 'charge.refunded', which updates the payment's refunded amount only and not the individual refund.

So a complete list needs the webhook to store each refund too. The agent looked at the event: it contains the charge with a refunds list, which is limited to the first 10 and not always expanded. A better event is 'refund.created' and 'refund.updated', which carry one refund each.

The plan has three steps. First, subscribe the webhook endpoint to both events and add a handler that upserts into the refunds table by the Stripe refund id. Second, a one-time backfill that lists all refunds from Stripe, with the checked list helper, and inserts the missing ones. Third, change the admin page to read from the table.

The agent started with the table. A column 'source' ('api' or 'dashboard') and a unique index on the Stripe refund id were needed. For old rows from the API the Stripe id is already stored, so the index can be created. A check found 3 rows with a null Stripe id, from failed refunds that never got an id, and the index allows nulls.

The migration was written and tested on a staging copy of the table, which has 2,140 refunds. It took under a second. The migration is not deployed yet, since it should go with the handler.

Open question for Mara: whether refunds made in the dashboard should also send the customer a receipt email. Today they do not. The agent will not change that without a decision.

summary: Implemented the refund.created and refund.updated webhook handlers with an upsert by Stripe refund id, and tests for out-of-order delivery.
body:
With the migration ready, the agent wrote the handlers. Both event types go to the same function, which takes the refund object, finds the payment by the charge or payment intent id and upserts a row into refunds.

Stripe does not promise the order of events. A refund.updated can arrive before refund.created. The upsert therefore uses the Stripe refund id as the key and only overwrites the status when the incoming event is newer, compared by the 'created' field of the event. For the refund object itself there is no version number, so the agent used the event's created time and stored it in a column 'last_event_at'.

Three tests cover: created then updated, updated before created, and the same event delivered twice. The third also checks that the payment's refunded total is not counted twice, since the total is calculated from the table with a sum and not incremented.

A fourth test covers a refund for a payment we do not know, for example from an old account. The handler then stores nothing and logs it as skipped, like the unknown customer case from a few days ago.

The agent sent a few test mode refunds through the Stripe CLI with 'stripe trigger refund.created' against a local server, and the rows appeared with source 'dashboard'. The webhook signature check passed with the local secret.

The handler and migration are ready for review. The deploy waits for Mara, and the backfill script will be written next.

summary: Wrote and ran the refund backfill against production in dry-run mode: 61 refunds exist in Stripe that are missing in the table, all created in the dashboard.
body:
The backfill script lists all refunds from Stripe with the pagination helper and compares them to the refunds table by the Stripe refund id. It has a dry-run mode that only prints the difference.

The agent ran it on production in dry-run mode, read-only. Stripe has 2,214 refunds, the table has 2,153. The 61 that are missing were all made in the dashboard, which matches the expectation. Total amount: 3,874.50 EUR and a few in USD.

The agent looked at the oldest few. The oldest is from about 14 months ago. Their payments are all known to the system, so the inserts will find their payment. Two refunds have a charge that belongs to an invoice of a customer that was deleted afterwards. The table has a foreign key to the payment, and the payment still exists since payments are kept for the accountants, so these two are fine as well.

The backfill sets the source to 'dashboard' and 'last_event_at' to the time of the refund. It does not send any email and does not change any invoice or credit note. The agent checked this twice, because the existing refund code creates a credit note for API refunds. For dashboard refunds a credit note is a finance decision and out of scope. The agent wrote the 61 refund ids and amounts into a file for Ines, who can see which ones have no credit note.

Mara reviewed the migration, the handlers and the script. She asked that the real run be done after the evening invoice run so there is no load at the same time. The agent will do that.

summary: Deployed the refund webhook handlers and ran the backfill after the evening run: 61 rows were added, counts match Stripe, and the admin page now loads in under 200 ms.
body:
The agent first deployed the migration, then the handlers, and then subscribed the webhook endpoint to refund.created and refund.updated in the Stripe dashboard. The order matters: subscribing earlier would send events to a handler that does not exist.

After the evening run finished with 216 invoices and a clean totals audit, the backfill was run for real. It inserted 61 rows in under 3 seconds. A second run said 'nothing to do', which confirms that it is safe to repeat.

The agent then compared Stripe and the table once more with the dry-run mode: 2,214 on both sides, and the sum of the amounts per currency was the same. The refunded total on the payments was recalculated from the table for the 58 payments concerned, and it matched the Stripe charge's amount_refunded for all of them.

The admin page was changed to read from the table. It showed a refund list of a customer with 14 refunds in 120 ms, against 3 seconds before. A note on the page says which refunds come from the dashboard. Support was told by message.

The webhook error rate stayed at zero in the hour after the deploy. One real refund was created by Ines on a test customer in the dashboard, to check the whole path, and the row showed up within 2 seconds.

The open question about receipts for dashboard refunds is still with Mara. The agent suggested one option: send nothing for now, and look at it again when finance has decided about credit notes. She agreed to wait.

There is nothing else open here. The agent added the topic to the notes in the repository: the table, the events, the backfill script path and the rule that API refunds still create a credit note while dashboard ones do not.

summary: Sent Ines the list of the 61 backfilled dashboard refunds with a column showing which of them have no credit note, 44 in total, so finance can decide.
body:
Ines needs to know for which dashboard refunds a credit note is missing, because the accountants want a credit note for each refund on an invoice.

The agent joined the 61 backfilled refunds with the credit notes table by payment and invoice. 17 refunds have a matching credit note, which finance had made by hand. 44 have none.

The sheet has these columns: refund id, date, amount and currency, invoice number, customer, reason if there is one, and whether a credit note exists. The amounts of the 44 add up to 2,611 EUR and 128 USD. The agent sorted the sheet by invoice date.

The agent did not create any credit notes, because the credit note numbers are a legal series. The agent offered a script that creates them in a batch, if Ines decides they are needed, with the original refund date on each. Ines will talk to the accountants.

summary: Looked at a slow query in the usage meter import and found a missing index on the usage counts by customer and day, which cut the import step from 40 to 3 seconds.
body:
The nightly usage import from nebula had grown slower. The log showed that the step 'upsert counts' took 40 seconds, up from about 10 two months ago.

The agent ran EXPLAIN ANALYZE on the upsert statement on a staging copy. It did a sequential scan on usage_counts, which has 5.2 million rows, to check the conflict on customer id and day. The unique constraint covered customer id, product and day, in this order, so a lookup by customer and day alone could not use it well.

The statement does include the product in the conflict target, so the constraint should be used. The agent looked closer: the import sent the product as a text value and the column is an enum, and the cast made the planner choose a scan in one of the code paths, the batch path with more than 500 rows. An explicit cast to the enum type in that statement fixed the plan.

After the change the plan used the unique index, and the step took 3 seconds on staging with the same data. A test with a batch of 2,000 rows was added.

No new index was needed, which is better, since the table is large. The change was deployed with the next release, and the next nightly import will show if the time holds.

summary: Wrote a test that checks that no invoice line is created twice when the usage import runs twice, after reading the import code for the cause of a worry Mara had.
body:
Mara worried that a repeated import, for example after a failed job, could create duplicate usage lines on an invoice. The agent read the code and wrote a test for it.

The import writes counts to usage_counts with an upsert by customer, product and day, so repeated runs overwrite and do not add. The invoice run reads from this table when the invoice is made at the end of the period. The lines are made from sums per product and not from individual import rows, so there is one line per product.

The test imports the same file twice for three customers, makes the invoices and checks the number of lines and the totals. It also changes one count between the two imports, the case of a late correction from nebula, and checks that the invoice uses the corrected value.

Both cases passed, so the design is safe as it is. The agent found one gap, though. If a correction arrives after the invoice was made, it has no effect on that invoice, and nothing reports it. The agent added a log line in the import when a count changes for a day that is already invoiced, with customer and difference. Three such lines came up in the data of last month, all for 1 or 2 units.

What to do about late corrections is a question for finance. The agent wrote the three cases down for Ines.

summary: Planned the work to speed up very large invoices by grouping usage lines per product per day, laying out three options with numbers and the effect on the PDF and totals.
body:
The PDF footer work made most invoices fast, but the largest ones still have 200 to 400 lines. The lines come from usage metering: one line per product per day for customers on daily metering. The agent wrote a plan for Mara on whether to change that.

The data first. Of last month's 5,900 invoices, 5,640 have fewer than 40 lines. 214 have between 40 and 100, 41 between 100 and 200, and 5 more than 200. The render time is under 4 seconds for all below 100 lines, so only about 46 invoices are slow, between 8 and 30 seconds. The full run is no problem with them.

Option one is to do nothing. The invoices are correct, the run is 11 minutes, and the timeout protects it. The cost is only the time of those few and a long PDF for a customer who has to read it.

Option two is to group the lines per product per week in the PDF only, with the full daily detail kept in an attachment page or a CSV link. The invoice lines in the database stay the same, so the totals and the audit are unchanged. The PDF would show a line per week and the sum, which are added from the daily lines, with rounding done per line as it is today. A risk is that the weekly sum of rounded daily lines differs from the rounding of the weekly total by a cent, which Ines would see as a mismatch. So the PDF would sum the already rounded daily amounts and not recalculate.

Option three is to change the lines themselves, to weekly lines in the invoice. This changes the data, the audit check, the credit notes and the finance exports. It is much more work and has a legal side, since the accountants have seen the daily form.

The agent recommends option one for now, and option two only if customers or finance ask for shorter PDFs. It has the smallest risk, and it does not need new tests of totals. The cost of option two was estimated at two days, including the CSV link.

The agent also mentioned that a different PDF renderer could solve the speed in a more basic way. That would be a larger project with its own rollout, and the question is whether it is worth it for 46 invoices a month. Mara will think about it and discuss it with Ines. No code was written.

summary: Built the per-product, per-day usage grouping behind a setting and compared it with the old lines on 30 customers: totals matched, and the biggest invoice dropped from 1,900 to 140 lines.
body:
Yesterday's plan named three options, and the second one, grouping usage lines per product per day, was chosen. Today the agent implemented it in src/invoice/lines.ts behind the setting USAGE_GROUPING, which is off by default.

The grouping sums the quantity per product and day and keeps one line with a description such as 'Events indexed, 12 Mar-style day label'. The unit price is not changed, and the amount is the quantity times the price, rounded once per line.

The agent then ran both modes on a staging copy for 30 customers, chosen to include the ten largest. In 29 cases the invoice total was identical to the cent. In one case the grouped total differed by 1 cent, because the old code rounded each usage line and the new code rounds the sum.

That difference is expected, and it is the same kind of problem Ines has pointed out before. The agent did not change the rounding, since it is a topic of its own. It wrote the case down with the customer id so Ines can look at it.

The largest invoice went from 1,900 lines to 140. The PDF render for it fell from 15 seconds to about 2, because the page count dropped from 38 to 4.

The invoice detail page and the CSV export still read the raw usage rows, so they are unchanged. A test now checks that the sum of the grouped quantities equals the sum of the raw quantities for each product.

Open points: the line description needs wording that Ines accepts, and the credit note code also builds lines and has not been checked. Next step is to show Ines three grouped sample PDFs.

summary: Showed Ines three grouped sample invoices; she accepted the grouping but wants the day range and the raw quantity in every line description, so the text was reworked.
body:
The agent generated three sample PDFs with USAGE_GROUPING on, one small, one medium and one with 140 lines, and sent them to Ines this morning.

Ina's answer, in short, came back within the hour: the grouping is fine for finance as long as an auditor can trace a line back to the usage data. She asked for two changes.

First, each line must show the day it covers in the same date format as the rest of the invoice, not a label made from the month name. Second, each line should show the quantity with the unit, such as '48,210 events', so nobody has to divide the amount by the price.

The agent changed the description template in src/invoice/lines.ts and added the thousands separator by locale, using the same helper as the receipts. This matters because the French and German number format bug of last week came from a similar place.

The agent also checked that the description does not break the layout. The longest product name plus the day and quantity fit in one line at the current column width, but only just. A product with a very long name wrapped into two lines in one sample, and the agent allowed wrapping in the description column.

The tests for the description text were rewritten for the English, French and German locales, 9 cases in total, and all pass.

The agent also looked at the credit note code. It builds lines from the invoice lines and not from the raw usage rows, so it follows the grouping without change. A credit note for a grouped invoice was created on staging and its total was correct.

Still open: the 1 cent difference of yesterday, which Ines wants to review with the customer id, and the decision when to switch the setting on.

summary: Looked into the 1 cent difference between grouped and ungrouped totals and found that per-line rounding of tiny usage lines was the cause; the grouped total is the more exact one.
body:
Ines asked why one customer's grouped invoice was 1 cent lower than the old calculation. The agent took the customer id from yesterday's comparison and recalculated the invoice by hand.

The customer had 31 days of usage for one product at a price of 0.0004 per event, with a daily count between 400 and 9,000. In the old mode every day became a line that was rounded to a cent. In the new mode the daily counts are added first and the sum is rounded once per product and day, so there is the same number of lines but no change.

The agent found that the difference came from something else: the same product also had a second usage row on some days, written by a late import run. The old mode made two lines for such a day and rounded each. The grouped mode merges them into one line and rounds once.

So on 4 days of the month two rows existed. The old way rounded 0.4 cents up twice, which gave 2 cents, while the merged value of 0.8 cents rounds to 1 cent. Over the month the totals differed by 1 cent.

The grouped result is closer to the exact amount, which was 6.8 cents for those days, so it is the more correct one. The agent wrote this down with the numbers for Ines in a short note.

It also checked how often late rows occur. In the last quarter 212 of 5,900 invoices had at least one day with two usage rows for the same product. The effect is at most a few cents for those.

The agent did not touch the rounding rule, which is a separate matter. Ines can decide whether the difference is acceptable when the setting is switched on.

summary: Answered Mara's question what happens to old invoices when USAGE_GROUPING is switched on: nothing, because grouping runs only when an invoice is created, and finalized invoices are not recomputed.
body:
Mara asked whether switching on USAGE_GROUPING would change invoices that already exist. The agent read the code path to be sure and not rely on memory.

The grouping happens in the function that builds the lines when an invoice is created in draft state. After finalization the lines are stored in the invoice_lines table, and the PDF job reads from that table only.

The only exception is a draft that was created before the switch and is finalized after it. Such a draft keeps the lines it already has, since the lines are written at creation. The agent checked this on staging with a draft created in the old mode.

The agent also confirmed that regenerating a PDF for an old invoice uses the stored lines and so looks exactly as before. Mara was happy with this and asked to keep it that way.

The answer is: no change for existing invoices, and the first grouped invoices are those created after the switch.

summary: Wrote the test that compares grouped and ungrouped invoices on generated data with random daily counts, and it found a bug where a product with zero usage on a day made an empty line.
body:
To be more sure about the grouping, the agent wrote a property-style test in tests/invoice/grouping.test.ts. It generates 200 customers with random products, random days and random counts, builds the invoice in both modes and compares the quantities.

The check is that for each product the total quantity is equal in both modes and that the grouped invoice has at most one line per product and day.

The test failed on the first run for 3 of the 200 cases. The cause was a day on which the usage row had a count of zero, which can happen when the meter reports a day without events. The grouped mode produced a line with quantity 0 and amount 0.00.

The old mode had skipped zero rows in an earlier filter, but the new code ran before that filter. The agent moved the filter in front of the grouping and added a case for it.

After the fix all 200 cases pass, and the test runs in about 1.5 seconds, so it stays in the normal suite. The seed is printed on failure so a case can be repeated.

summary: Switched USAGE_GROUPING on for the evening run in dry-run mode and compared 218 previews with the real ones: totals equal except 6 invoices that differ by 1 or 2 cents, all with late usage rows.
body:
After the tests were green, the agent ran the evening invoice run in preview mode with the grouping on, and compared the output with the preview without it. The run covered 218 invoices.

For 212 invoices the totals were exactly equal. For 6 the grouped total was lower by 1 or 2 cents. All 6 had days with two usage rows for the same product, which is the effect from earlier in the day.

The render time of the whole run in preview mode, with PDFs, went from 11 minutes to 6 minutes 40 seconds. The slowest invoice took 4 seconds instead of 15.

The agent made a list of the 6 invoices with both totals and sent it to Ines, so she is not surprised when she checks the month. She had asked for such a list for any change that moves a total.

The setting stays off in production until Ines has answered. If she agrees tomorrow, the first real run with grouping can be tomorrow evening.

The agent also saved the preview output of both modes in the staging bucket for a week, in case a question comes up.

One more thing was noticed: the preview log prints the mode only at the start of the run, and a person reading the middle of the log cannot see it. A line with the mode was added to every invoice log entry.

summary: Ines accepted the grouping with the 1-2 cent effect, and the setting went on for the evening run; all 221 invoices were created and the PDF step took 6 minutes.
body:
Ines wrote back in the morning that the six differences are fine and that the grouped invoices are easier to read, so she approved the switch. The agent turned USAGE_GROUPING on in the production config just before the evening run.

The run created 221 invoices. The agent watched the log through the run and compared the totals with the preview of the day before for the invoices that existed in both. There were no unexpected differences.

The PDF step took 6 minutes 5 seconds, against 11 minutes before the footer change and 23 minutes before that. The slowest invoice took 3.8 seconds. No render timeout fired, so the 90-second limit added earlier was not needed.

The emails with the PDF attached went out through Postmark as usual. The agent checked the delivery log and found 221 accepted, and 2 bounces within the first hour, both invalid addresses that were already known.

The agent opened five of the new PDFs by hand, among them the largest. The lines show the day, the quantity with the unit and the amount. The company VAT id is on every page, as Ines asked before.

One small issue came up. For a customer with usage in two currencies of the same plan, which happens for a few accounts that were moved from USD to EUR, the line grouping uses the currency of the invoice and this was right. The agent only wanted to make sure, and it checked that account in particular.

A second small issue was in the admin tool. The invoice page there shows the lines, and for grouped invoices the list is shorter, so support will see fewer lines than before. The agent wrote a short note for the support team that explains it.

The agent also removed the old code path for ungrouped lines from the hot path, but kept the setting for now. In two weeks, if no problem appears, the setting and the old code can be deleted.

Tomorrow's work is to look at the render path again, since the browser start is now the largest part of the time for small invoices.

summary: Measured the browser start cost per invoice and found that 1.1 seconds of every PDF is a fresh browser launch, so a pool of reused browsers is planned.
body:
With the big invoices fixed, the agent looked at the small ones, which are most of them. It added timing to the render function and ran 100 small invoices on staging.

The average time per invoice was 2.3 seconds. Of that, 1.1 seconds was the launch of a new headless browser, 0.4 seconds loading the HTML and fonts, 0.6 seconds printing to PDF and 0.2 seconds writing the file and the database row.

The job launches a new browser for every invoice, because that was the simplest way to get a clean state and to avoid a stuck page. The timeout added last week also relies on a fresh browser for the retry.

A pool of browsers that are reused for a number of invoices would save most of the launch time. For 220 invoices the saving would be about 4 minutes in a run that now takes 6.

The risks are memory growth and stuck pages. The agent therefore wants to restart a browser after 25 invoices and after any timeout, and to use a new page for each invoice and close it afterwards.

The agent tried a quick version on staging with a single browser reused for all 100 invoices. The time per invoice fell to 1.3 seconds, but the memory of the browser process grew from 180 MB to 640 MB over the run. That confirms that the restart limit is needed.

The plan is: pool size of 2, restart after 25 invoices, a new page per invoice and the existing timeout logic kept. The agent wrote the plan in the repository notes and will start with the pool class tomorrow.

It also noted that the planned new renderer, which has been discussed for later, would change this whole part, so the pool should stay small and simple and should not be tuned too much.

summary: Implemented a small browser pool class with a restart after 25 renders and tests with a fake browser, not yet used by the PDF job.
body:
The agent wrote src/pdf/browser-pool.ts. It holds up to two browser instances and hands one out with acquire(), taking back a used instance with release().

Each instance counts its renders. When the count reaches 25, or when the caller releases it with a failed flag, the pool closes it and starts a new one on the next acquire. This covers both the memory growth and the stuck pages.

A page is opened by the caller and has to be closed by the caller. The pool does not hide this, but the helper withPage() does it with a try and finally, so the job code does not forget it.

The tests use a fake browser with a counter for launches and closes. They check that 60 renders lead to 3 launches, that a failed release forces a restart, that two parallel acquires get different instances and that a third waits until one is released.

The tests also check shutdown. When the job ends, closeAll() has to close every instance, also those that are in use, and it must not hang if the browser is already dead. The agent added a 5-second limit for the close.

The pool is not connected to the PDF job yet. That is the next step, together with a staging run, so that the class can be reviewed on its own.

All 11 new tests pass in under a second.

summary: Connected the browser pool to the PDF job and ran 220 invoices on staging: 6 minutes fell to 2 minutes 50 seconds, with browser memory staying under 400 MB.
body:
The PDF job now takes pages from the pool through withPage() instead of launching its own browser. The 90-second timeout still applies per page. When it fires, the page is closed, the browser is released as failed, and the invoice is retried once, which now means a fresh browser from the pool.

The agent ran the job on a staging copy of the evening data with 220 invoices. The total time was 2 minutes 50 seconds, against 6 minutes before. The average per invoice fell from 2.3 to 0.7 seconds.

The memory of the biggest browser process peaked at 390 MB, just before a restart. It dropped back to about 150 MB after each restart. That is in line with the limit of 25 renders.

The agent also tested a failure. It put an invoice with an HTML page that never finishes loading, an image from an address that does not answer. The timeout fired after 90 seconds, the browser was restarted and the retry of that invoice failed again in the same way, as it should. The other invoices of the run were not delayed beyond that.

The result of the failed invoice is the same as before: it is marked as failed in the job table and the run report lists it. Nothing about the failure handling changed.

One more change was needed. The job used to delete the temporary folder of the browser after each invoice. With the pool, that folder is shared and may only be deleted at a restart, which the pool class now does.

The change goes to production with the evening run today, after the tests were run once more.

summary: Ran the evening run with the browser pool for a week of production load: 7 runs finished in under 3 minutes of PDF time, and one leaked browser process showed up and was fixed.
body:
After the pool went live on staging, it ran in production for the evening runs of the last week. This entry records what the seven runs showed and the one problem that came up.

PDF time for 218 to 224 invoices stayed between 2 minutes 40 seconds and 3 minutes 05 seconds, against 6 minutes before the pool. The slowest single invoice, a 140-line one, took 9 seconds. Browser memory peaked at 380 MB, below the 400 MB seen on staging.

On the fourth evening the process list showed one chromium process still alive after the job had finished. The cause was in the restart after 25 renders: when closing the old browser threw a timeout error, the pool logged it and went on without killing the process. The pool now calls kill on the process handle when close fails or takes longer than 5 seconds.

The fix is in src/pdf/browser-pool.ts, with a new test where the fake browser's close() never resolves. The test checks that the pool still hands out a fresh browser and that the old process gets the kill call. The run after the fix left no stray processes, which was checked with ps right after the job ended.

No invoice failed because of the pool in any of the seven runs, and the 90-second render timeout never fired. Ines saw no change in the PDFs. Mara asked that the pool size be a setting, so it is now PDF_POOL_SIZE with a default of 2. Next is to watch two more weeks and then drop the old launch-per-invoice path.

summary: Reviewed the Stripe SDK v16 deprecation warnings in the logs, listed 7 distinct ones and grouped them by what must change before the next upgrade.
body:
Mara asked the agent to prepare for the next Stripe SDK upgrade by looking at what the current version already warns about. The agent searched the production logs of the last two weeks for deprecation messages.

There were 7 distinct warnings, in about 4,100 log lines. Most of them came from two places, the dunning job and the refund report.

The first group is two warnings about the way list calls pass the parameter for the expand option. The code passes a string in some places and an array in others, and the SDK says the string form is going away. Five places in src/stripe use it.

The second group is three warnings about reading fields that were renamed in the API version the SDK uses. Two of them are in the invoice sync code, which reads the old name of a payment field, and one is in the webhook handler for payment intents.

The third group is two warnings about the two small shims in src/stripe/compat.ts. The shims were written for the old pagination and for a type that the first SDK versions did not have. The SDK now warns when they are used.

The agent made a table with the file, the line, the warning and what has to be done. Nothing was changed in code today, since the point was to see the size of the work.

The estimate is that the first and second group take about a half day, because they are simple edits with tests. The shims are riskier, because the refund report and the dunning job depend on the pagination one, and the pagination bug of a few weeks ago shows how easily a list can be truncated.

The agent therefore suggests to do the first two groups soon, in small commits, and to leave the shims for the actual upgrade, where their removal can be tested against Stripe test mode with the CI job that was added recently.

Mara agreed with this order. She asked to start with the expand parameter, since it touches the fewest tests.

The table is saved in the notes folder of the repository, so the next sessions can tick off the lines.

summary: Changed all five list calls to pass expand as an array and updated the tests; the two warnings from the expand group are gone on staging.
body:
The agent started with the first group of the table from yesterday. In src/stripe there are five list calls that pass expand as a string, for example expand: 'data.customer'. They were changed to arrays, such as expand: ['data.customer'].

The places are the refund report, the dunning job, the invoice sync, the customer export and one admin helper. In four of them the change is a one-line edit. In the customer export the expand value was built by joining several fields with a comma, which is not valid for the array form, so the code now builds an array from the start.

The unit tests that mock the SDK checked the exact argument, so eight of them had to be changed. The agent changed them and added one new case that checks that the export passes two fields as two entries.

The agent ran the comparison job against Stripe test mode, the one that checks the list helper against the database. It passed, and the expanded customer objects were present in all lists.

The deprecation warning for the string form no longer appears in the staging log after a full run of the dunning job, the refund report and the invoice sync. The other warnings of the table are still there, as expected.

One point in the review of the diff: the type of the expand parameter in the SDK is an array of strings, so the compiler would have complained earlier if the types of our helper had not been declared as any. The helper's own type was narrowed from any to string[] so that the compiler now catches this.

That narrowing found one more call in the test setup that used a string. It was fixed as well.

The change was deployed after the evening run. The next group in the table is the renamed fields.

summary: Replaced the three reads of renamed Stripe fields with the new names and added a fallback test, after finding that old webhook events in the retry queue still carry the old names.
body:
The second group of the warnings table was three places that read fields under their old names. Two are in the invoice sync and one is in the payment intent webhook handler.

Changing the names in the sync code was simple, since it reads objects that it fetches from Stripe with the current API version, so the new names are always there.

The webhook handler is different. Events are stored by the handler and processed by a job, and events that failed earlier are retried for several days. The agent looked at the table of stored events and found 14 that were created with an older API version and still use the old field names.

If the handler read only the new name, those 14 events would be processed with an empty value, and in one case that would mean a payment with a missing method. The agent therefore made the handler read the new name first and the old name as a fallback, with a comment on why.

A test was added with one event in each form. Both give the same result in the handler. The agent also put a log line in the fallback branch, so that it can be removed once the line is no longer seen for a few weeks.

The agent checked the deprecation warnings on staging with the replay of 200 stored events. The three warnings of the group are no longer present.

The replay also showed that no event was processed with an empty value, which was the real worry. The 14 old events were all in the replay and gave the right result.

The change is small, and the diff has 31 added lines, most of them in tests.

Only the shims group is left from the table, and it belongs to the upgrade. Nothing more is planned for today in this topic.

summary: Answered Mara's question how many invoices per month have more than 100 lines now that usage is grouped: 3 of about 5,900 last month, against 71 in the old format.
body:
Mara asked whether the work on big invoices still matters after the grouping. The agent counted the lines of the invoices of last month, in the stored form.

In the old, ungrouped form 71 of the 5,900 invoices had more than 100 lines, and 12 had more than 500. The largest had 1,900.

With the grouping, the agent recomputed the count from the raw usage rows. Only 3 invoices have more than 100 lines, and the largest has 140. The lines are now mostly one per product and day for the few customers that use many products.

So the problem of very large invoices is mostly gone, and the render time of the slowest invoice is about 4 seconds.

The agent told Mara that the remaining cost is the browser itself, which the pool has reduced, and that the further speedup would come from a new renderer rather than from more tuning of the current one.

Mara said that this matches her view and that the new renderer stays on the list as a later item, not an urgent one.

summary: Found that the reminder email for invoices due in three days showed the old due date after an invoice's payment terms were changed, and fixed it by reading the date at send time.
body:
A support ticket said that a customer got a reminder that the invoice is due in three days, with a date that was a week earlier than the date on the invoice in the portal. The agent started from the ticket's invoice id.

The invoice had been created with payment terms of 14 days. A week later, support changed the terms to 30 days at the customer's request, and the due date column was updated. The reminder had the old date.

The agent found that the reminders are planned as jobs. When an invoice is finalized, the code creates the reminder jobs with the data they need, including the due date as text, at that moment. A later change of the date does not touch the jobs that already exist.

So there were two faults. The email showed the old date, and the reminder was also sent at the old time, three days before the old due date, which is a week too early for the new terms.
