The fix has two parts. The reminder job now stores only the invoice id and loads the invoice when it runs, so the email uses the current date. The job also checks at the start whether it is still the right day: if the invoice is paid or the due date moved, it skips or reschedules itself.

For the rescheduling the agent used the existing job helper that sets the start time, and added a test with a due date that moves by 16 days. The job reschedules to three days before the new date and sends nothing.

There are still jobs in the queue that have the old format with the date as text. The agent made the job accept both forms: if there is no invoice id but only the old payload, it uses the old payload's invoice number to find the invoice. A query found 63 such jobs in the queue.

The agent also searched for other places that change the due date. Only the support tool does it, and it should recompute the reminders. A short comment was put there, and a ticket for the support tool was added to the notes.

All tests pass, and the 63 old jobs were run on a staging copy without a failure.

The customer from the ticket will get a correct reminder at the right time. The agent wrote a short reply for support.

summary: Checked the other emails for the same stale data problem as the reminder and found that the dunning email also copies the amount at scheduling time, so it now reads the open amount when it sends.
body:
After the reminder fix, the agent went through the other job types that send emails to see whether they also copy data when they are scheduled.

The receipt email is sent right after the payment, so its data is fresh. The reminder is fixed. The dunning email for a failed payment is the one that has the same pattern. It stores the amount and the currency in the job payload when the payment fails.

That gives a problem when a customer pays part of the amount, or when finance issues a credit note between the failure and the next dunning step. The email then asks for the full original amount. The retry schedule runs for up to 14 days, so this can happen.

The agent changed the dunning job to load the invoice and use the amount still open. If the open amount is zero, the job ends and sends nothing, and it writes the reason in the job log.

As with the reminder job, old jobs in the queue have the old payload, and the job accepts both. There were 9 such jobs.

A test with a partial payment checks that the email shows the open amount, with the currency code after the number, as in the other emails.

The agent made sure that the fix from a few weeks ago stays intact. The record that a dunning email was sent is still written before the call to Postmark returns, so a retry after a timeout does not send it twice. The test for that case still passes.

The agent also ran the query that counts duplicate emails per day, and it still finds none.

summary: Wrote the first plan for removing the old ungrouped line code and the USAGE_GROUPING setting after two weeks without problems, with a checklist of five places that read the setting.
Looked at why the evening run's database connection count peaks at 48 and found that the PDF pool and the email job each open their own connections, so both now share the main pool.
body:
Mara noticed in the monitoring that the Postgres connection count of billing-api peaks at 48 during the evening run, and the limit of the small database plan is 60. She asked whether that is a problem waiting to happen.

The agent logged the connections by application name for one run on staging. The web part uses 10, which is the configured pool size. The job runner pg-boss uses its own pool of 10. The PDF job and the email job each create a pool in their own module, with a size of 10 each, and the usage import has a fourth one with 8.

None of them needs that many. The PDF job renders with two browsers, so it can only use 2 connections at a time. The email job runs 4 sends in parallel.

The agent changed the PDF job, the email job and the usage import to use the shared database module instead of creating their own pools. The shared pool has a size of 20, and the web part keeps a separate pool of 10 so that web requests cannot be starved by a long run.

There is one catch. Jobs that start a transaction hold a connection for its whole length. The invoice creation job does that, and a run creates invoices in a loop. The agent checked that each transaction there is short, about 40 ms on average, so the pool is fine.

In the new setup the peak on staging was 27 connections: 10 for the web part, 20 at most for the shared pool and the job runner's 10 are now counted within it, as the runner can take the same pool instance.

That last point needed a change in the job runner configuration. pg-boss accepts an existing database object, so it uses the shared pool through a small adapter. The adapter had to implement executeSql only, and it was tested with the job table's maintenance queries too.

A load test with 5 times the usual number of jobs on staging stayed below 30 connections, and no job waited longer than 200 ms for a connection.

The change was deployed after the evening run. The agent will look at the monitoring after the run tomorrow to compare the peak.

summary: The evening run after the pool change peaked at 26 connections and took the same time as before, so the change is confirmed and Mara can lower the alert threshold.
body:
The agent looked at the monitoring this morning for the run of last night. The peak was 26 connections, against 48 before, and it came during the PDF step, when the web part and the shared pool were both busy.

The duration of the run was 2 minutes 38 seconds for 224 invoices, so it did not change. The job log shows no waits for a connection. The longest wait was 12 ms.

The agent also compared the web part. The 95th percentile of the response time for the admin tool and the API was the same as in the previous week, around 90 ms. The web pool did not see any change, which is the point of keeping it separate.

There were no errors with the message about too many clients in the database log, neither before nor after the change. So the change was a precaution and not a fix of a failure. Mara confirmed that this was what she wanted.

The alert for the connection count was set at 45. The agent suggested to lower it to 35, so that a real problem is noticed while the margin is still large. Mara will change it in the monitoring tool.

One observation: at the end of the run the connection count stays at 18 for some minutes, and does not drop to 10 immediately. The pool keeps idle connections for 30 seconds by default, and the job runner polls. That is fine.

The agent noted the numbers in the notes folder as a baseline. If the invoice volume grows a lot, the shared pool size of 20 can be raised, and the notes say what to check.

No more work is open in this topic.

summary: Began planning the move of the invoices table to partitions by writing down the facts: 1.9 million rows, 23 GB with indexes, and the three queries that are slow because they scan the whole table.
body:
The invoices table keeps growing, and Mara asked the agent to plan a way to keep it fast. Partitioning by time is the option that was already named in the earlier discussions, so the agent started by collecting numbers.

The table has 1.9 million rows. Together with its indexes it takes 23 GB, of which 14 GB are the indexes and 6 GB are the large text column that holds the stored line details. The rest is the table data itself. It grows by about 70,000 rows per month.

The agent used the slow query log of the last month and found three queries that matter. The first is the admin tool's search of the invoices of a customer, which takes 300 ms on average. The second is the monthly report for finance, which reads one month and takes 25 seconds. The third is the evening run's check for duplicates, which looks at the last 40 days and takes 4 seconds.

All three filter by a date range, and the dates come from the created column. The customer search also filters by customer id and would profit from a time range as well, which the admin tool can add by default, for example the last two years.

The partitioning key is therefore the created date, with one partition per quarter. A quarter has about 210,000 rows, which is a good size for the indexes.

The agent checked what points to the invoices table. There are foreign keys from the invoice lines and from the payments, and the email log has an invoice id column. A partitioned table needs the key column in the primary key, so the primary key will become the pair of the id and the created date. The foreign keys will have to carry the date as well, or be replaced by checks in the application.

That is the largest part of the work, and the agent counted five tables that refer to invoices. The next step is a closer look at each of them.

There is a second risk. The sequence for the invoice number is separate from the table, and the numbers must stay free of gaps, which is a legal requirement for finance. The agent verified that the number comes from its own sequence, so a move of the table does not affect it, but the sequence's ownership must be kept.

A rough estimate for the whole work is one week, including a rehearsal on a staging copy. The agent put the facts and the open points in the notes and will come back to them.

Mara asked that the plan includes a rollback that has been tried, not only written. This is now on the checklist.

summary: Tested how long a copy of the invoices table takes on a staging copy, 38 minutes for the full copy, and designed a two-step copy so that the final switch only moves the last day.
body:
To plan the switch, the agent measured how long the data copy takes. On the staging copy, which has the production size, an insert from the old table into a new partitioned table took 38 minutes, including the index builds on the partitions.

A copy of 38 minutes cannot happen in the middle of the day while invoices are written. Invoices are created mostly in the evening run, but payments update rows throughout the day, and a copy that misses updates gives wrong data.

The agent therefore designed a two-step approach. In step one, a copy of all rows older than two days is made at any time, since those rows are changed very rarely. In step two, in a quiet hour, the writes are paused and the rows of the last two days are copied, and the tables are renamed.

To be careful about the older rows that do change, the agent looked for updates. In the last month 140 invoices that were older than two days were updated, almost all of them by a payment arriving late or by a credit note. The step-two copy should therefore include all rows with an update time in the last few days, not only the new ones.

The table has an updated_at column, which is set by a trigger. The agent checked that the trigger is on every update path, including the payment webhook handler. It is.

So step two copies the rows with updated_at after the start of step one, and it deletes and re-inserts the same ids in the new table. That is simple, and tests on staging will show whether it is right.

The pause for writes is the delicate part. The agent suggested to stop the job runner and to put the web part into read-only mode for the invoice endpoints for the duration. The switch itself, two renames, takes less than a second, and the copy of two days of rows takes about a minute.

In the notes, the agent wrote the steps with commands and the checks after each: row counts per partition, a sum of the totals per month on both tables, and a comparison of random 1,000 rows by checksum.

Mara will review the steps tomorrow.

summary: Wrote the checksum and totals comparison script for the table switch and ran it against a staging copy: counts and the sum of totals per month match for all 33 months.
body:
For the checks of the switch, the agent wrote scripts/compare-invoices.ts. It takes two table names and compares them in three ways.

The first is the row count per month. The second is the sum of the total amount per month and currency, in cents, so that a rounding difference cannot hide. The third is a sample: 1,000 random invoice ids, for which it computes an md5 of the main columns on both tables and compares them.

The agent tested the script on staging by creating a plain copy of the invoices table and then changing it on purpose in three ways: one row deleted, one total changed by one cent and one status changed. The script found all three, with the month and the id in its output.

Then the agent ran it for the new partitioned table of the first test copy, made in the earlier step. For all 33 months the counts and the sums match. The sample of 1,000 rows had no difference.

The run of the script takes 50 seconds on the staging data, mostly for the sums. That is fast enough to run before and after the final switch.

One detail: the sample uses a random function, so a repeat gives other ids. The script takes an optional seed and prints it, which makes a failed check repeatable.

The script exits with a non-zero code for any difference, so it can be a step in the switch script and stop it.

The next step is the closer look at the five tables that refer to invoices.

summary: Ran the partition switch rehearsal on a fresh staging copy end to end: 41 minutes of copy, a 90-second switch, and all 33 months matched in the checksum script.
body:
Rehearsed the full plan for moving the invoices table to partitions on a fresh staging copy of production. The first copy step took 41 minutes, a little more than the 38 measured before, because the staging database was busy with another test. The second step, which moves only the rows of the last day, took 90 seconds, and that is the window in which invoice creation has to stop.

After the switch I ran the checksum and totals script from last week. Counts and the sum of totals per month matched for all 33 months, and the per-row checksum of the 2,000 sampled invoices matched too. I then ran the three slow queries against the new layout. The query for open invoices by customer fell from 7.4 seconds to 0.3 seconds, because it now reads only the recent partitions.

One thing broke. The foreign key from invoice_lines to invoices could not be kept as it was, because a unique key on a partitioned table has to include the partition column. I wrote down two options: add created_at to the key of invoice_lines, or drop the foreign key and rely on the code and a nightly check. Neither is decided.

The rollback was also tried: renaming the old table back took under a second, as long as no new rows were written in between. That limit goes into the plan. Next step is to talk with Mara about the foreign key and to decide on the quarter boundaries for the partitions.

summary: Compared the two options for the invoice_lines foreign key after partitioning and recommended adding the invoice's created_at to the key, with a nightly orphan check as a second guard.
body:
Mara agreed to look at the foreign key problem, so I wrote the two options down with their costs. Option one adds invoice_created_at to invoice_lines and makes the foreign key over (invoice_id, invoice_created_at). Option two drops the foreign key and only checks for orphans at night.

For option one I counted what changes. The lines table has 14 million rows, so adding and filling the new column takes about 25 minutes on the staging copy. Three queries in the code join lines to invoices and would now get the extra column in the join, which helps the planner prune partitions. The insert code for lines already has the invoice row in hand, so it can pass the date without an extra read.

For option two nothing changes in the code, but a bug could then leave a line without an invoice and nobody would see it before the night run. For a billing service I do not like that, because a lost line is lost money or a wrong total.

I recommended option one, and also a cheap nightly query for orphans, as a second guard. Mara has not answered yet. If she agrees, the column goes in as a separate step before the table switch, so each step can be rolled back by itself.

summary: Added the invoice_created_at column to invoice_lines with a batched backfill and tested it on staging; 14 million rows were filled in 22 minutes without long locks.
body:
Mara chose the composite foreign key, so I started with the column on invoice_lines. The migration adds invoice_created_at as nullable, and a separate script fills it in batches of 20,000 rows by joining to invoices. A batch takes about 0.9 seconds, and the script sleeps 200 ms between batches so the evening run is not slowed down.

On the staging copy the backfill took 22 minutes for 14.1 million rows. I watched pg_locks during the run and saw no lock longer than a few milliseconds. Replication lag on the staging replica stayed under 2 seconds.

The insert code in src/invoices/lines.ts now writes the column for new lines. I added a test that creates an invoice with three lines and checks that all three carry the date of the invoice. A second test covers the case where an invoice is created at 23:59 and its lines are written after midnight, because the date must come from the invoice row and not from the clock. That test failed at first, since one code path used new Date() for the lines. It was fixed to read the invoice row.

After the backfill I ran a check for rows where the column is still null or differs from the invoice: zero rows. The not-null constraint and the new key are still to come, and they should go in after the code is on production for a few days. The check query is saved as scripts/check-line-dates.sql so it can run again before the switch.

summary: Wrote the migration that creates the quarterly partitions and the switch procedure as a script with a dry-run mode, and ran it on staging twice.
body:
The next part of the partition work was the switch itself. I wrote scripts/partition-switch.ts, which does these steps: create the new partitioned table with one partition per quarter from the oldest invoice up to four quarters ahead, copy the old rows in two passes, take a short lock, move the last day, rename the tables and reset the sequences.

The script has a dry-run mode that prints each step with the row counts it would touch and does not write anything. It also refuses to start if the job runner has invoice jobs running, so the switch cannot happen in the middle of an evening run. That check reads the pg-boss job table for active jobs of the three invoice queues.

On staging I ran it twice from a clean copy. The first run failed in the sequence step, because the id column of the new table had no default linked to the old sequence, and the next insert gave a duplicate key error. I fixed that by setting the default to the existing sequence and by setting its value to the maximum id plus one after the rename. The second run went through, and a test insert after the switch got the right next id.

The lock window was 84 seconds in the second run. I also added a default partition so that a row with an unexpected date does not fail the insert, and a log line when anything lands in it. The new partitions for the next year are created by a monthly job, which I have not written yet. It goes on the list for tomorrow, together with a test for the rollback path.

summary: Wrote the job that creates future invoice partitions and an alert when fewer than two quarters are ahead, after noticing that nothing would otherwise add them.
body:
While reading the switch script again I saw that after four quarters, inserts would go into the default partition, and nobody would notice at once. So I wrote the maintenance job today.

The job runs on the first of every month in pg-boss. It looks up the latest partition and creates new quarterly partitions until there are four quarters ahead. It is safe to run twice, because it uses create table if not exists and checks the bounds first. If a partition with overlapping bounds exists, it stops and logs an error instead of guessing.

I added a second check that runs every night: if fewer than two quarters are ahead, or if the default partition holds any row, it sends a message to the alert channel. The query for the default partition is cheap because the partition is empty. I tested both paths with a staging database. In one test I dropped the future partitions and saw the alert come. In the other I inserted a row with a far future date and saw the alert about the default partition.

There are six tests for the job now. One of them covers the change of the year, since the quarter bounds are computed in code and I wanted to be sure about the edge. All pass. The job is not yet registered on production, because the table is still the old one. It will be registered right after the switch.

summary: Ran the switch rehearsal with the evening run active on a staging copy and found that the invoice job waits behind the lock for 84 seconds, then continues without error.
body:
Today I tested the thing I worried about most: what happens to a running invoice job when the switch takes its lock. For the test I started an evening run of 220 invoices on staging and started the switch script in dry-run off mode at the same time. I had to remove the safety check that refuses to run during jobs, using a flag only meant for this test.

The result was good. Jobs that wanted to insert an invoice waited on the lock, and after 84 seconds they went on. No job failed. Two jobs showed a lock wait of 83 and 84 seconds in the log, and the pg-boss default timeout is far above that, so no retry was needed. After the switch the new rows landed in the right partition, and I checked this with a query on the partition tableoid.

I also tested a worse case, a lock window of five minutes made by a sleep in the script. There the statement timeout of 60 seconds that the invoice code sets killed the waiting inserts, and pg-boss retried them later. After the lock was gone, all retried jobs finished, and no invoice was created twice. That match is thanks to the unique invoice number, which makes the second insert fail cleanly.

So the plan keeps the safety check, because it costs nothing, but the switch is not dangerous if a job slips in. I wrote the numbers into the plan document.

Open items are the rollback test and the not-null step on invoice_lines. I also want a last look at the three indexes, because partitioned tables need them per partition. Tomorrow I will check how long the index builds take on the big old partitions, since I expect them to be the slowest part of the first copy.

summary: Measured the index build times per partition on staging; the oldest quarters build in seconds and the whole set of five indexes takes 11 minutes, so they can be built before the final pass.
body:
After the lock test I looked at the indexes of the new table, because on a partitioned table each partition builds its own. The invoices table has five indexes: by customer and date, by status, by number, by Stripe invoice id and by due date.

On the staging copy I built them partition by partition after the first copy pass. The oldest quarters hold about 30,000 rows each and need only a few seconds per index. The last four quarters are bigger, about 250,000 rows each, and need up to 40 seconds per index. In total the five indexes took 11 minutes.

That changes the order of the steps a little. The indexes should be built after the first bulk copy and before the second pass, so that the final lock window does not include any build. I changed the script so that the second pass runs only after the index step reports success. The script also checks the index list on the new table against the old one and refuses to switch if one is missing.

The unique index on the invoice number needed a thought, since a unique index on a partitioned table must contain the partition key. I made the key (number, created_at). This still protects against double numbers in practice, because the number comes from one sequence, but the database no longer enforces it across quarters. I added a nightly check for duplicate numbers into the same job as the orphan check, and wrote the point down for Ines, since the invoice numbers matter to her.

summary: Tested the rollback of the partition switch on staging, which took 2 seconds if no new rows came in and needed a copy-back script if some had.
body:
Today I tried the way back. After a normal switch on staging I renamed the old table back and the partitioned one away, and it worked in about 2 seconds. This only works as long as no new invoice has been written to the new table.

For the case that rows were written, I wrote scripts/partition-rollback.ts. It copies every row newer than the switch time from the partitioned table into the old table and then renames. I tested it with 300 rows added after the switch. The copy took under a second, and the checksum script showed counts equal on both sides.

The lines table is the harder part, since it has the new key. The rollback script drops the composite key and puts the old foreign key back, which takes about 3 minutes on staging because the key is checked against all rows. I noted that time in the plan. If the rollback is needed, invoice creation would be stopped for those 3 minutes as well.

The plan now says that the old table is kept for 14 days after the switch, so a rollback stays possible. Disk space is fine for that, since 23 GB is little next to the free space. The drop of the old table will be a separate decision.

summary: Investigated why 9 customers got a receipt email twice this week and found that the Stripe webhook retry and the receipt job both queued a send for the same payment.
body:
Ines forwarded a note from support: nine customers got the receipt for the same payment twice this week. I started with the email log. In all nine cases the two sends were between 4 and 30 minutes apart and had the same payment id but different job ids.

The receipt is queued from two places. The normal path is the payment_intent.succeeded webhook handler, which queues a send_receipt job. The second place is a catch-up job that runs every hour and queues receipts for succeeded payments that have no receipt_sent_at. The catch-up job exists for the case that a webhook was lost.

The race is clear now. When the webhook handler had queued the job but the email provider call was still waiting in the queue, receipt_sent_at was empty, and the catch-up job queued a second one. In normal times the send takes seconds, but on those days the queue was behind, because the evening run sent 1,400 reminder emails at the same time. Both jobs then sent the mail.

I looked for the simplest fix. I added a receipt_queued_at column that is set in the same transaction that queues the job, and the catch-up job now only looks at payments where both receipt_queued_at and receipt_sent_at are empty. In addition, the pg-boss job gets a singleton key made from the payment id, so even a second queue attempt is dropped by the runner.

I wrote tests for it. One test queues from the webhook and runs the catch-up job at once and expects one job. Another starts with a lost webhook and expects the catch-up job to queue exactly one. Both pass.

I also checked past data: in the last 90 days, 31 payments had a double receipt, all on days with a busy queue. No other email type uses the catch-up pattern, so the problem is limited to receipts. The change is on staging and will go to production with tomorrow's release. I told Ines about the cause and the 31 cases, and that no customer was charged twice, since only the email was doubled.

summary: Deployed the double receipt fix and added a metric for the receipt queue age, then confirmed with a replay of last week's busy evening that only one email per payment goes out.
body:
The fix for the double receipts went to production this morning together with the migration for receipt_queued_at. The migration is quick, since the column is nullable and has no default. I also filled the column for payments of the last 7 days from the email log, so the catch-up job would not queue old ones by mistake.

To be sure, I replayed the busy evening on staging. I took the 1,400 reminder emails and the 220 receipts of last week's run and let them run through a slow fake email provider that needs 2 seconds per call. This made the queue about 25 minutes long, the same way as on the bad days. Before the fix the same replay produced 12 double receipts. After the fix, zero.

The replay showed one more thing. The receipts waited behind the reminders in the same queue, so a customer who paid at 19:00 might wait 20 minutes for the receipt. That is not a bug, but it is not nice. I gave the receipts their own queue with a higher priority, and the reminders keep the old one. The email worker has a limit of 5 calls per second against the provider, and I split this limit so that the receipts always have room.

I added a metric for the age of the oldest waiting job per queue and put it into the existing dashboard. Mara can set an alert on it. A sensible start is 10 minutes for the receipt queue.

I wrote a test for the priority, using a queue with 50 reminders and 1 receipt and checking that the receipt is sent before the reminders are done. It passes. I want to look at the result in production tomorrow evening, when the next run comes, and then say whether the split should stay.

summary: Checked the evening run on production after the receipt queue split: the oldest receipt waited 14 seconds, and there were no double emails.
body:
Looked at last night's run with the new receipt queue. The run created 224 invoices and sent about 1,350 reminders, and the receipts of that evening were 38.

The oldest waiting receipt had an age of 14 seconds at its peak, where before the split it could be 20 minutes. The reminders took the same total time as before, about 17 minutes, since they now share the rate limit with the receipts, but that has no real effect.

I searched the email log for payments with more than one receipt in the last night and found none. The catch-up job ran 24 times and queued nothing, as expected.

The age metric works and shows two lines in the dashboard. I told Mara she can set the alert at 10 minutes. I consider the receipt topic closed unless a new report comes in.

summary: Wrote the not-null step and the composite foreign key for invoice_lines and ran it on a staging copy; the key check took 4 minutes and no row failed.
body:
The code that writes invoice_created_at has been on production for six days now, so I went on with the constraint step. First the check script scripts/check-line-dates.sql on production: zero lines with a null date and zero with a date that differs from the invoice. Good.

The migration does three things. It sets the column to not null, it adds a unique key on invoices (id, created_at), and it adds the foreign key on invoice_lines (invoice_id, invoice_created_at) that points to it. On a table of 14 million rows, the not null step needs a full scan. To keep the lock short, I used the usual way: add a check constraint as not valid, validate it separately, then set not null, which can then skip the scan.

The foreign key is added as not valid first and validated afterwards. Validation takes only a weak lock, so inserts continue. On the staging copy the validation took 4 minutes and found no violating row. I also ran it while the evening-run replay was active, and the run was not slowed by more than a few percent.

The order matters for the switch. The unique key on invoices (id, created_at) has to exist on the partitioned table too, and there it has to include the partition column, which it does. I put the constraint step into the switch script as a step after the copy and before the lock. If the validation fails, the script stops before it takes the lock.

Another point was an ORM-like helper in our code that builds delete statements for lines by invoice_id. It still works because the key columns are only extra. I grepped for other deletes on lines and found only one in the admin tool for draft invoices. It works as well, since drafts use the same table.

The tests passed with the new constraints. I added one that tries to insert a line with a wrong invoice_created_at and expects a foreign key error. The migration is ready for production, and I will ask Mara for a time for it. It does not need downtime.

summary: Ran the constraint migration on production at low load: not null and the composite foreign key were validated in 6 minutes with no failed inserts.
body:
With Mara's agreement I ran the constraint migration on production this evening, after the invoice run had finished. The load was low, and I watched the dashboard during the migration.

The steps went as in staging. The check constraint was added as not valid and validated in 2 minutes 40 seconds. Setting not null was instant after that. The unique key on invoices (id, created_at) was built concurrently, which took 70 seconds. The foreign key was added not valid and validated in 3 minutes 10 seconds, so the sum was about 6 minutes in total.

During the migration the application logged no errors. I counted inserts into invoice_lines in that time, 412 of them from a late usage import, and all succeeded. The longest lock wait I saw in pg_stat_activity was 30 milliseconds.

After the migration I ran the orphan check query again and got zero rows. I also ran the checksum script on the new constraints, which only reads, and it showed the same counts as before.

Now everything the table switch needs is in place on production: the date column, the key, and the foreign key. The partition job is written and the switch script is rehearsed. What is left is the time for the switch itself and a message to Ines, since for 90 seconds no invoices can be created. I suggest a time after the evening run, when no job is active, and will write that down tomorrow.

summary: Answered Ines's question whether the partition switch can change any invoice number or total: it cannot, because rows are copied byte for byte and the checksum script compares them before the switch.
body:
Ines asked in the finance thread whether the move of the invoices table can change anything she checks each month, especially numbers and totals. I wrote her an answer and put the details here.

The switch copies rows as they are. No column is recomputed, and the invoice number comes from the stored value, not from the sequence. The checksum script builds a hash per row over all columns, including the total, tax and number, and compares the old and the new table for all 1.9 million rows, not only a sample. The switch script stops if one hash differs.

I also pointed out the one real change for her side. The uniqueness of the invoice number is now checked by a nightly query and no longer by the database across all quarters, since a partitioned table cannot do that. The number still comes from one sequence, so doubles are not possible in normal operation, and the nightly check would show it the next morning if one ever came.

For her monthly review nothing changes. The queries she uses read the table through the same name, and I ran her three saved queries on the staging copy after a switch. The results were identical to the old table, row for row, and two of them ran much faster.

She asked for the time of the switch. I said it will be after the evening run, with about 90 seconds in which new invoices wait, and I will tell her the evening before. She was fine with this and asked to get the checksum report as a file, so I made the script write its result to a text file with the counts per month.

summary: Fixed a flaky test in the dunning suite that failed one in ten runs because it compared a send time with the real clock.
body:
The dunning email tests failed about once in ten runs on CI, always in the test for the second reminder. I looked at the failure message: expected the send time to be 3 days after the first reminder, received 3 days minus 1 second.

The cause was that the test created the first reminder with the real clock and then computed the expected time with a second call to the clock. When the two calls fell on different seconds, the values differed. The code was fine, but the test was not.

I changed the test to use the fake timer that the other suites already use, and fixed the start time at a given moment. Now the expected time is a constant. I also searched the other test files for the same pattern of two clock reads and found two more places in the reminder tests, which I fixed as well.

I ran the dunning suite 200 times in a loop on my machine and got no failure. CI should be stable again. Nothing in the service code changed.

summary: Switched the invoices table to the partitioned layout on staging as the full dress rehearsal with the real script, then wrote the production runbook with times and stop conditions.
body:
Today was the last rehearsal before production, using a fresh copy made this morning. I ran the real script, not the dry-run, from the first step to the last, and took the time of each step to put into the runbook.

The numbers: first copy pass 41 minutes, index build 11 minutes, constraint step 5 minutes, second pass 6 minutes for the rows of the last two days, and the lock window 87 seconds. The checksum comparison over all rows ran for 9 minutes and matched everywhere. The total of about 72 minutes is mostly steps that run while the service works normally.

Two things were found. The first was that the second pass copied the rows of the last two days and not one day, since the first pass started before midnight. It does no harm, but the lock window depends on that number, so I made the script take the cut point from the end of the first pass. With this the lock window was 79 seconds in a second run.

The second was that a prepared statement cache in the app kept the old table's oid after the rename, and the first inserts after the switch failed with a cache lookup error in two of the workers. A restart of the workers fixed it. In production the runbook will have a step to restart the app and the job runner right after the rename. The restart takes about 20 seconds, so the pause for the customers goes up a little. I tested the restart in the rehearsal and the pause was 105 seconds in total.

The runbook has these parts: the checks before the start (no active jobs, free disk, a fresh backup), the steps with the expected time, the stop conditions, and the rollback with its times. A stop condition is, for example, a hash mismatch, a lock wait longer than 3 minutes, or an error rate above 2 percent after the restart. For each condition the runbook says what to do.

I also added the message texts for Ines and for the status page. The runbook is in docs/partition-switch.md. Mara will read it tomorrow, and then we pick the evening.

summary: Mara read the partition runbook and asked for two changes: a fresh backup restore test before the switch and a lower statement timeout for the final pass.
body:
Mara went through docs/partition-switch.md and had two requests. First, a backup is only worth something if it can be restored, so before the switch we restore last night's backup to a scratch database and run the count query on it. I added this as a step with the expected time of about 25 minutes, which can run in parallel with the first copy pass.

Second, she wanted the final pass to fail fast. I set the statement timeout for the second pass and the rename to 120 seconds, so a stuck lock cannot hold the invoice jobs for long. If it fires, the script rolls back that step and stops. I tested this by holding a lock from another session, and the script stopped after 120 seconds and left the old table untouched.

We agreed on the evening after next, after the run. I will write Ines the day before.

summary: Looked into a Stripe API error spike on the retry queue and found that 429 rate limit responses came from the backfill script running in parallel with the evening run.
body:
Mara noticed 38 failed jobs in the payment retry queue from last night and asked me to find out why. The error in the job log was the same in all of them: Stripe returned 429, rate_limit, and the SDK threw a StripeRateLimitError.

I first looked at the evening run itself. It makes about 220 calls to Stripe in a few minutes, which is far below the limit of 100 requests per second in live mode, so this could not be the reason. Then I looked at the time of the errors. They started at 21:12 and ended at 21:19, exactly the time of the consistency check I started by hand against the Stripe refunds, the one that lists all refunds and compares them with the table. That script reads pages of 100 without any pause and ran at about 90 requests per second, on top of the normal traffic.

So the limit was hit by my own script, and the payment retries that happened to run at the same moment got the 429. The retries are queued again by pg-boss, and I checked that all 38 jobs succeeded on their next try, within 30 minutes. No payment was lost, and no customer was charged twice, since the retry uses the same payment intent.

There are two lessons. The first is that the consistency script now sleeps 50 ms between pages and reads the Retry-After header when a 429 comes back. That brings it to about 15 requests per second. The second is that it should not run during the evening run at all, so I added a check at its start that stops if invoice jobs are active, like the switch script has.

I also looked at how the payment code handles the error. It does not handle 429 specially; the job fails and pg-boss retries with its backoff of 60 seconds, which works but fills the failure metric. I did not change that. A short note went into the docs for scripts that call Stripe in bulk. I ran the changed consistency script once on production during the day and got 14 requests per second at most, no 429. The result matched the table for all refunds. Nothing else remains for this topic.

summary: Ran the first copy pass of the production partition switch and the fresh-backup restore test; both finished, and the checksum comparison of the first pass matched for all rows copied so far.
body:
Today the preparation for tomorrow evening's switch began. The restore test came first. I restored last night's backup into a scratch database, which took 27 minutes, and ran the count query for invoices and lines. Counts were 1.93 million invoices and 14.3 million lines, equal to production at the backup time.

Then I started the first copy pass on production. The script copies in batches of 50,000 rows with a pause between batches and reads from the old table with a repeatable read snapshot per batch. The pass took 44 minutes and the load on the database stayed low: the CPU went up by about 10 percent, and the evening-run replay metrics did not show any change in query time for the app.

After the copy I built the five indexes on the new partitions. The build took 12 minutes. Then I ran the checksum comparison for the rows copied so far, which is all rows until the time the pass ended. The comparison took 10 minutes and showed no difference in the hash of any row.

One small surprise was disk usage. The new table with indexes takes 21 GB, compared with 23 GB for the old one, because the partitions are packed without the old bloat. Free disk is more than enough for both.

Until tomorrow the new table receives no writes, so it falls behind a little each hour. That is expected, and the second pass picks up everything newer than the cut point of the first pass. I noted the cut point in the runbook log. I also sent Ines the message with the time of the switch, after the run, and the 105 seconds of waiting. She confirmed and said that she would not run her review queries in that hour.

Left for tomorrow: the constraint step, the second pass, the lock, the rename and the restart of the workers.

summary: Prepared the production switch of the invoices table to quarterly partitions: reran the checks on a fresh copy and settled the window and stop conditions, without switching anything yet.
body:
I did not touch the production invoices table today. I used the day to get ready for the switch to quarterly partitions, following docs/partition-switch.md step by step on a copy of last night's backup.

The checks from the runbook all passed on the copy: no active jobs, enough free disk, a backup restored and readable, and no Stripe bulk script running at the time of the evening run. I added one more check to the list, a query that shows whether any pg-boss job is still holding a lock on the invoices table.

On the copy, the constraint step took 5 minutes, and the second pass for the last day and a half of rows took about 5 minutes 30 seconds. The window from lock to restart of the app and the job runner was 96 seconds, a bit better than the staging rehearsal. The statement timeout of 120 seconds was not reached, but with so little margin I will keep Mara's suggestion of a lower timeout for the final pass. After the rename I restarted the workers and saw no cache lookup error on the copy.

The checks after the switch on the copy were all fine: the checksum comparison over all rows matched, counts of invoices and lines were equal on both sides, and the sum of totals per month matched for all 34 months. The sequence gave the next id without a gap. A test invoice landed in the right quarter partition, which I confirmed with tableoid, and the default partition stayed empty.

I wrote the monthly partition job and the nightly check for orphans, duplicate numbers and the default partition, but did not register them on production. The plan is to keep the old table under the name invoices_old for 14 days so the rollback stays possible.

I sent Ines the checksum counts per month from the copy and a note that her monthly totals query should work as before. Next I will agree on the time of the real window with Mara, after an evening run has finished.

summary: Prepared to check the evening invoice run against the partition plan and listed the three slow queries to compare before the switch.
body:
The partition switch of the invoices table has not happened yet, so the evening run still used the single unpartitioned table. I took the numbers for the comparison that will matter afterwards. The average of the last ten evening runs was 39 minutes, and the invoice job showed no lock waits, which is the baseline I want to hold after the switch.

The three queries from the planning note are the open-invoices lookup, the monthly totals for Ines and the customer history page. I ran EXPLAIN on each one against staging and saved the plans next to the runbook. On the current table all three scan the whole table. The open-invoices lookup takes about 2.4 seconds, and that is the number I most want to see drop.

I also wrote down what to check for the composite foreign key on invoice_lines: the application logs for constraint errors and the nightly orphan check, which should keep returning 0 rows. I added a short query so I can run the orphan check by hand right after the switch instead of waiting for the night job.

One open point remains for the plan. The monthly totals query for Ines may still scan every partition when its month range spans a quarter edge, so I noted it as something to look at again once the layout exists. For rollback, the plan is to keep the old table renamed with an _old suffix for a week before dropping it. I asked Mara to review that part of the runbook.

summary: Wrote a plan for dropping the old invoices table after a quiet week, with the checks that must pass first and a rollback path kept until then.
body:
Started on the plan for removing the old invoices table once the switch to quarterly partitions has run for a while. The old table is 23 GB and is the only fast way back to the previous layout. Keeping it forever costs disk and invites mistakes, such as someone pointing a report at it, so I wrote a short plan with clear conditions instead of leaving it open.

There are three conditions. First, the nightly orphan check must be clean for seven nights in a row. Second, the checksum script must still match the partitioned table against the old one for all closed months. Third, nobody may read from the old table, which I will check by looking at the scan counters in pg_stat_user_tables. At the moment the counter for it is at 0, but the switch has not happened yet, so that number says little until the table has seen real traffic.

The copy-back script stays in the repository, with a note that after any drop it needs a backup restore as its source. Until the drop, it keeps working against the old table as it is.

I plan to take a final dump of the old table to cold storage before anything is dropped. A dump is cheap, and the accountants may ask Ines about old invoice data later.

I asked Mara to read the plan. She agreed with the seven nights and had no other changes. Nothing is dropped or switched by this plan; it only sets the order and the stop conditions for later.

summary: Found why the monthly totals report for Ines is slow, planned a created_at bound to make it prune partitions, and wrote down the assumption to check first.
body:
Ines reported that the monthly totals export was slow and asked if the planned partitioning of the invoices table would help. I looked at the query plan for the export and found that it filters on paid_at, while the planned partition key is created_at. With that filter Postgres has no way to prune, so after the switch the export would still scan every partition.

An invoice can be paid long after it was created, so the paid_at filter cannot simply be replaced. My idea is to keep it and add a lower bound on created_at of 120 days before the month start, which should match the longest payment terms we allow. I went through the plan catalog to check this and found no plan with longer terms, but I have not yet checked old custom plans and manually created invoices. I wrote down a list of those to look at next.

I also sketched a test that would fail if a plan with longer terms is ever added, so the assumption cannot break without notice. I ran the bounded query by hand on a copy of the data, and the numbers matched the current export for the last six months to the cent. I did not change the report yet. I told Ines what I plan to change and the assumption behind it, and asked her to tell me if finance knows of any invoice with terms longer than 120 days. Mara will read the plan before I touch the export.

summary: Upgraded the Stripe SDK from v13 to v14 on a test run, fixed two type errors around the invoice object, and found that the list helpers return a different page shape that our code relied on.
body:
The upgrade to v14 was planned for this week, and today I did the first part. I bumped the package, ran the type check, and got two errors. Both came from the invoice type, where a field that used to be a string is now typed as a string or null.

The first error was in the receipt builder, where I now handle a missing hosted invoice URL by leaving out the link. The second was in the dunning code, which read the same kind of field without a check. I fixed both and added a test for each.

The bigger finding came from the integration tests against the Stripe mock. Our listing code for customers reads the has_more flag and the last id of a page. In v14 the auto-pagination helpers behave a little differently when a limit is passed, and one of our loops stopped after the first page. That caused a test to see 100 customers instead of 240.

I did not want to change the loops everywhere, so I wrote a small shim in src/stripe/paginate.ts that walks the pages the way the old SDK did. Both loops now use it. The tests pass, with 412 of 412 green.

I did not deploy yet. The plan is to run the staging webhook replay tomorrow with the new SDK, since webhook parsing is where version changes tend to hurt. If it is clean, I deploy in the evening gap between runs. I noted in the shim file that it exists only because of this version, so it can be removed once we can use the native helpers.

summary: Prepared the Stripe SDK v14 upgrade by reading the list helper changes and checking the invoice code that relies on the old page shape, without deploying anything.
body:
I started on the v14 upgrade of the Stripe SDK by reading the changelog and listing everything in billing-api that touches the parts that changed. The first item is the invoice object, where a few fields have new types. I made the upgrade on a local branch and ran the type checker, which reported two errors around the invoice object, both small and both about fields that can now be null.

Then I looked at the part that worries me most, which is the list helpers. I searched the code for every place that pages through Stripe results, and found six. Three of them are in the payment retry job, one is in the nightly export for the accountants, and two are in the monthly totals report for Ines. Reading the new code, the list helpers seem to return a different page shape than the one our code expects, and our code reads the old shape directly. That would fail quietly instead of loudly, because an empty page looks like the end of the list. I have not confirmed this yet against a test account.

Nothing has been deployed and production still runs v13. The branch is local and has no tests added yet. Next I will write a test that pages through a list of at least three pages on the test account with both versions and compares the results. Then I will fix the six call sites one by one and run the evening invoice run on a test copy before I ask Mara to look at the change. I will also check that the webhook signature code is not affected by the upgrade.

summary: Deployed the v14 Stripe SDK to production between runs and watched the evening run; error rate stayed flat and no payment or webhook failed.
body:
I deployed at about 18:30, after the afternoon jobs were done and before the evening run. The deploy went through without problems and the health check was green within a minute.

During the evening run I watched three things: the Stripe error counter, the webhook failure counter and the payment success ratio. The error counter showed the usual two or three 402 card declines per hundred charges. The webhook failures stayed at 0. The payment success ratio was 96.8 percent, against 96.5 on the previous four evenings.

I also checked that the pagination shim was in use by the customer sync, and it logged its page counts as expected, 3 pages for 240 customers.

The SDK request logs show that the idle connections are now reused a bit more, which lowered the number of new TLS handshakes. This is a small gain and not a reason for the upgrade, but I noted it.

Nothing is left open for v14. The next steps are v15 in a week or two, which changes the error classes, and I will start by reading its changelog for what touches our error handling. I wrote the list of our places that catch Stripe errors so that the work is quick: eleven places, in payments, refunds, the customer sync and the webhook handler.

summary: Prepared an answer to Mara's question about what would happen to invoices being created while the partition switch runs, based on the rehearsal on the copy.
body:
Mara asked whether any invoice could end up half written when the partition switch runs on production. The switch has not happened yet, so I went back to the rehearsal I ran on the copy of the database and checked what it showed. In the rehearsal I started the invoice job during the switch window on purpose. The job waited behind the table lock for 84 seconds and then ran, and nothing was left half written.

After the lock was released in the rehearsal, the job continued and wrote 212 invoices into the new partitioned table. The count for that run matched the number of finalized subscriptions in the job log, and the checksum script showed no missing rows and no duplicates.

So my answer to Mara is that, going by the rehearsal, nothing should be lost and nothing written twice. The lock window on production may differ from the rehearsal, so I will keep the evening invoice run out of the switch time if possible. I wrote down the checks to repeat on the real run: the job log count against finalized subscriptions, and the checksum script on the final day. Mara agreed with the plan.

summary: Found a duplicate index on invoices.external_ref and prepared a migration to drop it, without running it on production yet.
body:
While looking at the index sizes, I saw two indexes on external_ref: one made by a unique constraint and one made by hand in the first version. The query planner only used the constraint's index.

I checked pg_stat_user_indexes. The hand-made index had 0 scans since the stats reset. The invoices table is still a single table, and the plan to split it by quarter is not done, so I looked at the one index pair only. Its size is about 600 MB, which is worth saving, and the same pair would later be copied into every partition.

I wrote a migration that drops the hand-made index and keeps the unique constraint. It ran on staging in under a second, and the lookup by external_ref still took 1 ms there afterwards. I did not run it on production. I wrote down the steps for it: pick a time of low load, drop the index with the concurrent option so that no lock blocks the invoice job, and watch slow queries for ten minutes. I asked Mara to read the migration before it goes out, and I kept the statement that recreates the old index in the same file in case a report turns out to need it.

summary: Investigated why the PDF renderer takes 40 seconds for invoices with 80 or more lines, and found that the headless browser reflows the table once for every row added by a script.
body:
Ines noticed that a few large invoices were arriving late in the evening, so I measured the renderer. A typical invoice with 10 lines takes 1.1 seconds. An invoice with 80 lines took 40 seconds in a test, which is far more than linear.

I profiled the render in the browser's performance trace. The page template builds the line table with a small script that appends one row at a time, and after each row it reads the table height to place a page break marker. That read forces a layout of the whole table, so the cost grows with the square of the rows.

I tried a fix in a scratch copy of the template. Rows are now built in a document fragment and the page break positions are computed once at the end. The 80-line invoice dropped to 3.4 seconds, and a 300-line one took 9 seconds. Quadratic growth is gone, though the cost is still not flat.

There is one risk. The page break logic changed slightly, so a row near a page edge could move to the next page. I rendered 40 real invoices from last month with the old and the new template and compared the PDFs as images. 38 were identical. In two, the last row of a page moved to the next page, which is acceptable but not exactly the same.

I did not change the production template yet. Since the new renderer is planned for later behind a flag, I want to ask Mara whether this fix is worth doing now. My view is that it is, because it is a change of 30 lines and the late invoices are a real problem for Ines. Next I will write a test that renders a 100-line invoice and fails if it takes more than 8 seconds.

summary: Shipped the document fragment fix for the invoice PDF template after Mara agreed, and added a render time test; large invoices now render in a fraction of the time.
body:
Mara agreed that the fix is small enough to go before the new renderer. I moved the change from the scratch copy into templates/invoice.html and the script that builds the table.

I added a test that renders an invoice with 100 lines and fails above 8 seconds. On my machine it takes 3.9 seconds, and the CI runner is slower, so I measured there too: 6.2 seconds. That leaves a small margin, and I left the limit at 8 for that reason.

I deployed before the evening run. During the run, the render times were logged for the first time per invoice. The median was 1.0 seconds. The slowest was an invoice with 212 lines that took 6.8 seconds, which would have taken more than 30 seconds before.

The total time of the PDF step fell from 9 minutes to 6 minutes.

There were two page layouts that changed, as expected from the test with images. I told Ines about it in case an accountant compares old and new copies of the same invoice. The numbers on both are the same, only a row sits on the next page.

Open points: the browser still starts fresh for every invoice, which costs about 0.6 seconds each. Reusing a browser would help more for the many small invoices, but it has memory risks. I wrote this down as a possible next step and did not start it.

summary: Started the Stripe SDK v15 upgrade by listing the eleven places that catch Stripe errors and checking which of them depend on the old error class names.
body:
The v15 changelog renames some error handling pieces, and our code catches Stripe errors in eleven places. I went through each.

Seven of them check the error type with a string, for example err.type === 'StripeCardError'. This still works in v15, since the type strings stay the same. Three use instanceof with the classes from the SDK, and the classes are still exported, but one of them is now a subclass of another, so the order of the checks matters. In the payment code the check for the general error came before the check for the card error, which would swallow the card errors. That order was fine in v14 and would be wrong now.

The eleventh place is the webhook handler, which catches signature errors. These keep their class.

I changed the order in the payment code and wrote a test that throws each kind of error and checks which branch handles it. The test found the problem before I fixed the order, which is a good sign that it tests the right thing.

The type check passes with v15 on a branchless local build, and 431 of 431 tests pass. I did not deploy. The webhook replay on staging is next, and I plan to run it tomorrow. One more thing I want to look at is the default retry count of the SDK, because a changelog line says that the default for network retries changed from 0 to 1 for some calls, and our refund calls must not retry silently.

summary: Checked the network retry default of Stripe SDK v15 and set maxNetworkRetries explicitly to 0 for refund calls, so a refund is never repeated silently by the client.
body:
The changelog line was about automatic retries on connection errors. I read the SDK source to see which calls it covers. The default now applies to all requests unless it is set on the client or per request.

For reads and charges with our own handling, a retry is harmless. For refunds it is not, because we do not send an idempotency key on refunds yet. A retried refund after a timeout could refund twice if the first call had actually gone through.

I set maxNetworkRetries to 0 on the client, and only the read paths set it to 2 per call. A test checks that the refund call is made with 0 retries. I noted in the refund code that an idempotency key would be the real fix, and I will bring it up with Mara as a separate task.

summary: Replayed the recorded webhook events through the v15 build on staging; all events were handled the same as with v14, with no differences in the database state.
body:
I replayed 2,800 events from the last five days, including retried ones and the refund and dispute events. All passed the signature check.

I compared the final state with the state from the v14 build. Invoices, payments and refunds were identical. The receipt emails queued were also the same.

The only log difference was a new deprecation notice about a field on the subscription object that we do not read. I left it alone. I plan to deploy v15 tomorrow before the evening run.

summary: Deployed Stripe SDK v15 and, during the evening run, found that card declines were now logged as unknown errors because the logger read a field that no longer exists.
body:
The deploy at about 18:20 went well, and the health check was green. During the evening run the payment success ratio looked normal at 96.6 percent, but the error log changed. Card declines, which are normal, were logged as errors of kind unknown instead of card_declined, and the alert for unknown errors fired twice.

I looked at the logger helper in src/stripe/errors.ts. It read err.raw.code to name the error kind. In v15 the raw object for card errors keeps the code in a different place for some declines, so the name came out empty and the helper fell back to unknown.

The payments were not affected. The decline handling does not use the helper. It uses the error type, which I had tested. But the dunning emails use the decline code to choose the text, and I checked this next. They read err.decline_code from the top level of the error, which still works. I verified this against the 14 declines of the evening: all 14 got the right dunning text.

I fixed the helper so that it reads the code from the top level first and from raw second. I added a test with samples of three decline shapes copied from the real log. The fix went out as a quick deploy at 21:00, and I silenced the alert for the rest of the run.

The lesson for the next upgrade is that the error tests I wrote cover the class order, but not the fields. I will add field checks for the log helper and the dunning code to the upgrade checklist.

summary: Confirmed after the logging fix that the v15 error names are right again: the late evening declines were logged as card_declined and the unknown error alert stayed quiet.
body:
After the quick deploy I watched the remaining part of the evening run. There were 6 more card declines, and all were logged as card_declined with the right decline code.

I also checked the earlier 14 declines in the log. They stayed as unknown, which is only a logging problem, but it affects the daily error report. I wrote a small query to count them and put a note in the report so that Ines is not surprised by the number.

The unknown error alert did not fire again. I re-enabled it at the normal threshold.

summary: Added field-level checks for Stripe errors to the upgrade checklist and a test file with real error samples, so the next SDK upgrade catches shape changes in logging and dunning.
body:
The v15 problem showed that checking class names is not enough. I wrote a fixtures file with eight real error payloads taken from the logs of the last months: three card declines of different codes, an insufficient funds case, an expired card, a rate limit, an invalid request and a SEPA-free generic API error.

A new test reads each fixture, builds the error with the current SDK and passes it through the logger helper and the dunning text selector. It checks that the kind and the text are the expected ones. For the card errors it checks the decline code as well.

I ran the test against v14 and v15, and both pass now. I also ran it against the old, unfixed helper to see if it fails, and it did, on exactly the three decline fixtures.

The upgrade checklist in docs/stripe-upgrades.md has now six steps: read the changelog, list the error catch sites, run the fixture test, replay the webhooks on staging, deploy between runs, and watch the first evening. I added the retry default check as a seventh, since it nearly caused a problem for refunds.

Mara read the checklist and asked me to add a step for the pagination shim, so that it is tested with a page size of 1. I added that. The shim has two tests now, one for a normal page size and one for a page size of 1, and both pass on v15.

summary: Answered Ines's question why two customers got an invoice total that differs by 1 cent from her spreadsheet, and showed that the spreadsheet rounds the sum while billing rounds each line.
body:
Ines sent two invoices where her check sheet and the PDF differ by 1 cent. I pulled both invoices and their lines.

The first has 7 lines. The PDF total is 214.37, the sheet says 214.38. I recomputed the lines by hand. Each line is quantity times unit price with VAT, rounded to the cent, and the sum of the rounded lines is 214.37. The sheet sums the unrounded values and rounds once at the end, which gives 214.38.

The second invoice shows the same pattern, with 11 lines and a difference of 1 cent in the other direction.

So billing is internally consistent: every line on the PDF is rounded, and the total is the sum of what is printed. A customer who adds the lines on the PDF gets our total. The sheet of Ines does not match what the customer sees.

This is a known gap that I noted earlier, since the accountants may prefer a different rule for the rounding of each line. I told Ines that I do not change the rounding on my own, and that she should ask the accountants which rule they want. If they name one, the change is small, since all rounding goes through one function in src/money.ts.

I added both invoices as examples to the note for the accountants. She will take it to the next meeting. Nothing else is open for me until she answers.

summary: Looked into a spike of failed receipt emails and found that the old email provider rejected addresses with a plus sign in 41 cases, which are now flagged for a different contact.
body:
The failed email report showed 41 bounces last week, up from the usual 5. I grouped them by the error returned by the provider. 38 had the same message about an invalid recipient, and the addresses all had a plus sign, such as name+billing@example.com.

The addresses are valid, and other providers accept them. I tested a send to my own test address with a plus sign through the current provider, and it was rejected in the same way. The provider's validation seems to have changed, since the same addresses worked a month ago. I checked old logs and found successful sends to 29 of them.

I cannot fix the provider. What I can do is find a way for the customers. I wrote a query that lists the affected customers: 41 in total, 33 of them with active subscriptions. For each, the account has a second contact address, or the owner's login address, in 36 of the cases.

I added a fallback in the receipt job. If a send fails with this specific error, the job tries the account owner's address once and logs which address was used. I tested it with a stub that returns the provider's error. The receipts for the 33 active customers will go out tonight from the retry.

This is another sign of the trouble with the provider. Customers also still write that receipts land in spam, and Mara knows about this. The fallback keeps the receipts moving until a better solution exists. For the 5 customers with no second address, I made a list for support, so someone can ask them for another contact.

I will check tomorrow whether the fallback sent all 36 and whether the bounce count returned to normal.

summary: Verified the receipt fallback: 36 of 36 receipts went to the owner address overnight, and the bounce count for the day fell to 4.
body:
This morning I checked the receipt job log. All 36 receipts that had bounced because of the plus sign went out to the account owner's address, and none bounced again.

The bounce count for the last 24 hours was 4. Three were full mailboxes and one was a closed domain, which is the usual noise. The list for support with the 5 customers without a second address is in the shared sheet, and Mara forwarded it.

I also looked at whether the fallback could send a receipt twice. Since the first send failed at the provider, there is no first email. I added a test that makes the first call fail and checks that exactly one email is queued per payment, which relates to the double receipts from earlier.

One more point: the fallback logs the address used, and I made sure that the log line writes only the domain and not the full address. Personal data should not sit in the logs for months. I changed two older lines that did the same mistake.

summary: Tracked down a slow query on the usage meter table that took 5 seconds in the evening run and cut it to 90 ms by adding a composite index on customer and period.
body:
The evening run log showed a query that reads the usage counts for a customer and a billing period, with a runtime of 5 seconds, executed once per customer. It was the largest part of the metering step.

EXPLAIN ANALYZE showed a sequential scan over usage_counts, which has 48 million rows. The table has an index on customer_id and a separate one on period_start, and the planner chose neither, because the customer filter returns many rows and the period filter does too.

I created a composite index on (customer_id, period_start) with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, which took 14 minutes at low load on production and did not block writes. After that the same query ran in 90 ms.

The whole metering step fell from 22 minutes to 4 minutes in a dry run on staging with a fresh copy of the data. The separate customer_id index is now redundant, since the composite one covers it, but I leave it for a week before I drop it, just to be careful.

The index adds 1.8 GB to the table. I think this is a fair price. I will look at the table size again in a month, since the usage table grows by about 2 million rows each month and may need a partition plan like the invoices table.

summary: Read the v16 Stripe SDK changelog and found two breaking changes that touch billing-api: a renamed field on payment intents and a changed type for expanded customers.
body:
Before I start the v16 upgrade, I read the whole changelog and searched the code for each item. Most items concern parts of the API that we do not use, such as the terminal and the issuing resources.

Two items touch us. The first is a renamed field on payment intents. We read the old name in three places: the payment confirmation, the SEPA-free reconciliation report and the receipt builder. The webhook handler also reads it, and old events in the retry queue may still carry the old name, which is a point to handle with a fallback.

The second is the type of the customer field when it is expanded. It is now a union with a deleted customer object. Our sync code assumes a live customer and reads the email directly, so a deleted customer would give an error. In production this is rare, but I found two deleted customers in the last month in our own data.

I wrote a list of changes: three renames with fallbacks, one guard for deleted customers, and the field tests for the log helper. I counted the work as a day.

I also checked the version of the pagination shim. In v16 the auto-pagination helper works the way our code needs, but the changelog says that the page size default changed from 10 to 100 in the list calls. Our loops pass explicit sizes, so I do not expect trouble. I will check this with the page size of 1 test.

Tomorrow I apply the changes, run the fixture tests and replay the webhooks on staging. Since the upgrade to v17 will come later, I do not want to remove the shim now. It stays until the key changes are in.

summary: Applied the v16 changes: three field renames with fallbacks, a guard for deleted customers, and updated fixtures; all 447 tests pass and the staging webhook replay matches v15.
body:
I made the changes from yesterday's list. The three reads of the renamed payment intent field now take the new name first and fall back to the old one, so events from the retry queue still work. I wrote a test with an old-format event and a new-format event for each place.

For the deleted customer case, the sync code checks the deleted flag and skips the customer with a log line. I wrote a test with a deleted customer object. Before the guard the test threw a type error, and after it, the sync completes.

The fixture file for errors got two new samples from this week's logs. Both the logger helper and the dunning text selector still give the right result with v16.

The pagination tests with page size 1 pass. The loops still go through the shim and the results are the same as before.

The full test suite has 447 tests and all pass. For the staging replay I used 3,300 events from the last week. All were handled, and the database state matches the v15 run for invoices, payments and refunds. The only difference was in a log line, which now shows the new field name.

I check the refund path again for the retry setting. maxNetworkRetries is still 0 for refunds, as set earlier, and the test for it passes.

I plan to deploy tomorrow morning, so that I can watch the first run of the day for payment errors, rather than at night. The evening run is the larger one, and I would see more there, but a morning deploy gives me a whole day to look at the logs.

summary: Deployed Stripe SDK v16 in the morning and found no errors; then looked at the payment retry schedule and found that failed payments were retried at the wrong hour for customers in other time zones.
body:
The v16 deploy went out at 08:40. The health check was green, and the first payment batch at 09:00 ran with no errors. The Stripe error counter showed one card decline in 40 charges, which is normal. The webhook handler processed 120 events without failures.

While watching the logs, I noticed something not related to the upgrade. The payment retry job schedules the second and third attempts for a failed payment at 'the same time of day' as the first failure. It computes this time in the server's time zone. For customers with a billing time zone, the retry came at an odd hour, such as 3 in the morning local time, where the card issuer's fraud check more often declines.

I looked at the data. 212 customers have a billing time zone that differs from the server's by more than 5 hours. Their retry success rate over the last quarter was 41 percent, against 58 percent for the others. That is not proof of a cause, since other things differ too, but it is a hint.

I changed the schedule so that the retry time is computed in the customer's time zone, targeting 10:00 local time. The change is limited to the function that picks the next attempt, and I added tests with three time zones, including one with a daylight saving shift on the retry day.

The change is not deployed yet. I want Ines to know about it, as the cash flow may shift by a day or so for some customers. I wrote her a short note with the number of customers affected and the way to measure the effect: compare the retry success rate of these 212 customers in a month.

The v16 upgrade has no open points. The dunning emails use the same schedule logic for their wording, and I checked that they read the retry time from the same function, so they stay consistent after the change.

summary: Deployed the local-time retry schedule after Ines agreed, and checked that the first 19 rescheduled retries were set to 10:00 in each customer's time zone.
body:
Ines replied that the shift of a day for some customers is fine, and that a better success rate matters more than the exact day of the money. I deployed the change before the noon batch.

The job rescheduled the open retries of the affected customers at the next planning step. I queried the retry table and found 19 rescheduled retries for customers in other time zones. Each had a next attempt at 10:00 in the customer's own zone, converted into the server's time. I checked five of them by hand, including one in a zone with a half hour offset, and all were right.

The dunning emails for these customers show the new retry date. I rendered three of them in the staging preview and the text was consistent with the schedule.
