One thing I had not considered was customers without a billing time zone set. For them the function falls back to the server zone, so nothing changes. 1,900 customers are in this group, which is most of them.

I set a reminder to measure the retry success rate for the 212 customers in a month, as I told Ines. Until then I will watch the retry table for odd times. For now, no errors, and the payment batch at noon ran with 97 percent success.

summary: Checked the first day of local-time payment retries and found 2 of 19 customers with a missing time zone, which fell back to 10:00 UTC, so a profile check now flags them.
body:
After the retry schedule went out this morning, I went through the retry queue for the full day. Of the 19 rescheduled retries, 17 ran at 10:00 in the customer's own time zone. Two ran at 10:00 UTC because their customer rows had no time zone at all.

Both customers came from the early import in the first version, when the country field was optional. I wrote a small query that lists active customers with a null timezone and found 31 of them. For these, the scheduler now derives a zone from the billing country, and uses UTC only when no country exists either.

I added a unit test for the fallback order: customer zone, then country default, then UTC. The scheduler logs which source it used, so Ines can see it in the retry report. Nothing was retried at night.

I also asked Ines whether she wants the 31 rows fixed by hand. She said the country-based guess is good enough for now, but she will look at the list of customers without a country. The dunning emails use the same send hour, so I checked that they read the same helper. They do, and no change was needed there.

Open: the 6 customers without a country stay on UTC until Ines has their data. The next step is a weekly count in the report so the list does not grow back.

summary: Found why some receipts arrived twice: the job runner retried the email job after a timeout even though the provider had accepted the message, so the job now records the send before it finishes.
body:
Two customers wrote that they got the same receipt twice. I pulled the job history from pg-boss and saw that both emails came from jobs with retry count 1. The first attempt had timed out after 30 seconds on the call to the old email provider, but the provider had in fact accepted the message.

The job marked the receipt as sent only after the call returned. A timeout therefore looked like a failure and the retry sent the mail again. I counted such cases over the last month and found 17 receipts that went out twice, all on slow evenings.

The fix has two parts. First, the job writes a row to receipt_sends with the invoice id before the call, in status pending, and sets it to sent afterwards. Second, a retry that finds a pending row older than two minutes checks the provider's message log by our own message id before sending again. If the log shows the message, it just marks the row as sent.

I wrote tests for three cases: normal send, timeout with accepted message, and timeout with no message. All three pass, and the full suite of 447 tests is still green. The log lookup is slow, about 800 ms, but it only runs on retries.

I deployed it in the evening and watched the next run. 112 receipts went out, none twice, and no retry needed the log. The old provider's slowness is one more reason the planned email move matters, but that is separate work. I will check the duplicate count again in a week.

summary: Answered Mara's question how many invoices a customer can have in a month: normally one, but a plan change in the middle adds a prorated one, and 212 customers had two last month.
body:
Mara asked whether any code assumes one invoice per customer per month. I looked at the invoice job and the report queries to answer.

The invoice job creates one invoice per subscription period. A plan change in the middle of a period closes the old period and creates a prorated invoice, so the customer gets two in that month. Last month 212 customers had two invoices and 9 had three, because they changed plan twice.

The monthly totals report groups by customer and period, so it is correct. The receipt email job reads by invoice id, which is also fine. One place does assume a single invoice: the customer page export joins on customer and month and would show only one row. I found it in export_customer_month.ts and wrote a failing test with two invoices.

I changed the join to include the invoice id and the test passes. I did not touch the invoice numbers, which are unique per invoice anyway. Mara read the change and agreed. The export runs for finance only, and Ines had not noticed the missing rows because the sums were still right through another sheet. I told her about the fix so she knows the old exports lacked the second row.

summary: Added a retry-after check for Stripe 429 responses to the backfill script so it waits as long as Stripe asks instead of hammering the API, which removed the rate limit spikes.
body:
The 429 spike from a few days ago had been traced to the backfill script, but I had only added a lower concurrency then. Today I made the script behave properly when it does get rate limited.

The Stripe error carries a Retry-After header in the raw response. The script ignored it and slept a fixed 200 ms. I changed it to read the header, wait that long plus a small random delay, and then continue with the same customer. The script also stops after 5 waits in a row and exits with a clear message, so nobody leaves it running unnoticed.

I tested it against the Stripe test mode with a loop that sends 150 requests quickly. Before the change it hit 38 rate limit errors. After the change there were 4, each followed by a pause, and the loop finished. The script still uses maxNetworkRetries of 2 because it does not touch refunds.

I ran it on production for the 3,000 customers of the backfill during the afternoon, outside the evening run. It finished in 41 minutes with 6 waits. The retry queue stayed clean, and the error alert did not fire. I added the notes about the header to the script's readme.

summary: Wrote a test suite for VAT reverse charge with 14 cases from real EU invoices after a customer in Ireland was charged VAT although his VAT number was valid.
body:
A customer in Ireland wrote that he was charged 23 percent VAT even though he had given a valid VAT number. I looked at his invoice and found that the number was saved with spaces and a lowercase country prefix, "ie 6388047v". Our validation call to the VAT service normalizes the input, but the reverse charge decision compared the saved string against a pattern that wanted uppercase and no spaces. It failed and treated him as a private person.

I fixed it in two steps. A normalize function now strips spaces and dots and upper-cases the prefix, and it is used both when saving and when deciding. A migration normalizes the 1,140 numbers already in the table. Of those, 23 changed, and 4 of the 23 belonged to customers who had paid VAT they should not have.

Then I wrote the test suite. It has 14 cases: valid and invalid numbers in several formats, Greece using EL instead of GR, Northern Ireland with XI, a customer in the same country as the company (VAT always applies), and a number that the service marks as unknown at that moment. The last case should not remove the reverse charge from an old customer, so it keeps the earlier result for 30 days.

All tests pass. I did not touch the four wrongly charged invoices. That is a decision for Ines, because corrections need credit notes, and I sent her the list with amounts. The sum is 318.40 euros in VAT. She will tell me tomorrow how the accountants want to handle it.

summary: Ines decided that the four wrong VAT invoices get credit notes, and I generated them with a script that dry-runs first and checks the sums against her list.
body:
Ines answered this morning that the accountants want credit notes and new invoices, not edits. I wrote a script for it. It takes the four invoice ids, creates a credit note that mirrors each invoice, and then creates a new invoice with reverse charge and the same lines.

The dry run prints the old total, the new total and the difference per customer. The four differences added up to 318.40 euros, the same as in my list to Ines. She checked the figures against her spreadsheet and they matched, line by line.

I ran it for real after her okay. The script used the normal invoice numbering, so the credit notes and the new invoices got the next numbers in the sequence. No payment was taken again, because the customers had already paid the gross amount. The difference is now a balance on the customer account, which Stripe applies to the next invoice.

I sent the four customers the corrected PDFs with a short text from Ines. The send went through the job queue and all four emails were accepted.

summary: Reviewed how coupon codes interact with proration after a plan change and found that a percent coupon was applied twice on the prorated invoice, which overcharged nobody but made the credit too large.
body:
Ines noticed a customer whose prorated credit after an upgrade looked too high. I traced the invoice lines for this customer, who had a 20 percent coupon.

The proration works in two steps: it credits the unused part of the old plan and charges the remaining part of the new plan. The credit line was calculated from the already discounted price of the old plan. Then the coupon was applied again to the credit line as a whole, so the credit was reduced twice. In this case the credit was 16 euros instead of 20, which means the customer was actually charged too much, not too little. I corrected my first guess after looking at the numbers again.

I checked how many invoices were affected. The query looked for prorated invoices with a coupon where the credit line had a discount line attached. It found 38 invoices over the last four months, with a total overcharge of 211.60 euros, the biggest single one being 14.20.

The fix is in the proration code. The coupon is now applied once, to the sum of the credit and the charge lines. I wrote six tests for percent coupons and fixed amount coupons, for upgrade and downgrade, and for a coupon that has expired between the two dates. One of the old tests had the wrong expected value and agreed with the bug, so I changed it and explained why in the commit message.

I did not deploy the fix yet. The correction of 38 invoices is a finance topic like the VAT one, so I wrote a list for Ines with invoice number, customer, amount and the corrected amount. Deployment waits until she says whether old invoices get credit notes, because the new numbers should not appear on one side only.

Next: the code review by Mara tomorrow, then deployment and the credit note script, which I can reuse from today.

summary: Ines confirmed that the 38 coupon proration invoices get credit notes too, so the fix can be deployed together with the correction run tomorrow morning.
body:
Ines read my list of 38 invoices and checked ten of them by hand. All ten matched. She asked for credit notes in the same way as for the VAT case, and for one email per customer, not one per invoice.

I changed the credit note script to group by customer. A customer with two affected invoices now gets one email with two corrected PDFs. The dry run shows 35 customers and the same total of 211.60 euros.

I also added a stop in the script: if a customer has an open payment retry, it skips that customer and prints the id. Otherwise a correction could meet a retry in the middle and charge the wrong amount. The dry run found 1 such customer, so I will handle that one separately after the retry ends.

Plan for tomorrow: Mara reviews, I deploy the fix in the morning, then run the correction.

summary: Deployed the proration coupon fix and ran the correction for 34 customers; one customer with an open retry waits until the payment settles.
body:
Mara reviewed the coupon change in the evening and asked only for one more test, for a coupon that ends exactly on the day of the plan change. I added it and it passed on the first run.

I deployed the fix and watched the evening invoice run. It created 640 invoices, 22 of them prorated, and 5 of those had coupons. I compared the five by hand with the numbers from a calculator and all matched to the cent.

Then I ran the correction script. The real run handled 34 customers and 37 invoices. For each one it created a credit note, a new invoice and a balance on the account. The sum of the differences was 205.10 euros, which is the total of 211.60 minus the one skipped customer's 6.50.

The skipped customer has a failed payment and the next retry is in two days. After the retry result, I will run the script for this one invoice. I put a note in the journal for that so I do not forget it.

The emails went out through the old provider. Of 34, 33 were accepted at once and one was delayed by 12 minutes, which I saw in the job log but did not need to fix. Finance now has a final sheet. Ines confirmed receipt of the sums and will give them to the accountants at the end of the month.

One thing I learned: the old test with the wrong expected value had been there for months, so tests that copy output from the code are a risk. I will watch for this in the next reviews.

summary: Looked at why the receipt page for customers loads slowly and found it counted all invoice lines of the customer for each page view; a limit and a cached count cut it from 1.8 s to 120 ms.
body:
A customer with a big account complained that the invoice list page took almost two seconds. I ran EXPLAIN on the query. It joined invoices with invoice_lines to compute a line count for each row, which is useless for the list, because the list shows only the totals.

The account in question has 410 invoices and about 31,000 lines. The join scanned all lines every time. I removed the line count from the list query and moved it to the detail page, where one invoice is loaded and the count is trivial.

I also added a limit of 50 rows with a cursor, because the endpoint returned everything before. The front end of nebula already sends a page size, so no change is needed there. A test with 120 invoices checks the cursor handling.

The response time for the big account fell from 1.8 seconds to 120 ms. For a normal account with 12 invoices it went from 90 ms to 25 ms. I deployed it before the evening run.

summary: Replied to a customer who asked why his trial ended one day early: the trial is counted in UTC days, and he started it late in the evening in a time zone ahead of UTC.
body:
A customer from Australia wrote that his 14 day trial ended after 13 days in his view. I checked his subscription. The trial started at 23:10 his local time, which was 13:10 UTC on the same date, and ended at the end of the 14th UTC day.

So the trial lasted 13 days and 11 hours. In the first version, I used a fixed end of day in UTC for simplicity. This was the cause, and it is not a bug in the narrow sense, but it is unfriendly.

I looked at what Stripe does. The trial_end timestamp can be any moment, so we can set it to exactly 14 times 24 hours after the start. The change is small: trial_end = start + 14 days, without rounding to the end of day. I wrote the change and a test with three start times, but did not deploy it yet. Existing trials keep their dates, since changing them would confuse people.

I replied to the customer, gave him one extra day by moving his trial end by hand in Stripe, and told him the rule will change for new trials. Mara agreed with the plan and said that I should mention it in the next release notes.

The trial reminder email says "ends tomorrow" and uses the date, so it must use the exact end time as well. I found that place and added it to the same change.

summary: Prepared Stripe webhook handling for slow database moments by making the handler acknowledge the event first and process it from a queue, after seeing two timeouts that made Stripe resend events.
body:
During the evening run, the webhook endpoint timed out twice. Stripe waits only a short time for an answer, and when the database was busy the handler needed more than that. Stripe then resent the events, which is expected, but it creates noise and double work.

The current handler does everything in the request: it checks the signature, loads the invoice, updates the status, and sends the receipt job. I changed it so that the request only checks the signature, writes the raw event into a table webhook_events with the Stripe event id as a unique key, and answers 200. A pg-boss job then processes the stored event.

The unique key also handles repeated deliveries cleanly: a second insert of the same event id does nothing, and the answer is still 200. Before, we relied on checks in the processing code, which worked but ran after the heavy part.

The processing job marks the row as done, or stores the error text and retries with a delay of one minute, up to 8 times. After that, the row stays in a failed state, and an alert fires. I wrote an admin query to list failed events, which Ines can also read.

Tests: I replayed the recorded events from the v15 check against the new flow on staging. All 214 events led to the same database state as before. I added tests for a duplicate event, an event for an unknown invoice, and a handler error followed by a successful retry.

Order is one risk. Events can arrive out of order, for example payment_intent.succeeded before invoice.finalized. The old code had the same problem and solved it with checks on the status. I kept these checks and added one more test where the order is reversed.

I deployed it after the evening run to avoid mixing the change with the load. The first events came in a few minutes later, and the median answer time of the endpoint fell from 340 ms to 35 ms. I will watch the queue depth tomorrow.

summary: Checked the webhook queue after the first hours: depth stayed under 5, median processing time was 210 ms, and no event failed.
body:
I looked at the new webhook flow late in the evening. Over the first hours it stored 188 events. The queue depth never went over 5, and the median time from storage to done was 210 ms. The slowest event took 3.1 seconds, a charge with many invoice lines.

No event ended in the failed state, and there were no resend warnings from Stripe in the dashboard. The answer time of the endpoint stayed around 35 ms.

One small thing: the raw event table will grow. Each event is about 4 KB, so with 6,000 events per day it is 24 MB per day. I will add a cleanup job that deletes done events after 30 days, but not today.

summary: Added the cleanup job for stored webhook events, which deletes processed rows after 30 days in batches, and kept failed ones for manual review.
body:
The webhook events table is now a regular part of the system, so it needs a retention rule. I wrote a pg-boss job that runs at night and deletes rows in state done that are older than 30 days.

The delete works in batches of 2,000 rows with a short pause in between, so it does not block the evening queries or fill the write-ahead log. On staging, with 400,000 generated rows, it removed all old rows in 90 seconds and the table size stayed flat afterwards.

Failed rows are never deleted by the job. They stay until someone looks at them and sets them to resolved by hand. A resolved row follows the same 30 day rule from the time of resolution. I added an index on state and received_at, which the cleanup query uses. Without it, the plan was a full scan.

I wrote tests for the three states and for the batch loop with a small batch size of 3. Mara asked if the job could delete a row that is still being processed. It cannot, because only the state done is selected and the processing job sets that as its last step. I added a comment explaining this.

The job is deployed and scheduled for three at night.

summary: Reviewed the webhook queue after a month of running: depth stayed low, one stuck event type was found and fixed, and the failed-event review list is now down to 3 rows.
body:
Mara asked whether the acknowledge-first webhook handling had held up since it went in, so I went through the queue numbers for the whole period instead of a single day. The depth stayed under 5 for almost all hours, with a peak of 31 during the evening invoice run on the busiest day. The median processing time was 190 ms and the 99th percentile was 1.4 seconds.

Over the period 412,000 events came through. 17 of them ended in the failed state, which is what I wanted to understand. Fourteen were the same case: invoice.finalized events for invoices that were deleted in the admin script before the event was processed, so the handler could not find the row and gave up after five attempts.

The handler now treats a missing invoice for that event type as already handled and logs it at info level. I replayed the 14 stored events on staging and all of them were marked processed without touching any invoice data. The other three failed rows are real problems and stay for manual review. Two are charge.dispute events for a customer whose Stripe account was merged, and one is a payout event with a shape the handler does not know.

I also checked the cleanup job from a few weeks ago. It deleted about 190,000 processed rows in batches of 2,000, the table is 60 percent smaller, and the batches did not block the evening run. No duplicate processing was seen: the unique constraint on the Stripe event id rejected 23 resent events, as intended.

Next I will write a short note in the runbook on how to read the failed list, and ask Mara whether the dispute events deserve their own handler. For now they only get logged.

summary: Mara asked whether the dunning emails can be sent in the customer's language, and I found that the templates exist in three languages but the choice always falls back to English.
body:
Mara forwarded a customer complaint about a German dunning mail in English. I checked the template code. There are templates for English, German and French, and the function that picks one reads customer.locale.

The locale is filled only for customers who set a language in the nebula profile. For all others it is null, and the function falls back to English. Of 2,300 active customers, 1,050 have no locale.

I suggested using the billing country as a second source: DE, AT and CH to German, FR and BE to French, everything else English. Mara agreed, with the point that a customer's own choice always wins. I will build it next.

summary: Built the locale fallback for dunning and receipt emails from the billing country, with the customer's own setting first, and tested it with 12 country cases.
body:
I wrote a small function pickLocale(customer) with the order: profile locale, then country mapping, then English. The mapping is a plain table in a file, so adding Spanish later means one line plus a template.

Switzerland was the only unclear country, because it has several languages. I mapped it to German, since most of our Swiss customers use it, and a profile setting overrides it anyway. Belgium goes to French for the same reason.

The tests cover 12 cases, including a null country, a lowercase country code and an unknown locale string like "de-AT", which should reduce to "de". The last case failed at first because the code compared the whole string. I fixed it by taking the part before the dash.

The receipt emails use the same function now. I rendered the dunning and receipt templates for each language into files and read them once to catch broken placeholders. The French receipt lacked the word for "tax" in one line, which showed the English word. I corrected it.

I deployed it before the evening run. Of the 31 dunning emails of the evening, 9 went out in German and 2 in French, which matches what I expected from the country counts.

summary: Checked the language fallback after a day of emails: 74 dunning and receipt mails went out in German or French, and no customer with a profile language got a different one.
body:
I compared the language of all emails of the day with the customers' settings. Of 622 emails, 74 were not in English. 41 of those came from the profile setting and 33 from the country mapping.

I looked for conflicts, meaning a customer with a profile locale who received another language. There were none. I also read five of the French and German mails for broken text, and they were fine.

One customer in Switzerland answered a mail to say he prefers English. I told him he can set it in his nebula profile, and that this will win over the country.

summary: Ines asked for a list of customers whose card expires within 30 days, and I wrote a query and a CSV export that she can run herself from the admin script.
body:
Ines wants to warn customers before their card expires, to cut down failed payments. I looked at what Stripe gives us. The payment method object has exp_month and exp_year, and we store a copy in payment_methods when a customer adds a card.

The query finds the default payment method of each active subscription and selects those that expire within 30 days. It found 87 customers today. Stripe updates the card details itself in some cases, for example when the bank issues a new card with the same number, so I also checked a sample of 10 against the live Stripe objects. Two had newer dates in Stripe than in our table, which means our copy lags.

I added a refresh of the copy when the webhook payment_method.automatically_updated arrives. That event was not handled before. The export now prints the customer, the email, the expiry and the plan, and writes a CSV. A reminder email is a possible next step, but Ines wants to see the list first.

summary: Wrote the card expiry reminder email with a 30 and a 7 day step and a guard so that customers who already updated their card, or pay by transfer, get nothing.
body:
After Ines saw the list she asked for an automatic reminder. I built it as a nightly pg-boss job that selects expiring default cards and sends one of two emails: one at 30 days before expiry and one at 7 days.

A table card_reminders stores the payment method id and the step, with a unique key on both. This prevents sending the same step twice, even if the job runs twice. It also survives a customer who changes the card and then the new one expires later, since the key uses the payment method id.

The guards are the main point. Customers whose subscription is cancelled get nothing. Customers whose default method is not a card get nothing. Customers with an open invoice in dunning already get dunning mails, so they are skipped too, to avoid two mails about the same problem. A customer whose card was refreshed by the new webhook handler is checked against the updated dates, so there is no mail for a card that already has a later expiry.

The email text is in English, German and French and uses the locale function from last week. It includes a link to the billing page of the nebula account where the card can be changed. Mara read the English text and asked to remove the sentence about service being stopped, because it sounds like a threat and is not exactly true, since we retry first. I removed it.

Tests cover the steps, the unique key, the four guards and a card that expires this month at the end of the day. I used a fake clock to avoid the kind of flaky test we had in the dunning suite.

I ran the job in dry mode on production data. It would send 87 mails for the 30 day step and 19 for the 7 day step. Ines looked at the dry output and wanted to start slowly, so the job has a daily limit of 40 mails for the first week.

Deployment is planned for the evening.

summary: Deployed the card expiry reminders and found the 7 day step would have mailed 6 customers whose card had been replaced, because the check read an old row; fixed before the first send.
body:
I deployed the reminder job in the evening with the sending switched off, meaning it only wrote what it would send. This was a good choice. The 7 day list contained 6 customers who, according to Stripe, already had a new default card.

The cause was that the job read the default payment method from our payment_methods table, where the is_default flag is updated only on a certain webhook, customer.updated. When a customer changed the default through the billing page, the flag was updated, but when it changed through a support action in the Stripe dashboard, it was not, because we did not look at that event type properly.

I looked at the handler. It processed customer.updated only when invoice_settings was in the previous attributes, and the dashboard action produced a different shape. I changed the handler to compare the default payment method of the object itself with our row, which is independent of the event details.

Then I wrote a repair script that compares our default flags with Stripe for all active customers. It checked 2,310 customers and found 11 with a wrong flag, 6 of them from the reminder list and 5 others. I corrected all 11.

After the repair, the dry run listed 81 customers for the 30 day step and 13 for the 7 day step. I checked ten at random against Stripe and all were correct.

A second small thing came from the dry run. One customer appeared in both steps at once, because the card expires in 7 days and the 30 day mail had never been sent to him, since he joined 12 days ago. I changed the rule so that a customer in the 7 day window who never got the first step receives only the 7 day mail.

Tests were added for both fixes. I switched on sending with the limit of 40 per day. The first batch went out with 40 mails, all accepted by the provider. I will check bounce counts and the number of cards updated after the reminders over the next days.

summary: Measured the first reminder day: 40 mails sent, 6 customers updated their card within hours, and the bounce rate was 5 percent, mostly addresses that were already known bad.
body:
I looked at the results of the first sending day. 40 mails left, and the provider accepted all of them. Two bounced at once, which makes 5 percent, a bit above our normal level of about 3 percent.

Both bounced addresses were already on the list of known bad contacts from the plus sign problem of last week, so they are not new. The receipt fallback to the owner address does not apply to these reminders, since the mail is about the card of that very person. I flagged the two accounts for Ines, so she can ask for a different contact.

Six customers had replaced their card by the evening. Since the mails went out around noon, that is a response rate of 15 percent in a few hours, which Ines considers very good. I checked that for these six, the new card was saved as default and that the next invoice will use it. The refreshed flags were right in all six cases.

I also checked that the dunning job did not send anything extra to the same customers. It did not. The guard against open dunning worked for 3 customers who would otherwise have gotten both mails.

One issue turned up: the mail contains the last four digits and the expiry date. For a customer with two cards, the text did not say which card was meant, since it used the default card but the customer's old second card has the same last four digits. This is rare, but the confusion is possible. I added the card brand to the text, for example "Visa ending 4242".

The daily limit stays at 40 for the week, then I raise it to 100. At the current numbers the 81 customers of the first step need three days. The remaining step is to include the reminder counts in the weekly finance report, which I will do next.

summary: Followed up the card expiry reminders by checking the 6 customers who updated their card, and found 2 whose new card was declined at the next charge, so a retry now waits for it.
body:
After the first reminder day I went through the 6 customers who updated their card within hours. For 4 of them the next charge went through on the new card without trouble. Two had a new card that Stripe declined with a generic decline code.

Both cases showed the same pattern. The customer had added the card in the portal, but the subscription still pointed at the old payment method. The default payment method on the Stripe customer was updated, but the subscription had its own default set, which wins over the customer one.

I looked at the code that handles the payment method update webhook. It only changed the customer default and never touched the subscription. I wrote a small change that clears the subscription default when it equals the old card, so the customer default is used again.

I added a test with a fixture for a subscription that has its own default and one that does not. Both pass, and the full suite of 447 tests still passes. I did not deploy yet because I want Ines to see the two customers first.

I also wrote down the two customer ids and the dates of their failed charges in a note for her. She can decide whether the dunning email that went out to them should be followed by a short apology. The dunning schedule itself is unchanged.

One open question is how many older customers have the same split default. I wrote a read-only query that lists subscriptions whose default differs from the customer default. It returned 17 rows, which I will check next before deciding on a correction run.

Next step is to deploy the webhook change tomorrow morning together with the list for Ines.

summary: Checked the 17 subscriptions with a split default payment method and found 11 were intended, such as company cards, so only 6 need the fix.
body:
The query from this afternoon listed 17 subscriptions whose own default payment method differs from the customer default. I went through them one by one in the Stripe dashboard and our own tables.

Eleven of them were deliberate. These are customers with a company card on the subscription and a personal card on the customer, set up by our support at the customer's request. Changing them would have moved their charges to the wrong card, so they stay as they are.

Six were the same case as the two declined customers. The customer had updated the card in the portal after the old one expired, and the subscription still pointed at the expired card. For those six the next charge would have failed.

I extended the query with a condition on the expiry of the subscription card, so that only subscriptions with an expired or soon expiring own default are returned. It now returns exactly those 6 rows.

I wrote a correction script with a dry run that prints what it will change and the next invoice date for each. The real run asks for a confirmation and logs each change. Ines read the dry run output and agreed that the 6 can be corrected.

I ran the script and all 6 subscriptions now use the customer default. A manual retry of the two earlier declined invoices went through, so both customers are paid.

The webhook change is deployed too, and the first payment method update after the deploy was handled correctly. I will look at the next reminder day to see whether any new split appears.

summary: Planned the move from one flat table of dunning attempts to a per-invoice attempt log, after Ines asked why she cannot see which email went with which retry.
body:
Ines asked a simple question during her monthly check: for a failed invoice, which dunning email went out after which payment retry? Today the answer needs three tables. The retries are in the payment attempts table, the emails are in the job runner history, and the link is only the customer id and a rough time.

I looked at how the dunning job is built. It schedules an email job and a retry job separately, each with its own delay. There is no shared id between them, so nothing stores the pairing.

I wrote down a plan for a dunning step table. Each row would have the invoice id, the step number, the retry id, the email job id, the template name, the language and the result of each. The rows are written when the step is planned and updated when the retry and the email finish.

The plan has three parts. First, add the table and write to it from the dunning planner, without reading from it. Second, backfill the last 90 days from the existing tables, using a time window to match emails to retries. Third, give Ines an export that reads from it.

The backfill is the weak point. The time window match is a guess, and for invoices with several retries on the same day it may pair wrongly. I decided to mark backfilled rows with a flag so they can be told apart from exact ones.

I checked the size. Last month had about 1,900 failed invoices with an average of 2.6 steps, so roughly 5,000 rows a month. That is small and needs no special index beyond the invoice id.

I also thought about the SEPA debits, which will fail with other reason codes and later timing than cards. The table has a free text reason column and a code column so that those can be added without a change.

Mara read the plan and asked that the step number be fixed in the template names, so that a template rename does not break old rows. I added the template key as a stable string next to the display name.

Nothing is built yet. The migration is the next piece, and I will start with it tomorrow.

summary: Created the dunning step table and wrote to it from the planner, with no reads yet, and the first 31 failed invoices produced 31 rows.
body:
I added the migration for the dunning step table with the columns from the plan: invoice id, step number, retry id, email job id, template key, language, and the two results. There is a unique index on invoice id and step number.

The dunning planner now inserts a row when it plans a step. The retry job and the email job update their own part of the row when they finish. Both updates are written so that they only touch their columns.

I ran the planner against staging with 31 failed invoices from a copy of last week. It produced 31 rows with step 1, and the email and retry results filled in after the jobs ran. One row had a failed email result, which matched a known bad address.

The tests for the planner grew by 6 cases, and all 453 pass. The backfill and the export come after this has run in production for a few days.

summary: Answered Mara's question about why the usage meter shows a lower count than nebula for one customer: the meter reads closed hours and the customer had a spike in the current one.
body:
Mara noticed that a customer's event count in the billing usage meter was about 4,000 lower than the number in the nebula dashboard, and asked whether we were losing usage.

I compared the two for the same customer and period. The difference was exactly the events of the last open hour. The meter reads counts from nebula in closed hourly buckets, and the dashboard also shows the hour that is still running.

The customer had a burst of ingestion in the last hour, which made the gap look large. For earlier hours the two numbers matched to the event.

I checked a second customer with a steady load, and the gap was 130 events, again the open hour. So nothing is lost, and the meter will catch up at the next run.

I also looked at the end of the billing period. The invoice run happens after the last bucket is closed, with a margin of 20 minutes, so the final hour is included in the invoice. I confirmed this with the last month's invoices for five customers and found no missing hours.

I added a line to the admin usage page that says the current hour is not included. Mara agreed that this is enough for now and no code change in the meter is needed.

summary: Wrote the backfill for dunning steps from the last 90 days and marked 412 of the 3,870 rows as guessed, because several retries fell on one day.
body:
The dunning step table has been filled by the planner for a few days, so I wrote the backfill for the older history. It reads the payment attempts and the email job history of the last 90 days and pairs them by invoice and time.

The matching takes each retry and looks for an email job for the same customer in the window of 2 hours before to 6 hours after the retry. If exactly one email matches, the pair is exact. If none or more than one matches, the row is marked as guessed.

The result was 3,870 rows. Of these, 412 were marked as guessed, mostly invoices with two retries on the same day after a manual retry by support. I kept those, because a row with a flag is more useful to Ines than a gap.

I ran it first on staging and compared 25 random rows by hand against the job history. All 25 were right, including 3 of the guessed ones.

The real run took 40 seconds and wrote the rows in batches of 500 without locking the live table for long. It is safe to run twice, because of the unique index and an insert that skips existing rows.

Next is the export for Ines, with the guessed flag as a visible column.

summary: Built the dunning export for Ines with one row per step, showing the email, the retry result and a guessed flag, and she found one wrong template name on the first look.
body:
I wrote the export that reads the dunning step table and joins the invoice and customer. It gives one row per step with invoice number, customer, step, template key, language, email result, retry result and the guessed flag.

It runs from the admin script, like the card expiry list, so Ines can start it herself. It takes a period and writes a CSV. For the last 30 days it returned 1,160 rows and took 2 seconds.

Ins looked at the file and noticed that for some French customers the template name showed the German version. I checked and found that the planner stored the template key before the locale fallback was applied, so the stored key was the default one.

The emails themselves were sent in the right language, because the sender applies the fallback again. Only the stored key was wrong, in 63 rows.

I fixed the planner to store the key after the fallback and corrected the 63 rows from the language column. The unit test now checks that the stored key and the sent template agree.

Ines will use the export for the month check next week. If she finds more mismatches, the first thing to compare is the language column.

summary: Investigated why the invoice PDF for a customer with 1,400 lines took 38 seconds to render and found the headless browser waits for fonts and images for every page.
body:
A customer with a large plan of many small items had an invoice with 1,400 lines, and the PDF took 38 seconds. The job runner has a 30 second timeout for it, so it failed and was retried twice.

I started by timing the steps. Building the data took 0.4 seconds. The HTML template took 0.6 seconds. The rest, about 37 seconds, was inside the headless browser, between loading the page and the print call.

I compared invoices of different sizes. 50 lines took 2.1 seconds, 400 lines took 9 seconds, and 1,400 lines took 38 seconds. That is more than linear, so something grows with the number of lines per page.

The template repeats the table header on every page, and each row has a small icon image loaded from our own static server. The browser requests the icon for each row, even if the URL is the same, because the cache header is missing. I saw 1,400 requests in the log.

I tried the same invoice with the icon inlined as a data URI in the CSS, which removed the requests. The time fell to 21 seconds. That helped, but is still slow.

Then I looked at the layout. The table has rows with a fixed height but the CSS uses a page break rule that makes the browser recompute the layout of the entire table for every page break. Changing the rule for rows to avoid breaks inside rows only, instead of avoiding breaks after every row, brought it to 12 seconds.

The remaining time seems to be the browser itself with the long table. I did not find a big gain in more tuning.

I shipped the icon and the CSS change. The customer's invoice now renders in 12 seconds, and the job succeeds on the first try. The test render of 10 typical invoices produced the same output as before, which I checked by comparing page counts and the total line.

This suggests the old renderer has a limit. If invoices keep growing, a different approach to the PDF may be needed, and I wrote that as an idea for later.

summary: Looked at the Stripe SDK pagination use in the backfill and invoice sync and listed the three places that use a hand-written pagination shim instead of auto-pagination.
body:
Before the next SDK upgrade I wanted to know how much of our code depends on the pagination shims. I searched for the helper that loops over starting_after and has_more.

It is used in three places. The backfill script uses it to list charges. The invoice sync uses it for listing subscriptions per customer. The reconciliation job uses it for balance transactions.

The newer SDK versions have auto-pagination on list calls, so the helper would not be needed. But our helper also does something else: it catches the rate limit error and waits, which came in with the retry-after check from a while ago.

So replacing it with the SDK method means we have to keep the wait on rate limits in some other way. The SDK has its own retry count for network errors, but that does not respect the retry-after header for our case.

I wrote a table in the notes with each use, the page size, the typical number of items and whether the rate limit matters. For the backfill it matters a lot, because it runs for a long time. For the sync it hardly does.

I did not change code today. The upgrade to the next major version is not yet planned, and I only wanted a clear list. I will come back to it when the changelog is read.

summary: Wrote a test for the dunning step table that makes sure a step is never planned twice for the same invoice, after seeing one duplicate in staging.
body:
While running the planner on staging, I saw one invoice with a step 2 planned twice, which failed on the unique index and logged an error. In production the same would have caused the job to retry.

I looked at the cause. The planner runs every 15 minutes, and a slow run overlapped with the next one for a short time. Both read the invoice as due for step 2 before either had written the row.

The unique index protected the data, but the error was noisy and made the job fail. I changed the insert to skip on conflict and to continue to the next invoice, with a debug log line.

I also added an advisory lock around the planner run, so that two planner runs cannot overlap at all. If the lock is taken, the run exits at once.

The new test starts two planner runs at the same time on a set of 20 invoices and checks that there are exactly 20 rows with step 2 and no error. It passed 10 times in a row.

All 454 tests pass with it. I will deploy the planner change with the next release.

summary: Deployed the dunning planner lock and watched the first hour: no overlapping runs, no conflict errors, and 9 steps planned.
body:
I deployed the planner with the advisory lock together with the skip on conflict. The release went out without any change in the other jobs.

I watched the job runner for the first hour. The planner ran four times, and each run took less than 3 seconds. Nothing was skipped because of the lock, so there was no overlap in this period.

It planned 9 dunning steps in total, and all 9 rows are in the step table with the right template key and language. The retries and emails for those ran at the expected times.

The error log has no unique index errors. In the earlier days, I saw one or two per day.

I also checked the lock itself in Postgres. It is released when the run ends, and I saw no lock remain after a run that was stopped on purpose in staging.

I consider this finished. The next look will be with the export of Ines at the end of the month, where any wrong pairs would show.

summary: Switched the dunning reads to the new per-invoice step table behind a flag and found that the old flat table and the new rows disagree for 14 invoices, all from the guessed backfill.
body:
After the planner lock and the backfill, I added a read path that builds the dunning view from the step table. It sits behind the flag dunning_steps_read, off by default. I ran both paths side by side over the last 90 days and compared the number of attempts per invoice.

The two paths agreed for 3,856 of 3,870 rows. The 14 differences were all invoices where several retries fell on one day, so the backfill had to guess the order of the emails. In 11 cases the guessed order is plausible, and in 3 cases the retry result was attached to the wrong email.

I did not fix these by hand. The guessed flag already marks them, and Ines said the export shows that flag. The comparison script is in scripts/compare-dunning.ts and prints the invoice ids that differ. Next I will turn the flag on for the admin view only and ask Ines to look at ten invoices before the customer-facing pages read from the new table.

summary: Made the bank transfer matching run twice a day and added a check before each dunning email that skips invoices paid in the last hour, which removed the late reminder case.
body:
Following Ines's question, I looked at the transfer matching job. It reads the bank statement file that finance drops into a shared bucket, matches the reference to invoice numbers and marks invoices paid. It runs once a day at 06:00.

The bank provides the file twice a day, in the morning and around 14:00. The job just never read the second one. I changed the schedule so that it runs at 06:00 and 14:30, and made the job remember which file it has already processed, by name and checksum.

That helps for transfers that arrive in the afternoon, but a window remains. A reminder can still be sent between the arrival of the money and the next match. To close this, I added a guard before each dunning email.

The guard checks the invoice status again at send time, not at planning time. If the invoice is paid, the email is skipped and the step is marked skipped in the step table. This was easy now that the table exists.

I also thought about transfers that are in the bank file but have no matching reference, which happens when customers type the number wrong. Those are not marked paid, so the guard does not help them. There were 14 such rows last month, and Ines handles them by hand.

I wrote tests for the guard with three cases: invoice open, invoice paid before sending, and invoice paid but then refunded. In the third case the email should be sent again if the invoice is open, and the test checks that.

I replayed the last two weeks of dunning on staging with the new guard. Out of 640 steps planned, 11 would have been skipped because the invoice was already paid at send time. Of those, 4 were transfers that arrived in the afternoon.

The second file job ran today for the first time at 14:30 in production. It found 23 new payments and marked them paid, and nothing was processed twice, which I checked by running it a second time and seeing zero.

The skipped steps now show in the export for Ines, in the retry result column as skipped. I told her about the new value.

The annual customer who complained got an apology from support, and I added a link to this change in the ticket.

summary: Read the plan for a new invoice PDF renderer and listed what must be compared against the old one: page breaks, totals position, fonts, and the credit note layout.
body:
The slow rendering for large invoices keeps coming back, so I started to look at what a new renderer would need. This is only a list for now, with no code.

The old renderer builds HTML and prints it with the headless browser. The new one would build the PDF directly from the data, without a browser, which should be much faster for long tables. I looked at two libraries and wrote down what each can do with tables that span pages.

The comparison list has four items. First, page breaks: the old layout repeats the table header and avoids a break inside a line. Second, the totals block, which must stay together on the last page with the VAT lines. Third, the fonts, because the accountants have a corporate font with its license. Fourth, the credit note layout, which shares most of the template but has other wording and a minus sign on every amount.

I also looked at how many different layouts exist. There are the invoice, the credit note, the prorated invoice, and a version with the reverse charge note. That makes four, and each needs a sample.

I picked 20 real invoices of different sizes as a test set, from 1 line up to the 1,400 line one. I removed the customer names and kept the numbers, so that the set can be stored in the repo.

The next step is a small prototype for the largest invoice, to see the time. I will not decide anything before I have that number.

summary: Built a prototype of the PDF renderer without a browser and rendered the 1,400 line invoice in 1.6 seconds, but the totals block broke across pages in two of the 20 samples.
body:
I built the prototype with the library that draws tables directly into a PDF. It takes the same invoice data object as the old renderer, so I did not have to touch the data layer.

The largest invoice with 1,400 lines rendered in 1.6 seconds, compared with 12 seconds in the old renderer after the CSS fix. A typical invoice of 30 lines took 60 ms, against 1.9 seconds.

I rendered all 20 samples and compared them with the old output. For comparison I converted both PDFs to images and looked at them side by side, since a pixel diff would be useless with different engines.

Most samples looked right. The header repeats on every page, and the amounts are right-aligned. The fonts need a registration step, and I used a free font as a stand-in because I do not have the corporate one in the repo.

Two samples had a problem. The totals block, with the net amount, the VAT lines and the total, was split between two pages, with the total alone on the last page. The old renderer keeps this block together.

The library has no keep-together option for a block. I measured the height of the block before drawing it, and if it does not fit on the remaining page, I start a new page. This solved both samples.

I then compared the totals as numbers. I extracted the text of each PDF and compared the total line of the new one with the old one for all 20, and all 20 matched. This matters given the rounding work that was done before.

The credit note layout is not done. I did the invoice and the prorated version only, and the reverse charge note is still missing.

One more issue is text extraction. Some customers feed our PDFs into their accounting tools, and the new one writes the numbers with spaces between the characters in some cases. I need to check whether this is the library or my font setup.

I wrote down the open points in the notes: credit note layout, reverse charge note, corporate font, text extraction. The prototype is promising on speed, but it is not close to replacing the old one.

summary: Found that the odd spacing in the extracted PDF text came from a missing font mapping, and fixed it by embedding the font with a proper character map.
body:
The numbers in the prototype PDF had spaces between the characters when I copied the text out. I checked with two tools for text extraction, and both showed the issue.

The cause was the font. I had registered the stand-in font as a simple subset without the mapping of glyphs to characters, so the viewers had to guess the text. They got it wrong for digits with a narrow width.

I changed the registration to embed the full font with its character map. The file size per invoice grew from 18 KB to 61 KB, which is fine for email attachments.

After the change, the extracted text of the total line was right in both tools. I ran the check over all 20 samples and compared each extracted number with the data. All amounts matched.

The corporate font will need the same registration, and I wrote it into the notes.

summary: Added the reverse charge note and the credit note layout to the prototype renderer, and 19 of the 20 samples now match the old output in the total and the page count.
body:
I continued with the missing layouts in the prototype. The reverse charge note is a short text block under the totals, with the VAT number of the customer and the legal sentence. The text is in the template data, so I used the same source.

For the credit note, the title and the wording change, and every amount gets a minus sign. I handled this by passing a flag in the render options and formatting the amounts through the same helper as before, so that the sign and the rounding come from one place.

I then rendered all 20 samples again and compared the total line and the page count with the old renderer. 19 matched in both.

One sample, an invoice with a very long customer address of seven lines, took one page more than the old one. The old template shrinks the address font when it is long, and mine did not. I added the same rule, and then the page count matched too, so all 20 agree.

I also tried the invoice in German and French. The labels come from the same translation files as the emails. The long French words for the VAT lines fit in the column, but only just, so I widened the column by a few points.

I checked the rounding path with a handful of invoices with odd amounts. Because the lines already come rounded from the data layer, the renderer does no rounding itself, and the totals on the PDF equal the totals in the database in all cases I tried.

What is not done: the corporate font, a test with a real printer-like viewer, and any plan for how to roll it out. For the last point, I expect a flag, so both renderers can run side by side. I will write that down in a separate note when the font question is answered.

I asked Ines if she can get the corporate font license file for use in the service. She said she would ask the accountants and the brand people.

summary: Wrote a comparison script that renders any invoice with both renderers and reports differences in total, page count and render time, and ran it over 300 real invoices.
body:
To trust the new renderer I needed more than 20 samples, so I wrote a script that takes a list of invoice ids and renders each with both renderers. It extracts the text and compares the invoice number, the net, the VAT lines and the total. It also records the page count and the time.

I ran it over 300 invoices from last quarter, chosen at random but with all four layouts included. It took about 12 minutes, mostly because of the old renderer.

In 294 cases, the numbers and the page count were identical. In 6 cases something differed. Four were page count differences by one page, caused by the address rule on very long company names, which wrap at a different place.

Two were real differences in text. In both, the customer name contained an ampersand, and the new renderer wrote it as the escaped entity from our HTML-safe string. The old browser rendered the entity correctly, but my renderer took the string as it was. I used the raw name for the new one, and both cases now match.

The time comparison is clear. The median for the old renderer was 1.8 seconds and for the new one 70 ms. The slowest old invoice was 13 seconds, the slowest new one 1.7 seconds.

I also looked at the file sizes. The new files are on average three times larger, because of the embedded font, with a median of 58 KB. That is acceptable, but the email provider has a limit for attachments, and we are far from it.

For the four page count cases, I looked at the output by eye. The new layouts look fine, and the difference is a wrapped line. I would accept this, but it is a change that customers may notice, and I will tell Ines.

The script will be reused later when the corporate font is in. It prints a table, and exits with a failure code if any total differs, so it can run in the test pipeline for a small set.

summary: Got the answer on the corporate font license and found it allows embedding in PDFs but not in a server-side bundle, so the font file will be loaded from a private bucket.
body:
Ines came back from the accountants with the license text for the corporate font. I read it with her. It allows embedding in documents sent to customers, which is what we need.

It does not allow redistributing the font file in a software package. That means we cannot commit the file to the repo or bake it into the image, since the image can be pulled by others in the company.

We decided to keep the file in a private bucket and load it at start-up. The service already reads other secrets and files from there, so there is a known access path. If the font is missing, the renderer falls back to the free font and logs a warning, so that a missing file does not stop invoices.

I wrote the loader with a cache in memory, so the file is read once per process. The test environment uses the free font through the same fallback, which keeps the tests independent of the license.

I then rendered the 20 samples with the corporate font on my machine, using a local copy. The widths differ from the free font. Three samples changed their page count by one page, since the corporate font is a bit wider.

I adjusted the column widths of the table to the new font, and the three samples are back to the old page count. The total and the VAT lines are right-aligned as before.

The text extraction works with the corporate font too, which I checked on the totals of all samples.

The open points are now small. What remains is the rollout, and I will think about it next, with the flag and the comparison script as the base.

summary: Checked how the credit note copies its VAT rate and found the invoice line stores no rate of its own, so the original rate has to be rebuilt from the tax rules table by invoice date.
body:
Following the finding that credit notes use the VAT rate of today, I looked at where the original rate could come from. The invoice lines store the net amount and the tax amount, but no rate column. The rate was only ever read from the tax rules table at render time.

I first tried to divide tax by net per line. That gives the right rate for most lines, but rounding on small lines gave results such as 18.9 percent instead of 19, so it cannot be trusted.

The second option was to look up the rule that was valid on the invoice date. The tax rules table keeps valid-from and valid-to columns, so this works for all the EU countries. I wrote the lookup as a function and ran it over 2,300 credit notes from the last year. In 2,291 cases it returned the same rate as the stored tax amount implies.

The 9 other credit notes are the ones with VAT differences that Ines is already tracking. This confirms that they are the only affected ones. The next step is to change the credit note builder to use this lookup and to add a rate column to new invoice lines, so the lookup is not needed in future.

summary: Changed the credit note builder to use the VAT rate of the original invoice and added a stored rate column to invoice lines, so refunds after a rate change keep the original tax.
body:
I changed the credit note builder so that it no longer reads the current tax rule. It now takes the rate from the original invoice line. For older lines without a rate it uses the date lookup that I tested yesterday.

A migration adds a nullable tax_rate column to the invoice lines. New invoices write it when the lines are created, and a small backfill job fills it for older lines in batches of 500, using the same lookup. The backfill ran on staging over all lines and wrote 118,000 rows in a few minutes. I did not touch the invoices table partitions, so the migration only added the column.

I added tests for four cases: a rate change between invoice and credit note, a partial credit note, a reverse charge invoice with zero VAT, and a line with no stored rate. The existing 460 tests still pass, and the new ones pass too.

One case surprised me. A credit note for an invoice from a country that changed its rate in the same month used the new rate in the old code for the whole note. The new code keeps the rate per line, so this is correct now.

I checked the totals of 50 recent credit notes with the old and new builder, and they are the same, because no rate changed in that period. Ines will see differences only in the nine notes she already corrected. I will deploy the code first and the backfill after it, and then check the first credit notes created.

summary: Checked all five places that render invoice PDFs and found that two ignored the stored renderer version, the receipt email and the admin download; both are fixed.
body:
I went through the five call sites that render an invoice PDF. They are the invoice email, the receipt email, the customer portal download, the admin download and the nightly archive for the accountants.

The invoice email and the portal download already passed the invoice object to the render function, so they picked up the stored version without change. The nightly archive does the same.

The receipt email and the admin download had their own small wrapper that called the render function with fixed options. They did not pass the version, so they would have used the default.

The default is v1 today, so nothing was wrong yet. But when v2 comes, those two would have produced the wrong layout for some invoices. I changed both to pass the version from the invoice.

I wrote a test that goes through all five call sites with a fake renderer that records the version it gets. It uses an invoice with a version v1 and checks all five calls. Then I made the default parameter required, so that the compiler complains if someone forgets it in the future.

The TypeScript build found one more call in a script for support, which I had not found by search. It rendered a sample invoice for a template check. I gave it the version v1 explicitly.

All 457 tests pass. The change is deployed, and I looked at the rendered receipts of the afternoon, which came out as before.

I will now go back to the rollout note and add the stored version as a rule that the flag does not override: the flag only decides about new invoices.

summary: Looked into a customer whose SEPA-like transfer refund came back as a credit note with the wrong VAT, and found the credit note copies the VAT rate of today instead of the original invoice.
body:
Ines forwarded a case. A customer in Austria got a credit note for an invoice from four months ago, and the VAT on the credit note was different from the VAT on the invoice. She asked how this can happen.

I opened both documents. The invoice had 20 percent, which was the rate at that time. The credit note had 19 percent, which is the rate of the customer's billing country as we have it now. The customer had changed the billing country from Austria to Germany two months earlier.

I read the credit note code. It builds the credit note lines by copying the amounts of the invoice, but takes the VAT rate from the current tax rules for the customer. That was done because the tax tables are by country, and nobody had thought of the case where the customer moved.

A credit note must mirror the invoice it corrects, with the same rate. Otherwise the VAT return of the accountants does not balance, since the VAT paid on the invoice would not be the VAT given back.

I changed the code to copy the rate and the tax country from the invoice lines. The current rules are used only for credit notes that are not linked to an invoice, which does not happen today, but the path exists, so I kept it.

I wrote tests for four cases. Same country, a customer who moved country, a reverse charge invoice, and a prorated invoice. In the moved case, the credit note now has 20 percent as in the invoice.

Then I looked for older credit notes with this problem. I wrote a query that compares the rate of each credit note line with the rate of the invoice line it refers to. It returned 9 credit notes out of about 2,100 in the last year.

The differences in money are small. The biggest was 11.40 in VAT, and the total of all nine was 41.72. Ines will decide how to correct them, probably with a new credit note for the difference, and she asked for the list as a CSV.

The fix is deployed. The nine cases wait for her decision, and I put the CSV in the shared folder with the invoice numbers, rates and amounts.

summary: Ines chose to correct the nine credit notes with VAT differences by one adjustment each, and the dry run shows a total of 41.72 that matches her list.
body:
Ines looked at the CSV of the nine credit notes and decided that each gets a small adjustment document, not a cancellation and a new credit note, since the amounts are tiny and the accountants prefer fewer documents.

I used the correction script from the earlier VAT work, which first does a dry run and compares the sums with a list. The dry run produced nine adjustments with a total of 41.72, and her list had the same total and the same invoice numbers.

I ran the real run. Nine documents were created, each linked to its credit note, and no emails went out because Ines wants to send a short explanation herself. The invoice PDFs are rendered with the v1 version, as the stored version rule says.

I checked one of the new documents by hand. The rate and the tax country match the original invoice, and the amount is the difference.

summary: Ines found that 3 of the 9 credit notes had their PDF cached with the old VAT rate, so I listed the cached files and set them to regenerate from the stored rate.
body:
Ines wrote early this morning that the credit note PDFs she had opened for her month check still showed the wrong VAT line on three of the nine corrected notes. The database rows were right, since the adjustment had moved the stored rate, so I suspected the files rather than the numbers. I compared the stored renderer version and the file timestamps for all nine notes. Six PDFs were rebuilt after the correction, and three were older than the correction, which explains what she saw.

The cause was in the PDF cache. It is keyed by the invoice id and the renderer version, and it does not include the stored rate of the lines. A correction that changes only the rate therefore leaves the old file in place. The same gap would hit any later correction of a line, so it is not specific to these credit notes.

For now I deleted the three cached files and let the download path render them again. I opened each of them and compared the VAT line and the total with the rows. The totals match, and the three notes carry the original rate. I also searched for other cached files that are older than the last change of their invoice lines. The query found 4 more, all from invoices with a manual line edit months ago, and none is a credit note. I did not touch those four, because their totals still match the rows, but I put them on a list for Ines.

The real fix is to add a hash of the line data to the cache key, so that any change of a line makes a new file. I wrote the change down but did not start it, because the new renderer behind the flag will need its own cache key anyway and I want to do both in one step. I told Ines that her three files are now right and that the note about the other four is in her list. Next I will write the cache key change with a test that edits a line after the first render and expects a different file.

summary: Ines checked the adjustment output and found one credit note with a rounded line that differed by a cent from her sheet; the cause was her sheet, not the script.
body:
Ines went through the nine printed lines and said that one of them showed 4.13 where her sheet said 4.14. I recomputed that credit note by hand. It has three lines, and the VAT of each line is rounded before the sum, while her sheet rounded the sum once.

The invoice itself uses the per line rounding, so the script is right and the sheet was off. She changed her sheet and the total is still 41.72 because the other direction was off by the same cent on a neighbor row. I told her the rule once more so she can apply it to the next list.

No code was changed. She approved the run, and I will do it this afternoon.

summary: Ran the nine VAT adjustments on production and checked every credit note afterwards; all nine now carry the original rate and the total moved by 41.72.
body:
I ran the adjustment script on production after taking a backup of the nine credit note rows and their lines. The output listed nine written adjustments and no skips.

After the run I did three checks. First, I summed the adjustments from the database and got 41.72. Second, I rendered the nine PDFs with the old renderer and the prototype and compared totals; they match. Third, I looked at the customer balance for each one, because a credit note with a changed total can change the amount that is left to refund.

Two of the customers had an open balance that moved by a few cents. For both, the difference was inside the credit that is not yet paid out, so no money had to go back to Stripe. One customer had already been refunded the full amount of the old credit note, and the adjustment is 0.38 less than what was paid out. Ines said finance will absorb that and not ask the customer for it.

I wrote the list of the nine with the before and after into the finance folder as she asked. The credit note builder had already been fixed, so no new case should appear. I will watch the next refund that comes in after a rate change, but there is none known right now.

summary: Wrote a nightly check that compares each credit note's VAT rate with the rate of its original invoice, so the bug of the wrong rate would be seen the same night if it came back.
body:
After the adjustments today I wanted a guard and not only a fix. The check is a SQL query run by a pg-boss job at night. It joins credit notes to their original invoice lines and flags any line where the stored rate differs.

On production it returns zero rows after today's adjustments. I tested it on staging by changing one rate by hand, and it flagged exactly that line with the invoice number.

The job sends a short email to the finance alias only when there are rows, so there is no daily noise. I added the job to the schedule list and a test that the email is not sent for an empty result.

One thing I noticed: older credit notes from before the stored rate column have a null rate on the line. The check skips those, and I wrote that in a comment. A backfill of the old lines would need the tax rules lookup by date, which is what I did for the nine, but doing it for all of them is a bigger job and nobody asked for it yet. I left it as a note for Ines and Mara.

summary: Looked at the Stripe SDK pagination shims again and chose to replace the one in the invoice sync first, because it is the simplest and has a test.
body:
The earlier list had three places with a hand-written pagination loop around the Stripe list calls. They exist because older SDK versions did not give a good auto-pagination for our use. I looked at each of them this morning.

The invoice sync shim is about 30 lines. It calls list with a starting_after cursor and stops when has_more is false. It has a test with a fake client, which makes it the safest to change. The backfill one has a custom delay between pages. The third is inside the customer import script and is rarely run.

I did not change any code yet, since the SDK is still on the version where the shims were written. The upgrade to the next major version is planned, and the shims should be removed together with it, so a change now would only be done twice. I wrote this down as a plan so the upgrade entry can refer to it.

I did check that the invoice sync test covers the case of an empty page and a single page, which it does. The last page case with exactly 100 items is missing, so I added that test. It passed on the old shim.

summary: Answered Mara's question on why a receipt email showed a total different from the PDF: the email was built from the draft invoice, before a late usage line was added.
body:
Mara asked about a customer who got a receipt of 212.40 while the PDF said 214.90. I found the invoice in the database and the timeline of events.

The receipt email is queued when the invoice is finalized, but it reads the amounts when the job runs. In this case the job ran before the late usage line of the last closed hour was written, and so the amounts of the email were from the draft.

The PDF was rendered later and is correct. The customer was charged 214.90 by Stripe, so no money issue. I sent the customer a corrected receipt by hand. The proper fix is to have the email job read the finalized snapshot, and I will do that next.

summary: Made the receipt email read the finalized invoice snapshot instead of live rows, and added a test that fails when a line is written after finalization.
body:
This follows Mara's question from this morning. The receipt job loaded the invoice with its lines at the time it ran, which could be after a late usage line was added.

The invoice table already has a finalized_at column and a totals snapshot written during finalization. I changed the receipt job so that it takes the total and lines from the snapshot and refuses to send if the snapshot is missing. In that case it retries with the usual backoff, so a race with the finalization only delays the mail.

I wrote three tests. One writes a line after finalization and checks that the email still shows the snapshot total. A second sends with a missing snapshot and expects a retry. A third checks the email total against the PDF total for ten fixtures.

While doing this I looked at where else the live rows are read after finalization. The dunning email reads the amount due from the invoice header, which is fine, but the admin download rebuilds the lines from the live table. That could show a late line that is not in the charged total. I did not change it today because the PDF path was already fixed for the renderer version, and I want to look at it with the new renderer work.

I ran the whole test suite: 412 tests passed, and the receipt tests take 3 seconds. I deployed in the afternoon and saw 26 receipts go out with matching totals. I will look again tomorrow for any retry noise in the job logs.

summary: Checked the receipt retry noise after the snapshot change: 11 retries in a day, all from invoices finalized seconds before, and none stuck.
body:
I looked at the job logs of the last day. The receipt job had 11 retries, and in all of them the snapshot was missing on the first try and present on the second, a few seconds later.

That is the race that the retry is designed for. The longest delay was 20 seconds, and no job went beyond two attempts. There were no failed receipts and no duplicates; I checked this by counting sent receipts per invoice and every invoice had one.

I also compared the totals of 140 receipts with the PDFs of the same invoices, and all matched to the cent. Before the change, the one mismatch was the case Mara found.

The admin download is the remaining place that reads live lines. I wrote the change for it: it now reads lines from the snapshot for finalized invoices and from live rows only for drafts. The download of a draft is useful for finance when they check usage before the invoice is closed, so it stays.

Tests: I added a test with a late line, as for the receipt, and one for a draft. Both pass. I deployed it in the same release.
