Left: the snapshot is only a total and a line list, and not the tax breakdown. For the reverse charge note the PDF reads the tax rules, which could change after the fact. The stored rate column helps for lines. I will keep the breakdown in mind for the new renderer.

summary: Reviewed what the SEPA-like transfer customers see in the dunning emails and found that the text still talks about card retries, which is wrong for them.
body:
Ines forwarded a mail from a customer who pays by bank transfer and got a dunning mail that said we would try the card again. They have no card.

I read the dunning templates. There are three steps, and each has a block about the retry that is shown whenever the planner has a retry date. For transfer customers the planner writes a date anyway, because the step table has one row per step with a date for all of them.

The guard I wrote for card expiry emails already checks the payment method kind, but the dunning path does not. I changed the template data so that retry_date is empty for customers without a card, and the template shows a line with the bank details and the invoice number instead.

I made fixtures for card, transfer and no method, and rendered all three languages. Everything looks right. I will deploy with the next release.

summary: Deployed the dunning text fix for transfer customers and found that 23 open dunning steps would have shown the wrong card retry text.
body:
I deployed the template change and then ran a query for the dunning steps that are planned but not sent yet. Of 97 open steps, 23 belong to customers who pay by transfer. Those would have gotten the card retry text.

After the deploy I rendered three of them in the preview and they show the bank details block. The first send ran at noon and 6 of those mails went out with the new text. I checked the content in the Postmark activity view.

No more work is needed here, but Ines may want to look at the English wording of the bank block, which I wrote quickly.

summary: Started the plan to make the dunning email carry a link to the payment page, after Ines noticed that customers reply to the mail with questions instead of paying.
body:
Ines said that many customers answer the dunning email, and her team spends time on it. She asked whether the mail could link directly to a place where they can pay.

Stripe has a hosted invoice page, and each invoice we create there has a hosted_invoice_url. I checked how many of our invoices have it: all invoices from the card path do, but the transfer invoices created by our own flow do not, since they are only stored here.

Two options: create a Stripe invoice object for every transfer invoice, or build a small page in billing-api that shows the amount and bank details. The first changes how reconciliation works, because the Stripe invoice would then be a second source of truth. The second is more work but keeps the current model.

I wrote the facts into a short note with what each option changes and sent it to Ines and Mara. For card customers I can add the hosted link at once, since the data is there, so I started with that.

The change in the dunning template data is small: payment_url from the hosted invoice. I added it to the card branch only, with a test for the empty case in which no URL exists, and in that case the button is not shown.

I rendered the mail in German and French and the link text fits on one line. The click tracking of Postmark is off for these mails on purpose, so the link stays the real Stripe address and customers can see where it goes.

I did not deploy yet, because I want Ines to look at the preview. Mara's answer on the transfer option is still open.

summary: Mara chose the small payment page over Stripe objects for transfer invoices, so I sketched its shape: a signed link, amount, bank details and the invoice number as reference.
body:
Mara answered the note quickly. She does not want a second Stripe invoice for transfers, so the page lives in billing-api.

I sketched what it needs. The link carries the invoice id and a signature made with a server secret, so nobody can guess the invoices of others. It shows the amount due, the due date, the IBAN of the company and the invoice number as the payment reference. No login is needed.

The signature should expire, but a dunning mail can be opened weeks later. I chose a long life of 60 days and a fresh link in each new mail, instead of a permanent one.

For the paid state the page shows a plain message that the invoice is paid, which stops a customer from paying twice after the transfer matching has run.

Route: GET /pay/:token under the public Fastify scope. Rate limit like the other public routes. I wrote the token helper and its tests: valid, wrong signature, expired, and tampered invoice id. All four pass.

The page template is next, and it should use the same fonts and language fallback as the emails.

summary: Built the payment page for transfer invoices with the language fallback of the emails and checked it against 8 invoices in staging.
body:
I wrote the page template and the route. It uses the locale fallback built earlier, so the language follows the customer setting first and the billing country next.

The states are: open, paid, and unknown link. Unknown and expired links show the same neutral text, with the support address, so the page does not tell anyone whether an invoice exists.

In staging I tried 8 invoices: 4 open, 2 paid, 1 with a credit note that lowers the amount due, 1 with a partial payment. The credit note case showed the right amount due. The partial payment case showed the full total, which is wrong. The amount due must be total minus payments matched so far, and I fixed the query to subtract them.

After the fix all 8 show the correct amount. I also checked that the page sends no-store cache headers, so a paid invoice does not show as open from a cache.

The link is now added to the transfer branch of the dunning mails. I will deploy tomorrow and let Ines look at the page first.

summary: Deployed the payment page and the dunning links and watched the first sends: 31 mails with a link, 5 opened pages and 2 invoices paid within the hour.
body:
After Ines approved the page text I deployed in the evening. The next dunning run sent 31 mails, 19 for card customers with the Stripe link and 12 for transfer customers with the new page link.

In the access log I saw 5 page views for transfer links. Two of those customers paid by transfer within the hour, but matching only runs twice a day, so the invoices still show as open on our side until then.

That gap is a problem for the page: a customer who has paid still sees the amount due until the next matching. I noted this on the page as a small line that says payments may take up to a day to show. It is not nice but it is honest.

No errors in the logs, and no 500 responses. The signature check rejected one request, which was a link where the mail client had broken the token at a line end. I looked at the mail source and the link was cut by a mail client wrap in a plain text part, so I made the text part use a shorter token format.

The tokens were base64url with a long signature. I cut the signature to 22 characters of the HMAC, which is enough for this use, and kept the old format valid for 60 days so no sent link breaks.

Tests for both formats pass. I will deploy this fix tomorrow morning.

summary: Shortened the payment link token and kept the old format valid, then checked in staging that old and new links both open.
body:
The broken link in the plain text part came from a long token that some mail clients wrapped. I changed the token to carry a 22 character signature instead of the full one.

The verification now accepts both: if the signature part has the old length it is compared fully, and if it has the new length it is compared as a prefix of the HMAC with a constant time compare. I was careful to check the length first so that a short guess cannot match by accident of an empty prefix.

I wrote tests for: new valid, old valid, new with one wrong character, old with one wrong character, empty signature, signature of a wrong length. All pass.

The length of a full link went from 118 characters to 86. Mail clients wrap at 76 in plain text, so it still wraps in some cases, but the mail now puts the link on its own line, which clients do not break.

In staging I opened an old link made yesterday and a new one. Both show the same invoice. A tampered copy of each gives the neutral page.

I also looked at the rate limit. A test with 200 requests per minute from one address got blocked after 60, as configured.

One more point: the page is reachable without login, so I checked that the response contains no customer name or address. It shows only the amount, the due date, the bank details, and the invoice number.

I deployed it in the evening, and the next dunning run will be the check. I am ending the work on the page here, unless Ines has more wishes for the text.

summary: Checked the dunning run after the token change: 28 mails, none with a broken link, and the payment page has been opened 9 times with 4 invoices paid.
body:
I looked at the last run in Postmark and in our logs. 28 dunning mails went out and none of the links was rejected by the signature check. The one rejection of before did not happen again.

The page was opened 9 times by 7 customers. Four of those invoices were paid, 2 by card on the Stripe page and 2 by transfer, which will be visible after the next matching. Compared with an earlier week where roughly one in ten late invoices was paid within two days, this looks better, but the sample is small and I will not claim a result yet.

Ines said her team received fewer replies to the dunning mails this morning, 3 instead of the usual 10 or so. I asked her to count again after a full week.

I also fixed the line about payments taking a day: the matching runs twice a day, so it now says a few hours. Small text change, no logic.

summary: Began the Stripe SDK upgrade to the next major version by reading the changelog and running the tests on a local branch of the main checkout, which showed 14 failing tests.
body:
I started the SDK upgrade work today, using the plan of the pagination shims from earlier. I work in the main checkout, so I did the upgrade as an uncommitted change first, to see the size of it.

I read the changelog from our version to the next. The breaking changes that matter for us are the changed type of some webhook event objects, a renamed parameter on the invoice upcoming call, and a new default for the API version used by the client.

After the install, the TypeScript build gave 23 errors. Most come from two things: the upcoming invoice call, which we use for the preview of the next invoice, and the types of the subscription items.

I fixed the type errors, and then ran the tests: 14 of 412 failed. Eleven fail because fixtures contain fields that the new types do not allow; three fail in the webhook handler tests because the event type of one payload changed.

I looked at the three webhook failures with care, since a wrong handler in production could miss a payment. The cause was that our test fixture used an old shape of the charge object. The real events from Stripe will come in the API version we pin on the account, so the handler is not wrong, but the fixtures should match the real shape. I replaced them with payloads copied from the Stripe dashboard event log.

That leaves the 11 fixture failures. I fixed 6 of them and stopped there, because I want to review the pinned API version before going on.

On the pinned version: the client takes the account default unless we set apiVersion. Our code sets it explicitly, and the new SDK expects a newer one. If I change it, the shape of every response may change. I will compare our version with the one the SDK is typed for, and decide whether to pin the old version and live with a type mismatch or move.

Nothing is committed. The shims stay for now.

summary: Compared the pinned Stripe API version with the one the new SDK expects and decided to move the pin in a separate release, after the SDK upgrade is live.
body:
I spent the evening on the API version question. Our client pins an API version from the first version of the service. The new SDK is typed for a newer one, and sets it by default.

I listed what changed between the two API versions for the objects we use. For invoices the main change is that the charge field is replaced by a list of payments in one case, and some fields moved on the subscription. The change in the tax fields touches the code that checks VAT on invoices created by Stripe, which we do not use for our own invoices, but the dunning side reads some of them.

Two choices: do both moves at once or separate them. Doing them together makes any problem hard to place. I chose to separate: first the SDK, with the pin kept, so responses are unchanged; later the API version.

The SDK allows the old pin with a cast. I added the cast in one place, the client factory, with a comment that it is temporary. The compiler no longer complains about the string.

Then I finished the fixtures. The remaining 5 failures were fixtures with a removed field. After the fix all 412 tests pass.

I ran the integration tests against the Stripe test mode: create customer, attach card, create subscription, pay an invoice, refund, and the webhook round trip with the CLI forwarding. All steps passed. The refund and the webhook paths took the most time to check, since they touch money.

One warning appeared in the log: a deprecation notice for a call in the usage sync. I noted it and did not change it today.

The diff is 190 lines, half of it fixtures. I want to run it on staging for a day before the production deploy, and then handle the pagination shims in a second step. Not committed yet; I will commit tomorrow after a last read.

summary: Deployed the SDK upgrade to staging and ran the nightly jobs against Stripe test mode, finding that the usage sync warning comes from a renamed call that still works.
body:
I put the upgrade on staging tonight. It started clean and the health check passed.

The nightly jobs I ran by hand were the invoice sync, the usage sync, the dunning planner, and the card expiry job. All finished, with the same row counts as the run with the old SDK on the same data: 1,212 invoices in the sync, 340 usage records, 31 dunning steps, 40 expiry candidates.

The warning in the usage sync is about the name of the usage record call. The new name is the same function in a different namespace, and the old name still works with a notice. I changed it to the new one. The sync ran again with no warning and the same 340 records.

I checked the response shapes by logging the keys of ten invoices and ten customers in both versions. They are the same since the pin stayed.

I looked at the error classes as well. The SDK raises its error types with a changed type field for rate limits. Our error handler maps card errors to dunning outcomes and checks the type string. I read the code: it checks for card_error and for the idempotency errors, not for the rate limit, so it is not affected. A rate limit error goes to the generic branch and is retried by pg-boss.

To be sure, I forced a card declined case with the test card 4000000000000002 and the dunning outcome was the same as before: declined, planned a retry. And a test card for insufficient funds gave the expected code.

Nothing else showed up. The plan is to leave it on staging overnight, and to deploy to production in the morning if the night run is clean.

summary: Prepared the Stripe SDK upgrade for production by reading the staging night run and writing down the checks to run for the first hour after a deploy.
body:
The staging night run finished without errors, and the counts of jobs matched the previous night. I did not deploy anything to production this evening. The upgrade is still on staging, and I used the time to prepare the release.

I wrote a short checklist for the first hour after a deploy, with three things to watch. Webhooks: every event should pass the signature check, and the handler should write the expected rows. Charges: card payments and SEPA transfers should match the invoices they belong to. Jobs: pg-boss should show no failed jobs and the queue should stay short.

I also pulled the response times of calls to Stripe from our logs as a baseline. The median was 240 ms, and the slowest call was 1.4 seconds for a list call. After the release I will compare against these numbers.

One thing to expect: the client puts the SDK version in the user agent, so the Stripe dashboard will show the new version in the request log after the upgrade. That is normal and no cause for worry.

I asked Ines whether she could prepare a small refund of a test invoice that I can run in the live system after the release. She agreed. I noted that the refund endpoint has no protection against a retried request. A client that sends the call twice could refund twice. Stripe would reject a refund above the charge amount, but partial refunds could add up. That is a topic for later.

The pagination shims are a separate step. The three places are still on the old loops, which work with the new SDK according to the local tests, so I will replace them one at a time in later changes so each can be checked.

I also wrote in the notes that the API version pin is still old and that moving it is a separate job after the upgrade is live. Tomorrow I will decide on the time of the production deploy.

summary: Prepared the check of the Stripe SDK upgrade by setting the baseline numbers for errors, webhooks, payments and dunning, before anything is changed.
body:
I went through the logs of the last day to write down the baseline that the Stripe SDK upgrade will be measured against. The upgrade itself has not started in production, and I only read the current state. The error rate from Stripe calls was 0.3 percent, the same as the week before, and those errors are declined cards that the dunning flow expects.

The webhook handler processed 640 events with no signature failure and no handler exception. I counted the events by type and compared with the previous day: invoice.paid, charge.failed and charge.refunded were within a few percent of the usual numbers. I saved the counts in a note so that I can compare them after the upgrade.

For the money, I compared the sum of payments recorded in billing-api with the sum of Stripe charges of the same day, and both were 18,942.60 in total. Ines asked for this check because the upgrade will touch the payment code, so she wants to see the same comparison before and after. She also looked at three invoices and the receipts and said they were correct, and we agreed that she will look at three again after the change.

The dunning planner made 27 steps and the outcomes had the same split of recovered and failed as in the days before. The card expiry job sent its reminders as usual.

No issue to fix today. For the next steps I listed in order: do the SDK upgrade on a local branch and look at the failing tests, then replace the invoice sync shim, the backfill shim and the import script one, and after that move the API version pin. I also want idempotency on refunds, which is a separate ticket for Mara to prioritize.

summary: Moved the Stripe API version pin to the one the new SDK expects, in its own release, and checked 40 test-mode charges plus the webhook payload shapes before and after.
body:
As planned two days ago, the pin moved in a separate release from the SDK upgrade. The change is one line in the Stripe client setup, plus the matching version in the webhook test fixtures.

Before deploying I read the API changelog between the old pin and the new one. Three changes touch us: a renamed field on the invoice object, a changed default for expanded payment intents, and a new status value on charges. I checked each against the code. The renamed field is read in the invoice sync, so I added a fallback that reads either name.

The expanded payment intent default affected the refund code, which expected the payment intent to be a string id in one place. I made it accept both an id and an object. A test covers both shapes now.

On staging I ran 40 charges in test mode with cards, a failing card and a transfer-style invoice. All produced the same outcomes as before the pin move. The webhook payloads for invoice.paid and charge.refunded had the new field name, and the handler parsed them.

I deployed to production in the afternoon and watched the webhook log for an hour. No signature errors, no parse errors, and the usage sync ran clean. The old pin stays documented in the release note in case of a rollback.

Left for later: the fallback for the renamed field can go after a week of clean runs.

summary: Answered Mara's question on why two customers were charged on the first of the month instead of the invoice due date: the trial end was stored in local time and crossed midnight.
body:
Mara asked about two customers whose card was charged a day early compared with the date on the invoice. I looked at their subscriptions. Both trials were created late in the evening by customers in a timezone ahead of ours.

The trial end is stored as a timestamp, but the billing job compares it to a date computed in the server timezone. For a trial ending near midnight that date can be one day earlier than the customer sees. The charge itself was correct under our rules, but the invoice showed the later date.

I checked how many accounts are affected by listing trials that end within two hours of midnight in any timezone we have on file. There are 17 open trials like that, and 2 had already been charged.

The fix is to compute the due date from the customer timezone, which the account already has. I wrote the failing test for the two cases first and the change is small. I did not deploy yet, because Ines should know that the dates on those 17 invoices will move by one day.

I sent her the list. The two charged customers get a short email from Mara explaining it.

summary: Fixed the due date calculation to use the customer timezone and deployed it after Ines agreed on the 17 open trials, with the test for the midnight cases passing.
body:
Ines replied that moving the due dates by one day on 17 trials is fine as long as the invoice and the reminder agree. So I went on with the timezone change.

The due date now comes from a helper that takes the trial end and the account timezone and returns a calendar date. The billing job, the invoice builder and the reminder scheduler all call it. Before, the invoice builder and the job had their own copies, and that was part of why the dates differed.

I removed the two copies and added tests. They cover an account ahead of the server, one behind it, a daylight saving change on the trial end, and an account with no timezone, which falls back to the server one. The old tests still pass.

I also checked the reminder scheduler. It scheduled the first reminder three days before the due date, and with the new helper the reminder moves along with it. A dry run printed the old and new dates for the 17 trials. 15 moved by one day, and 2 did not change because the customers sit in our timezone.

Deployed in the evening. After the deploy I ran the dry run again, and it showed no more differences between the invoice date and the job date. The two customers who were charged early got the explanation email.

Next I will check next week's trials ending around midnight and watch that the first charges happen on the right date.

summary: Compared the old customer sync pagination helper with the SDK's auto-pagination on a test account, found it stops at 100 customers, and planned the replacement.
body:
Started on the second pagination shim, after the invoice sync. The customer sync uses a helper that fetches pages with starting_after and a loop. I read it through and wrote a small script that runs it next to the SDK's own auto-pagination iterator, without changing any production code.

I ran the script against a test account with 230 customers. The iterator returned all 230. The old helper returned 100. Reading the helper again, a condition on has_more is checked against the wrong variable when a page comes back with exactly the limit, so the loop ends early. Production has not hit it so far because the sync runs per batch and no batch is that large, but it is a real bug and it explains an odd count I saw in a test run a while ago.

I wrote down the plan for the change. The sync will read the iterator until the end and write in chunks of 50. I drafted two tests, one with 230 fake customers and one with exactly 100, which is the case that breaks. The second one fails against the current helper, as expected, so it shows the bug well.

The subscriptions sync also uses this helper, so it needs the same care. I left the helper and the customer sync untouched for now. Next I will write the replacement and compare the output on staging before anything goes out. I told Mara about the finding so she knows the old helper should not be copied into new code.

summary: Read the old customer sync pagination helper and the SDK iterator side by side on a test account, and wrote down the checks to run before the sync is changed.
body:
I ran the old customer sync helper and the SDK's auto-pagination against the same test account in the evening. The test account holds 4,812 customers, the same count as our table. The old helper read 100 customers and stopped, while the iterator went through all the pages.

I counted the API calls for a full read with the page size of 100. The iterator needed 49 calls. That is the number I want to see in the log after the change, with no extra calls beyond the page count. I also noted the run time of the current sync, so I can compare it later.

Nothing was changed in the sync code and nothing was deployed. I wrote down the checks for the first run after the change: the count of customers read against the count in the database, the number of calls, the run time and any errors in the log. The subscriptions sync uses the same old helper and stays as it is for now. I will plan it after the customer sync, and I will ask Mara to look at the plan first.

summary: Looked into slow rendering for invoices with many lines and found that the prototype renderer spends most of its time on one font load and one table layout per line, then fixed the font load.
body:
The prototype renderer is meant to be faster than the old one for big invoices, but the comparison script showed that for invoices with more than 300 lines it was only a little better. I profiled one invoice with 520 lines.

Out of 4.1 seconds, about 1.3 seconds went to loading the corporate font. The font was fetched from the private bucket on each render. The rest was mostly table layout, with a separate layout pass for every line.

For the font I added a cache in memory for the process, keyed by the file version. The first render fetches it and later ones reuse it. The 520-line invoice dropped to 2.8 seconds on the second run.

The layout is a harder problem. Each line is a table row with wrapped description text, and the browser recalculates the layout when a row is added. I tried building the whole table as one HTML string instead of adding rows one at a time. That cut another 0.9 seconds, to 1.9.

I ran the comparison script over the 300 real invoices again. Totals and page counts still match on all of them, except the one invoice that differed before and has a known cause with a page break. Median render time fell from 1.2 seconds to 0.7. The slowest invoice went from 6.0 to 2.6 seconds.

The font cache has one risk: the font file is licensed for private use, so the cache is memory only and never writes to disk. I checked that no temporary file is created.

Next I want to look at the page break difference and at memory use, because a cached font plus several parallel renders could grow the process.

summary: Measured memory use of the prototype renderer with the font cache under 8 parallel renders and found it stable at about 410 MB with no growth over 500 renders.
body:
After the cache change I worried about memory. I ran 500 renders of mixed invoices with 8 in parallel and sampled the process memory every 10 seconds.

Memory rose to about 410 MB in the first minute and stayed there. The font adds about 2 MB, which is nothing next to the browser pages. No growth trend after the first 100 renders.

One thing I noticed is that pages are closed correctly after an error. I forced 20 failures with a bad template and the count of open pages returned to zero each time.

Good enough for now. I will repeat the test with the biggest invoices later.

summary: Found why one invoice breaks to a new page differently in the prototype renderer: a row with a tall description is allowed to split across pages, and the old renderer kept rows whole.
body:
The one invoice whose page count differed turned out to have a line with a very long description of 14 lines. The prototype lets a table row split across two pages. The old renderer never splits rows.

I added the CSS rule that keeps rows together, break-inside avoid, on the line rows. After that the invoice has the same 3 pages as the old output.

I worried that a row taller than a page could loop. A test with a 90-line description renders fine, because the browser splits it anyway when it cannot fit. I checked that the header row repeats on each page, and it does.

The comparison script now shows no page count differences on the 300 invoices. Totals match everywhere. Next step is to compare the visual output, which Ines will do on a sample.

summary: Looked at the subscriptions sync's use of the old pagination helper and planned how to move it to the SDK iterator, without changing any code yet.
body:
The subscriptions sync is the last user of the old pagination helper, apart from the admin export. Today I read through it to see what a move to the SDK iterator would need. The sync filters on status, and I wrote down that the filter has to be passed to the iterator the same way, so that cancelled subscriptions are not read by mistake.

On staging I counted what the current code reads: 212 test subscriptions, the same number as in the database. I saved the ids and statuses to a file, so that later I can compare them with the output of the new code and see any difference at once.

I also wrote the test case I want before any change: two full pages and then an empty last page. The old helper handles that case, and I want to be sure the iterator does the same. The test is written and fails for now, because the new code is not there yet.

The admin export also uses the helper, and it sorts the results. I will look at it separately, because I want to check that the order stays the same, and I have not started on it.

The next step is to swap in the iterator in the subscriptions sync and run the comparison on staging. Nothing is changed in the service yet, and there is nothing to deploy.

summary: Checked the admin export that still used the old pagination helper and planned to keep its newest-first order with an explicit sort once it moves to the SDK iterator.
body:
Looked at the admin export that still used the old pagination helper and found that it relies on the order of the results. The export lists invoices from Stripe for the finance team. It relied on Stripe returning newest first, which the helper kept.

With the SDK iterator the order should be the same, but I did not want the export to depend on that. I planned to collect the results and sort by created, descending, before writing the file, and I wrote that down as a step of the move without changing any code yet.

To have a baseline, I ran one export of 640 rows with the current code and saved the file. After the move I will compare a new export against it, and I expect the files to differ only in the generation timestamp in the header.

The old helper still has this user, and the subscriptions sync as well, so it stays in the code for now. I added the export to the list of places to move, next to the subscriptions sync.

summary: Investigated a SEPA debit that Stripe marked failed after the account had been shown as paid, and found that the webhook for the late failure was processed before the pending state was saved.
body:
Ines forwarded a case where a customer's invoice showed as paid in our system, but Stripe said the SEPA debit had failed two days after. The reminder emails never started.

I followed the events for that invoice in the webhook log. The payment started as pending, and our code marked the invoice paid when the payment intent reached processing, not when it succeeded. That was a mistake in how I handled the SEPA states. For cards the two points are the same moment, so it never showed.

Then the failure event arrived. The handler looked for an invoice in state pending to move it to failed, and found one in state paid, so it skipped it. No error was logged, because skipping is a normal path for duplicate events.

There are two fixes. First, the invoice should be paid only on the succeeded event for SEPA, and should stay in a state called payment_pending while the debit runs. The account stays active while pending, as before. Second, a failure event on a paid invoice should not be skipped silently. It should reopen the invoice and start the dunning, and log a warning.

I wrote the tests first. One test replays the event sequence of the case: processing, then failed two days later. Another covers succeeded after processing, which must mark the invoice paid. A third sends the failure on a paid invoice and expects a reopened invoice and a dunning step.

The changes are in the webhook handler and in the invoice state helper. The existing state diagram in the docs got the new state.

I then looked for other cases. A query on invoices paid by SEPA in the last 60 days where Stripe's payment intent is not in succeeded found 3 invoices, including the one from Ines. The other two are also failed debits, from the same cause.

I have not touched them yet. I will deploy the fix first, then fix the three by hand with Ines.

summary: Deployed the SEPA state fix and replayed the failure events for the three invoices, which reopened them and started their reminder emails.
body:
After the tests passed I deployed the fix. The first SEPA events went through with the new state, and an invoice in processing now shows payment_pending.

For the three affected invoices I replayed their failure events from the stored webhook log. Each one reopened and a dunning step was created. The reminder emails went out through Postmark, and I checked that they carry the transfer-style payment link, as planned for SEPA customers who cannot retry the debit.

I told Ines which invoices were reopened, with the amounts. She will write to the customers herself.

summary: Added a nightly check that compares SEPA invoices marked paid with the Stripe payment intent status, so a mismatch like the late failure would be seen the next morning.
body:
After the SEPA state bug I wanted a check that does not depend on the webhook. The nightly job takes all invoices paid by SEPA in the last 90 days and reads the payment intent status from Stripe.

If an invoice is paid in our system and the intent is not succeeded, the job writes a line to the finance report and logs a warning. It reads in batches of 100 with the iterator.

A first run found no mismatches, which fits the three repaired invoices. A test with a fake mismatch makes the report line appear.

summary: Planned the next step for the invoices table, the partitioning by quarter, after checking that the table has 3.1 million rows and the largest queries scan most of it.
body:
The invoices table keeps growing, and the monthly queries from Ines are getting slower. I looked at the numbers to see whether partitioning is worth doing now.

The table has 3.1 million rows and about 9 GB with its indexes. The query for the monthly finance report takes 11 seconds, and the plan shows a scan over most of the table because the filter on the invoice date uses an index that is not selective for old quarters.

The idea is one partition per quarter, by invoice date. Queries for the current quarter would read one partition. The old quarters stay as they are for now.

I listed what depends on the table as it is. There are two foreign keys from credit notes and payments, which point at the invoice id. In a partitioned table the primary key must include the partition column, so those references need care. Options are to add the date to the references, or to drop the foreign keys and check the link in the code. I prefer to keep the date out of the references and use a unique index on the id in each partition, plus a check job.

There is also the invoice number sequence, which is not affected, and three reports that query the table by id only. Those would scan all partitions without the date, so I looked at how often they run. Two run a few times a day, and one runs per customer request. The last is the risk.

For the per-customer query I can add the customer id and a recent-first order, which the index supports on every partition.

Plan: try the layout on a copy of production data from last night, time the five main queries before and after, and write down the migration steps. No change to production yet. I will ask Mara to review the plan before I start.

summary: Built the partitioned copy of the invoices table on a staging database with real data and timed the five main queries: the finance report fell from 11 seconds to 1.4.
body:
I restored last night's copy to the staging database and created a second table partitioned by quarter on the invoice date. Then I loaded the rows into it, which took 7 minutes for 3.1 million rows.

The five main queries, before and after:
- monthly finance report: 11.0 s to 1.4 s
- invoices of one customer: 40 ms to 35 ms
- open invoices for dunning: 380 ms to 120 ms
- usage close for the month: 2.2 s to 0.6 s
- lookup by invoice number: 3 ms to 9 ms

The lookup by number got slower because the number is not tied to the date, so the planner checks each partition. With 14 partitions it is still fast, but it will grow. I can improve it by adding the quarter to the lookup when the number format allows it. The numbers contain the year, so I can derive the likely quarter and search there first, then fall back.

The foreign key question: on the copy I dropped the two foreign keys and kept the unique id index per partition. The credit note and payment inserts work. I wrote a check query that finds credit notes without an invoice, and it returns zero rows on the copy.

The migration steps I wrote down are:
1. Create the partitioned table with the same columns.
2. Attach the current quarter first, and copy older quarters one at a time at night.
3. Switch the name in one short lock.
4. Keep the old table for a week.

I sent this to Mara for review and asked her about the lock time. I measured it on the copy and it was under a second, but production has more write traffic.

summary: Mara reviewed the partition plan and asked for a rollback path, so I added a step that keeps the old table writable through a trigger for the first day.
body:
Mara read the plan and had two questions. What happens if the switch goes wrong, and are the invoice writes lost in the window between copy and switch?

For the second one, the plan copies rows while the service keeps writing. I added a trigger on the old table that copies new and changed rows to the new one until the switch, and a count comparison before the switch.

For the rollback I added the reverse trigger after the switch, so the old table receives the writes for the first day. If we must go back, the old table is current and the name switch can be reversed.

She also asked about the lookup by invoice number. I will put the quarter guess in the lookup code and test it on numbers from every quarter.

I updated the written plan with both changes. Mara approved it on that basis. The next step is a rehearsal on staging, with write traffic from a script.

summary: Rehearsed the whole partition migration on staging with a script writing 20 invoices per second, and found the trigger copy missed updates to rows that were not yet copied.
body:
I ran the full migration on staging with a load script writing new invoices and updating existing ones at 20 per second, which is above our peak.

The steps worked in order, and the switch took 0.4 seconds. But the count comparison before the switch showed 37 rows that differed between the old and the new table. I looked at them. All were updates to rows from older quarters that the nightly copy had not reached yet.

The trigger copied inserts and updates into the new table, but an update to a row that does not exist there yet did nothing, because the trigger used a plain update. So the changed row was never copied, and the later batch copy took the old values from a snapshot taken earlier.

The fix is to make the trigger an upsert on the invoice id. Then an update to an uncopied row inserts it, and the batch copy later skips rows that already exist, using on conflict do nothing. I changed both.

I ran the rehearsal again from a fresh restore. This time the comparison at the switch showed zero differences in count and in a checksum over the id, total and status columns.

I also tested a failure in the middle. I stopped the copy job after 6 quarters and restarted it. It continued from the next quarter and did not duplicate rows, because of the conflict rule.

The rollback path also got a test. After the switch I reversed the names and checked that the old table had all writes from the load script during the first minutes. It had.

The lookup by number with the quarter guess now takes 2 ms on the copy for numbers of all quarters. For a number whose year part is wrong the fallback finds it in 9 ms.

There are two small things left: the docs for the schema, and the report that reads a view over the old table name. The view must point at the new table after the switch, so I added it to the migration script.

I think the plan is ready for production, but I want one more look at the disk space, because the copy needs 9 GB more during the migration.

summary: Checked the disk space and the backup schedule for the partition migration and found enough room, but the nightly backup overlaps the copy window, so the copy moves to start after it.
body:
The migration needs about 9 GB for the new table and indexes while the old one still exists. I looked at the production database volume: 62 percent used of 200 GB, so there is room with a wide margin.

Then the backup. The nightly backup starts at two in the morning and takes about 40 minutes. The copy job is planned for the night too, and both read the large table. On staging I ran them together and the backup took 70 minutes, and the copy slowed down by half.

I moved the copy window to start at three, after the backup. The job takes one quarter at a time, with a pause of 30 seconds between quarters, so the database does not get a long heavy load.

I also checked the replication lag during the rehearsal, because a bulk copy writes a lot. The replica lagged by up to 12 seconds, which is fine for the reports that read from it. The job now reads the lag and pauses if it is above 60 seconds.

The last point was the vacuum. After the copy, the new partitions have no statistics, so the planner may choose badly at first. I added an analyze for each partition at the end of each copy step.

I also wrote a short runbook for the night:
- check the backup finished
- start the copy job
- watch the count comparison in the log
- switch in the morning, when Mara is in

I tested the pause on lag by setting the threshold to 5 seconds on staging, and the job did pause and resume.

The migration is ready. The remaining decision is the day, and I suggested to Mara to do it in a quiet week, not in the week of the month end, when Ines runs the reports.

summary: Wrote the log and alert for the partition migration and agreed with Mara and Ines to start the copy in a week, after the month end close.
body:
Mara and Ines looked at the runbook. Ines asked that nothing happens during the close, because her reports must not change under her. We agreed to start the copy the night after the close is finished, which is in about a week.

I added logging to the copy job: one line per quarter with the row count, the time and the lag. A failure also writes to the channel the team watches. I tested it by making a quarter fail on staging.

I added an alert for the period after the switch. It fires if the count of the old and new table differs by more than a few rows in the first day, because the reverse trigger keeps them in step. A test on staging made it fire when I deleted rows by hand.

One more check on the code: every query that names the invoices table by date now has the date range in it. I grepped for queries with an invoice id only, and found two more in the admin tool. Those are rare, so I left them, but I put them in the runbook as a thing to watch.

The plan stays as written. Waiting for the close.
